TypeScript Mastery

TypeScript is JavaScript with a second layer on top: a description of what your values are supposed to look like. This course teaches that layer from the ground up. First what its guarantees really promise, and where they are deliberately not airtight. Then how it follows the if checks you already write, how to design data so that impossible situations cannot even be written down, how to write code that works for many types, and how to compute new types from old ones. It finishes with how a package tells the people who install it what its types are, and with the places where untyped data still sneaks in, usually through the any type.

How to use this course

  • This course sits between JavaScript and React. It assumes you have already learned JavaScript, from the JavaScript course or elsewhere: values, closures, classes and modules are used here without being explained again. TypeScript adds a second layer that only exists while you write and build your code. Most of the confusion people have with it comes from mixing up which layer a thing belongs to, so §1 starts by separating them.
  • Everything here was compiled or run. Every line marked ✅ (accepted) or ❌ (rejected) was really compiled, so the mark is what the compiler said, not what the author believed. Code that runs was executed under Node 24. That habit changed the course while it was being written: it caught a wrong claim about NoInfer, and a decorator example (a decorator is a function that wraps a class or method) that passed the type checker and then looped forever when it ran.
  • It is written against TypeScript 7. The compiler used throughout is tsc 7.0.2, the rewrite of the compiler in a faster native language. TypeScript 6.0 was a bridge release that marked some old options as deprecated, and 7 removes them: target: es5, outFile, baseUrl, moduleResolution: classic and node10, module: amd, umd and system, esModuleInterop: false and downlevelIteration now all fail with an error. If a configuration file you find online uses them, it was written for an older version, and §14 shows what to use instead.
  • The authority is the TypeScript Handbook and the compiler. The topics come from the Handbook, the Reference and the Modules Reference (read on 2026-08-31) and from all 136 options in the tsconfig reference. Where a documentation page and the installed compiler disagreed, the compiler won.
  • The course climbs from types to programs. §1–§7 are the everyday language: the two layers, the basic types, narrowing, functions, objects, classes and generics. §8–§10 show how to compute types from other types, the ready-made utility types, and how TypeScript decides whether one type fits another. §11–§15 cover what surrounds a real project: modules, declaration files (the .d.ts files that describe a package's types), configuration, project structure and the few features that produce extra JavaScript. §16–§17 apply everything to real code and cover writing clean types and keeping the compiler fast, and §18 builds a fully typed service.
  • Each section has numbered subsections, examples with the compiler's real error messages, and exercises with worked solutions. If an error message in the course differs from yours, check your tsconfig first: most differences come from one setting.

You need Node and TypeScript 7 in the project. Check both before starting:

node --version    # v24 or newer
npx tsc --version # Version 7.x

Versions every example in this course was produced against: TypeScript 7.0.2 · Node 24.

What you are actually learning

Not a list of type syntax, but five ideas that explain almost every error message you will meet:

  1. Two layers. The types are removed (the technical word is erased) before your program runs, so the running program cannot look at a type to decide anything. Whatever the program must decide while it runs needs a real value: a label field, a class, a validation function. A whole family of "cannot find name" errors is just this one rule (§1).
  2. Types match by shape. TypeScript does not care what a type is called. It checks whether the members fit, one by one, with a few deliberate exceptions where it is more relaxed than strictly safe. For example, it is relaxed about method parameters but strict about properties that hold functions. Knowing where those exceptions are lets you predict an error instead of arguing with it (§10).
  3. Narrowing and impossible states. When you write typeof, a truthiness check, in or instanceof, TypeScript learns exactly as much as that check proves, and no more. A discriminated union (a group of shapes that share one label field) plus an exhaustiveness check (making sure every case is handled) means that adding a new case produces a compile error everywhere it matters (§3).
  4. Types computed instead of copied. Tools like keyof, indexed access, conditional types, infer, mapped types and template literals build one type out of another, so the two can never drift apart. The compiler has a limit: 999 repeated steps of a certain kind before it gives up (§8).
  5. The edges of your program. JSON.parse and res.json() return any, a caught error is unknown, and the type you pass to querySelector is a claim, not a check. Your types are only as trustworthy as the places where outside data comes in, which is why the course ends by teaching how to parse data rather than just describe it (§16).

By the end you should be able to set up the compiler on purpose, publish types that other people can use, trace any error message back to the rule that caused it, and make your types true at the edges instead of merely declared, all without looking anything up.

SECTION 1

The Type Layer and the Compiler

TypeScript is JavaScript plus a second layer that only exists while you write and build your code. By the time your program runs, that layer is gone. Most of the trouble people have with TypeScript comes from mixing the two layers up: an error about a type that "should be right" is usually a question about the type layer that someone tried to answer with a fact about the running program, or the other way round.

So this section is not a tour of syntax. It explains what kind of thing TypeScript is: what it checks, what it produces, what it does not promise, and the few places where it knowingly gives an answer that is not quite safe, because a perfectly safe answer would make ordinary JavaScript impossible to check. Get this straight first and the rest of the language is much smaller than it looks. Skip it and you will be surprised for a year.

Three facts frame everything that follows:

  • Types are erased. They are removed before the code runs, so a type can never change what your program does.
  • Types are structural. A type describes a shape (which members something has) and never depends on a name.
  • The checker is deliberately unsound in a few specific places. "Unsound" means it sometimes accepts code that could still fail. Each case is a documented trade-off in favour of being usable, not a bug.

By the end of this section you will be able to say which of these three facts explains any surprise you meet.

1.1 Runtime Versus Compile Time

The difference between runtime versus compile time is the first thing to get straight. Two completely separate machines are involved. They run at different times, and they know different things.

Compile time is when tsc reads your source. It can see the whole program, it knows every declared type, and it can prove things about code that never runs. Runtime is when a JavaScript engine runs the output. It only has values, and no types at all.

type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; r: number } | { kind: 'square'; side: number };

function area(s: Shape): number {
  // `s.kind` is a real runtime property — this test works.
  return s.kind === 'circle' ? Math.PI * s.r ** 2 : s.side ** 2;
}

console.log(area({ kind: 'square', side: 3 }));
// @ts-expect-error `Shape` is not a value, so it cannot be used in an expression
const nothing: unknown = Shape;

9

The first check works because kind is data, a real value that exists while the program runs. The second is rejected because Shape is a type, and nothing called Shape exists in the JavaScript that comes out, so there is nothing to take the typeof of. This one question, "is this name a value or a type?", explains most "cannot find name" errors in a beginner's first week.

A compile-time guarantee is what the type layer sells, so it helps to be exact about what it covers. If tsc reports no errors, then under the assumptions you gave it, the operations in your program are consistent with each other: you never read a property that the declared type lacks, and you never pass an argument the function refuses. What it does not cover is data that comes from outside the program. Suppose you say a JSON response is a User. TypeScript checks every use of it against User, but never checks it against the real bytes that arrived over the network. So the guarantee is only as true as your annotations, and §16.21 shows how to make them true instead of merely claimed.

The practical rule that follows: anything the program must decide while it runs needs a real value to decide with. That can be a discriminant property (a field whose value tells you which kind of object you have), a Symbol, a class you can test with instanceof, or a validator that returns a boolean. Every attempt to make a decision from a type alone ends in the same error, and the fix is always to put the information into a value.

The rest of the course leans on two terms collected here: a compile-time guarantee and a discriminant property.

1.2 Type Erasure

Type erasure is what makes everything in §1.1 true: the compiler deletes the type layer and writes out JavaScript. This is not "translation" in the usual sense. For nearly every construct it is plain deletion, and the output is your source with the annotations removed.

// input.ts
export interface User { id: number; name: string }
export type Id = User['id'];

export function rename(user: User, name: string): User {
  return { ...user, name };
}

Compiled with tsc and no options at all, this is the whole transformation:

export function rename(user, name) {
    return { ...user, name };
}

The interface and the type alias produced nothing at all, and the function only lost its annotations. That is what makes TypeScript cheap to adopt and cheap to leave: the output looks like the code you wrote.

The emit pipeline has three stages. It helps to know their names, because error codes point at them. The parser turns text into a syntax tree and reports TS1xxx errors, which are real syntax mistakes. The checker walks that tree, works out the types and reports TS2xxx and higher, which are the type errors. The emitter writes the JavaScript and, separately, declaration files (§12.14). Importantly, the emitter runs even when the checker found errors, unless you ask it not to: by default tsc still writes output for a program with type errors, and noEmitOnError is the setting that changes this. That surprises people who expect a compiler to refuse.

Four constructs are the exceptions to erasure. They produce code instead of disappearing, and §15 covers all four: enum, namespace, decorators and parameter properties. Everything else in the type layer vanishes, which is why erasableSyntaxOnly (§14.11) exists. It forbids exactly those four, so that any tool that only strips types produces correct output.

The consequence to carry into every later section: a type cannot affect what the program does. It cannot change a value, cannot be tested, and cannot be inspected while the program runs. When a design seems to need that, what it actually needs is a value that mirrors the type. That is the idea behind discriminated unions (§3.12), as const objects (§8.1) and runtime validators (§16.21).

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: the emit pipeline.

1.3 A Structural Type System

A structural type system decides whether two types are compatible by comparing their members, not their names. If a value has the right members, it counts as that type.

interface Point { x: number; y: number }

function show(p: Point): string { return `${p.x},${p.y}`; }

const literal = { x: 1, y: 2 };
console.log(show(literal));                     // never mentions Point — and is fine

class Vector { constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {} }
console.log(show(new Vector(3, 4)));            // no `implements Point` anywhere

const extra = { x: 5, y: 6, z: 7 };
console.log(show(extra));                       // extra members are fine via a variable

1,2
3,4
5,6

None of those three says anything about Point. In a nominal type system, such as Java, C# or Rust, each of them would have to declare the relationship explicitly, and the compiler would reject an unrelated class that has identical fields. TypeScript takes the opposite position because it describes JavaScript, where an object that comes out of a JSON parse has no class and no declared interface and is still a perfectly good Point.

Two consequences follow, one pleasant and one that surprises everyone once.

You can type existing code without touching it. An interface that describes a shape someone else produces needs no cooperation from them, which is what makes it possible at all to add types to an untyped library (§12.20).

Two unrelated ideas with the same shape are the same type. Metres and Feet as number, UserId and OrderId as string, Celsius and Fahrenheit: the structural system cannot tell them apart, and will happily let you pass one where the other was meant. This is a real gap and a source of real bugs. The standard fix is the branded types of §8.11: you intersect the type with a marker that nothing else can produce, which gives you nominal behaviour inside a structural system.

One refinement is worth knowing early, because it looks like a contradiction. Object literals written directly in a call or assignment get an extra check, called excess property checking (§5.4). So show({ x: 5, y: 6, z: 7 }) written inline is an error, while passing the same object through a variable is not. This is a usability rule added on top of the structural rule, not a change to it. A freshly written literal with an extra key is almost always a typo, while a variable that happens to have more members is almost always fine.

To have in hand before moving on: a nominal type system.

1.4 Type Annotations and Type Inference

A type annotation is a colon followed by a type. Type inference is the compiler working the type out from what you wrote. The everyday skill is knowing which to use where, and the default is stronger than newcomers expect: annotate the boundaries, infer everything else.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// Inferred, and correctly.
const count = 3;                      // 3, a literal type — const never widens
let mutable = 3;                      // number — let widens
const names = ['a', 'b'];             // string[]
const lookup = new Map<string, number>([['a', 1]]);

type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof count, 3>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof mutable, number>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<typeof names, string[]>>;

// Inferred from the body — the return type needs no annotation.
function double(n: number) { return n * 2; }
type _4 = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof double>, number>>;

console.log(count, mutable, names, lookup.get('a'), double(21));

3 3 [ 'a', 'b' ] 1 42

Parameter types must be annotated, because there is nothing to infer them from, and that is the one place annotations are mandatory. Under noImplicitAny (§2.4) an unannotated parameter is an error instead of a silent any.

A return type annotation is optional, and often worth writing anyway, for a reason that has nothing to do with the compiler needing it. An annotated return type is checked at the function, so a mistake is reported where the mistake is. An inferred one travels onward and is reported at some distant call, sometimes in another file. On an exported function, the annotation also stops a later change from quietly altering your public API. Most teams settle on this rule: annotate exported functions, infer local ones.

Do not annotate what inference already gets right. const names: string[] = ['a', 'b'] adds nothing, and in the as const case it actively loses information. An annotation that does earn its place is one that is deliberately narrower or wider than what would be inferred: const level: Level = 'warn' checks the literal against a union, and let current: Node | null = null widens a variable that starts out empty: it gives it a broader type than null alone, so it can hold a Node later.

Inference also works in the other direction. Contextual typing (§2.5) means the surrounding code supplies the type. In names.map((s) => s.length), the parameter s gets its type from the array, not from an annotation. That is what makes callbacks pleasant to write, and it is why the advice about parameter order in §7.2 matters.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: a type annotation.

1.5 Gradual Typing

Gradual typing means a program can be partly typed and partly not, with the boundary moving over time. It is TypeScript's central design commitment, and it is the reason the language exists at all instead of being a brand-new language that merely looks like JavaScript.

Concretely, four things follow from it.

Every JavaScript file is a valid TypeScript file. Rename .js to .ts and it compiles. It may produce errors under strict settings, but it parses and produces output. There is no rewrite step.

any is a legal type, and it switches checking off locally (§10.12). This escape hatch is what makes a step-by-step migration possible: a module you have not typed yet does not break the build.

Strictness is a dial, not a switch. strict is a family of about a dozen settings (§13.6) that you can turn on one at a time, so a large codebase can tighten gradually: turn on noImplicitAny, fix what breaks, commit, then move to the next. §16.25 calls this a strictness ratchet, and it is the standard migration strategy.

Types can be added from outside. A .d.ts file describes a library that has no types of its own, without modifying it (§12.1), and JSDoc comments give types to a .js file without converting it (§12.24).

The cost of gradual typing is worth being honest about: a gradually typed program's guarantees are only as good as its worst-typed edge. A single any flowing through a well-typed core removes checking everywhere it reaches (§10.21), and a .d.ts file that lies is believed completely. Gradual typing buys easy adoption, and the price is that a green build does not mean what it means in a sound, fully typed language.

The practical advice: use the dial. A new project should start at maximum strictness, because the cost of strictness grows with how much untyped code you already have, and on day one that is zero.

1.6 The tsc Compiler and the TypeScript 7 Native Port

The tsc compiler is the reference implementation. It checks types, writes JavaScript, writes declaration files, and every other tool is measured against it. The TypeScript 7 native port is what it now is: a rewrite of the compiler in Go, shipped as a native executable instead of as JavaScript.

That is not a small detail. It changes what you install and how you use the compiler from code. Measured on the installed copy:

$ node_modules/.bin/tsc --version
Version 7.0.2

$ file node_modules/@typescript/typescript-linux-x64/lib/tsc
ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, statically linked, Go BuildID=..., stripped

$ ls -l node_modules/@typescript/typescript-linux-x64/lib/tsc
-rwxrwxr-x  24101026  tsc

The typescript package itself now contains just five small files. Its bin/tsc is a Node shim that execves the platform binary, and the binary arrives through one of twenty optionalDependencies (@typescript/typescript-linux-x64, @typescript/typescript-darwin-arm64, and so on), of which your package manager installs exactly one.

The programmatic API moved, and this is the breaking change most likely to affect you. require('typescript') used to give you the whole compiler. Now it gives you two properties:

$ node -e "const ts = require('typescript'); console.log(Object.keys(ts))"
[ 'version', 'versionMajorMinor' ]

The real API now lives under explicit subpaths: typescript/unstable/sync, typescript/unstable/async, typescript/unstable/ast and others. The unstable in those names is a deliberate signal that the API may still change. Any tool that did import * as ts from 'typescript' and then used ts.createProgram needs updating, and the subpath it needs is typescript/unstable/sync.

The reason for the rewrite was speed, and speed is worth measuring rather than repeating. On this machine, a synthetic project of 200 files and 400 exported declarations, checked with strict and noEmit:

run 1: 1.73s   103 MB
run 2: 1.84s   102 MB
run 3: 1.86s   102 MB

That is the number to compare your own project against, and §17.6 covers what to do when yours is much worse. The point for now is that the tsc compiler is a native binary with a native binary's start-up cost, about a tenth of a second rather than a second. That is what makes it practical to run in a pre-commit hook.

1.7 Checking Without Emitting, and Type Checking as a Gate

Checking without emitting is tsc --noEmit: run the checker, report errors, write no files. It is the most-used way to run the compiler in modern projects, because in most build setups something else does the emitting.

$ tsc --noEmit                 # check the whole project, produce nothing
$ tsc --noEmit --watch         # and keep checking as files change

A bundler (a tool that combines many source files into a few files for shipping), Vite, esbuild, swc or Node's own type stripping (§15.24) converts each file quickly by deleting the types without checking them. It is fast precisely because it skips the expensive part. So the modern setup splits the two jobs: the fast tool writes the output, and tsc --noEmit does the checking.

Type checking as a gate is what makes that split safe. If nothing runs the checker, the types are just documentation, and documentation drifts out of date. The gate belongs in three places, listed from cheapest and most frequent to most costly and least frequent:

The editor, continuously, through the language server (§1.10). This catches nearly everything and costs you nothing.

A pre-commit hook, on the changed files or the whole project. With a native compiler and --incremental (§14.3), which reuses the results of the previous run, this takes a second or two.

CI, on every pull request, as a required check. This is the one that must exist, because it is the only one that cannot be skipped with --no-verify.

The failure this prevents is specific and common. A team uses a bundler during development, and on release day discovers forty type errors, because nothing has run the checker since the bundler never did. Adding tsc --noEmit to CI from the first commit is a ten-minute job that prevents it entirely.

One setting goes with this. noEmitOnError makes the emitter refuse to write output when the checker found errors. It only matters when tsc is your emitter, and it is worth turning on there, since the default of writing out code that has type errors surprises everyone at least once.

1.8 A Type Error, and How to Read One

A type error is the checker's claim that two types are incompatible. It has a structure that is worth learning: a code, a top-level message, and an indented chain of increasingly specific reasons.

type User = { id: number; profile: { name: string; age: number } };
declare function save(u: User): void;
// @ts-expect-error age is a string here
save({ id: 1, profile: { name: 'Ada', age: '36' } });

error TS2345: Argument of type '{ id: number; profile: { name: string; age: string; }; }'
is not assignable to parameter of type 'User'.
  The types of 'profile.age' are incompatible between these types.
    Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

Read a type error from the bottom up. The last, most indented line is the actual disagreement, here that string is not a number, and every line above it is the path the checker took to get there. On a deeply nested type the top line can be a page long while the bottom line is one short clause, and the bottom line is the one that tells you what to fix.

The error code is worth searching for. TS2345 is always "argument not assignable to parameter", TS2322 is "type not assignable to type" in an assignment, TS2339 is "property does not exist", TS2551 is the same with a spelling suggestion, and TS7006 is an implicit any parameter. A handful of codes cover most of the errors you will see. Searching for the code, instead of the message, finds explanations instead of one person's particular case.

The position of an error is where the checker noticed the problem, not necessarily where the mistake is. An inferred return type travels onward: annotate the function (§1.4) and the same mistake is reported at the function instead of at the call. This is the single most effective technique for a confusing error, and §17.1 develops it.

Two things the message will not tell you, and that are worth checking yourself. First, whether the two types are different declarations of the same shape, which happens when two copies of a package are installed. The message then reads absurdly, comparing User to User, and the fix is to remove the duplicate dependency. Second, whether the error is caused by an earlier error: tsc carries on after a failure, so a cascade of twenty errors often has a single cause, and fixing the first is worth more than reading the rest.

1.9 File Extensions: .ts, .tsx, .mts and .cts

TypeScript has four source file extensions, and each one means something to the compiler. They are not a matter of style.

A .ts file is ordinary TypeScript. Whether it produces ESM output (the standard import/export module format) or CommonJS output (Node's older require/module.exports format) depends on the module setting and, under nodenext, on the type field of the nearest package.json (§11.10).

A .tsx file turns on JSX syntax (§16.11). That has a real cost: in a .tsx file, <T>expr is not a type assertion, because it is read as JSX. The angle-bracket assertion is therefore unavailable and you must write expr as T. That is one of two reasons this course uses the as form throughout. The other is that it reads better in a chain.

A .mts file always produces ESM and a .cts file always produces CommonJS, whatever any package.json says. They are the escape hatches that let one package hold both formats, and they are why export = can be legal in one file and an error in its neighbour (§11.7). Their outputs are .mjs and .cjs.

Two declaration-file extensions go with those: .d.mts describes an ESM module and .d.cts describes a CommonJS one, and a package published in both formats needs both (§11.16). A plain .d.ts follows the same package.json rule as a .ts.

The practical advice is short. Use .ts everywhere, .tsx where there is JSX, and use .mts or .cts only when you must fix a file's format. In practice that means a build script that has to stay CommonJS, or a single ESM entry point in an otherwise CommonJS package. A codebase that uses .mts everywhere has usually mistaken the extension for a strictness setting.

In summary, the vocabulary here is a .ts file and a type assertion.

1.10 The Language Server, Editor Integration and the Playground

The language server is the same compiler, running as a long-lived background process that answers questions about the file you are editing. Editor integration (the red squiggles, autocomplete, go-to-definition, rename and quick fixes) is entirely that server, talking to your editor over the Language Server Protocol.

This matters for a practical reason: the language server and tsc can disagree, and when they do, the editor is usually the one that is wrong. There are three causes, from most to least common:

The editor is using a different TypeScript version, its own bundled copy instead of your project's. Every editor has a "use workspace version" setting, and setting it is the first thing to do in a new project. A course, a tutorial or a colleague reporting an error you cannot reproduce is very often this.

The editor is using a different tsconfig, because the file you have open is not covered by any project's include. The language server then falls back to guessed defaults, which are much looser than yours.

The server's state is out of date. Renaming files, changing package.json or installing a dependency can leave it stale, and restarting it fixes that. Learn where that command is in your editor before you need it.

One habit pays for itself immediately: hover over things. The inferred type of a variable, the resolved type arguments of a generic call and the specific overload that was chosen (when a function declares several signatures, the one this call matched) are all one hover away. Reading them is how you find out that a const widened when you thought it had not. This course's Expect<Equal<...>> harness (§8.1) exists to write those hovers down in a form a build can check. In your editor, the hover is the interactive version of the same thing.

The TypeScript playground is the language server in a web page, and it is the right place to reproduce a problem in isolation. Two of its features are underused. The config panel exposes every compiler option, so "does this depend on strictNullChecks?" takes ten seconds to answer. And a playground link encodes the whole program in the URL, which makes it the right way to ask a question about a type error instead of pasting a screenshot.

What to carry forward from this subsection: the typescript playground.

1.11 Type Soundness

Type soundness is a precise property. A type system is sound if a program that type-checks cannot go wrong at runtime in the ways the types describe. If the checker says a value is a string, a sound system guarantees that at runtime it is a string.

TypeScript is not sound, and its own design goals say so, so this is not a discovery. The relevant non-goal is "apply a sound or 'provably correct' type system; instead, strike a balance between correctness and productivity."

It is worth seeing why a sound checker for JavaScript would be unusable, instead of taking the trade-off on faith. Here are ways a checked program can still fail:

const nums: number[] = [1, 2, 3];
const n = nums[10];                        // typed number; actually undefined
console.log(n, typeof n);

const parsed = JSON.parse('{"id": "x"}') as { id: number };
console.log(parsed.id, typeof parsed.id);  // typed number; actually a string

const anything: any = 'not a number';
const alsoNum: number = anything;          // any turns checking off
console.log(alsoNum, typeof alsoNum);

undefined undefined
x string
not a number string

Three checked expressions, and three runtime types that contradict their static ones. The first is fixed by a setting (noUncheckedIndexedAccess, §5.19). The second is fixed by validating instead of asserting (§16.21). The third is any doing exactly what it is documented to do (§10.12).

The useful way to hold this: TypeScript's guarantee is "consistent with what you told it", not "true of the running program". Every unsound case above is a place where what you told it was false. That view is what makes the type system worth trusting in practice. The failures are not mysterious. They sit exactly at the boundaries where you asserted something instead of checking it, and you can list those boundaries in your own codebase.

1.12 Unsoundness by Design

Besides the escape hatches you open yourself, the checker has a small number of deliberate holes: places where it accepts something it could prove might be wrong, because rejecting it would break too much ordinary JavaScript. Unsoundness by design is the name for these. Knowing the list turns them from surprises into known hazards.

// 1. Arrays are covariant, and mutable.
type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };
const dogs: Dog[] = [{ name: 'Rex', bark() {} }];
const animals: Animal[] = dogs;            // accepted
animals.push({ name: 'Whiskers' });        // a cat is now in dogs
console.log(dogs.length, typeof dogs[1]!.bark);

// 2. Method parameters are bivariant.
type Handler = { handle(e: Animal): void };
const dogHandler: Handler = { handle(d: Dog) { console.log('handled', d.name); } };
dogHandler.handle({ name: 'Whiskers' });   // no bark, but it type-checked

// 3. Optional properties do not have to be absent-or-valid without a flag.
type Opts = { retries?: number };
const o: Opts = JSON.parse('{"retries": null}');
console.log(o.retries);                     // typed number | undefined; actually null

2 undefined
handled Whiskers
null

Array covariance is the famous one. Covariance means the relationship carries over in the same direction: because a Dog is an Animal, Dog[] is assignable to Animal[], because refusing it would break huge amounts of code that works in practice. The price is that pushing through the widened alias corrupts the original array. readonly Animal[] is the sound version, and it is the right parameter type for anything that only reads (§7.14).

Method bivariance is the second. A method's parameters are checked in both directions, so a handler that accepts a narrower type is assignable where a wider one was wanted. strictFunctionTypes (§10.5) fixes this for properties that hold functions and deliberately does not fix it for methods, because the built-in Array<T> and Promise<T> signatures depend on the looser rule.

Missing versus undefined is the third. Without exactOptionalPropertyTypes (§5.18), an optional property may be explicitly set to undefined, and nothing at all stops a null that came from outside.

The pattern across all three is the same, and it is the honest summary of TypeScript's design: where soundness and existing JavaScript conflicted, existing JavaScript won, and a setting was added later for people who want the strict answer. Every setting named above is off by default and worth turning on in new code.

The terms above, gathered: an optional property.

1.13 What TypeScript Deliberately Does Not Do

Several things people expect from a typed language are missing on purpose, and the list is short enough to learn. Knowing what TypeScript deliberately does not do saves you from searching for a feature that will never arrive.

It does not check anything at runtime. There is no reflection, no runtime type test and no automatic validation of an API response. Everything the types say is erased (§1.2), and any runtime checking is code you write or a library you call (§16.21).

It does not add runtime features to JavaScript. With four historical exceptions (§15), the language adds only type syntax. Optional chaining, #private fields and decorators all arrived through the JavaScript standards process. TypeScript implemented them but did not invent them, and its policy is now to wait for standardisation instead of leading it.

It does not aim for soundness (§1.11), and it does not aim to catch every error. A program can type-check and still divide by zero, deadlock or be wrong about the business.

It does not provide nominal types. There is no newtype (a type that is a separate copy of another, as in Haskell) and no opaque type alias (a type whose real structure is hidden from the rest of the program). The structural rule is the rule, and the branding of §8.11 is a pattern, not a feature.

It does not model effects, ownership, lifetimes or nullability at the reference level. There is no throws clause, so a function's signature says nothing about what it can throw (§10.20). There is no async-versus-sync distinction beyond the return type, and there is no borrow checker.

It does not change how your JavaScript behaves. The output is your code with the types removed, and TypeScript will not turn a == into a === or insert a runtime conversion. If the JavaScript was wrong, the TypeScript is wrong in exactly the same way.

The productive attitude is to see these as boundaries, not gaps. Each one is a place to bring a different tool, such as a validator, a linter or a test, and knowing where the boundary is lets you bring the tool at the right moment instead of arguing with the compiler.

1.14 The DefinitelyTyped Ecosystem and Semantic Versioning of Types

A library written in JavaScript has no types of its own, so someone else has to write them. The DefinitelyTyped ecosystem is where those types live: one very large repository whose packages are published to npm under the @types scope.

npm install --save-dev @types/node        # types for Node's built-in modules
npm install --save-dev @types/express     # types for a library that ships none

Three rules make this work in practice.

Check whether you need it at all. A package that ships its own types (most modern ones do, and package.json's types field, or the types condition of an exports map, says so, §12.19) needs no @types package, and installing one anyway gives you two competing declarations. npm ls @types/foo tells you whether you have one you no longer need.

@types packages are devDependencies, always, because they are erased. The exception that catches people: if your own package publishes declaration files that refer to a type from an @types package, that package becomes a real dependency for your users, because their compiler must find it too.

Version them against the library, not against TypeScript. The DefinitelyTyped convention is that @types/foo@4.17.x targets foo@4.17.x: the major and minor numbers follow the library, and the patch number is the types' own revision.

Semantic versioning of types is the harder half, because a change that is safe for JavaScript can break a TypeScript build. Adding an overload, narrowing a return type, making an optional property required, or adding a required type parameter can each turn a program that compiled into one that fails, while changing no runtime behaviour at all. The community convention is that a types-only breaking change deserves a major version, and it is followed inconsistently.

The defence is the same as for any dependency, and it is worth saying because people skip it for types: pin your @types versions in the lockfile, and treat a types upgrade as a change that needs CI to pass. A tsc --noEmit step in CI (§1.7) turns "the types moved under us" from a mystery into a failing build on the pull request that bumped them.

What This Section Established

Two layers. The type layer exists at compile time and is erased before anything runs, so no runtime decision can be made from a type: put the information into a value instead. Types are structural: a shape, never a name. That is what lets you type code you did not write, and it is why Metres and Feet are the same type until you brand them.

The compiler is now a Go binary reached through a Node shim, with its programmatic API moved to typescript/unstable/*, and require('typescript') returns two properties and nothing else. tsc --noEmit in CI is the gate that keeps the types honest when something faster does the emitting, and reading an error from the bottom up is the skill that makes the messages useful.

And the honest part: TypeScript is not sound, on purpose. Array covariance, method bivariance and optional-versus-undefined are the three holes built in by design. any, assertions and unvalidated external data are the three you open yourself. Everything the checker guarantees depends on your annotations being true, which is why the sections on narrowing, assignability and runtime validation are where the real safety comes from.

Exercises

1. Value or type? For each name, say whether it exists at runtime, at compile time, or both, and give the reason: an interface, a class, a type alias, an enum, a const object with as const, a namespace containing only types, a function parameter's annotation. Then write one program that shows the "both" cases being used in each position.

2. Find the unsoundness. Write three short programs that type-check but produce a runtime value that contradicts its static type: one using array covariance, one using an assertion on external data, and one using an out-of-range index. For each, name the setting or the practice that would have prevented it.

3. Read three errors. Produce the errors TS2345, TS2339 and TS7006 on purpose, quote each message in full, and for each say which line of the message points to the actual mistake and what the smallest fix is.

Solution

1. Value or type?

Name Exists at Why
interface compile time only Pure type declaration; emits nothing (§1.2).
class both Declares a constructor value and an instance type with the same name.
type alias compile time only Erased entirely.
enum both Emits a real object; one of the four non-erased constructs (§15.1).
const object as const both An ordinary value; typeof it reaches its type (§8.1).
namespace of types only compile time only A namespace with no value members emits nothing (§15.10).
a parameter annotation compile time only Deleted with the rest of the type layer. 
class Box { constructor(public value: number) {} }
enum Direction { Up = 'UP', Down = 'DOWN' }
const LEVELS = ['debug', 'info'] as const;

// Each of the three used as a VALUE:
const b = new Box(1);
const d = Direction.Up;
const first = LEVELS[0];

// ...and each used as a TYPE:
const alsoBox: Box = b;
const alsoDir: Direction = d;
type Level = (typeof LEVELS)[number];
const alsoLevel: Level = first;

console.log(alsoBox.value, alsoDir, alsoLevel, Object.keys(Direction));

1 UP debug [ 'Up', 'Down' ]

The class row is the one that causes real confusion, because Box in a type position means the instance, while Box in a value position means the constructor. typeof Box is how you name the constructor's type (§8.1), and that difference is why InstanceType<typeof Box> exists.

2. Three unsound programs.

// (a) Array covariance — a mutable widening alias.
type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };
const dogs: Dog[] = [{ name: 'Rex', bark() {} }];
const asAnimals: Animal[] = dogs;
asAnimals.push({ name: 'Whiskers' });
console.log('a:', typeof dogs[1]!.bark);

// (b) An assertion on external data.
const fromApi = JSON.parse('{"id": "seven"}') as { id: number };
console.log('b:', typeof fromApi.id, fromApi.id * 2);

// (c) An out-of-range index.
const nums: number[] = [1, 2, 3];
const missing = nums[99];
console.log('c:', missing, typeof missing);

a: undefined
b: string NaN
c: undefined undefined

Read line b carefully, because it is the sharpest of the three. The checker's static claim was number. At runtime typeof reports string, so fromApi.id * 2 is NaN instead of 14. An assertion produces a wrong answer quietly: no throw and no warning, just arithmetic on a string. A validator would have failed at the boundary with a message naming the field.

The preventions, one per case. (a) Type the widened alias as readonly Animal[], which is still covariant and is also sound, because it cannot be pushed to. (b) Parse instead of asserting (§16.21): a schema validator returns { id: number } only if the data really has that shape. (c) Turn on noUncheckedIndexedAccess (§5.19), which gives nums[99] the type number | undefined and forces you to check.

Notice that only one of the three is fixed by a compiler setting. The other two are fixed by practices, preferring readonly and validating at boundaries. That is the point of §1.11 again: the guarantee depends on what you told the compiler.

3. Three errors.

declare function save(u: { id: number }): void;
// @ts-expect-error TS2345
save({ id: '1' });

const point = { x: 1, y: 2 };
// @ts-expect-error TS2339
console.log(point.z);

error TS2345: Argument of type '{ id: string; }' is not assignable to parameter of
type '{ id: number; }'.
  Types of property 'id' are incompatible.
    Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

error TS2339: Property 'z' does not exist on type '{ x: number; y: number; }'.

error TS7006: Parameter 'item' implicitly has an 'any' type.

TS2345: the last line is the mistake, string where number was wanted. The first two lines are the path. The smallest fix: save({ id: 1 }).

TS2339: a single line that names both the property and the type it is missing from. The two possible fixes are genuinely different and the message cannot choose between them. Either z is a typo (TS2551 is the variant that says "Did you mean 'y'?"), or the type is too narrow and the property needs adding to it.

TS7006: produced by const f = function (item) { return item; }; under noImplicitAny. The parameter has no annotation and nothing to infer it from. It is worth checking what does not produce it, because the common explanation is wrong: [1, 2].forEach(function (item) { ... }) is fine, because contextual typing (§2.5) applies to a function expression exactly as it does to an arrow function, and item is number. The difference is not arrow versus function. It is whether the function sits in a position that supplies a type. The fix is an annotation, and the better fix is usually to move the function back into the position that was typing it.

SECTION 2

Everyday Types

This is the vocabulary section. Nearly everything you write in TypeScript on an ordinary day is here: the basic types, arrays, object shapes, unions (a value that can be one of several types), aliases (a name for a type), interfaces, and a few operators for telling the checker something it could not work out by itself.

It is also where your habits form, and two of them decide how pleasant the next year will be. The first is letting inference do its job. Inference means the compiler works out a type from the value, so writing the type yourself on a const it already understands is noise, and writing it wrongly (for example, turning a value you wanted exact into a broad one) is worse than noise. The second is treating an assertion as a debt. An assertion (as) does not convince the checker, it silences it, so every use is a place where you promised something that nobody checked.

The order goes from the least to the most surprising. Basic types and arrays are unremarkable. Unions are where TypeScript starts describing real data honestly. Literal types and widening are where inference stops being obvious. And null and undefined under strictNullChecks (the setting that stops them from sneaking into every type) are the biggest source of both benefit and annoyance in the whole language.

2.1 string, number and boolean

JavaScript has seven primitive types (the simplest kinds of value), and TypeScript names each of them in lower case. Three carry almost all the traffic.

The string type covers every string, whatever its length or encoding. The number type covers every JavaScript number. JavaScript stores all numbers the same way (as a 64-bit floating-point value, the IEEE-754 double), so integers and decimals are the same type, and NaN and Infinity are numbers too. The boolean type has exactly two values.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const title: string = 'Mastery';
const count: number = 42;
const ratio: number = 0.5;
const ready: boolean = true;

type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof title, string>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof count, number>>;

// One number type, so these are all the same type.
console.log(Number.isInteger(count), Number.isInteger(ratio), typeof NaN, typeof Infinity);

true false number number

Two rules about the names themselves, and both are enforced.

Write string, not String. The capitalised names String, Number and Boolean are the types of wrapper objects, and you almost never want them. const s: String = 'x' compiles, but then s cannot be passed to a parameter typed string, which produces a baffling error. The lower-case names are the real primitives. The capitalised ones exist to describe new String('x'), which no modern code writes.

There is no int, float, char or double. JavaScript does not have them, so TypeScript does not either. A function that needs an integer has to say so in a way the type system cannot check (a name, a comment, a branded type from §8.11), or check it while the program runs.

The other four primitives are bigint and symbol (§2.16), and null and undefined (§2.14). Each has enough behaviour to earn its own subsection. object, unknown and never are types too, but not primitives, and they belong to §4.

One line each, for reference: the string type, the number type and the boolean type.

2.2 An Array Type

An array type is written two ways and they mean exactly the same thing: T[] and Array<T>.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const names: string[] = ['Ada', 'Grace'];
const scores: Array<number> = [1, 2, 3];
type _1 = Expect<Equal<string[], Array<string>>>;

// Nested and union element types need parentheses to say what you mean.
const grid: number[][] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];
const mixed: (string | number)[] = ['a', 1];
const arrayOrString: string | string[] = 'either';

type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof grid, number[][]>>;
console.log(names.length, grid[1]?.[0], mixed, arrayOrString);

2 3 [ 'a', 1 ] either

The parentheses in (string | number)[] matter. Without them, string | number[] means "a string, or an array of numbers", which is a completely different type. It compiles happily and then fails at the first .map. This is the most common precedence mistake in TypeScript annotations, and reading the annotation aloud catches it: "string or number-array" versus "array of string-or-number".

T[] is the usual spelling and the one to prefer. Array<T> is needed in only one situation, where the element type is written with a keyof or a conditional that would otherwise group the wrong way. Otherwise it is a matter of taste, and a lint rule should decide it for the whole codebase.

A tuple is different (§5.11): [string, number] is an array of fixed length with one type per position, and it is what you want for a pair or a coordinate. An ordinary array type says nothing about length, which is why names[10] type-checks and is undefined at runtime unless noUncheckedIndexedAccess is on (§5.19).

readonly T[] is the version to use for parameters you only read. It accepts every array, forbids push, sort and assigning to an index, and it is the safe counterpart of the covariance hole from §1.12. ReadonlyArray<T> is the long form.

2.3 Annotations: Variables, Parameters and Returns

An annotation can go in three places, and the right advice differs for each.

// A variable annotation — usually unnecessary.
const port: number = 8080;             // the annotation adds nothing
const level: 'debug' | 'info' = 'debug';   // the annotation adds a check

// A parameter type annotation — mandatory (nothing to infer from).
function greet(name: string, times: number): string {
  return `${name} `.repeat(times).trim();
}

// A return type annotation — optional, and often worth writing.
function parsePort(raw: string): number {
  const n = Number(raw);
  return Number.isInteger(n) ? n : 8080;
}

console.log(greet('Ada', 2), parsePort('80'), parsePort('nope'));

Ada Ada 80 8080

A variable annotation is redundant when the starting value already says it. const port: number = 8080 and const port = 8080 differ only in that the second remembers the exact literal 8080. Write the annotation when it does real work: to widen on purpose (let current: Node | null = null), to check a literal against a union (level above), or to declare a variable that has no starting value.

A parameter type annotation is the one that is not optional. Under noImplicitAny (§2.4), a parameter with no annotation and no type from its context is an error. That is good, because an unchecked parameter type is where most any enters a codebase.

A return type annotation is optional, and it is the one worth debating. Writing it costs a few characters and buys two things: the error appears at the function instead of at the call, and an exported function's public shape cannot change by accident. The cost is that inference is often more precise than what you would write. A function returning 'a' | 'b' is easy to annotate as string by mistake, and you lose the union.

Most teams end up with this rule, and this course follows it: annotate exported functions, infer local ones, and never annotate a const whose starting value is already exactly right.

2.4 The any Type and noImplicitAny

The any type is the off switch. A value typed any can be assigned to anything, called, indexed, and have any property read from it, with no checking at all.

const raw: any = JSON.parse('{"id":1}');
console.log(raw.id, raw.nope, raw.a?.b?.c);       // none of these are checked
const asNumber: number = raw;                     // and it flows anywhere
console.log(typeof asNumber);

1 undefined undefined
object

asNumber is annotated number and holds an object. That is the any type doing exactly what it is documented to do, and it is why any is called contagious (§10.21): once one value is any, everything derived from it is any too, and checking stops quietly instead of loudly.

noImplicitAny is the setting that stops any from appearing without you asking for it. Without it, a parameter with no annotation is silently any. With it, you get TS7006: Parameter 'x' implicitly has an 'any' type.

// With noImplicitAny on (it is part of `strict`):
// @ts-expect-error Parameter 'item' implicitly has an 'any' type.
const identity = function (item) { return item; };
console.log(typeof identity);

function

The setting separates implicit any from explicit any. It says nothing about a deliberate x: any, which stays legal because gradual typing (§1.5) needs an escape hatch. What it removes is the silent kind, the kind you did not choose.

The better alternative is unknown (§10.13). It accepts any value exactly as any does, but allows nothing until you narrow it, so the checking is postponed instead of deleted. Wherever this course would once have written any, the answer is unknown plus a narrowing step. In two sentences: any means "stop checking"; unknown means "check later".

2.5 Anonymous Functions and Contextual Typing

An anonymous function passed as an argument usually needs no annotations at all, because contextual typing gives its parameters their types from the position it is in.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const words = ['alpha', 'be', 'gamma'];

// `w` is `string` and `i` is `number`, with nothing written down.
const lengths = words.map((w) => w.length);
const indexed = words.map(function (w, i) { return `${i}:${w}`; });

type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof lengths, number[]>>;
console.log(lengths, indexed);

[ 5, 2, 5 ] [ '0:alpha', '1:be', '2:gamma' ]

Contextual typing applies to function expressions exactly as it does to arrow functions. The common claim that arrows get types from context and function expressions do not is false, and the example above is the proof: w and i are typed in both. What decides it is the position. A function written directly as an argument, as the starting value of a typed variable, or as the value of a typed property gets its parameter types from that context.

Move it out of that position and the types vanish:

// @ts-expect-error no context here, so `w` is an implicit any
const extracted = (w) => w.length;

// Two ways to restore it.
const annotated = (w: string) => w.length;
type Mapper = (w: string) => number;
const contextual: Mapper = (w) => w.length;

console.log(annotated('abcd'), contextual('abc'));

4 3

The second fix is the interesting one. Giving the variable a function type means its parameters get their types from it, so the annotation is written once, on the type, instead of on every parameter. That is the usual way to declare a handler, a reducer or a comparator, and it scales far better than annotating parameters one by one.

Contextual typing also reaches into object literals and return positions, which is why const config: Options = { onError(e) { … } } gives e a type. It is also why the ordering advice in §7.2 matters: a callback can only be typed from information the checker already has, so the value that determines the type must come first in the parameter list.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: an anonymous function.

2.6 An Object Type and Optional Properties

An object type is written inline, listing the members it has. It is structural (§1.3), so it describes a shape and nothing else.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function describe(user: { id: number; name: string; nickname?: string }): string {
  return `${user.nickname ?? user.name} (#${user.id})`;
}

console.log(describe({ id: 1, name: 'Ada' }));
console.log(describe({ id: 2, name: 'Grace', nickname: 'Amazing Grace' }));

Ada (#1)
Amazing Grace (#2)

An optional property is marked with ?. Under strictNullChecks that means two things at once: the property may be missing, and reading it gives T | undefined.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type User = { id: number; nickname?: string };
declare const u: User;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof u.nickname, string | undefined>>;

// @ts-expect-error 'u.nickname' is possibly 'undefined'.
const upper = u.nickname.toUpperCase();

// The three honest ways to deal with it.
const a = u.nickname?.toUpperCase();          // optional chaining: string | undefined
const b = u.nickname ?? 'anonymous';          // a default: string
const c = u.nickname !== undefined ? u.nickname.toUpperCase() : 'none';   // narrowing (§3.1)
console.log(a, b, c);

undefined anonymous none

The separator inside an object type may be ;, , or a newline, and the convention in this course — and in the handbook — is ; on one line and newlines when multi-line.

Two things to know before §5 covers object types properly. An excess property check applies to an object literal written directly: describe({ id: 1, name: 'Ada', extra: true }) is an error, while the same object passed through a variable is not (§5.4). And an inline object type gets unwieldy quickly: as soon as the same shape appears in two signatures it deserves a name, which is what §2.8 and §2.9 are about.

2.7 Union Types, and Operating on One

A union type means "one of these", written with |. It is the feature that lets TypeScript describe real JavaScript data honestly, because real JavaScript functions really do accept a string or a number.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Id = string | number;

function format(id: Id): string {
  // Operating on a union: only what EVERY member supports is available.
  return id.toString().padStart(6, '0');
}

console.log(format(42), format('7'));

declare const someId: Id;
// @ts-expect-error Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'string | number'.
type Upper = ReturnType<typeof someId.toUpperCase>;

000042 000007

Operating on a union follows one rule, and it is the one that trips people up: you may only use members that every part of the union has. toString() exists on both string and number, so it is allowed. toUpperCase() exists on only one of them, so it is not, even when you are certain which one you have.

The answer is not an assertion. It is narrowing (§3.1), which is the whole of the next section:

type Id = string | number;

function format(id: Id): string {
  if (typeof id === 'string') return id.toUpperCase();   // here `id` is string
  return id.toFixed(0).padStart(6, '0');                 // and here it is number
}

console.log(format('abc'), format(42.7));

ABC 000043

The other everyday use of a union is a union of literal types, such as 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn'. It is the closest thing TypeScript has to an enum that produces no code (§15.9). It gives you autocompletion, exhaustiveness checking (§3.14) and a compile error on a typo, at no cost at runtime.

A union spreads over most type operators, and the exceptions are a real source of surprises. keyof (A | B) gives the intersection of their keys, meaning only the keys that both members have, which is what makes Omit unsafe on a union (§9.5). It is worth knowing now, because a union type is the first thing you will apply a utility type to.

2.8 Type Aliases

A type alias gives a name to any type at all: type Name = .... It does not create a new type. It is only a name, and the checker treats the alias and its definition as identical.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type UserId = string;
type Point = { x: number; y: number };
type Callback = (err: Error | null, value?: string) => void;
type Level = 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn';
type Pair<T> = [T, T];

type _1 = Expect<Equal<UserId, string>>;                 // an alias IS its definition
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Pair<number>, [number, number]>>;

const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 };
console.log(p, ('warn' satisfies Level));

{ x: 1, y: 2 } warn

A type alias can name anything: a union, an intersection, a primitive, a function type, a tuple, a conditional type, a mapped type. That is its main advantage over an interface, which can only describe an object shape (including a callable or constructable one).

type UserId = string creates no distinction. UserId and string can be swapped for each other in both directions, so this alias documents your intent and prevents nothing. If you want a UserId that a plain string cannot be passed as, you need a brand (§8.11). An alias on its own is a comment with syntax.

Aliases can be generic (§7.3), and can be recursive when the recursion is lazy (type Json = string | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json }). They cannot be merged: declaring type Point twice in one scope is a duplicate-name error. That last point is a real difference from interfaces, and the subject of §2.10.

2.9 Interfaces

An interface describes an object shape, and for that job it is interchangeable with a type alias in almost every respect.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

interface Point { x: number; y: number }
interface Point3D extends Point { z: number }

// Declaration merging: two declarations of one interface combine.
interface Config { host: string }
interface Config { port: number }
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Config, { host: string; port: number }>>;

const p: Point3D = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 };
const c: Config = { host: 'localhost', port: 8080 };
console.log(p, c);

{ x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 } { host: 'localhost', port: 8080 }

Two capabilities are an interface's own, and both are about extension.

extends builds a new interface from one or more others. Unlike an intersection, the compiler checks that the members are compatible, so a clash between x: string and an inherited x: number is an error at the declaration, not a silently impossible type.

Declaration merging means two declarations with the same name in the same scope are combined instead of clashing. That looks like a trap, but it is actually the mechanism behind module augmentation (§12.6) and global augmentation (§12.5): it is how you add a property to Window, or a method to a library's interface, without editing the library. It is also why an interface is the right choice for anything that users of your code might need to extend.

An interface can also describe callable and constructable shapes, such as interface Fn { (x: number): string } and interface Ctor { new (x: number): Thing } (§4.2, §4.3), so "interfaces are only for objects" is an oversimplification. What an interface cannot be is a union, an intersection, a primitive alias, a conditional type or a mapped type.

2.10 Alias Versus Interface

The alias versus interface question comes up in every codebase. The honest answer has three parts: a rule for the cases where it matters, a default for the cases where it does not, and one measurable difference.

Use an interface when the type is an object shape that others may extend or augment. That means a public API, anything a plugin might add to, and anything in a .d.ts file. Declaration merging is a feature there.

Use a type alias for anything else, or when you specifically want merging to be impossible. A union, a function type, a tuple, a mapped or conditional type, a generic transformation: an interface cannot express any of these.

For a plain internal object shape, either is fine, so pick one and be consistent. The difference is small enough that a lint rule that settles it is worth more than a debate.

The measurable difference, and the reason the compiler team's own guidance leans towards interfaces for large object shapes:

// An intersection is re-checked structurally at each use, and its errors
// are deferred to the use site.
type A = { a: string };
type B = { b: number };
type Intersected = A & B;

interface IA { a: string }
interface IB extends IA { b: number }

const one: Intersected = { a: 'x', b: 1 };
const two: IB = { a: 'x', b: 1 };
console.log(one, two);

{ a: 'x', b: 1 } { a: 'x', b: 1 }

Both work, but the compiler does different things behind them. An interface is a single named type that gets cached. An intersection is a composite that the checker may have to work out again at each use, and §17.8 is the subsection that measures the cost. For two members it does not matter. For a deeply composed type used across hundreds of files it does, and "interfaces are cheaper than intersections" is the finding that most often speeds up a slow build.

The one difference in behaviour that is not about performance: an intersection with conflicting members silently produces an impossible type, while interface … extends with a conflict is an error at the declaration. { x: number } & { x: string } has an x of type never, and you find out at the first assignment.

2.11 Type Assertions and the as Operator

A type assertion tells the checker to treat an expression as a type it could not work out itself. The as operator is the syntax: expr as T.

// The legitimate case: you know something the checker cannot.
const el = document.getElementById('app') as HTMLCanvasElement;
console.log(typeof el);

// The check that stops the worst mistakes.
const n = 42;
// @ts-expect-error Conversion of type 'number' to type 'string' may be a mistake
const bad = n as string;

object

An assertion is not a conversion. Nothing happens while the program runs: as is erased like every other type construct (§1.2), so n as string would leave a number sitting in a variable that the checker believes is a string. That is why it is the most dangerous everyday syntax in the language.

The compiler applies one guard: the two types must be related, meaning one must be assignable to the other. 42 as string is refused, and 42 as number | string is allowed. That guard catches typos and nothing else, and it can be bypassed by going through unknown (§10.15), which is exactly why a double assertion is a red flag that reviewers should stop.

The angle-bracket form <T>expr means the same thing and should not be used. It is unavailable in .tsx files, where it is read as JSX (§1.9), so as is the only spelling that works everywhere.

Three rules for using assertions well.

Prefer satisfies when you want checking without changing the type (§8.10). Most uses of as on a configuration object should be satisfies.

Prefer a type predicate when you are narrowing (§3.9). x as Dog after an if is a claim. isDog(x) is a check the compiler can carry forward.

When you must assert, do it at a boundary, never in the middle. One assertion inside a validated parser (§16.21) is a contract you can audit. Twenty assertions scattered through business logic are twenty unverified claims.

2.12 Literal Types, Widening and Inference

A literal type is a type with exactly one value: 'debug', 42, true. They are what make a union of strings useful, and they appear and disappear according to rules that are worth learning precisely.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const fixed = 'hello';               // const: the literal type is kept
let variable = 'hello';              // let: widened to string
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof fixed, 'hello'>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof variable, string>>;

// A property of an object literal always widens, even under const.
const obj = { k: 'v' };
type _3 = Expect<Equal<typeof obj, { k: string }>>;

// An array literal widens too, and loses its length.
const arr = [1, 2];
type _4 = Expect<Equal<typeof arr, number[]>>;

// A const's literal type is lost the moment it is copied to a mutable place.
let copied = fixed;
type _5 = Expect<Equal<typeof copied, string>>;

// But a contextual type of a literal union keeps it.
type Level = 'debug' | 'info';
const lv: Level = 'debug';
type _6 = Expect<Equal<typeof lv, 'debug'>>;

console.log(fixed, variable, obj, arr, copied, lv);

hello hello { k: 'v' } [ 1, 2 ] hello debug

Literal inference is the rule that produces the literal type, and literal widening is the rule that discards it. Both are about whether the value can change. A const binding cannot change, so its literal type stays true forever. A let binding can change, so keeping 'hello' would be wrong the moment it is reassigned. Every widening in the list above follows from that: an object's property can change, an array's elements can change, and copying into a let creates a home that can change.

The consequences bite in one specific place, and it is worth recognising the error:

type Method = 'GET' | 'POST';
function request(url: string, method: Method): string { return `${method} ${url}`; }

const opts = { url: '/api', method: 'POST' };
// @ts-expect-error Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Method'.
const broken: string = request(opts.url, opts.method);

// Three fixes, in increasing order of preference.
console.log(request(opts.url, opts.method as Method));            // assertion: unchecked
const typed: { url: string; method: Method } = { url: '/api', method: 'POST' };
console.log(request(typed.url, typed.method));                    // annotation: checked
const frozen = { url: '/api', method: 'POST' } as const;
console.log(request(frozen.url, frozen.method));                  // const assertion: checked and precise

POST /api
POST /api
POST /api

That error, "string is not assignable to 'GET' | 'POST'" on an object property you can see is 'POST', is the most common confusion caused by widening, and it has nothing to do with the value being wrong. The property can change, so the checker refuses to promise that it will still be 'POST' when the call happens.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: literal widening and literal inference.

2.13 A Const Assertion

A const assertion, written as const, is the instruction that turns widening off for one expression.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const config = { retries: 3, mode: 'fast' } as const;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof config, { readonly retries: 3; readonly mode: 'fast' }>>;

const levels = ['debug', 'info', 'warn'] as const;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof levels, readonly ['debug', 'info', 'warn']>>;
type Level = (typeof levels)[number];
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Level, 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn'>>;

console.log(config.mode, levels.length);
// @ts-expect-error a const assertion makes every property readonly
config.retries = 4;

fast 3

It does three things at once, and all three matter.

Literal types are kept at every depth, so you get 'fast' instead of string. Every property becomes readonly, all the way down. An array literal becomes a readonly tuple, keeping both its length and the type at each position.

That combination is what makes the "declare the data, derive the types" pattern work (§8.1): a single as const object is both the value your code uses at runtime and the source of every type that describes it. Pulling out the union with (typeof levels)[number] is the idiom you will write most often.

A const assertion only exists at compile time. It does not call Object.freeze, and the object can still be changed while the program runs: (config as { retries: number }).retries = 4 works, and so does any change from untyped code. If you need the guarantee at runtime too, Object.freeze is a separate call.

Two limits. It only works on a literal: as const on a variable or a function call is an error, because there is no literal for it to preserve. And in a generic API you usually want const on the type parameter instead (§7.8), so the caller does not have to remember as const at every call.

2.14 null, undefined and strictNullChecks

JavaScript has two empty values, and TypeScript has a type for each. What matters is strictNullChecks, the setting that decides whether they are tracked at all.

With strictNullChecks off (the default before 2016, still found in old configs), null and undefined can be assigned to every type, so string means "a string, or null, or undefined" and the compiler never mentions it. Every "cannot read properties of undefined" crash is invisible to the checker.

With it on (it is part of strict, and it is the single most valuable setting in the language), they are separate types that you have to handle.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function firstWord(text: string | null): string {
  if (text === null) return '';
  return text.split(' ')[0] ?? '';        // narrowed to string here
}

// The same body without the guard — declared, never called, so only the type is at issue.
function firstWordBroken(text: string | null): string {
  // @ts-expect-error 'text' is possibly 'null'.
  return text.split(' ')[0] ?? '';
}

const found: string | undefined = ['a'].find((s) => s === 'z');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof found, string | undefined>>;

console.log(firstWord('hello world'), `[${firstWord(null)}]`, found, typeof firstWordBroken);

hello [] undefined function

It is worth keeping the difference between the two values, because TypeScript keeps it. undefined means "not there": a missing property, a variable that was never assigned, a function with no return, an index out of range. null means "deliberately empty": a value someone set. The convention that pays off is to use undefined everywhere in your own code and let null appear only where an outside API produces it. Then ?. and ??, which treat both the same way, are the only places you need to think about it.

?. and ?? are the everyday tools, and they are runtime JavaScript, not type syntax. a?.b gives undefined instead of crashing when a is null or undefined, and a ?? b supplies a default only for null and undefined, not for 0 or ''. That is the bug || has and ?? fixes.

Turning strictNullChecks on in an existing codebase produces a lot of errors, and that number is an honest measure of how much of your code was already wrong. §16.25's ratchet shows how to do it a little at a time.

2.15 The Non-Null Assertion Operator

The non-null assertion operator is a ! placed after a value, which removes null and undefined from its type. It is an assertion (§2.11) with a shorter spelling and the same risk.

const numbers = [1, 2, 3];

const first = numbers[0];         // number, because noUncheckedIndexedAccess is off here
const found = numbers.find((n) => n > 10);

function neverCalled(): string {
  // @ts-expect-error 'found' is possibly 'undefined'.
  return found.toFixed(0);
}

const assertedAway: number = found!;   // compiles — and holds undefined
console.log(first, assertedAway, typeof assertedAway, typeof neverCalled);

1 undefined undefined function

That output is the whole argument. found! compiled, told the checker that assertedAway was a number, and it printed undefined. The ! does nothing while the program runs: it deletes a check and leaves the bug.

There are places where it is right, and they share one property: you have information the checker cannot have.

const byId = new Map<string, { name: string }>([['u1', { name: 'Ada' }]]);

// A Map you just populated: `get` is typed as possibly undefined, and you know it is not.
console.log(byId.get('u1')!.name);

// A regex you wrote, whose group must match if the match succeeded.
const m = /(\d+)-(\d+)/.exec('10-20');
if (m) console.log(Number(m[1]!) + Number(m[2]!));

Ada
30

Three rules keep it honest. Never use ! on data from outside the program (an API response, a DOM query, a parsed file), because there the checker is right and you are guessing. Prefer a narrowing check where one is possible: if (found !== undefined) costs one line and is verified. And prefer ?? with a real default where one exists, which turns an assertion into a value.

A lint rule (@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion, §17.18) that requires a comment on every ! is a good middle position: it does not ban the operator, but it makes each use a decision that someone wrote down.

2.16 bigint and symbol

Two primitives are rarely written, and worth knowing precisely for when they are.

The bigint type is an integer of any size, written with an n suffix. It exists because number is a double and loses precision for integers above 2⁵³.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const big = 9007199254740993n;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof big, 9007199254740993n>>;   // a bigint literal type

console.log(big.toString(), Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2);

function alsoATypeError(): bigint {
  // @ts-expect-error Operator '+' cannot be applied to types 'bigint' and 'number'.
  return big + 1;
}
console.log(typeof alsoATypeError);

9007199254740993 true
function

The second value printed is why bigint exists: at that size, two different numbers compare equal. TypeScript refuses to mix bigint and number in arithmetic, which mirrors JavaScript's own TypeError, so this is one of the few places where the type error and the runtime error agree exactly.

The symbol type is a unique key. TypeScript adds a refinement that JavaScript does not have:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const key = Symbol('cache');       // `const` + Symbol() => the type is `unique symbol`
let notUnique = Symbol('cache');   // `let` => just `symbol`
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof notUnique, symbol>>;

const store = { [key]: 1 };
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof store, { [key]: number }>>;

console.log(store[key], key.description, key === Symbol('cache'));

1 cache false

unique symbol is a type with exactly one value, the way 'debug' is.
