It can only be produced by a const declaration initialised with Symbol() or Symbol.for(), and it is what allows a symbol to be used as a property key in the type layer. That is the machinery behind branded types (§8.11) and behind Symbol.iterator in the standard library's own declarations.

Symbol.iterator, Symbol.asyncIterator and the other well-known symbols are all typed as unique symbol in lib.es2015.symbol.wellknown.d.ts, which is why { [Symbol.iterator]() { … } } makes an object structurally iterable.

To have in hand before moving on: the bigint type and the symbol type.

What This Section Established

The primitives are lower-case, (string | number)[] needs its parentheses, and a parameter annotation is the only mandatory one. any stops checking and unknown postpones it. Contextual typing gives an anonymous function its parameter types, function expressions included (contrary to the usual claim), and it is the position, not the syntax, that decides.

Unions describe real data, and you may only use what every member has, which is why narrowing exists. An alias names any type and cannot merge. An interface names an object shape, can extends, can merge, and is measurably cheaper than the equivalent intersection at scale.

Assertions are erased, guarded only by whether the types are related, and belong at boundaries. Widening throws literal types away wherever the value could change, as const turns that off, and strictNullChecks plus ?. and ?? is where most everyday safety comes from. ! is an assertion in one character, and the example above prints undefined from a variable the checker believed was a number.

Exercises

1. Fix five annotations. Each of these is legal and wrong in a different way. Explain the defect and give the better version: const port: Number = 8080; let ids: string | number[] = []; const level: string = 'warn' where level is passed to something wanting 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn'; function handler(e) { return e.type } inside a .map; const el = document.querySelector('.x') as HTMLInputElement.

2. Widening, three ways. Write one object literal that fails to satisfy a function expecting a literal-union parameter, then fix it three ways — with an assertion, with an annotation, and with as const — and say precisely what each fix does and does not check. Prove the difference with a fourth case where the assertion silently accepts a wrong value and the other two do not.

3. An alias-versus-interface decision table. For each of these, choose alias or interface and justify it in one sentence: a union of three string literals; a shape a plugin author must be able to add fields to; a function type used as a callback parameter; a generic Result<T, E>; the props of a component in a published library; a mapped type deriving a form model from an entity.

Solution

1. Five annotations.

// (a) `Number` is the wrapper object type, not the primitive.
const portWrong: Number = 8080;
// @ts-expect-error a Number is not assignable to a number parameter
const asPrimitive: number = portWrong;
const port = 8080;                       // better: infer, or annotate `number`

// (b) `string | number[]` is "a string OR an array of numbers".
declare let idsWrong: string | number[];
// @ts-expect-error 'push' does not exist on type 'string | number[]'
idsWrong.push(1);
let ids: (string | number)[] = [];       // better: parenthesise
ids.push(1, 'a');

// (c) Annotating `string` throws the literal type away.
type Level = 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn';
declare function log(level: Level): void;
const levelWrong: string = 'warn';
// @ts-expect-error 'string' is not assignable to 'Level'
log(levelWrong);
const level: Level = 'warn';             // better: annotate the union, or omit it entirely
log(level);

console.log(port, ids, level);

8080 [ 1, 'a' ] warn

Note that idsWrong is declared without a starting value. Writing let idsWrong: string | number[] = [] would narrow it by assignment (§3.7) to number[] on the spot, and .push(1) would then be perfectly legal. The declared type is still the union, but the checker knows what is in there right now. That is worth remembering as a diagnostic: a union that seems not to cause the error you expected has often been narrowed by its own starting value.

(d) function handler(e) { return e.type } taken out of a .map. Written inline as an argument it gets its types from context and is fine. Assigned to a variable first, it loses that context and e is an implicit any (TS7006). The better version gives the variable a function type, const handler: (e: Event) => string = (e) => e.type, so the annotation is written once and the parameter is typed from it (§2.5).

(e) document.querySelector('.x') as HTMLInputElement. There are two problems in one line. The assertion throws away the | null that querySelector correctly returns, so a missing element becomes a crash at runtime instead of a check. And it claims the element type with no evidence. The better version checks both: const el = document.querySelector('.x'); if (el instanceof HTMLInputElement) { … }, one check that establishes both facts, verified instead of claimed.

2. Widening, three ways.

type Method = 'GET' | 'POST';
function request(url: string, method: Method): string { return `${method} ${url}`; }

const opts = { url: '/api', method: 'POST' };
// @ts-expect-error 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Method'
const broken = request(opts.url, opts.method);

// Fix 1 — assertion: changes the type, checks nothing about the value.
console.log(request(opts.url, opts.method as Method));

// Fix 2 — annotation: checks the literal against the union at the declaration.
const annotated: { url: string; method: Method } = { url: '/api', method: 'POST' };
console.log(request(annotated.url, annotated.method));

// Fix 3 — const assertion: keeps the literal type, and makes it readonly.
const frozen = { url: '/api', method: 'POST' } as const;
console.log(request(frozen.url, frozen.method));

// The fourth case: a wrong value.
const wrong = { url: '/api', method: 'PATCH' };
console.log(request(wrong.url, wrong.method as Method));   // accepted — and wrong

// @ts-expect-error 'PATCH' is not assignable to type 'Method'
const wrongAnnotated: { method: Method } = { method: 'PATCH' };
// @ts-expect-error 'PATCH' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Method'
const wrongConst = request(wrong.url, ({ method: 'PATCH' } as const).method);

POST /api
POST /api
POST /api
PATCH /api

The assertion is the only fix that does not check the value. wrong.method as Method compiles with 'PATCH' in it, and the request goes out with a method the server will reject, which is exactly the failure the union was written to prevent.

The annotation and the const assertion both catch it, for different reasons. The annotation checks the object literal against { method: Method } at the declaration, so 'PATCH' fails there. The const assertion keeps the type as the literal 'PATCH', so the failure happens at the call, where 'PATCH' is not assignable to Method.

Prefer as const when the object is data, and the annotation when it is a contract. as const also gives you readonly and keeps every other literal in the object for later use (§8.1), while the annotation gives you a name to reuse. satisfies (§8.10) gives you both, and is the right answer when you want the check and the precise type.

3. Alias versus interface.

Type Choice Why
A union of three string literals alias An interface cannot be a union at all.
A shape a plugin author must extend interface Declaration merging and extends are the extension mechanism (§12.6).
A callback's function type alias Reads better, and gives the parameters contextual types (§2.5); an interface with a call signature works but is unidiomatic.
A generic Result<T, E> alias It is a union of a success and a failure variant.
Props of a component in a published library interface Consumers may need to augment it, and the error messages name it rather than expanding it.
A mapped type deriving a form model alias A mapped type is not expressible as an interface.

Four of the six are forced, which is the useful observation: the alias-versus-interface debate is only alive for a plain object shape that nobody needs to extend, and there the answer is "be consistent". The two rows that really needed judging both went to interface for the same reason: someone outside your codebase might need to extend the type, and merging is the only mechanism that lets them.

The tiebreaker when it really is a coin flip is error messages. An interface's name survives into the error text, while a large alias is often expanded inline, which produces the page-long messages of §17.1. That is a small effect for a two-field shape and a large one for a twenty-field entity used across a hundred files.

SECTION 3

Narrowing and Control Flow

§2.7 left a promise unpaid. A union type describes real data honestly, but then you may only use what every member of the union has in common, which would make unions nearly useless if that were the end of the story. It is not. Narrowing is how TypeScript turns a union back into one specific type inside a branch of your code, and it is what makes TypeScript feel like it understands your program instead of just checking it.

Narrowing works because TypeScript reads the same checks JavaScript programmers already write: typeof x === 'string', if (value), 'kind' in obj, x instanceof Error, x === null. None of these is TypeScript syntax. They are checks you would have written anyway, and the compiler follows them. That is the design choice that makes the language pleasant: the type system grows out of the habits you already have.

This section covers every form of narrowing. Then it shows three ways to teach the compiler about checks it cannot see through by itself (type predicates, assertion functions and discriminated unions, which are groups of shapes sharing one label field). Then comes the payoff, exhaustiveness checking, which turns "I added a new case" into a compile error everywhere that case matters. It ends with the two situations where narrowing is lost. Both were measured rather than remembered, because the widely repeated version of one of them is wrong.

3.1 Type Narrowing and Control Flow Analysis

Type narrowing is the compiler making a variable's type more specific inside a region of code, because a test had to succeed for the code to get there. Control flow analysis is how it does that: the checker follows every path through a function and keeps track of what is known about each variable at each point.

function describe(value: string | number | null): string {
  // Here: string | number | null
  if (value === null) return 'nothing';
  // Here: string | number — the null branch returned
  if (typeof value === 'number') return value.toFixed(2);
  // Here: string — the number branch returned
  return value.toUpperCase();
}

console.log(describe(null), describe(3.14159), describe('quiet'));

nothing 3.14 QUIET

Read the three comments as the point of the whole section: the type of value is different on each line, and nothing was annotated or asserted to make that happen. The checker knows that a return ends a path, so the code after the first if can only run when the test failed.

Control flow analysis handles every control structure, not just if: return, throw, continue, break, &&, ||, ?:, switch, and the body of a loop versus its exit. It also narrows in the false branch, which is what makes early returns so effective: each one removes a member of the union from everything that follows.

Two properties worth fixing early.

Narrowing applies to a variable or property, not to a type. value is narrowed, but string | number | null is not. Two variables with the same union narrow independently, and narrowing a tells the checker nothing about b.

A narrowing is cancelled by anything that could change what it refers to. An assignment narrows again from the new value (§3.7). A function call can cancel the narrowing of a property, and §3.16 measures exactly when.

The rest of this section is a catalogue of what counts as a test. Every one of them is ordinary JavaScript.

3.2 A typeof Type Guard

A typeof type guard is the most direct form: typeof x === 'string' narrows x to string.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function size(v: string | number[] | (() => number)): number {
  if (typeof v === 'string') return v.length;
  if (typeof v === 'function') return v();
  return v.length;
}

console.log(size('hello'), size([1, 2, 3]), size(() => 42));

5 3 42

The strings typeof can produce are a fixed set: 'string', 'number', 'bigint', 'boolean', 'symbol', 'undefined', 'object' and 'function'. The checker knows all eight, so a typo in the string is a compile error instead of a branch that never runs.

The trap is typeof null === 'object', a bug JavaScript has had since 1995 and can never fix. A typeof guard for 'object' therefore does not exclude null:

function len(v: string[] | null): number {
  if (typeof v === 'object') {
    // @ts-expect-error 'v' is possibly 'null'.
    return v.length;
  }
  return 0;
}

function lenFixed(v: string[] | null): number {
  return v !== null ? v.length : 0;
}

console.log(lenFixed(['a', 'b']), lenFixed(null), typeof null);

2 0 object

The checker is right and typeof is misleading, which shows the type system modelling how JavaScript really behaves and not an idealised version. To ask "is this a non-null object?", test v !== null first, or use a truthiness check (§3.3) when falsy values are acceptable.

typeof also cannot tell object shapes apart: every array, every class instance and every plain object is 'object'. To tell those apart you need instanceof (§3.6), in (§3.5) or a discriminant (§3.12).

3.3 Truthiness Narrowing

Truthiness narrowing is what a bare if (value) does. The true branch removes every type that can only be falsy, and the false branch removes types that can never be falsy.

function greet(name: string | null | undefined): string {
  if (!name) return 'Hello, stranger';
  return `Hello, ${name.toUpperCase()}`;   // string here
}

function count(items: number[] | undefined): number {
  if (items && items.length > 0) return items.length;   // && narrows too
  return 0;
}

console.log(greet(null), greet(''), greet('Ada'), count(undefined), count([1, 2]));

Hello, stranger Hello, stranger Hello, ADA 0 2

Notice the second call: greet('') took the "stranger" branch, because the empty string is falsy. That is truthiness narrowing behaving exactly as JavaScript does, and it is the reason to be careful with it.

The hazard is that truthiness treats "absent", "empty" and "zero" as the same thing. A number | undefined narrowed with if (n) also throws away 0, which is almost never what you meant:

function retryDelay(configured: number | undefined): string {
  const wrong = configured ? `${configured}ms` : 'default';   // 0 becomes 'default'
  const right = configured !== undefined ? `${configured}ms` : 'default';
  return `${wrong} / ${right}`;
}

console.log(retryDelay(0), retryDelay(500), retryDelay(undefined));

default / 0ms 500ms / 500ms default / default

retryDelay(0) is the whole argument: "retry immediately" turned into "use the default". The rule that avoids this is to narrow against the specific value you mean (!== undefined, !== null, or != null for both), and to use truthiness only when every falsy value should really take the same branch.

?? (§2.14) is the same distinction applied to values, and it is why configured ?? 500 is correct where configured || 500 is not.

3.4 Equality Narrowing

Equality narrowing uses ===, !==, == and !=, and it narrows both sides of the comparison.

function compare(a: string | number, b: string | boolean): string {
  if (a === b) {
    // Both are narrowed to the only type they can share: string.
    return a.toUpperCase() + b.toLowerCase();
  }
  return 'different';
}

console.log(compare('Hi', 'Hi'), compare(1, true));

HIhi different

Inside the if, a is string and b is string, because the only way a === b can be true is if both are strings, and the checker works out that overlap for you. That is genuinely clever, and it is why comparing two unions is worth doing when it expresses what you mean.

The loose operators are narrowed correctly too, including the special case for null and undefined. x != null excludes both null and undefined, and the checker knows it:

function trim(v: string | null | undefined): string {
  if (v != null) return v.trim();     // both null and undefined excluded
  return '';
}

console.log(`[${trim(null)}]`, `[${trim(undefined)}]`, `[${trim('  x  ')}]`);

[] [] [x]

!= null is the one place where a loose comparison is normal in TypeScript, and it is checked, not just tolerated: the checker models JavaScript's loose equality precisely enough to know that null == undefined and that nothing else is loosely equal to either.

Comparing against a literal narrows a union of literals. This is the mechanism behind discriminated unions (§3.12): if (s.kind === 'circle') narrows s itself, not just s.kind. It is a special rule for a discriminant property, and the reason such unions work so well.

3.5 The in Operator

The in operator narrowing tests whether a property exists, and narrows a union to the members that declare it.

type Fish = { swim(): string };
type Bird = { fly(): string };
type Human = { swim?(): string; walk(): string };

function move(animal: Fish | Bird): string {
  if ('swim' in animal) return animal.swim();
  return animal.fly();
}

console.log(move({ swim: () => 'swimming' }), move({ fly: () => 'flying' }));

swimming flying

This is the guard to reach for when the members of the union share no label field and are not classes, which describes most types that come from a JSON API.

An optional property puts its type in both branches. That is correct, and it surprises people:

type Fish = { swim(): string };
type Human = { swim?(): string; walk(): string };

function describe(x: Fish | Human): string {
  if ('swim' in x) {
    // x is Fish | Human here — Human MIGHT have `swim`
    return x.swim?.() ?? 'a human who cannot swim';
  }
  // and here x is Human, since Fish must have `swim`
  return x.walk();
}

console.log(describe({ swim: () => 'fish swimming' }), describe({ walk: () => 'walking' }));

fish swimming walking

The reason is that 'swim' in x being true does not rule out Human, because Human's swim is optional and might be there. The checker is being exact. A guard that narrowed to Fish here would be unsafe.

in also narrows the negative branch, removing every member that requires the property. That is often the more useful half, and it is why putting the check for the required property first tends to produce cleaner code.

One limitation: in is a runtime check that also looks along the prototype chain, not just the object's own properties, so it is true for an inherited method. If you need to check own properties only, Object.hasOwn(x, 'swim') is the right call, but it does not narrow, because its signature has no type predicate. Wrapping it in your own predicate (§3.9) is the fix.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: the in operator narrowing.

3.6 instanceof Narrowing

instanceof narrowing works on anything that has a prototype: classes, and the built-in constructors.

class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(public status: number, message: string) { super(message); }
}

function report(e: unknown): string {
  if (e instanceof HttpError) return `HTTP ${e.status}: ${e.message}`;
  if (e instanceof Error) return `${e.name}: ${e.message}`;
  return `unknown: ${String(e)}`;
}

console.log(report(new HttpError(404, 'not found')));
console.log(report(new TypeError('bad')));
console.log(report('a string'));

HTTP 404: not found
TypeError: bad
unknown: a string

Order matters, and the subclass must come first. HttpError is an Error, so testing e instanceof Error first would catch it too. The compiler will not report that bug, because both branches type-check. Check this every time you see a chain of instanceof.

This is the main narrowing tool for catch (§10.20), where the caught value is unknown under useUnknownInCatchVariables and instanceof Error is the honest first question.

Two limits are worth knowing before you rely on it.

It fails across realms. An Error created in an iframe, a worker or a different Node context is not an instanceof your own realm's Error, because the constructors are different objects. Library code that has to work across realms tests a brand or a Symbol.toStringTag instead.

It cannot be used with a type that has no constructor. An interface, a type alias or a plain object shape does not exist at runtime (§1.2), so x instanceof MyInterface is not just unsupported, it does not mean anything. That is the wall people hit first, and the three ways past it are in (§3.5), a discriminant (§3.12) and a type predicate (§3.9).

3.7 Narrowing by Assignment

Narrowing by assignment means the checker narrows a variable again from whatever you just assigned to it. It applies to let variables and to parameters.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

let value: string | number = 'hello';
// Right here, `value` is string — narrowed by the initialiser.
console.log(value.toUpperCase());

value = 42;
// And now it is number.
console.log(value.toFixed(1));

function neverCalled(): string {
  // @ts-expect-error 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'number'
  return value.toUpperCase();
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

HELLO
42.0
function

The rule is that the declared type stays the same, and the narrowed type follows the assignments. value is always declared string | number, so assigning either is legal. What changes is what you may do with it at each point.

Two consequences that are easy to get wrong.

A declaration with no starting value begins at its declared type, and under strictNullChecks a let x: string that is used before it is assigned is caught by definite-assignment analysis, not by narrowing.

Assigning a value outside the declared type is still an error. Narrowing never widens what is allowed: value = true above is rejected whatever value currently holds.

The case that catches people is loops. A variable narrowed before a loop is widened again inside it if the loop body assigns to it, because the checker has to allow for the second pass seeing the assigned value. That is correct and occasionally annoying, and the usual fix is to narrow inside the loop body instead of outside it.

3.8 Narrowing an Optional Chain

Narrowing an optional chain is the everyday way to check a nested value. a?.b gives undefined when a is null or undefined, so testing the result narrows a as well as a.b.

type User = { profile?: { name?: string; age: number } };

function label(u: User): string {
  if (u.profile?.name) {
    // Both `u.profile` and `u.profile.name` are narrowed here.
    return u.profile.name.toUpperCase() + ` (${u.profile.age})`;
  }
  return 'anonymous';
}

console.log(label({ profile: { name: 'ada', age: 36 } }), label({}), label({ profile: { age: 1 } }));

ADA (36) anonymous anonymous

The checker carried the guard through two levels: inside the if, u.profile is known to be there and u.profile.name is known to be a non-empty string. That is control flow analysis following the meaning of the optional chain, and it is why the chained form reads better than two nested ifs.

The ! at the end of a chain is a different operator, and a worse idea. u.profile!.name asserts instead of checking (§2.15), while u.profile?.name produces undefined and lets you handle it.

A chain narrows only the exact expression you wrote. u.profile?.name narrows u.profile, not a local copy of it, and not getUser().profile. A chain that starts with a function call narrows nothing at all, because the checker cannot know that a second call returns the same object:

type User = { profile?: { name: string } };
const store = { current: { profile: { name: 'ada' } } as User };
function getUser(): User { return store.current; }

function broken(): string {
  if (getUser().profile) {
    // @ts-expect-error 'Object is possibly 'undefined'' — a second call could differ
    return getUser().profile.name;
  }
  return '';
}

function fixed(): string {
  const u = getUser();                 // one call, one reference to narrow
  return u.profile ? u.profile.name : '';
}

console.log(fixed(), typeof broken);

ada function

Save the result of the call in a const first. That one habit fixes the whole family of "object is possibly undefined" errors on expressions you can see you have just checked.

3.9 A Type Predicate and a User-Defined Type Guard

When a check is too complicated for the built-in forms, you can teach the checker about it. A user-defined type guard is a function that returns boolean, with a return type written as a type predicate: param is Type.

type Fish = { kind: string; swim(): string };
type Bird = { kind: string; fly(): string };

function isFish(animal: Fish | Bird): animal is Fish {
  return typeof (animal as Fish).swim === 'function';
}

function move(animals: (Fish | Bird)[]): string[] {
  return animals.map((a) => (isFish(a) ? a.swim() : a.fly()));
}

console.log(move([
  { kind: 'trout', swim: () => 'swim' },
  { kind: 'robin', fly: () => 'fly' },
]));

[ 'swim', 'fly' ]

A type predicate is a promise the compiler does not check. isFish could return true every time and the compiler would believe it. The only thing verified is that Fish is a possible narrowing of the parameter's declared type. That makes a type predicate an assertion in disguise, so treat it with the same care as as (§2.11): the body must really establish the claim, and it belongs in one reviewed place instead of being scattered around.

The two places a user-defined type guard earns its keep:

Filtering. arr.filter(isFish) gives Fish[], which a plain boolean function cannot do. §3.10 shows that the simplest case is now automatic.

A check with no built-in form. Validating a parsed JSON shape, testing a branded type (§8.11), or checking a property whose presence in cannot express are all cases where the check is real code, and the predicate is how its conclusion reaches the type layer.

Write the body carefully, because nothing else will check it. typeof (animal as Fish).swim === 'function' is the honest check. return 'swim' in animal would also work here. return true would compile and lie. A predicate whose body is a single as and no test is a bug waiting for its data.

For a generic guard, arg is T works with a type parameter: function isArrayOf<T>(v: unknown, check: (x: unknown) => x is T): v is T[]. That is the composable form worth writing once per codebase.

3.10 An Inferred Type Predicate

Since TypeScript 5.5 the compiler will work out a type predicate by itself for a function whose body is a single return of a narrowing expression. An inferred type predicate removes the most common reason to write one by hand.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const mixed = [1, null, 3];

// No predicate written anywhere — and the result is number[], not (number | null)[].
const numbers = mixed.filter((x) => x !== null);
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof numbers, number[]>>;

console.log(numbers, numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0));

[ 1, 3 ] 4

Before this existed, that filter produced (number | null)[], and every codebase had a notNull helper with a hand-written predicate or, worse, an assertion at the call. Now the inference covers it.

The conditions are specific, and knowing them tells you when to write the predicate yourself. The compiler infers x is T when the function has no explicit return type, has exactly one return statement, does not assign to its parameter, and returns an expression that narrows the parameter.

Add an if/else, an intermediate variable that gets reassigned, or an explicit : boolean return type, and the inference switches off, silently, because returning boolean is a perfectly legal thing for a function to do.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const mixed = [1, null, 3];

// An explicit `: boolean` turns the inference off.
const stillMixed = mixed.filter((x): boolean => x !== null);
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof stillMixed, (number | null)[]>>;

// And an explicit predicate turns it back on, precisely.
const numbers = mixed.filter((x): x is number => x !== null);
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof numbers, number[]>>;

console.log(stillMixed.length, numbers.length);

2 2

The practical rule: do not annotate the return type of a small predicate. It is the one place where an annotation does harm, because it replaces the precise inferred predicate with a plain boolean, and the symptom shows up at the call, not at the function.

3.11 An Assertion Function

An assertion function narrows by throwing instead of returning. Its return type is asserts x is T, and the checker treats everything after a successful call as narrowed.

function assertIsString(v: unknown): asserts v is string {
  if (typeof v !== 'string') throw new TypeError(`expected a string, got ${typeof v}`);
}

function assertDefined<T>(v: T, what: string): asserts v is NonNullable<T> {
  if (v == null) throw new Error(`${what} is missing`);
}

function shout(v: unknown): string {
  assertIsString(v);
  return v.toUpperCase();        // `v` is string from here to the end of the scope
}

console.log(shout('hello'));
try { shout(42); } catch (e) { console.log((e as Error).message); }

HELLO
expected a string, got number

The difference from a type predicate is scope. A predicate narrows inside the branch that tested it. An assertion function narrows everything after the call, because execution only continues if the assertion held. That makes assertion functions a natural fit for preconditions at the top of a function.

There is one rule that will catch you, and its error message is hard to read:

const assertString = function (v: unknown): asserts v is string {
  if (typeof v !== 'string') throw new TypeError('nope');
};

function use(v: unknown): number {
  // @ts-expect-error Assertions require every name in the call target to be declared with an explicit type annotation.
  assertString(v);
  return (v as string).length;
}

// The fix: annotate the binding, not just the function's return type.
type StringAssert = (v: unknown) => asserts v is string;
const assertString2: StringAssert = (v) => {
  if (typeof v !== 'string') throw new TypeError('nope');
};

function useFixed(v: unknown): number {
  assertString2(v);
  return v.length;
}

console.log(useFixed('abcd'), typeof use);

4 function

TS2775, "Assertions require every name in the call target to be declared with an explicit type annotation", appears whenever the thing you call is a const whose type was inferred. A function declaration is fine. A const holding a function expression needs its own type annotation. The reason is that the assertion changes how the checker follows control flow, so the checker wants the fact that it is an assertion to be visible in the declaration and not worked out from a body it may not have read yet.

Node's own assert module is typed this way, which is why assert(x) narrows x. That is worth knowing, because it means an existing assertion library often gives you narrowing for free.

3.12 A Discriminated Union and Its Discriminant Property

A discriminated union is a union of object types that all share one property, and in each member that property has a different literal type. A discriminant property is that shared property, and it is what lets the union narrow with a single comparison.

type Shape =
  | { kind: 'circle'; radius: number }
  | { kind: 'rectangle'; width: number; height: number }
  | { kind: 'triangle'; base: number; height: number };

function area(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s.kind) {
    case 'circle': return Math.PI * s.radius ** 2;
    case 'rectangle': return s.width * s.height;
    case 'triangle': return (s.base * s.height) / 2;
  }
}

console.log(
  area({ kind: 'rectangle', width: 3, height: 4 }),
  area({ kind: 'triangle', base: 6, height: 4 }),
  area({ kind: 'circle', radius: 1 }).toFixed(4),
);

12 12 3.1416

Inside each case, s is one specific member, so s.radius is available in the first case and a compile error in the others. The compiler did all that from one switch on one property.

Three requirements make a union discriminated, and getting any of them wrong turns it into an ordinary union that will not narrow.

The property must exist on every member. A member missing kind breaks the whole mechanism.

Its type must be a literal type in each member, 'circle' and not string. This is where widening (§2.12) bites: { kind: 'circle', radius: 1 } stored in a variable with no type from context has kind: string, and the union stops working. Annotate the variable, or use as const.

The literals must be different from each other. Two members with kind: 'circle' both match.

The discriminant does not have to be a string. A boolean works, and it is the standard shape for a result type, { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }. A numeric literal works too, and so does null versus an object on a shared field. What matters is that the checker can tell the members apart by comparing one value.

A discriminated union is the single most valuable modelling tool in the language, because it makes illegal states unrepresentable. { loading: boolean; data?: T; error?: E } allows eight combinations, of which only three make sense. The three-member discriminated union allows exactly those three. Everything §3.14 does depends on having modelled the data this way.

3.13 Narrowing a Constant Indexed Access

A discriminant does not have to be a named property. Narrowing a constant indexed access means the checker narrows through obj[k] and tuple[0] when the index is a literal.

type RpcResult =
  | ['ok', { rows: number }]
  | ['error', { message: string }];

function handle(r: RpcResult): string {
  if (r[0] === 'ok') return `${r[1].rows} rows`;   // r[1] is narrowed by testing r[0]
  return `failed: ${r[1].message}`;
}

console.log(handle(['ok', { rows: 3 }]), handle(['error', { message: 'timeout' }]));

3 rows failed: timeout

That is a discriminated tuple, and it is the shape used by Node's callback convention and by many RPC protocols. Testing element 0 narrows element 1, which is the same rule as for a named discriminant property, applied to a numeric index.

The same works for an object indexed by a literal key, including a key stored in a const:

type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; r: number } | { kind: 'rect'; w: number };

const KEY = 'kind';                       // a const, so its type is the literal 'kind'

function area(s: Shape): number {
  if (s[KEY] === 'circle') return Math.PI * s.r ** 2;
  return s.w;
}

console.log(area({ kind: 'rect', w: 5 }), area({ kind: 'circle', r: 2 }).toFixed(2));

5 12.57

const KEY = 'kind' is what makes this work. Its type is the literal 'kind' (§2.12), so s[KEY] is an indexed access with a literal index, and narrowing applies. Declare it with let and the type widens to string, so the index is no longer constant, and the narrowing stops silently.

That "silently" is the reason this subsection exists. Nothing warns you. You just get an error on s.r that looks like the discriminated union stopped working. The check is always the same: is the index a literal type?

3.14 Exhaustiveness Checking and never in a Default Branch

Exhaustiveness checking is the payoff for modelling with a discriminated union: the compiler tells you when you have missed a case. The mechanism is the never type in a default branch.

type Shape =
  | { kind: 'circle'; radius: number }
  | { kind: 'rectangle'; width: number; height: number };

function area(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s.kind) {
    case 'circle': return Math.PI * s.radius ** 2;
    case 'rectangle': return s.width * s.height;
    default: {
      const exhaustive: never = s;              // every case handled => `s` is never
      throw new Error(`unhandled shape: ${JSON.stringify(exhaustive)}`);
    }
  }
}

console.log(area({ kind: 'rectangle', width: 2, height: 5 }));

10

Now add a member and watch what happens:

type Shape =
  | { kind: 'circle'; radius: number }
  | { kind: 'rectangle'; width: number; height: number }
  | { kind: 'triangle'; base: number; height: number };

function area(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s.kind) {
    case 'circle': return Math.PI * s.radius ** 2;
    case 'rectangle': return s.width * s.height;
    default: {
      // @ts-expect-error Type '{ kind: "triangle"; base: number; height: number; }' is not assignable to type 'never'.
      const exhaustive: never = s;
      throw new Error('unhandled');
    }
  }
}

console.log(area({ kind: 'circle', radius: 1 }).toFixed(2));

3.14

The error names the missing case exactly, { kind: "triangle"; … }, which is why this pattern is worth the four lines it costs. Adding a member to a union in one file produces a compile error at every switch that does not handle it, in every file, with the missing member printed. That is refactoring guided by compiler errors, and it is the strongest argument for discriminated unions over a bag of optional fields.

Two details make it work reliably.

The never assignment must be in a default branch, not after the switch. After the switch, control flow analysis has already merged the paths, and s is the full union again.

Throw instead of returning silently. The never check is a compile-time guarantee that assumes the input matches its declared type. Data arriving from outside the program can still carry an unknown kind (§1.11), and the throw is what turns that into a clear runtime failure instead of undefined.

A helper is worth having: function assertNever(x: never): never { throw new Error(\unexpected: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`); }, called asdefault: return assertNever(s);`. It is the same check in one line, and it reads better.

In summary, the vocabulary here is the never type in a default branch.

3.15 An Aliased Condition

Since TypeScript 4.4 the checker follows a condition that is stored in a const. An aliased condition means you can give a test a name and still get the narrowing.

type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number } | { kind: 'rect'; width: number };

function area(s: Shape): number {
  const isCircle = s.kind === 'circle';     // a named condition
  if (isCircle) return Math.PI * s.radius ** 2;   // and `s` is narrowed by it
  return s.width;
}

function normalise(input: string | null | undefined): string {
  const hasValue = input != null && input.length > 0;
  if (!hasValue) return '';
  return input.trim();                      // narrowed through the alias, two tests deep
}

console.log(area({ kind: 'rect', width: 4 }), `[${normalise(null)}]`, normalise(' hi '));

4 [] hi

Before this existed, moving a condition into a well-named variable cost you the narrowing, so readable code and narrowed code pulled in opposite directions. That is resolved: name the condition, and the narrowing follows.

The requirement is that the alias is a const and that the tested variable is never reassigned. A let holding the condition is not tracked, because the checker cannot know that its value still reflects the test. This is the same rule as everywhere else in the section: narrowing survives exactly as long as the checker can prove that nothing changed.

There is a second requirement that is easy to miss, and worth measuring, because the feature is usually described more generously than it behaves: an aliased condition narrows a variable, not a property.

type Input = { value?: string | null };

function viaVariable(v: string | null | undefined): string {
  const hasValue = v != null;
  if (!hasValue) return '';
  return v.trim();                          // ✅ the variable is narrowed
}

function viaProperty(i: Input): string {
  const hasValue = i.value != null;
  if (!hasValue) return '';
  // @ts-expect-error 'i.value' is possibly 'null' or 'undefined'.
  return i.value.trim();
}

console.log(viaVariable(' x '), typeof viaProperty);

x function

Both functions test the same thing, and only one narrows. The first example in this subsection is not a counter-example: const isCircle = s.kind === 'circle' narrows s, the variable, by its discriminant. It does not narrow s.kind as a property in its own right. When the thing you need narrowed is a property, put it in a const first, which is the same fix as in §3.16.

The practical use is guard clauses. const isAdmin = user.role === 'admin' && user.active; followed by if (!isAdmin) throw … reads better than the inline version and narrows the same way, which means the readable version is now also the one that type-checks.

Note that an aliased condition is not the same as an inferred type predicate (§3.10). The alias holds a boolean whose origin the checker remembers within one function. A predicate is a function signature that carries the narrowing across a function call. If you move the condition into a function, you need the predicate.

3.16 Narrowing That Is Lost Across a Closure

Two situations lose narrowing, and the difference between them is precise. It is worth measuring instead of trusting the usual summary, because "narrowing is lost inside callbacks" is only half true.

function keepsIt(v: string | undefined): string {
  if (v === undefined) return '';
  const f = () => v.toUpperCase();     // ✅ narrowing survives: `v` is never assigned
  return f();
}

function alsoKeepsIt(v: string | undefined): string {
  let w = v;
  if (w === undefined) return '';
  const g = () => w.toUpperCase();     // ✅ still fine: `w` is not assigned after this
  return g();
}

console.log(keepsIt('a'), alsoKeepsIt('b'));

A B

function losesIt(v: string | undefined): string {
  let w = v;
  if (w === undefined) return '';
  const f = () => {
    // @ts-expect-error 'w' is possibly 'undefined'.
    return w.toUpperCase();
  };
  w = v;                               // THIS is what invalidated the narrowing above
  return f();
}

type Box = { v?: string };
function alsoLosesIt(b: Box): string[] {
  if (b.v === undefined) return [];
  return [1].map(() => {
    // @ts-expect-error 'b.v' is possibly 'undefined'.
    return b.v.toUpperCase();
  });
}

console.log(typeof losesIt, typeof alsoLosesIt);

function function

Read those four functions together, because the rule is exact.

A variable captured by a function keeps its narrowing unless it is assigned somewhere in the enclosing function. keepsIt and alsoKeepsIt both work, while losesIt fails because of the w = v two lines below the closure. The checker cannot know when the closure will run, so any assignment anywhere in the function cancels the narrowing inside it. The fix is a const: copy the narrowed value into one, and it can never be cancelled.

A narrowed property is always lost inside a callback. b.v in alsoLosesIt fails even though nothing assigns to it, because the checker cannot prove that the callback will not run after something else changed b. The fix is the same: write const v = b.v; after the guard, then use v.

One behaviour is worth knowing because it is the opposite of what people assume: a property narrowing survives an await.

type Box = { v?: string };

async function survivesAwait(b: Box): Promise<string> {
  if (b.v === undefined) return '';
  await Promise.resolve();
  return b.v.toUpperCase();            // ✅ still narrowed after the await
}

console.log(await survivesAwait({ v: 'ok' }));
export {};

OK

That is genuinely unsafe, since another task could have changed b during the await, and it is a deliberate usability trade-off of the same kind as the list in §1.12. Knowing that it is unsafe is the point: if the object is shared and can change, copy the value into a const before the await instead of trusting the narrowing.

The one habit that covers all three cases: after a guard, put the narrowed value in a const. It costs one line, and it is safe against closures, assignments and awaits alike.

What This Section Established

Narrowing is control flow analysis reading the checks you already write. There is typeof (remember that null is 'object'), truthiness (remember that 0 and '' are falsy), equality (which narrows both sides and treats != null exactly), in (which puts an optional property in both branches), and instanceof (subclass first, and useless across realms).

When those are not enough there are three extensions. A type predicate carries a narrowing across a call, and is an unchecked promise. An assertion function narrows everything after it, and needs an explicit type annotation on its binding or you get TS2775. And a discriminated union narrows through one comparison, including through a constant index, as long as the discriminant is a literal type in every member.

The payoff is exhaustiveness: const exhaustive: never = s in a default branch turns a new union member into a compile error that names the missing case. And the losses are precise: a captured variable loses its narrowing only if something assigns to it, a property always loses it inside a callback, and a property narrowing survives an await even though it should not. One const after the guard fixes all three.

Exercises

1. Narrow six values. Write one function per input that returns a string, narrowing without any assertion: string | number; string[] | null; Date | string; { a: number } | { b: number }; unknown (report the typeof); and Error | { message: string } where only the first is a real Error. For each, say which guard you used and why the others would not work.

2. Make an illegal state unrepresentable. Take type State = { loading: boolean; data?: User[]; error?: string } and list three combinations it allows that should be impossible. Rewrite it as a discriminated union, write a renderer with exhaustiveness checking, then add a fourth state and show the exact compile error that appears.

3. Find the lost narrowing. Write a function where a narrowing is silently lost, using each of the three mechanisms in §3.16: a reassigned captured variable, a property inside a callback, and an index that stopped being a literal. Fix each with the smallest change, and say what the fix relies on.

Solution

1. Six narrowings.

function a(v: string | number): string {
  return typeof v === 'string' ? v.toUpperCase() : v.toFixed(1);
}

function b(v: string[] | null): string {
  return v !== null ? v.join('|') : 'none';        // NOT `typeof v === 'object'`
}

function c(v: Date | string): string {
  return v instanceof Date ? v.toISOString().slice(0, 10) : v.trim();
}

function d(v: { a: number } | { b: number }): string {
  return 'a' in v ? `a=${v.a}` : `b=${v.b}`;
}

function e(v: unknown): string {
  return typeof v;
}

function f(v: Error | { message: string }): string {
  return v instanceof Error ? `${v.name}: ${v.message}` : `plain: ${v.message}`;
}

console.log(a(3.14159), b(null), c(new Date('2026-09-01T00:00:00Z')), d({ b: 2 }), e([]), f(new RangeError('x')));

3.1 none 2026-09-01 b=2 object RangeError: x

(b) is the one with a trap. typeof v === 'object' is true for null, so it does not narrow away the null — §3.2's measured point. v !== null is the check that works.

(c) and (f) both need instanceof, because Date and Error are classes with real prototypes, and no structural property reliably tells them apart. A { message: string } from a JSON payload has a message exactly as an Error does, so in would match both.

(d) needs in, because neither member is a class and neither has a discriminant. This is the shape that in exists for.

(e) is the reminder that unknown allows nothing until you narrow it. typeof v is legal on unknown because it is legal on every value, but v.length would not be.

2. Illegal states.

type User = { id: number };

// The old shape permits, among others:
//   { loading: true,  data: [...], error: 'x' }  — loading AND done AND failed
//   { loading: false }                            — done, with neither data nor error
//   { loading: false, data: [...], error: 'x' }   — succeeded and failed at once
type State =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'loaded'; data: User[] }
  | { status: 'failed'; error: string };

function render(s: State): string {
  switch (s.status) {
    case 'idle': return 'Nothing requested yet';
    case 'loading': return 'Loading…';
    case 'loaded': return `${s.data.length} users`;
    case 'failed': return `Error: ${s.error}`;
    default: return assertNever(s);
  }
}

function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error(`unexpected state: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`);
}

console.log(render({ status: 'loaded', data: [{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }] }), '|', render({ status: 'loading' }));

2 users | Loading…

Adding a fifth member — | { status: 'refreshing'; data: User[] } — without touching render produces exactly this at the assertNever call:

error TS2345: Argument of type '{ status: "refreshing"; data: User[]; }' is not
assignable to parameter of type 'never'.

The error names the state you forgot, in every file that switches on it. The boolean-bag version cannot do that: with { loading: boolean; … } there is no new member to be missing, so adding a "refreshing" idea means adding another boolean and finding every place by hand.

The three impossible combinations listed above all became unrepresentable, and the count is an honest measure: { loading: boolean; data?: User[]; error?: string } has 2 × 2 × 2 = eight combinations by presence, of which four are meaningful, while the union has exactly four members and every one of them is meaningful.

3. Three lost narrowings.

type Box = { v?: string };

// (a) A captured variable that is assigned later in the function.
function lostA(input: string | undefined): string {
  let w = input;
  if (w === undefined) return '';
  const f = () => {
    // @ts-expect-error 'w' is possibly 'undefined'.
    return w.toUpperCase();
  };
  w = input;
  return f();
}

function fixedA(input: string | undefined): string {
  let w = input;
  if (w === undefined) return '';
  const narrowed = w;                 // a const cannot be invalidated
  const f = () => narrowed.toUpperCase();
  w = input;
  return f();
}

// (b) A property narrowing inside a callback.
function lostB(b: Box): string[] {
  if (b.v === undefined) return [];
  return [1, 2].map(() => {
    // @ts-expect-error 'b.v' is possibly 'undefined'.
    return b.v.toUpperCase();
  });
}

function fixedB(b: Box): string[] {
  const v = b.v;
  if (v === undefined) return [];
  return [1, 2].map(() => v.toUpperCase());
}

// (c) An index that stopped being a literal type.
type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; r: number } | { kind: 'rect'; w: number };
let mutableKey = 'kind';              // widened to string
const constKey = 'kind';              // the literal type 'kind'

function lostC(s: Shape): number {
  // @ts-expect-error 'mutableKey' is not a literal, so nothing narrows
  if (s[mutableKey] === 'circle') return 1;
  return 2;
}

function fixedC(s: Shape): number {
  if (s[constKey] === 'circle') return Math.PI * s.r ** 2;
  return s.w;
}

console.log(fixedA('a'), fixedB({ v: 'b' }), fixedC({ kind: 'rect', w: 3 }), typeof lostA, typeof lostB, typeof lostC);

A [ 'B', 'B' ] 3 function function function

(a) relies on the value never changing. const narrowed = w creates a binding that nothing can assign to, so the checker's rule ("cancel on any assignment to the captured name") cannot apply. Note that the later w = input is still there: the fix does not require removing it.

(b) relies on turning a property into a local variable. The checker refuses to narrow b.v inside a callback because it cannot say when the callback runs relative to a change to b. A const v is not a property of anything, so there is nothing to change.

(c) relies on the index being a literal type. const constKey = 'kind' has the type 'kind', while let mutableKey = 'kind' has the type string. The runtime behaviour is identical and only one of them narrows, which is why the failure is confusing when you meet it and trivial once you know to check the type of the index. Hovering over the key is a ten-second diagnosis.

SECTION 4

Functions

Functions are where a type system either earns its keep or gets in the way. TypeScript gives you a lot to work with here: two ways to write the type of a function, three special return types that mean genuinely different things, overloads (several signatures for one function) whose rules surprise everyone once, and one deliberate place where the rules are looser than strictly safe.

The idea that organises the section is that a function type is a contract that points in two directions. The parameters are what the caller must provide. The return type is what the caller may rely on. Nearly every rule below follows from that: why a function that takes fewer parameters can stand in where more were expected, why a callback that returns a value is fine in a slot that says void, why never and void are different things, and why overloads are checked from the caller's point of view but written from the implementer's.

Along the way the section introduces four types that are not really about functions but appear first here because this is where they matter: void (nothing useful is returned), object (any non-primitive value), unknown (a value you know nothing about yet) and never (a value that can never exist). unknown and never are the two most useful types in the language after the basic ones, and §8 and §10 both lean on them.

4.1 A Function Type Expression

A function type expression is the arrow-shaped syntax for describing a function: (a: string) => number. It is what you write in an annotation, a type alias, or a parameter position.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Formatter = (value: number, digits: number) => string;

const fixed: Formatter = (v, d) => v.toFixed(d);           // parameters typed by context
const percent: Formatter = (v, d) => `${(v * 100).toFixed(d)}%`;

function render(value: number, format: Formatter): string { return format(value, 1); }

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Parameters<Formatter>, [value: number, digits: number]>>;
console.log(render(0.25, fixed), render(0.25, percent));

0.3 25.0%

Two things about the syntax itself.

The parameter names are part of the type, but only as documentation. (value: number) => string and (v: number) => string are the same type. The names show up in editor hints and in the labelled tuple of Parameters<T> (§9.8), and nothing checks that an implementation uses the same ones.

A parameter name is mandatory, even when it means nothing. (number) => string does not mean "takes a number". It means "takes a parameter called number, of type any", which is a common and silent mistake. Under noImplicitAny it is an error, which is one more reason that setting is not optional.

Writing the type once, as Formatter above, is what gives each implementation its parameter types from context (§2.5). That is the best argument for naming a function type instead of writing it inline: const fixed: Formatter = (v, d) => … needs no annotations at all, while an inline arrow needs two.

A function type expression cannot describe an overloaded function, a constructor, or a function that also has properties. For those you need a call signature (§4.2) or a construct signature (§4.3).

4.2 A Call Signature

A call signature is a member of an object type that says "this object can be called": { (a: string): number }. It exists for the case a function type expression cannot cover, a function that also has properties.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Counter = {
  (label: string): string;      // the call signature
  count: number;                // and a property on the same value
  reset(): void;
};

function makeCounter(): Counter {
  const fn = ((label: string) => `${label}: ${++fn.count}`) as Counter;
  fn.count = 0;
  fn.reset = () => { fn.count = 0; };
  return fn;
}

const hits = makeCounter();
console.log(hits('a'), hits('b'), hits.count);
hits.reset();
console.log(hits.count);

a: 1 b: 2 2
0

That is a real pattern, not a curiosity. jQuery, express, debug and many middleware factories are callable objects, and a call signature is the only way to describe one.

An ordinary function can only be assigned to a type with a call signature if the properties are there too, which is why the implementation above needs the assertion: the arrow does not have count until the next line. That assertion is one of the few that is truly unavoidable, and the alternative, Object.assign(fn, { count: 0, reset }), is worth knowing because it is checked instead of asserted.

Generic call signatures put the type parameter in a different place from a generic function type, and the difference matters:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type GenericFn = <T>(x: T) => T[];          // generic at CALL time
type FnOfT<T> = (x: T) => T[];              // generic type, fixed when you name it

const wrap: GenericFn = (x) => [x];
const s = wrap('a');                        // T solved per call
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof s, string[]>>;

const wrapNumbers: FnOfT<number> = (x) => [x];
type _2 = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof wrapNumbers>, number[]>>;

console.log(wrap('a'), wrapNumbers(1));

[ 'a' ] [ 1 ]

GenericFn stays generic, and each call works out T for itself. FnOfT<number> is one concrete function type. Getting these the wrong way round is the usual cause of "T is unknown here" in a callback type.

4.3 A Construct Signature

A construct signature describes something you can call with new: { new (a: string): Thing }, or new (a: string) => Thing in the standalone form.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Ctor<T> = new (...args: never[]) => T;

class Connection {
  constructor(public host: string, public port = 5432) {}
  describe(): string { return `${this.host}:${this.port}`; }
}

// A class's static side has the construct signature; the class name alone does not.
type _1 = Expect<Equal<ConstructorParameters<typeof Connection>, [host: string, port?: number]>>;

const factory: new (host: string) => Connection = Connection;
console.log(new factory('db.internal').describe());

db.internal:5432

typeof Connection is the constructor and Connection is the instance. This is the §8.1 distinction, and the reason a construct signature is always written against typeof TheClass.

A type may have both a call signature and a construct signature. That is how Date is declared: Date('x') returns a string and new Date('x') returns a Date, and the standard library declares one of each.

An abstract class needs abstract new. A plain construct signature is (correctly) not satisfied by an abstract class, since you cannot create one directly. abstract new (...args: never[]) => T is the constraint that accepts both kinds, and it is what a mixin (§6.25) or a registry of subclasses needs.

The parameter list matters more than it looks. new () => T rejects every class whose constructor takes arguments, and new (...args: any[]) => T accepts everything and checks nothing. The version that accepts every class and still checks the arguments uses a generic tuple: new (...args: A) => T with A extends readonly unknown[]. That is the shape §7.9 builds a factory from.

4.4 Generic Functions, Inference and Explicit Type Arguments

A generic function declares its type parameters before its parameter list, type argument inference works them out from the arguments, and specifying type arguments overrides that when you need to.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function firstOrNull<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | null {
  return items.length > 0 ? items[0]! : null;
}

const inferred = firstOrNull([1, 2, 3]);
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof inferred, number | null>>;

// Specifying the type argument: needed when nothing can be inferred.
const empty = firstOrNull<string>([]);
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof empty, string | null>>;

// And useful for pinning a wider type than inference would choose.
const widened = firstOrNull<number | string>([1, 2]);
type _3 = Expect<Equal<typeof widened, number | string | null>>;

console.log(inferred, empty, widened);

1 null 1

§7 covers generics in full. Three points belong here because they are about functions specifically.

Inference runs left to right through the parameter list, so a callback placed after the value it works on gets its parameter types for free. Put them the other way round and you get implicit anys.

If you specify one type argument, you must specify all of them, unless the rest have defaults. pair<string>('a', 1) is an error for pair<A, B>. You must write pair<string, number>(…) or nothing.

Partial application is not available, which makes the case "one type argument I want to give, one I want inferred" awkward. The usual workaround is a curried factory, withKind<'circle'>()( … ), where the outer call fixes the explicit parameter and the inner call infers the rest.

What to take from this subsection: type argument inference and specifying type arguments.

4.5 Optional and Default Parameters

An optional parameter is marked ? and may be left out. A default parameter type is worked out from the default value, and the parameter becomes optional automatically.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function withOptional(a: number, b?: number): number { return a + (b ?? 0); }
function withDefault(a: number, b = 10): number { return a + b; }

// Both produce the same PARAMETER type — optional, with the default inferred.
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Parameters<typeof withOptional>, [a: number, b?: number]>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Parameters<typeof withDefault>, [a: number, b?: number]>>;

console.log(withOptional(1), withOptional(1, 2), withDefault(1), withDefault(1, 2));

1 3 11 3

The difference is entirely inside the function. In withOptional, b has type number | undefined and every use has to handle that. In withDefault, b has type number, because the default has already been applied, so the body is simpler. Prefer a default whenever a sensible one exists: it moves the ?? 0 from every use into one place.

Three rules that are enforced.

Optional parameters must come last. (a?: number, b: number) is an error, because there is no way to give b without a.

A default parameter may come before a required one, unlike an optional one. But then the caller must pass undefined explicitly to get the default, which is worse than reordering. Treat this as legal but best avoided.

? and a default together are an error. b?: number = 10 is rejected: the default already makes it optional.

What matters at the call is what undefined means. withOptional(1, undefined) and withOptional(1) behave the same, and so do the two forms for withDefault, because a default applies to undefined and not to null. Under exactOptionalPropertyTypes (§5.18) the same difference becomes visible for object properties, where it is enforced and not just a convention.

The terms above, gathered: an optional parameter and a default parameter type.

4.6 Rest Parameters and Rest Arguments

A rest parameter type must be an array or tuple type, and rest arguments spread an array or tuple into a call. Together they keep functions that take any number of arguments typed.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function sum(...values: number[]): number { return values.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }

// A TUPLE rest parameter fixes the arity and the type at each position.
function tagged(label: string, ...rest: [count: number, urgent: boolean]): string {
  return `${label}/${rest[0]}/${rest[1]}`;
}

console.log(sum(1, 2, 3), tagged('x', 2, true));
// @ts-expect-error the rest tuple requires exactly two more arguments
tagged('x', 2);

// Rest ARGUMENTS: spreading into a call.
const args = [1, 2, 3] as const;
console.log(sum(...args));

6 x/2/true
6

The as const on args is doing real work. Spreading a plain number[] into a function with a fixed number of parameters is an error ("A spread argument must either have a tuple type or be passed to a rest parameter"), because the checker cannot know how many elements it has. sum takes a rest parameter, so it accepts either. tagged would not.

A tuple rest parameter is how you say "these arguments come as a group". It is the mechanism behind the generic factory of §7.9, and behind Parameters<F> being spreadable back into a call.

Labelled tuple elements, such as [count: number, urgent: boolean], are worth writing, because the labels show up in editor hints at the call. Without them the hint reads rest_0, rest_1, which tells the caller nothing.

One asymmetry: a rest parameter cannot be optional and cannot have a default, because it already means "zero or more". ...values: number[] = [] is a syntax error, and spreading nothing simply gives an empty array.

One line each, for reference: a rest parameter type.

4.7 Parameter Destructuring Types

Parameter destructuring types annotate the pattern as a whole, not each variable inside it.

function draw({ x, y = 0, label }: { x: number; y?: number; label?: string }): string {
  return `${label ?? 'point'} at ${x},${y}`;
}

function head<T>([first]: readonly T[]): T | undefined { return first; }

console.log(draw({ x: 3 }), draw({ x: 1, y: 2, label: 'origin' }), head([10, 20]));

point at 3,0 origin at 1,2 10

The annotation goes after the whole pattern, and its shape mirrors the shape of the pattern. Annotating inside, with { x: number, y: number } as the pattern, does not do what it looks like: in JavaScript destructuring, { x: number } means "put x into a variable called number", so that form silently renames your variables.

That is worth saying plainly, because it produces one of the most confusing errors in the language: function draw({ x: number, y: number }) declares two variables that are both called number, and the error is a complaint about a duplicate name that says nothing about types.

Defaults inside the pattern and optionality in the type work together. { y = 0 } supplies the default and y?: number allows it to be left out. You need both, and then the type of the parameter inside the body is number instead of number | undefined.

For a function with more than about three parameters, an options object with destructuring is usually the better interface, and this is how to type it. Give the object type a name, type DrawOptions = { … }, as soon as it appears twice. That also gives callers something to check against with satisfies (§8.10).

4.8 Declaring this in a Function

Declaring this in a function is done with a fake first parameter called this. It is checked, and then removed from the output.

function toHex(this: number, pad = 2): string {
  return this.toString(16).padStart(pad, '0');
}

console.log(toHex.call(255), toHex.call(10, 4));

function neverCalled(): string {
  // @ts-expect-error The 'this' context of type 'void' is not assignable to method's 'this' of type 'number'.
  return toHex();
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

ff 000a
function

this must be the first parameter, and it does not count as one. It is removed from the JavaScript output entirely, and Parameters<typeof toHex> is [pad?: number], with the this parameter left out. ThisParameterType and OmitThisParameter (§9.9) exist to reach it.

The three places to use it:

A callback whose this the caller sets. DOM handlers, jQuery-style APIs and the optional thisArg of Array.prototype.map all set this, and declaring it is what lets the body type-check.

A method in an object literal that uses this. Under noImplicitThis (part of strict), a function inside an object literal gets its this from the literal, but one taken out into a variable does not. That is where the annotation goes.

A function you plan to call with .call, .apply or .bind. With strictBindCallApply (§13.10) on, those three are checked against the declared this and the parameter list, so the wrong receiver is an error instead of a surprise at runtime.

Note that an arrow function cannot declare this, because it does not have one: it uses the this of the code around it. That is not a limitation to work around. It is the reason arrows are the right default for callbacks.

4.9 The void Type and Return Type void Assignability

The void type is the return type of a function that returns nothing useful. It is not undefined, and the difference is the subject of one of TypeScript's most useful deliberate rules.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function logIt(msg: string): void { console.log(msg); }

// A function whose DECLARED return type is void may not return a value.
function alsoNeverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'void'.
  return 1;
}

// But a function ASSIGNED to a void-returning type may return one, and it is ignored.
type VoidFn = () => void;
const returnsNumber: VoidFn = () => 42;
const result = returnsNumber();
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof result, void>>;

console.log(result, typeof alsoNeverCalled);

42 function

Read that 42. result has the static type void and holds the number 42 at runtime. The value was not thrown away, it was only declared uninteresting. That is the exact meaning of the two rules, which look contradictory and are not: a declared void return means "this function produces nothing"; a void in a target type means "the caller will ignore whatever comes back". Nothing at runtime enforces the second, because nothing needs to.

Return type void assignability is the second rule, and it exists for one very common pattern:

const source = [1, 2, 3];
const target: number[] = [];

// `push` returns a number; `forEach`'s callback is declared to return void.
source.forEach((n) => target.push(n));

console.log(target);

[ 1, 2, 3 ]

Without the rule, (n) => target.push(n) would be an error, and every callback like it would need a block body and a discarded result. The rule makes the short form legal, and it is safe because the caller really does discard the value: forEach never looks at what its callback returned.

A void-typed value may still hold something, and you may not use it. result above really is 42, and the type layer refuses to let you find that out: assigning a void to anything other than void, any or unknown is an error. void means "do not rely on this", which is a weaker and more honest claim than "this is undefined".

The related trap is Promise<void>. An async function with no return value has that type, and void there means the same thing: awaiting it is fine, and using the result is not.

4.10 The object Type

The object type, written in lower case, means "any non-primitive value". It is narrower than it looks and useful in exactly one situation.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function countKeys(o: object): number { return Object.keys(o).length; }

console.log(countKeys({ a: 1, b: 2 }), countKeys([1, 2, 3]), countKeys(() => {}));

function stillNeverCalled(): number {
  // @ts-expect-error Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'object'.
  return countKeys('abc');
}
console.log(typeof stillNeverCalled);

2 3 0
function

Arrays and functions are objects, so they are accepted. Strings, numbers, booleans, null and undefined are not. That is its whole meaning, and it is the right parameter type for a helper like Object.keys that must reject primitives.

Three types are easy to confuse and mean entirely different things.

object means any non-primitive. You cannot read any property from it without narrowing.

Object (capitalised) is the wrapper interface, and nearly everything is assignable to it, including 42 and 'abc'. It is almost never what you want, and a lint rule should ban it.

{} means "anything except null and undefined". That is also nearly everything, and it is the cause of the disaster in §9.5 where Omit on a union collapses to it.

For "a plain dictionary object" the right type is Record<string, unknown>, not object, because it allows indexing and object does not. For "some value I will narrow", the right type is unknown (§4.11). object is for the narrow case of "not a primitive, and I do not care what else".

4.11 The unknown Type

The unknown type is the safe counterpart of any. Every value can be assigned to it, but nothing can be taken out of it without narrowing.

function describe(value: unknown): string {
  if (typeof value === 'string') return `string of length ${value.length}`;
  if (typeof value === 'number') return `number ${value.toFixed(1)}`;
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return `array of ${value.length}`;
  if (value instanceof Error) return `error: ${value.message}`;
  if (value === null) return 'null';
  return `something else (${typeof value})`;
}

console.log(describe('abc'), '|', describe(3.14159), '|', describe([1, 2]));
console.log(describe(new RangeError('x')), '|', describe(null), '|', describe({ a: 1 }));

function lastNeverCalled(): number {
  const v: unknown = 'abc';
  // @ts-expect-error 'v' is of type 'unknown'.
  return v.length;
}
console.log(typeof lastNeverCalled);

string of length 3 | number 3.1 | array of 2
error: x | null | something else (object)
function

The contrast with any is the whole point. Both accept every value, but any then allows every operation and unknown allows none. any deletes the checking; unknown postpones it to a narrowing step you must actually write.

Three places where unknown is the right answer and any is the wrong one.

A caught error. Under useUnknownInCatchVariables (§10.19), which is part of strict, the variable in a catch is unknown, because anything can be thrown. instanceof Error is the honest first question (§10.20).

A parsed JSON payload. JSON.parse returns any in the standard library for historical reasons, and assigning the result to an unknown straight away is the cheapest thing you can do for a codebase's safety. §16.21 is the full treatment.

A parameter or constraint you do not want to restrict. T extends unknown and an unconstrained T are the same, but unknown as a parameter type, (value: unknown) => …, is how you say "any value, and I will check it".

unknown absorbs everything in a union: unknown | string is unknown. In an intersection it changes nothing: unknown & string is string. Those two facts make it the top of the type hierarchy, and never (§4.12) is the bottom.

4.12 The never Type

The never type is the type with no values. Nothing can be assigned to it (except never itself), and it can be assigned to everything.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// A function that never returns normally.
function fail(message: string): never { throw new Error(message); }

function parsePort(raw: string): number {
  const n = Number(raw);
  if (!Number.isInteger(n)) fail(`not a port: ${raw}`);
  return n;                                   // reachable only if fail() did not run
}

// never is the empty union: it disappears from one.
type _1 = Expect<Equal<string | never, string>>;
// and it absorbs an intersection.
type _2 = Expect<Equal<string & never, never>>;
// An impossible narrowing produces it.
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Extract<'a' | 'b', 'c'>, never>>;

console.log(parsePort('8080'));
try { parsePort('x'); } catch (e) { console.log((e as Error).message); }

8080
not a port: x

Four uses, and each appears elsewhere in this course.

A function that never returns, like fail above. Annotating it never instead of void is what lets control flow analysis know that the code after a call to it cannot run, which is why if (!ok) fail(…) narrows for the rest of the function.

Exhaustiveness checking (§3.14): const exhaustive: never = s fails exactly when s still has members.

Filtering in a mapped type (§8.7): a key remapped to never is removed, which is how Omit and every "pick the properties that…" helper works.

A deliberately impossible parameter, as in (...args: never[]) => unknown (§8.4), which matches every function without bringing in any.

Be exact about how it differs from void: void means "returns, with nothing useful"; never means "does not return". A function annotated void that always throws is legal but loses the control flow benefit. Annotate it never and its callers get narrowing.

4.13 The Function Type

The Function type, capitalised, is the global interface that describes any function. It is legal, it is dangerous, and it should almost never appear in your code.

const anything: Function = (a: number) => a * 2;

// Every one of these compiles: the arguments are unchecked and the return is `any`.
const wrong: string = anything('not a number', 1, 2, 3);
console.log(typeof wrong, wrong);

number NaN

wrong is annotated string and holds NaN. The Function type accepts any argument list and returns any, so it is any wearing the shape of a function, with all of any's spreading effect (§10.21) and none of the warning that a literal any would give a reviewer.

It also carries the members of Function.prototype (call, apply, bind, length, name), which is sometimes the reason people reach for it.

The replacement is a call signature with never[] arguments:

type AnyFunction = (...args: never[]) => unknown;

function describe(fn: AnyFunction): string { return `${fn.length} declared parameters`; }

const add = (a: number, b: number) => a + b;
console.log(describe(add), '|', describe(() => {}));

2 declared parameters | 0 declared parameters

(...args: never[]) => unknown matches every function, because a never[] can be passed to any parameter list, while the return is unknown instead of any, so nothing leaks. That is the constraint used throughout this course (§8.4, §9.8), and @typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-function-type is the lint rule that enforces the swap.

The one legitimate use of Function is in a type test: typeof x === 'function' narrows unknown to Function, and that is the checker's own choice, not yours.

4.14 Function Assignability

Function assignability is the rule that decides whether one function type may be used where another was expected. It has two halves that pull in opposite directions.

type Handler = (event: { type: string; detail: number }) => void;

// FEWER parameters is fine: the extra argument is simply ignored.
const ignoresIt: Handler = () => console.log('something happened');
const usesIt: Handler = (e) => console.log(e.type, e.detail);

// MORE parameters is not.
// @ts-expect-error Target signature provides too few arguments.
