const wantsTwo: Handler = (e: { type: string; detail: number }, extra: string) => {};

ignoresIt({ type: 'click', detail: 1 });
usesIt({ type: 'click', detail: 1 });

something happened
click 1

Parameter count: a function may have fewer parameters than its target type. That is not a concession, it is a requirement: arr.forEach((x) => …) would be an error otherwise, since the callback type of forEach declares three parameters and almost nobody uses all three.

Return type: covariant. Covariant means the direction follows the types. A function returning Dog can be used where one returning Animal was wanted, because the caller gets something at least as specific as promised.

Parameter types: contravariant, in principle. Contravariant means the direction is reversed. A function accepting Animal can be used where one accepting Dog was wanted, because it can handle more than it needs to. §7.10 has the full argument.

And here is the deliberate hole. TypeScript checks the parameters of a method bivariantly, meaning in both directions, so a handler that accepts a narrower type is accepted too:

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

// A METHOD: parameters are checked bivariantly.
type WithMethod = { handle(a: Animal): void };
const m: WithMethod = { handle(d: Dog) { d.bark(); } };   // accepted — and unsound

// A PROPERTY of function type: checked strictly under strictFunctionTypes.
type WithProperty = { handle: (a: Animal) => void };
// @ts-expect-error Types of parameters 'd' and 'a' are incompatible.
const p: WithProperty = { handle: (d: Dog) => d.bark() };

try { m.handle({ name: 'Whiskers' }); } catch (e) { console.log((e as Error).constructor.name); }

TypeError

The cat reached a handler that calls .bark(), and it threw. strictFunctionTypes fixes this for properties that hold functions, and deliberately does not fix it for methods (§10.5), because the methods of Array<T> itself (push, concat, indexOf) depend on the looser rule. Writing the callback as a property instead of a method is how you switch on the strict check, and it is worth doing for any interface you own.

4.15 Overloads

A function overload is a set of public signatures over one implementation. An overload signature is one of those public entries, and an implementation signature is the one with the body. The implementation signature cannot be called from outside.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function reverse(input: string): string;
function reverse<T>(input: T[]): T[];
function reverse(input: string | unknown[]): string | unknown[] {
  return typeof input === 'string' ? [...input].reverse().join('') : [...input].reverse();
}

const asString = reverse('abc');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof asString, string>>;
const asArray = reverse([1, 2, 3]);
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof asArray, number[]>>;

console.log(asString, asArray);

function unreachable(): unknown {
  // @ts-expect-error No overload matches this call.
  return reverse(42);
}
console.log(typeof unreachable);

cba [ 3, 2, 1 ]
function

The implementation signature is invisible to callers. Only the two overload signatures can be called, which is why reverse(anyStringOrArray), a union that matches only the implementation, is an error. That surprises people, and it is the rule that makes overloads worth having: the public contract is narrower than the implementation's.

Overloads are tried in the order they are declared, and the first match wins. Put the most specific one first, because a general signature at the top hides everything after it.

Writing good overloads comes down to three habits.

Prefer a union parameter to two overloads when the return type does not change. function pad(v: string | number): string is simpler than two signatures and gives better errors: the message for overloads ("No overload matches this call") is much worse than a plain assignability failure.

Prefer a generic to overloads when the relationship is the same every time. function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined covers infinitely many cases that overloads would have to list one by one.

Do not add an overload for the union of the others. reverse(x: string | unknown[]) as a third public signature would let callers pass a union, and then the return type is a union too, so every call needs narrowing. This is the mistake that turns an overloaded API into an unpleasant one.

The implementation signature must be compatible with every overload, and the compiler checks that loosely. It is one of the places where an assertion inside the body is truly unavoidable, and where the type test (Expect<Equal<…>> above) is what actually pins down the intended behaviour.

Gathered here, because the rest of the course uses them: a function overload, an overload signature, an implementation signature and writing good overloads.

4.16 Higher-Order Function Types and Callback Parameter Types

A higher-order function type takes a function or returns one, and a callback parameter type is the shape of the function it takes. Getting these right is most of what makes a library pleasant to use.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function debounce<A extends readonly unknown[]>(
  fn: (...args: A) => void,
  waitMs: number,
): (...args: A) => void {
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
  return (...args) => {
    if (timer !== undefined) clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), waitMs);
  };
}

const log = (label: string, count: number) => console.log(label, count);
const debounced = debounce(log, 10);
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Parameters<typeof debounced>, [label: string, count: number]>>;

debounced('a', 1);

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error the wrapper kept the original parameter types
  debounced('a', 'b');
}
void neverCalled;

await new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 40));
export {};

a 1

Three design rules are visible in that signature.

Take the arguments as a tuple type parameter. A extends readonly unknown[] with (...args: A) => void keeps both the number of arguments and their labels, so debounced has exactly the parameters of log. Writing (...args: any[]) => void would type-check and lose all of that.

Put the value to infer from before the callback. debounce(fn, waitMs) works out A from fn immediately. The reverse order would work here only because waitMs adds nothing, and in general it breaks typing from context (§2.5).

Use ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> instead of number or NodeJS.Timeout. The two runtimes disagree about what setTimeout returns, and deriving the type means the same source compiles in both.

For a callback parameter type, the rules are the mirror image. Declare every parameter the callback may receive, because a caller that takes fewer is always allowed (§4.14), while one that wants the third argument cannot get it if you did not declare it. Declare the return as void if you will ignore it, since that is what makes the short arrow form legal (§4.9). And declare the callback as a property, not a method, in any interface you own, so strictFunctionTypes checks its parameters properly.

The term this subsection introduced, in one line: a higher-order function type.

4.17 NoInfer

NoInfer, added to the standard library in TypeScript 5.4, marks a position that should not contribute a candidate to type inference. It solves a specific and common problem: an argument that ought to be checked against a type parameter instead widens it.

function pick<T extends string>(options: T[], preferred: NoInfer<T>): T {
  return options.includes(preferred) ? preferred : options[0]!;
}

console.log(pick(['red', 'green'], 'green'));
// @ts-expect-error 'blue' is not one of the options
pick(['red', 'green'], 'blue');

// Without NoInfer, the second argument widens T and the check silently disappears.
function pickLoose<T extends string>(options: T[], preferred: T): T { return preferred; }
console.log(pickLoose(['red', 'green'], 'blue'));

green
blue

That output is the argument. pickLoose(['red', 'green'], 'blue') compiled and returned 'blue', because T was worked out from both arguments as 'red' | 'green' | 'blue', and once 'blue' is part of T it is a perfectly good option. The check the signature seemed to make had quietly disappeared.

NoInfer<T> fixes it by taking the second argument out of the candidates for inference: T is worked out from options alone, and preferred is then checked against the result.

The pattern applies to any API where one argument defines the type and the other must conform to it:

  • a default value that must match a set of allowed values;
  • a state machine transition whose target must be one of the declared states;
  • an animation whose to must have the keys of from;
  • a form field whose default must be in its option list.

Before NoInfer existed, the workaround was a second type parameter with a constraint, <T extends string, U extends T>. It mostly worked and gave worse error messages. NoInfer<T> is a single wrapper in the signature and needs no extra parameter.

Note that it is an inference instruction only. It does not restrict anything, does not change the type, and does not exist at runtime: it just removes one place where a candidate could come from. If the parameter should genuinely widen T, do not use it.

What This Section Established

A function type expression names a contract and gives its implementations their parameter types for free. A call signature adds properties to something callable. A construct signature describes new, always against typeof TheClass, and needs a generic tuple to accept every constructor while still checking arguments.

Optional parameters and defaults produce the same parameter type and differ only inside the body, so prefer the default. Rest parameters take arrays or tuples, and a spread argument needs a tuple type or as const. Destructured parameters are annotated as a whole, and { x: number } in the pattern renames instead of typing.

Four types arrived here. void means "produces nothing" as a declaration and "the result is ignored" as a target, which is what makes forEach((x) => arr.push(x)) legal. object means non-primitive and is rarely what you want, while Record<string, unknown> usually is. unknown is any with the checking postponed instead of deleted. never is the empty type, and the engine behind exhaustiveness, unreachable code and filtering in mapped types.

Function is any in disguise: the example returned NaN from a variable annotated string. Function assignability allows fewer parameters, is covariant in the return and contravariant in the parameters, except that methods are bivariant on purpose and strictFunctionTypes only fixes properties that hold functions. Overloads present a narrower contract than the implementation, so prefer a union or a generic where either will do. And NoInfer is how you stop an argument from widening the very type parameter it was supposed to be checked against.

Exercises

1. Type four callables. Write the type, not the implementation, for: a function with a cache property and a clear() method; a class constructor taking (host: string, port?: number) that any subclass also satisfies; a generic function that stays generic when assigned to a variable; and a callback receiving (value, index, array) whose return is ignored. For each, say which of the four forms in §4.1–§4.3 you used and why the others cannot express it.

2. Break and fix bivariance. Write an interface with a method taking a wide type, implement it with a handler taking a narrow one, and show that it compiles and then throws at runtime. Change one thing so the compiler catches it, and explain both why the original is allowed and why the fix works.

3. Make an API that cannot be misused. Write transition(states, from, to) where states is a readonly array of state names and both from and to must be members of it, using a literal type so that a typo is a compile error. Show one correct call and two rejected ones, then say exactly which two features from this section and §7 the signature depends on.

Solution

1. Four callables.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// (a) A callable with properties — needs a call signature (§4.2).
type Memoised = {
  (key: string): number;
  cache: Map<string, number>;
  clear(): void;
};

// (b) A constructor any subclass satisfies — an abstract construct signature (§4.3).
type ConnectionCtor = abstract new (host: string, port?: number) => { host: string };

// (c) Generic at call time — a generic call signature, NOT a generic type alias (§4.2).
type Wrap = <T>(value: T) => { value: T };
const wrap: Wrap = (value) => ({ value });
const wrapped = wrap('a');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof wrapped, { value: string }>>;

// (d) A callback whose result is ignored — a function type expression with a void return (§4.1, §4.9).
type EachCallback<T> = (value: T, index: number, array: readonly T[]) => void;

const shout: EachCallback<string> = (v, i) => console.log(i, v.toUpperCase());
['a', 'b'].forEach(shout);
console.log(wrapped);

0 A
1 B
{ value: 'a' }

(a) A function type expression cannot carry properties — it describes a call and nothing else — so a call signature inside an object type is the only form that works.

(b) abstract new is required if a subclass constructor should satisfy it; a plain new (…) => T rejects an abstract base, and typeof SomeClass would pin it to one specific class.

(c) The distinction that matters: type Wrap = <T>(v: T) => … keeps T open at each call, while type Wrap<T> = (v: T) => … would have to be instantiated as Wrap<string> at the annotation and would stop being generic.

(d) void rather than undefined is what makes (v, i) => console.log(…) legal, since console.log returns undefined — and it would make an arrow returning a number legal too (§4.9). Declaring all three parameters lets a caller use as few as they like (§4.14).

2. Break and fix bivariance.

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

// A METHOD — parameters are checked bivariantly, so this compiles.
interface MethodHandler { handle(a: Animal): void }
const broken: MethodHandler = { handle(d: Dog) { d.bark(); } };

let thrown = 'nothing';
try { broken.handle({ name: 'Whiskers' }); }
catch (e) { thrown = (e as Error).constructor.name; }
console.log('runtime result:', thrown);

// The one-word fix: declare it as a PROPERTY of function type.
interface PropertyHandler { handle: (a: Animal) => void }
// @ts-expect-error Types of parameters 'd' and 'a' are incompatible.
const caught: PropertyHandler = { handle: (d: Dog) => d.bark() };

const fine: PropertyHandler = { handle: (a) => console.log('handled', a.name) };
fine.handle({ name: 'Whiskers' });

runtime result: TypeError
handled Whiskers

Why the original is allowed. TypeScript checks method parameters in both directions, which is unsafe and deliberate (§1.12). The reason is Array<T> and every other built-in generic: push, concat and indexOf are methods whose parameter types must vary with T, and checking them strictly would make Dog[] impossible to assign to Animal[], which would break an enormous amount of code that works in practice.

Why the fix works. strictFunctionTypes, part of strict, checks properties that hold functions contravariantly, and only those properties. Writing handle: (a: Animal) => void therefore switches on the strict rule with no other change, and the same mistake becomes a compile error at the declaration.

The practical advice: in an interface you own, whose implementations you do not control, declare callbacks as properties. Use method syntax only where you actually want the looser rule, which in application code is almost never.

3. An API that cannot be misused.

function transition<const S extends readonly string[]>(
  states: S,
  from: NoInfer<S[number]>,
  to: NoInfer<S[number]>,
): string {
  if (!states.includes(from) || !states.includes(to)) throw new Error('unknown state');
  return `${from} -> ${to}`;
}

const STATES = ['idle', 'loading', 'done'] as const;

console.log(transition(STATES, 'idle', 'loading'));
// @ts-expect-error 'loadng' is a typo, not a state
transition(STATES, 'idle', 'loadng');
// @ts-expect-error 'failed' is not in this state list
transition(STATES, 'failed', 'done');

idle -> loading

Two features carry the signature, and removing either one silently switches the check off.

const S, a const type parameter (§7.8), is what keeps S as readonly ['idle', 'loading', 'done'] instead of string[]. Without it, S[number] is string and every typo is accepted. Note that STATES is already as const here, so const S is a second safeguard, but it is what makes the function correct for a caller who passes an array literal directly.

NoInfer<S[number]> (§4.17) is what stops from and to from contributing to inference. Without it, S would be worked out from all three arguments and 'loadng' would simply join the union, which is exactly the pickLoose failure measured earlier in this section, where the call compiled and returned the wrong value.

S[number] is an indexed access type (§8.2) that turns the tuple into the union of its elements. It is the third piece, and the one that connects the array's value to the parameters' types.

The runtime check is still there and still necessary, because a caller holding an any, or data from outside the program, can defeat any of this (§1.11). The type-level work removes the mistakes a developer makes while typing, and the throw covers the ones that arrive while the program runs.

SECTION 5

Objects, Interfaces and Tuples

Most of the data a program handles is shaped like an object, so most of the types you write describe objects. This section is the complete account of how: the modifiers you can put on a property, the two ways to combine shapes, the index signature for keys you cannot list in advance, tuples for data where position matters, and four strictness settings that decide how honest all of this is.

Three ideas run through it:

  • A property has three independent settings. Is it required or optional, can it be changed or is it read-only, and what is its type. TypeScript lets you be exact about each one.
  • There are two ways to combine shapes, and they are not interchangeable. extends checks the combination where you declare it. & (an intersection) just builds it, and can quietly produce a type nothing could ever satisfy.
  • An index signature is a promise you can almost never keep. Record<string, T> claims that every possible string key holds a T, which is false for every real dictionary. The noUncheckedIndexedAccess setting is what makes the type admit that.

The four settings in §5.18–§5.21 are all off by default, even under strict. Each one closes a real gap, each one produces errors in existing code, and each is worth turning on in a new project on day one, because that is the cheapest day.

5.1 An Object Literal Type

An object literal type is written inline, with braces, and lists the members. It is the unnamed form; interface and type give the same thing a name.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function ship(order: { id: string; items: { sku: string; qty: number }[]; note?: string }): string {
  const total = order.items.reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0);
  return `${order.id}: ${total} items${order.note ? ` (${order.note})` : ''}`;
}

console.log(ship({ id: 'o1', items: [{ sku: 'a', qty: 2 }, { sku: 'b', qty: 1 }] }));
console.log(ship({ id: 'o2', items: [], note: 'gift' }));

o1: 3 items
o2: 0 items (gift)

Members are separated by ;, , or a newline, and a nested object literal type is just another one in a member position.

Give it a name as soon as it appears twice. An inline object literal type used in one signature is fine. The same shape written out in three places is three chances for the copies to drift apart, and error messages then print the whole expansion instead of a name (§17.4).

Three other kinds of member can sit beside plain properties, and each has its own subsection later: a method (greet(): string), which is checked bivariantly (§4.14); a call or construct signature (§4.2, §4.3); and an index signature (§5.5).

An object literal type is structural like everything else (§1.3), with one extra rule on top: the excess property check of §5.4, which applies to an object literal written directly and not to a variable.

5.2 A Property Modifier

A property modifier is ? or readonly, written before or after the property name, and the two are independent of each other.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Record_ = {
  id: number;                   // required, mutable
  name?: string;                // optional, mutable
  readonly createdAt: string;   // required, immutable
  readonly tag?: string;        // optional, immutable
};

declare const r: Record_;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof r.name, string | undefined>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof r.tag, string | undefined>>;

? means two things at once under strictNullChecks: the property may be missing from an object literal, and reading it gives T | undefined. Those two ideas can be separated, and exactOptionalPropertyTypes (§5.18) is the setting that separates them.

All four combinations are meaningful, and worth choosing deliberately. A required property that can change is the default. An optional one is a field with a default, or a value that may really be missing. A readonly required property is something set once, such as an identity or a creation timestamp. A readonly optional property is rarer and usually means "worked out at construction, and may not apply".

Mapped types keep modifiers as they are unless you change them on purpose (§8.6). That is what makes Partial, Required and Readonly (§9.2) exact.

One habit worth forming: do not reach for ? when the property is always there but sometimes empty. tags?: string[] and tags: string[] differ in that the second cannot be forgotten, and [] is a perfectly good empty value. Optional is for "this may genuinely not exist", not for "I did not feel like writing it".

5.3 The readonly Modifier

The readonly modifier stops assignment through that reference. It is a compile-time rule with no effect at runtime at all.

type Config = { readonly host: string; readonly ports: number[] };

const config: Config = { host: 'localhost', ports: [80, 443] };

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Cannot assign to 'host' because it is a read-only property.
  config.host = 'elsewhere';
}

// But readonly is SHALLOW — the array itself is still mutable.
config.ports.push(8080);
console.log(config.ports, typeof neverCalled);

// And it is not enforced across an alias.
const alias: { host: string } = config;
alias.host = 'elsewhere';
console.log(config.host);

[ 80, 443, 8080 ] function
elsewhere

Both of those outputs are the point. readonly is shallow: it protects the variable, not what the variable points at, so config.ports.push(…) is legal, and readonly ports: readonly number[] is what you actually wanted. And readonly is not part of assignability: a { readonly host: string } can be assigned to a { host: string }, so one alias removes the protection entirely and the compiler says nothing.

That second behaviour is deliberate, and is another entry in the list in §1.12. Checking readonly on assignment would break a lot of ordinary code, such as passing a frozen config to a function that declares a mutable parameter, and the trade-off went the usual way.

readonly pays off inside a single type. It documents your intent, it catches the direct mistake, and it composes: Readonly<T> (§9.2), readonly T[] (§5.16) and a readonly tuple (§5.15) are all built from it. as const (§2.13) applies it everywhere at once.

For a real guarantee at runtime you need Object.freeze, which TypeScript understands: Object.freeze(x) returns Readonly<T>, so the type and the runtime agree. It is the only construct in this subsection where they do.

5.4 An Excess Property Check

An excess property check is a rule added on top of structural typing: an object literal assigned directly to a typed target may not carry properties that the target does not declare.

type Options = { url: string; timeout?: number };

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'timeoutMs' does not exist in type 'Options'.
  const bad: Options = { url: '/api', timeoutMs: 500 };
}

// The same object through a variable is accepted — structural typing's actual rule.
const loose = { url: '/api', timeoutMs: 500 };
const fine: Options = loose;

console.log(fine.url, typeof neverCalled);

/api function

Both lines describe the same value, and only one is rejected. The check exists because a stray key in a freshly written literal is almost always a typo, and timeoutMs instead of timeout is exactly the mistake it catches. Once the value has passed through a variable, that assumption no longer holds, because the object may have been built for several purposes, so the plain structural rule applies.

Three ways to switch it off, from most to least honest. Assign through a variable, as above, which is what the checker itself treats as the signal. Add an index signature to the target if extra keys are really expected. Assert, which throws away the check along with everything else.

The check also fires on function arguments and return values, which is where it does most of its work: request({ url: '/api', timeoutMs: 500 }) is caught at the call.

It does not fire on a spread. { ...loose } is a freshly written literal, but the properties that come from the spread are not checked as excess. That is a documented gap, and a place where typos survive. When a config object is built by spreading, satisfies (§8.10) is the tool that brings the check back.

5.5 An Index Signature

An index signature describes keys you cannot list in advance: { [key: string]: number }.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Counts = { [word: string]: number };

function tally(words: readonly string[]): Counts {
  const counts: Counts = {};
  for (const w of words) counts[w] = (counts[w] ?? 0) + 1;
  return counts;
}

console.log(tally(['a', 'b', 'a']));

// The key type may be string, number, symbol, or a template literal type.
type Headers_ = { [k: `x-${string}`]: string };
const h: Headers_ = { 'x-request-id': 'abc' };
console.log(h['x-request-id']);

{ a: 2, b: 1 }
abc

Three rules are enforced and each has a reason.

Every declared property must be compatible with the index signature. { [k: string]: number; name: string } is an error, because obj['name'] would have to be both. The fix is to widen the value type of the index signature to a union, or to use two types.

A string index signature also covers numeric keys, because a JavaScript property key is always a string (§8.1). That is why keyof { [k: string]: T } is string | number.

The key type may be a template literal type (§8.8), which is genuinely useful: { [k: \data-${string}`]: string }` describes exactly the data attributes and nothing else.

The honest problem with an index signature is that it lies. Counts claims that every string key holds a number, so counts['nonexistent'].toFixed(0) type-checks and then crashes. That is the gap noUncheckedIndexedAccess (§5.19) closes, and it is the single most valuable setting in this section.

Prefer Record<K, V> (§9.3) with a finite union of keys when you can list the keys: it checks that every key is handled, instead of making a promise. Keep the index signature for keys that are really open-ended.

5.6 Extending an Interface

Extending an interface builds a new one from one or more existing ones, and the compiler checks the combination at the declaration.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

interface Entity { id: string; createdAt: string }
interface Named { name: string }
interface User extends Entity, Named { email: string }

type _1 = Expect<Equal<keyof User, 'id' | 'createdAt' | 'name' | 'email'>>;

const u: User = { id: 'u1', createdAt: '2026-09-01', name: 'Ada', email: 'a@b.c' };
console.log(u.name, u.id);

Ada u1

Extending several interfaces is allowed, and is the normal way to combine the traits of an entity.

A member may be narrowed but not contradicted. interface Admin extends User { name: 'root' } is legal, because 'root' is assignable to string, while { name: number } is an error at the declaration, with a message naming both types. That check is the main practical difference from an intersection (§5.8).

An interface may extend a type alias whose definition is an object shape, and a class (§6.6), which is how you say "this shape matches that class's instances".

The style worth adopting: small named traits such as Entity, Timestamped and SoftDeletable, combined with extends at the leaves. It reads better than one long interface, the traits can be reused, and each combination is checked where it is written, not at some far-away use.

5.7 An Intersection Type

An intersection type combines types with &: a value must satisfy all of them.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Entity = { id: string };
type Timestamped = { createdAt: string };
type Post = Entity & Timestamped & { title: string };

const p: Post = { id: 'p1', createdAt: '2026-09-01', title: 'Hello' };
console.log(p.title, p.id);

// An intersection can also combine a union with a constraint.
type Level = 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error';
type Severe = Level & ('warn' | 'error');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Severe, 'warn' | 'error'>>;

Hello p1

& works on any types, not only object shapes, which is its advantage over extends. The Severe line above is an intersection of unions, and the branded types of §8.11 are an intersection of a primitive with an object.

Conflicting members produce never instead of an error, and this is the behaviour to know about:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Bad = { x: number } & { x: string };
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Bad['x'], never>>;

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'never'.
  const b: Bad = { x: 1 };
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

function

The type is built without any complaint and becomes impossible to satisfy. The error arrives at the first attempt to create a value, possibly in another file, with a message about never that does not mention the two declarations that caused it. That is the argument for extends when both sides are object shapes.

Intersecting two functions produces an overload: ((a: string) => void) & ((a: number) => void) can be called with either, which is occasionally the neatest way to express that.

5.8 Interface Extension Versus Intersection

The interface extension versus intersection decision comes down to three differences that matter, and they are not just style.

Where the error appears. interface A extends B is checked at the declaration, while A & B is checked at each use. A conflict is therefore reported once and precisely with extends, and repeatedly and confusingly with &.

What happens to a conflict. extends reports it. & produces a member of type never and says nothing (§5.7).

Cost. An interface is one named type that the checker works out once and caches. An intersection is a composite that it may have to work out again at each use, and its error messages spell out the contents instead of naming an alias.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

interface Base { id: string }
interface ViaExtends extends Base { name: string }
type ViaIntersection = Base & { name: string };

// Structurally identical — the difference is in the checker's treatment, not the result.
const a: ViaExtends = { id: '1', name: 'x' };
const b: ViaIntersection = a;
const c: ViaExtends = b;
console.log(a.name, b.id, c.id);

x 1 1

Use extends when both sides are object shapes and you control the declaration. Use & when at least one side is not an object shape (a union, a generic parameter, a mapped or conditional type), or when you are combining types you did not declare.

The rule extends to the custom utilities of §9.10: RequireKeys<T, K> = Omit<T, K> & Required<Pick<T, K>> has to use &, because its parts are computed. That is fine. The advice is about declared shapes, where you have a choice.

§17.8 measures the performance side of this. The short version: for two small shapes it does not matter, and for a widely used entity type built from four traits it is one of the most valuable changes available to a slow build.

5.9 Merging Interfaces

Merging interfaces means that two declarations of the same interface name in the same scope are combined into one.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

interface Settings { theme: string }
interface Settings { locale: string }

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Settings, { theme: string; locale: string }>>;

const s: Settings = { theme: 'dark', locale: 'en-GB' };
console.log(s);

{ theme: 'dark', locale: 'en-GB' }

Inside one file this looks like a hazard, and it is one: a mistyped second declaration silently adds members instead of reporting a duplicate. A type alias would have reported "Duplicate identifier".

Its purpose is extension from outside. The same mechanism, used inside declare global or declare module, is how you add a property to Window, a method to Express.Request, or a field to a library's options interface without editing it. §12.5 and §12.6 cover it fully, and it is the reason interfaces are the right choice for anything that users of your code might need to extend.

Three rules constrain merging.

Non-function members must be identical. Two declarations of theme: string are fine. theme: string and theme: number is an error.

Function members become overloads, with the signatures of the later declaration placed first. That order is what lets an augmentation add a more specific overload that wins.

Merging happens per scope. Two interface Settings in different modules are unrelated. Only declarations in the same declaration space merge, which is why augmenting a module needs the declare module wrapper.

5.10 A Generic Object Type

A generic object type turns a shape into a template with a type parameter, and it is the usual way to describe a container, an envelope or a repository.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

interface Page<T> {
  items: readonly T[];
  total: number;
  next?: string;
}

type UserPage = Page<{ id: string; name: string }>;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<UserPage['items'], readonly { id: string; name: string }[]>>;

function firstOf<T>(page: Page<T>): T | undefined { return page.items[0]; }

const page: Page<string> = { items: ['a', 'b'], total: 2 };
console.log(firstOf(page), page.total);

a 2

Everything from §7 applies (constraints, defaults, and variance, which is how a type parameter affects whether one instantiation fits another), and two points are specific to object shapes.

Put the parameter where things vary, and nowhere else. Page<T> uses T once, in items, while total and next do not depend on it. A parameter that appears in no member is a phantom (§7.13) and should be there on purpose.

A generic interface is open to extension and a generic alias is not. A user can augment interface Page<T> but not type Page<T>. For the public envelope type of a library, that is a real consideration.

Instantiation, meaning filling in the type parameter as in Page<string>, is structural: Page<string> and any object with a readonly string[] and a number are the same type, so a caller does not need to import Page to satisfy it.

5.11 A Tuple Type

A tuple type is an array type with a fixed length and a type for each position: [string, number].

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Point = [number, number];
type Entry = [key: string, value: number];

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Point['length'], 2>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Point[0], number>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Point[number], number>>;

const p: Point = [3, 4];
const [x, y] = p;
console.log(Math.hypot(x, y), Object.fromEntries([['a', 1]] as Entry[]));

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Type '[number, number, number]' is not assignable to type 'Point'.
  const bad: Point = [1, 2, 3];
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

5 { a: 1 }
function

length is a literal type on a tuple, 2 and not number. That is what makes arithmetic on tuples possible in the type layer (§8.9), and what lets the checker reject the wrong number of elements.

Three places where tuples are the right tool, not a curiosity. A pair or a coordinate, where a name for each element would be noise. A function's parameter list, which is exactly what Parameters<F> produces (§9.8) and what a rest parameter consumes (§4.6). A discriminated result, where element 0 is the discriminant (§3.13), the shape used by Object.entries, useState and Go-style error returns.

A tuple is still an array at runtime, with every array method, so push exists and will happily make it the wrong length. readonly (§5.15) is what closes that, and it is why as const produces a readonly tuple and not a mutable one.

5.12 A Named Tuple Element

A named tuple element has a label: [start: number, end: number]. The label is documentation, for people and for editor hints, and it changes nothing about assignability.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Span = [start: number, end: number];
type Unlabelled = [number, number];

// The labels do not affect the type.
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Span, Unlabelled>>;

function length_(span: Span): number { return span[1] - span[0]; }
console.log(length_([3, 10]));

7

The labels show up at a call that spreads the tuple, and in Parameters<F> (§9.8). Without labels an editor hint reads arg_0: number, arg_1: number. With them it reads start: number, end: number, which is the whole return on writing them.

Labels are all or nothing within one tuple. Mixing them, as in [start: number, number], is an error: either every element is named or none is.

The label of a rest element names the whole rest, as in [first: string, ...rest: number[]], and that is what the hint shows for every extra argument.

Write labels on any tuple that appears in a public signature. They cost a few characters, and they are the difference between a hint that tells the caller what to pass and one that does not.

5.13 An Optional Tuple Element

An optional tuple element is marked ?, and it makes the length of the tuple a union.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Span = [start: number, end?: number];

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Span['length'], 1 | 2>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Span[1], number | undefined>>;

function width(s: Span): number { return (s[1] ?? s[0]) - s[0]; }

console.log(width([3]), width([3, 10]));

0 7

length becomes 1 | 2, which is exactly right and is what lets a switch (s.length) narrow the tuple.

The rules mirror optional parameters (§4.5): optional elements must come after all the required ones, and reading one gives T | undefined. That is not a coincidence, because a function's parameter list is a tuple type, and Parameters<typeof f> for a function with an optional parameter produces exactly this shape.

A rest element may follow optional elements, so [a: string, b?: number, ...rest: boolean[]] is legal and describes the matching parameter list.

The everyday use is describing a function signature instead of declaring one: a callback whose second argument is optional, or an event tuple whose payload is sometimes absent.

5.14 A Rest Element in a Tuple

A rest element in a tuple stands for any number of elements: [string, ...number[]].

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Command = [name: string, ...args: string[]];
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Command['length'], number>>;

// A rest element may sit in the MIDDLE or at the start.
type Trailing = [first: string, ...middle: number[], last: boolean];

const c: Command = ['build', '--watch', '--minify'];
const t: Trailing = ['start', 1, 2, 3, true];

console.log(c[0], c.slice(1), t[0], t[t.length - 1]);

build [ '--watch', '--minify' ] start true

A rest element in the middle or at the start is legal, which is more than a rest parameter allows. [...number[], boolean] describes "any number of numbers, then a boolean", and the checker matches from both ends.

Only one rest element per tuple, and its length becomes number. The number of elements is no longer known, so arithmetic on tuples (§8.9) stops working on it.

The main use is describing the parameters of a function that takes any number of arguments, so they can be passed on. (...args: Command) => void accepts exactly the shape above, and spreading a Command into such a call type-checks. That is the mechanism behind the wrapper types of §4.16 and §9.8.

Combined with a generic, [first: T, ...rest: R] with R extends readonly unknown[], it becomes the type-level way of taking a list apart that the recursive types of §8.9 loop over.

5.15 A Readonly Tuple

A readonly tuple is written readonly [A, B], and it forbids both assigning to an element and the array methods that change it.

type Point = readonly [x: number, y: number];

const p: Point = [3, 4];
console.log(Math.hypot(p[0], p[1]));

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Cannot assign to '0' because it is a read-only property.
  p[0] = 5;
  // @ts-expect-error Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly [x: number, y: number]'.
  p.push(6);
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

5
function

as const on an array literal produces exactly this (§2.13), which is why the two features are almost always seen together.

A mutable tuple can be assigned to a readonly one, but not the other way round, which is the correct direction: promising less is safe, and promising more is not. That makes readonly [A, B] the right parameter type for anything that only reads, exactly as readonly T[] is (§5.16).

The one point of friction: a function declared to take a mutable [number, number] rejects an as const argument, and the error ("The type 'readonly [1, 2]' is 'readonly' and cannot be assigned to the mutable type '[number, number]'") is common enough to recognise on sight. The fix is nearly always to make the parameter readonly, not to remove the as const.

5.16 The Array Type and the ReadonlyArray Type

The Array type is T[] or Array<T>, and the ReadonlyArray type is readonly T[] or ReadonlyArray<T>. The difference is which methods exist.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type _1 = Expect<Equal<number[], Array<number>>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<readonly number[], ReadonlyArray<number>>>;

function total(xs: readonly number[]): number { return xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }

const mutable = [1, 2, 3];
const frozen: readonly number[] = mutable;      // widening to readonly is always safe
console.log(total(mutable), total(frozen));

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly number[]'.
  frozen.push(4);
  // @ts-expect-error The type 'readonly number[]' is 'readonly' and cannot be assigned to the mutable type 'number[]'.
  const back: number[] = frozen;
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

6 6
function

ReadonlyArray<T> declares every method that does not change the array (map, filter, slice, concat, reduce, includes, iteration) and leaves out push, pop, splice, sort, reverse and assigning to an index. Nothing is frozen at runtime. The protection exists only in the type.

Take readonly T[] for every parameter you only read. It accepts more for the caller, it documents that you will not change the array, and it is the safe answer to array covariance (§1.12): you cannot push a cat into a readonly Animal[].

readonly is one word in the annotation and a large change in the API, so the migration cost in an existing codebase is real: a readonly T[] cannot be passed where a T[] was expected, and the errors spread outwards until they reach code that genuinely changes the array. Working from the leaves inwards, parameters before return types, keeps it manageable.

The two spellings are interchangeable, and readonly T[] is the usual one. ReadonlyArray<T> is needed only when the element type would otherwise group the wrong way, and readonly cannot be applied to a type alias for an array: type Xs = number[]; readonly Xs is not valid syntax.

5.17 A Recursive Type Alias

A recursive type alias refers to itself. It is how you describe a tree, a nested configuration or a JSON value.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Json =
  | string | number | boolean | null
  | Json[]
  | { [key: string]: Json };

const doc: Json = { name: 'Ada', tags: ['x', 'y'], meta: { deep: { deeper: [1, true, null] } } };

type TreeNode<T> = { value: T; children: TreeNode<T>[] };

function count<T>(node: TreeNode<T>): number {
  return 1 + node.children.reduce((n, c) => n + count(c), 0);
}

const tree: TreeNode<string> = {
  value: 'root',
  children: [{ value: 'a', children: [] }, { value: 'b', children: [{ value: 'c', children: [] }] }],
};

console.log(count(tree), JSON.stringify(doc).length);

4 72

Recursion in an object type is unrestricted, because it is lazy. The checker expands a branch only when something asks for it, so Json and TreeNode<T> cost nothing however deep they go.

That is very different from recursion in a conditional or mapped type, which is eager and limited: 999 tail-recursive instantiations, and 47 otherwise (§8.9). A recursive alias that describes a shape is cheap. A recursive alias that computes something is not.

The Json type above is worth keeping in a codebase. It is the honest type for the result of JSON.parse, where the standard library says any, which is a hole (§16.6), and assigning the result of a parse to a Json straight away is the cheapest safety improvement available at the edge of an API.

One limitation: a type alias may not refer to itself in a position that the checker must resolve eagerly. type Bad = Bad[] is fine (lazy), while type Worse = Worse & { a: 1 } is a circular-reference error, and the message names the alias.

5.18 exactOptionalPropertyTypes

exactOptionalPropertyTypes separates the two meanings of ?: with it on, an optional property may be missing, but may not be present and holding undefined.

// With --exactOptionalPropertyTypes
type Options = { retries?: number };

const absent: Options = {};                       // ✅ the property is not there

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Type 'undefined' is not assignable to type 'number' with 'exactOptionalPropertyTypes: true'.
  const explicit: Options = { retries: undefined };
}

// Opt back in where you mean it:
type Loose = { retries?: number | undefined };
const alsoFine: Loose = { retries: undefined };

console.log(absent, alsoFine, typeof neverCalled);

{} { retries: undefined } function

The distinction is not academic. 'retries' in options is false for the first and true for the second. Object.keys(options).length is 0 and 1. JSON.stringify writes {} for both, because it drops undefined values, which is a third behaviour again. Any code that loops over keys, merges objects or compares them cares which one it has.

The setting is off by default, even under strict, because turning it on in an existing codebase produces errors in one specific and common pattern: building an options object with { retries: maybeUndefined }. The fix is to leave the key out instead of setting it to undefined, which usually means a conditional spread, ...(retries !== undefined && { retries }), and that is a real edit at every such place.

Turn it on in a new project. The pattern it forbids is one you would rather not have, and the | undefined escape hatch is available wherever an explicit undefined really is part of the interface.

Note that it does not affect parameters: f(a?: number) still accepts f(undefined), because that is how JavaScript defaults work, and changing it would break every call that passes an optional value along.

5.19 noUncheckedIndexedAccess

noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds | undefined to the result of every index access on an array or an index signature. It closes the biggest silent hole in the type system.

// With --noUncheckedIndexedAccess
type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const nums = [1, 2, 3];
const first = nums[0];
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof first, number | undefined>>;

const dict: Record<string, number> = { a: 1 };
const got = dict['a'];
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof got, number | undefined>>;

// The three honest ways to proceed.
console.log(nums[0] ?? 0, nums.at(0), nums[10]);
for (const n of nums) console.log(n.toFixed(0));   // iteration is not an index access

1 1 undefined
1
2
3

Without the setting, nums[10] has type number and holds undefined, the unsoundness shown in §1.11. With it, the type tells the truth and every access must be handled.

The cost is real, and concentrated in loops. for (let i = 0; i < xs.length; i++) xs[i].foo needs a ! or a check, even though the loop bound makes it safe. Three ways to reduce it, in order of preference: loop with for...of, which is not an index access and is unaffected; destructure, since const [first] = xs also gives number | undefined but reads better with a default; and use ! deliberately where a bound really does guarantee the value, with the reasoning in a comment.

A tuple is unaffected at known positions. const p: [number, number] = [1, 2]; p[0] is number, because the length is known, which is one more argument for tuples over arrays when the number of elements is fixed.

Of the four settings in this section, this is the one to turn on first. Every "cannot read properties of undefined" from an array or a dictionary lookup is a bug it would have caught.

5.20 noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature

noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature requires bracket syntax for a property that comes from an index signature, and saves dot syntax for properties that were actually declared.

// With --noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature
type Env = { NODE_ENV: string; [key: string]: string };

declare const env: Env;

const declared = env.NODE_ENV;        // ✅ a real, declared property
const other = env['HOME'];            // ✅ bracket syntax for an index-signature key

function neverCalled(): string {
  // @ts-expect-error Property 'HOME' comes from an index signature, so it must be accessed with ['HOME'].
  return env.HOME;
}
console.log(typeof declared, typeof neverCalled);

string function

The value is that the syntax now records what you know. env.NODE_ENV is a documented key that someone declared, and env['HOME'] is a lookup that may find nothing. Without the setting both are written with a dot and the difference is invisible, so a typo in a declared name, env.NODE_EVN, silently falls through to the index signature and type-checks as string.

That is the bug it catches, and a good one: a misspelled property on a type with a string index signature produces no error at all by default.

Combine it with noUncheckedIndexedAccess and the pair is genuinely strong: brackets are required and give string | undefined, so a missing environment variable becomes a case you handle instead of the string "undefined" two layers further on.

The cost is a mechanical edit, dots to brackets, concentrated on process.env, configuration objects and header maps. It is much smaller than for either of the previous two settings, and it is the one most likely to be worth turning on in an existing codebase.

5.21 An Empty Object Type

An empty object type, written {}, does not mean "an object with no properties". It means anything except null and undefined.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Empty = {};

const a: Empty = { anything: 1 };
const b: Empty = 42;
const c: Empty = 'a string';
const d: Empty = [];

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Type 'null' is not assignable to type '{}'.
  const e: Empty = null;
}

// Which is why NonNullable is defined as T & {} (§9.6).
type _1 = Expect<Equal<NonNullable<string | null | undefined>, string>>;
console.log(a, b, c, d, typeof neverCalled);

{ anything: 1 } 42 a string [] function

Every primitive can be assigned to {}, because every primitive has methods ((42).toFixed works), so structurally a number does satisfy "an object type with no required members". Only null and undefined have no properties at all, and they are the only two that are excluded.

That is why {} is nearly useless as an annotation and genuinely useful as a filter: T & {} removes null and undefined, and it is the definition of NonNullable<T> (§9.6).

The failure to recognise is a derived type collapsing to {}. Omit on a union does it (§9.5), and so does Pick<T, never>. The symptom is that the editor offers no completions and every assignment is accepted, which means an annotation that has stopped checking. When a computed type stops rejecting things, check whether it has become {}.

@typescript-eslint/no-empty-object-type is the lint rule that flags a bare {} in an annotation. It is worth having on, with an exception for the T & {} idiom.

5.22 Weak Type Detection

Weak type detection is a second rule of thumb, next to excess property checking, for a type whose properties are all optional.

type Options = { retries?: number; timeout?: number; verbose?: boolean };

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Type '{ retires: number; }' has no properties in common with type 'Options'.
  const typo: Options = { retires: 3 };
}

const good: Options = { retries: 3 };
const empty: Options = {};              // ✅ an empty object IS a valid Options
console.log(good, empty, typeof neverCalled);

{ retries: 3 } {} function

Without the rule, { retires: 3 } would be perfectly assignable: every property of Options is optional, so an object with none of them satisfies it structurally, and a typo would go unnoticed.

The rule: if every property of the target is optional, the source must have at least one property in common. Note the wording, at least one and not all, which is why {} is still accepted and why an object with one correct key and one typo passes.

That limit is the thing to know. Weak type detection catches an options object that is entirely misspelled, and misses one that is partly misspelled:

type Options = { retries?: number; timeout?: number };

// Caught: nothing in common.
function a(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error no properties in common
  const x: Options = { retires: 3 };
}

// Also caught, by the excess property check this time.
function b(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error 'timout' does not exist in type 'Options'
  const y: Options = { retries: 3, timout: 100 };
}
console.log(typeof a, typeof b);

function function

The second is caught by excess property checking (§5.4) and not by weak type detection, which is why the two rules together cover the case, and why an object built through a variable or a spread escapes both. satisfies (§8.10) is the tool that brings the check back for those.

What This Section Established

A property has three independent settings, and ? mixes two of them until exactOptionalPropertyTypes separates them. readonly is shallow, is not checked on assignment, and gives real safety only within a single type. Object.freeze is the version the runtime knows about.

Excess property checking and weak type detection are two rules that protect object literals from typos, and both are defeated by going through a variable or a spread, where satisfies is the fix. An index signature is a promise that every key is present, which is false: noUncheckedIndexedAccess makes the type say so, and it is the first setting to turn on.

extends checks a combination at the declaration and reports conflicts. & builds it lazily and turns a conflict into a silent never. Use extends for declared object shapes and & for anything computed. Interface merging is a hazard inside one file, and the whole mechanism for extending types you do not own.

Tuples are arrays with a known length and a type for each position, with labels for the hints, optional and rest elements that mirror parameter lists, and a readonly form that as const produces. And {} means "not null and not undefined", which is why a derived type that collapses to it stops checking anything at all.

Exercises

1. Model a shape four ways and choose. Describe a User with a required id, an optional nickname, an immutable createdAt and an open bag of string metadata: as an inline object literal type, as an interface with extends, as an intersection, and as a generic. Say which you would ship and why, and show one thing that each of the other three cannot do.

2. Turn on the three settings. Take a small module that uses process.env, an array index in a loop, and an options object built with a possibly undefined value. Show the errors that exactOptionalPropertyTypes, noUncheckedIndexedAccess and noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature each produce, and fix each without an assertion.

3. Find the silent failures. Write four types that compile and are wrong: one where & produced a never member, one where a typo in an object literal escaped both rules, one where a derived type collapsed to {}, and one where readonly was defeated by an alias. For each, give the change that makes the compiler catch it.

Solution

1. Four models.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// (a) Inline object literal type.
type UserInline = {
  id: string;
  nickname?: string;
  readonly createdAt: string;
  meta: { [key: string]: string };
};

// (b) Interface with extends — the one to ship.
interface Entity { id: string; readonly createdAt: string }
interface UserIface extends Entity {
  nickname?: string;
  meta: { [key: string]: string };
}

// (c) Intersection.
type UserIntersection = Entity & { nickname?: string; meta: { [key: string]: string } };

// (d) Generic in the metadata value type.
interface UserGeneric<M = string> extends Entity {
  nickname?: string;
  meta: { [key: string]: M };
}

type _1 = Expect<Equal<UserIface['meta'], UserInline['meta']>>;

const u: UserIface = { id: 'u1', createdAt: '2026-09-01', meta: { source: 'signup' } };
const typed: UserGeneric<number> = { id: 'u2', createdAt: '2026-09-01', meta: { visits: 3 } };
console.log(u.meta.source, typed.meta.visits);

signup 3

Ship (b). Entity can be reused across every other record type, the combination is checked at the declaration (§5.8), the name survives into error messages, and, decisively for anything public, a user can extend UserIface through declaration merging (§5.9).

What the other three cannot do. (a) cannot be reused: the Entity half would be copied into every record type and would drift. (c) turns a conflicting member into a silent never instead of an error, and is worked out again at each use. (d) is the only one that makes the metadata value type a parameter, so it is what you want if the metadata values vary, and over-engineering if they do not (§7.14).

2. The four flags.

# noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature
error TS4111: Property 'NODE_ENV' comes from an index signature,
so it must be accessed with ['NODE_ENV'].

# noUncheckedIndexedAccess
error TS18048: 'rows[i]' is possibly 'undefined'.

# exactOptionalPropertyTypes
error TS2375: Type '{ retries: number | undefined; }' is not assignable to type
'Options' with 'exactOptionalPropertyTypes: true'. Consider adding 'undefined'
to the types of the target's properties.

type Options = { retries?: number };

// (a) process.env — bracket access, and handle the miss rather than asserting.
const env: Record<string, string | undefined> = { NODE_ENV: 'production' };
const mode = env['NODE_ENV'] ?? 'development';

// (b) The loop — for...of is not an index access, so the flag does not apply.
const rows = [{ n: 1 }, { n: 2 }];
let total = 0;
for (const row of rows) total += row.n;

// (c) The options object — omit the key rather than setting it undefined.
const maybe: number | undefined = undefined;
const options: Options = { ...(maybe !== undefined && { retries: maybe }) };

console.log(mode, total, options, 'retries' in options);

production 3 {} false

Each fix removes an assertion instead of adding one. ?? 'development' supplies the value that the type says might be missing. for...of avoids the index access entirely. And the conditional spread produces an object where the key is genuinely missing, which 'retries' in options reports as false, the distinction that exactOptionalPropertyTypes exists to make visible.

3. Four silent failures.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// (a) An intersection produced a `never` member — no error at the declaration.
type Conflicted = { status: number } & { status: string };
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Conflicted['status'], never>>;

// (b) A typo escaped both heuristics, because the object went through a variable.
type Options = { retries?: number; timeout?: number };
const built = { retries: 3, timout: 100 };
const escaped: Options = built;

// (c) A derived type collapsed to {} and stopped checking.
type Shape = { kind: 'a'; x: number } | { kind: 'b'; y: string };
type Collapsed = Omit<Shape, 'kind'>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Collapsed, {}>>;
const anything: Collapsed = { completely: 'unrelated' };

// (d) readonly defeated by an alias.
const config: { readonly host: string } = { host: 'a' };
const alias: { host: string } = config;
alias.host = 'b';

console.log(escaped, anything, config.host);

{ retries: 3, timout: 100 } { completely: 'unrelated' } b

(a) Use interface … extends. Two interfaces with a conflicting status produce an error at the declaration that names both types, while the intersection produces never and postpones the failure to the first value.

(b) Use satisfies. const built = { retries: 3, timout: 100 } satisfies Options brings back the excess property check at the point where the object is written, which is where the typo is. Assigning to a variable first is exactly the escape hatch that the check treats as intentional (§5.4).

(c) Use a distributive Omit, one that is applied to each variant of the union separately. type Collapsed = Shape extends unknown ? Omit<Shape, 'kind'> : never keeps the variants apart (§9.5). The sign to notice is that the editor offered no completions on Collapsed.

(d) There is no compiler fix, and that is the point. readonly is not part of assignability (§1.12), so the alias is legal by design. What works is Object.freeze, which makes the change fail at runtime in strict mode and returns a Readonly<T> that the checker also understands, the only construct in the subsection where the type and the runtime agree.

SECTION 6

Classes

A TypeScript class is a JavaScript class with a type layer added on top, and you can see where the two meet. Some of what this section covers is only a type annotation that disappears when you build: implements, abstract, private and the this type. Some of it produces extra code: parameter properties (a shortcut that declares a field in the constructor) and the rules for setting up fields, which the useDefineForClassFields setting selects. Knowing which is which is the difference between predicting what a class does and being surprised by it.

So the section is organised around two questions: what does the type layer add (visibility, abstract classes, this types, generic parameters, mixins) and what did the running language already have (fields, constructors, #private, static blocks, super). For the second group, TypeScript's job is to describe things accurately. Where it does not, as with private versus #private, you should know about it instead of having it glossed over.

Three things here trip up even experienced people:

  • private is erased. It exists only for the checker, so it protects nothing while the program runs.
  • A base class constructor cannot see a subclass's field initialisers. This is measured below. It produces an undefined that no type says is possible.
  • A static member cannot use the class's type parameter. The reason is obvious once you hear it and puzzling until then.

6.1 A Class Field

A class field is a property declared in the body of the class. TypeScript adds an optional type annotation and the same modifiers as a property of an object type.

class Account {
  id: string;                       // declared, assigned in the constructor
  balance = 0;                      // inferred `number` from the initialiser
  readonly openedAt: string;        // readonly: assignable only in the constructor
  nickname?: string;                // optional: `string | undefined`

  constructor(id: string, openedAt: string) {
    this.id = id;
    this.openedAt = openedAt;
  }
}

const a = new Account('acc-1', '2026-09-01');
a.balance += 100;
console.log(a.id, a.balance, a.openedAt, a.nickname);

acc-1 100 2026-09-01 undefined

A field with a starting value has its type inferred, exactly as a const does, except that a field can be changed, so a literal widens: balance = 0 is number, not 0. Annotate the field when you want something else.

A field declared without a starting value must be assigned in the constructor, under strictPropertyInitialization (§6.12). That setting is what makes the id declaration above safe.

readonly on a field allows assignment in the constructor and nowhere else. It gives the same shallow, assignment-only guarantee as on an object property (§5.3): a readonly array field can still be pushed to.

Fields are where the runtime rules changed with ES2022, and §6.14 covers what useDefineForClassFields chooses. The short version, needed already: a field's starting value is set at construction, in the order of declaration, after super() returns, which is why the base class in §6.19 cannot see it.

6.2 A Class Constructor

A class constructor is a method named constructor, and TypeScript lets you overload it exactly as you can overload a function (§4.15).

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

class Money {
  readonly cents: number;

  constructor(cents: number);
  constructor(major: number, minor: number);
  constructor(a: number, b?: number) {
    this.cents = b === undefined ? a : a * 100 + b;
  }

  toString(): string { return `${(this.cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`; }
}

type _1 = Expect<Equal<ConstructorParameters<typeof Money>, [major: number, minor: number]>>;

console.log(String(new Money(1234)), String(new Money(12, 34)));

12.34 12.34

A constructor has no return type annotation, because it always produces an instance, and writing one is an error.

ConstructorParameters<typeof Money> gives only the last overload's parameters, which the type test above confirms: it is [major: number, minor: number], not a union of both signatures. That is how ConstructorParameters and Parameters behave on any overloaded signature, and it is a real limitation of those utilities, not a quirk of this example.

A derived class's constructor must call super() before it touches this, and the compiler enforces that. If the derived class declares no constructor at all, one is created for it that passes every argument along.

A private or protected constructor stops code outside from creating instances, which is how a singleton, or a class that can only be made by a factory, is written:

class Registry {
  private static instance: Registry | undefined;
  private constructor(readonly createdAt: number) {}
  static get(): Registry {
    Registry.instance ??= new Registry(0);
    return Registry.instance;
  }
}

console.log(Registry.get() === Registry.get());

true

6.3 A Class Method

A class method is a function stored on the prototype. TypeScript types it exactly like a function, with one important difference from a property that holds a function.

class Cart {
  private items: { sku: string; qty: number }[] = [];

  add(sku: string, qty = 1): this { this.items.push({ sku, qty }); return this; }
  count(): number { return this.items.reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0); }
  find(sku: string): { sku: string; qty: number } | undefined {
    return this.items.find((i) => i.sku === sku);
  }
}

const cart = new Cart().add('a', 2).add('b');
console.log(cart.count(), cart.find('a')?.qty, cart.find('z'));

3 2 undefined

The parameters of a method are checked bivariantly (§4.14). That is the deliberate looseness that makes the methods of Array<T> work. A field that holds an arrow function is checked strictly under strictFunctionTypes. So for an interface you own where the callbacks matter, declaring handle: (e: E) => void instead of handle(e: E): void gives you a real check.

A method lives on the prototype, and an arrow field lives on each instance. That is a runtime difference with three consequences. The arrow is created again for every instance. The arrow captures this from where it is written, so it survives being passed around as a callback. And only the method is shared, so only the method can be patched. §6.17 is where this matters most.

Methods can be overloaded with the same syntax as functions, can be static, abstract, private, protected or override, and can declare a this parameter (§6.18), which is how you write a method that only makes sense on a particular receiver.

6.4 A Class Getter

A class getter is an accessor, and TypeScript infers its type from what it returns. The setter that goes with it may take a different type, which is one of the more useful things about the pair.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

class Temperature {
  #celsius = 0;

  get celsius(): number { return this.#celsius; }
  set celsius(value: number | string) {
    this.#celsius = typeof value === 'string' ? Number.parseFloat(value) : value;
  }

  get fahrenheit(): number { return this.#celsius * 9 / 5 + 32; }   // read-only: no setter
}

const t = new Temperature();
t.celsius = '21.5';                       // the setter accepts a string
console.log(t.celsius, t.fahrenheit);

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Cannot assign to 'fahrenheit' because it is a read-only property.
  t.fahrenheit = 100;
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

21.5 70.7
function

A getter with no setter is readonly from outside, which is the cleanest way to expose a value that is worked out from other fields.

The setter's parameter type may be wider than the getter's return type. Reading t.celsius gives number, while writing accepts number | string. This has been supported since TypeScript 4.3, and it is exactly right for a value that is cleaned up on the way in.

A getter's return type must be assignable to the setter's parameter type, and the compiler checks it, so the pair cannot describe a property you can write but not read back.

Getters are also where useDefineForClassFields causes trouble in inheritance: under the modern rules, a field in a derived class with the same name as an accessor in the base class hides it with a plain data property, and silently switches the accessor off. §6.14 covers it.

6.5 A Class Index Signature

A class index signature works exactly like the one in an object type (§5.5), and it is uncommon for good reason.

class Bag {
  [key: string]: number | ((k: string) => number);

  count = 0;
  get(k: string): number { return typeof this[k] === 'number' ? (this[k] as number) : 0; }
}

const b = new Bag();
b['apples'] = 3;
console.log(b['apples'], b.count, b.get('apples'), b.get('pears'));

3 0 3 0

Every member must be compatible with the index signature, methods included. That is why the signature above has to include a function type, and why the class ends up with an awkward union everywhere. It is the reason class index signatures are rare: adding one changes the type of every member.

The three alternatives are almost always better. A Map, when the keys are data. A private field holding a Record<string, T>, with typed accessors, which keeps the index signature off the class itself. A generic class (§6.15) that takes the value type as a parameter.

A class index signature is really right when you are describing an existing runtime object with dynamic properties, such as a .d.ts for a library whose instances carry arbitrary keys. In your own code, prefer composition.

To have in hand before moving on: a generic class.

6.6 The extends and implements Clauses

An extends clause creates a real prototype link. An implements clause is a check at the type level that a class satisfies an interface, and it produces no code.

interface Serialisable { toJSON(): unknown }
interface Identified { readonly id: string }

class Entity implements Identified {
  constructor(readonly id: string) {}
}

class Post extends Entity implements Serialisable {
  constructor(id: string, public title: string) { super(id); }
  toJSON(): unknown { return { id: this.id, title: this.title }; }
}

const p = new Post('p1', 'Hello');
console.log(JSON.stringify(p), p instanceof Entity);

{"id":"p1","title":"Hello"} true

implements is a check, not inheritance. It verifies that the class has the members and it adds nothing: no defaults, no method bodies, and, importantly, no types from context for the members:

interface Handler { handle(event: { type: string }): void }

class Broken implements Handler {
  // @ts-expect-error Parameter 'event' implicitly has an 'any' type.
  handle(event) { console.log(event.type); }
}

class Fixed implements Handler {
  handle(event: { type: string }): void { console.log(event.type); }
}

new Fixed().handle({ type: 'click' });
console.log(typeof Broken);

click
function

That surprises everyone once: the interface names the parameter type, and the class must still write it out. implements checks afterwards. It does not supply types beforehand. The workaround, when the shape is a callback, is to declare the member as a property with a function type and let its starting value take its types from that.

A class may implement several interfaces, and extend exactly one class. A class may also be used as an interface. implements SomeClass checks the shape of the instance, including private members, which makes it effectively impossible for an unrelated class to satisfy it (§10.10).

Gathered here, since each is referred to later: an implements clause and an extends clause.

6.7 Member Visibility and the public Modifier

Member visibility in TypeScript has three levels, and all three exist only at compile time. The public modifier is the default and is almost never written.

class Session {
  public readonly id: string;         // `public` is redundant here
  token: string;                      // ...and identical to this

  constructor(id: string, token: string) {
    this.id = id;
    this.token = token;
  }
}

const s = new Session('s1', 'secret');
console.log(s.id, s.token, Object.keys(s));

s1 secret [ 'id', 'token' ]

Write public in exactly one situation: on a parameter property (§6.11), where the modifier is what creates the field, and leaving it out would make the parameter an ordinary one.

The three levels in one line each. public: reachable everywhere, and the default. protected (§6.8): reachable in the class and its subclasses. private (§6.9): reachable only in the class that declares it.

All three are erased. The JavaScript that comes out has plain properties, and Object.keys(s) above lists everything regardless. That is the fact that makes the warning in §6.9 necessary, and the # field of §6.10 the real answer.

TypeScript's visibility is part of the type, so it affects assignability (§10.10): a class with a private member can only be assigned to another type that declares the same private member from the same declaration. That is the one place where TypeScript's shape-based typing becomes name-based, and it is occasionally exactly what you want.

6.8 The protected Modifier

The protected modifier makes a member visible inside the class that declares it and inside its subclasses, and invisible outside.

abstract class Repository {
  protected constructor(protected readonly table: string) {}
  protected query(sql: string): string { return `[${this.table}] ${sql}`; }
  abstract all(): string;
}

class UserRepository extends Repository {
  constructor() { super('users'); }
  all(): string { return this.query('SELECT *'); }        // protected: visible here
}

const repo = new UserRepository();
console.log(repo.all());

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Property 'query' is protected and only accessible within class 'Repository' and its subclasses.
  repo.query('SELECT 1');
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

[users] SELECT *
function

A subclass may widen a protected member to public by redeclaring it, which is the documented way to expose an inherited implementation detail. It may not narrow a public member to protected.

A protected member can be reached through this and through instances of the same subclass, but not through instances of the base class or of a sibling class. That last restriction catches people who write a compare(other: Base) method: other.protectedField is an error inside a subclass if other is typed as the base. Typing the parameter as this (§6.20) is the usual fix.

A protected constructor allows subclassing while forbidding a direct new. It is the shape used above, and it is how you write a base class that is abstract in spirit but must still be constructible by its subclasses.

Like every visibility modifier, protected is erased. Its value is in communicating the design and in a check at compile time, not in hiding anything.

6.9 The private Modifier

The private modifier limits a member to the class that declares it, at compile time only.

class Vault {
  private secret = 'hunter2';
  reveal(other: Vault): string { return other.secret; }   // same class: allowed
}

const v = new Vault();
