console.log(v.reveal(new Vault()));

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Property 'secret' is private and only accessible within class 'Vault'.
  console.log(v.secret);
}

// But at runtime it is an ordinary property.
console.log(JSON.stringify(v), Object.keys(v), (v as unknown as { secret: string }).secret);

hunter2
{"secret":"hunter2"} [ 'secret' ] hunter2

Read the last line. The "private" field can be listed, saved to JSON, and read with one assertion. private is a design rule for people reading your code, not a security boundary, and putting a credential behind it and calling it protected is a real mistake.

private is accessible across instances of the same class, as reveal shows. That is deliberate and matches C# and Java: privacy is per class, not per instance.

A private member makes the class name-based in its typing (§10.10). Two classes with identical shapes and private members cannot be assigned to each other, because the check compares the declaration the member came from. That is occasionally useful, since it acts as a cheap brand, and occasionally the cause of a baffling "Types have separate declarations of a private property" error when two copies of a package are installed.

Use #private (§6.10) instead in new code. It is real, it is JavaScript, and the only reasons to prefer private are that it can be reached from a subclass in some patterns and that # fields do not work with some older tools.

6.10 A Private Field in a Class

A private field in a class is written with #. It is a JavaScript feature, not a TypeScript one, and it is genuinely private while the program runs.

class Vault {
  #secret = 'hunter2';
  reveal(other: Vault): string { return other.#secret; }
  static isVault(x: unknown): x is Vault { return #secret in (x as object); }
}

const v = new Vault();
console.log(v.reveal(new Vault()));
console.log(JSON.stringify(v), Object.keys(v));
console.log(Vault.isVault(v), Vault.isVault({ secret: 'x' }));

hunter2
{} []
true false

Reaching for v.#secret from outside the class body is not merely a type error. It does not even parse, in TypeScript or in JavaScript:

error TS18013: Property '#secret' is not accessible outside class 'Vault'
because it has a private identifier.

{} and []: the field does not appear in JSON.stringify or Object.keys, because it is not a property at all. It is stored in a private slot per instance, and only code written inside the class body can name it.

#secret in x is the brand check, and it is the only test in JavaScript that cannot be faked. Vault.isVault({ secret: 'x' }) is false, and no amount of copying properties can make it true. That makes it the correct way to implement a this is T guard, or a replacement for instanceof across realms.

Three practical points.

Accessing #x on a value that does not have it is a TypeError, not undefined. That is why the in form exists: it tests without throwing.

A # field cannot be accessed from a subclass. Unlike private, there is no protected version. If a subclass needs the value, it must be protected or exposed through an accessor.

It survives every transform. private is erased and # is not, so the guarantee holds under esbuild, swc and Node's type stripping, which is exactly the property that private lacks.

6.11 A Parameter Property

A parameter property declares a field and assigns it from a constructor parameter, by putting a visibility modifier (or readonly) on the parameter. It is one of the four TypeScript constructs that produce code (§1.2).

class Point {
  constructor(
    public readonly x: number,
    private y = 0,
  ) {}
  sum(): number { return this.x + this.y; }
}

const p = new Point(3, 4);
console.log(p.sum(), Object.keys(p), new Point(1).sum());

7 [ 'x', 'y' ] 1

The constructor that comes out contains this.x = x; this.y = y;. Nothing else in the type-level material of this course does that.

The modifier is what creates the field. constructor(x: number) declares an ordinary parameter and no property, while constructor(public x: number) declares both. So public is not redundant here, unlike everywhere else (§6.7).

It is forbidden by erasableSyntaxOnly (§14.11), along with enum, namespace and legacy decorators, because a tool that only strips types cannot produce the assignment. If your build uses Node's type stripping, or esbuild without a TypeScript-aware step, parameter properties will silently not work: the field will be undefined.

The trade-off is real. Parameter properties remove a tedious repetition (declare, parameter, assign), and they are used constantly in Angular and NestJS codebases. The alternative is three lines per field, or a plain field with an options object as the parameter. If your project sets erasableSyntaxOnly, use ordinary fields. Otherwise this is a reasonable convenience.

6.12 strictPropertyInitialization

strictPropertyInitialization requires every non-optional field to be assigned by the end of the constructor. It is part of strict and depends on strictNullChecks.

class Config {
  host: string;
  port = 5432;
  nickname?: string;

  constructor(host: string) { this.host = host; }
}

console.log(new Config('db').host, new Config('db').port);

db 5432

Remove the assignment and the error names the field:

error TS2564: Property 'host' has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor.

The check is deliberately shallow. It looks for a direct assignment in the body of the constructor and does not follow into a helper method, so constructor() { this.reset(); } with reset() doing the assignment still fails. That is a false alarm from the point of view of what the code does, and a defensible one: a subclass could override reset, so the compiler cannot prove the field is set.

There are three legitimate ways past it, in order of preference. Assign in the constructor, including through a parameter property (§6.11). Give the field a default, which is usually what "it starts empty" means. Use the definite assignment assertion (§6.13) when a framework assigns the field, and only then.

The bug it catches is the classic one: a field that the constructor forgot, read later as undefined while its type says string. Without the setting that is invisible. With it, it is a compile error at the class.

6.13 The Definite Assignment Assertion

The definite assignment assertion is a ! after a field name (or a variable name), telling the compiler that something it cannot see assigns the value.

class Component {
  element!: HTMLElement;          // assigned by the framework before any method runs
  #ready = false;

  mount(el: HTMLElement): void { this.element = el; this.#ready = true; }
  render(): string { return this.#ready ? this.element.tagName : '(unmounted)'; }
}

const c = new Component();
console.log(c.render());

(unmounted)

element!: HTMLElement compiles under strictPropertyInitialization, and the field is undefined until mount runs, which is exactly what the code above demonstrates, and exactly the risk.

It is an assertion, with all the caveats of §2.11. It silences the checker and verifies nothing. this.element.tagName on a component that has not been mounted is a crash at runtime that the type system was told not to worry about, and the #ready guard above is doing the real work.

Three cases where it is the right tool, all sharing one property: something outside the constructor really does the assignment. A dependency-injection framework, a test fixture assigned in beforeEach, and a field filled in by a deserialiser.

And in each case the honest alternative is a union. element: HTMLElement | null = null says what is true, costs one narrowing per use, and that narrowing is exactly where the bug would have been. The ! trades that check for brevity, so keep it for cases where the framework's guarantee is really strong and the alternative would be a null check on every line.

The same ! on a let declaration, let x!: string;, does the same job for a variable that is assigned in a callback the checker cannot follow.

6.14 useDefineForClassFields

useDefineForClassFields chooses between two ways the running program sets up class fields, and it changes what the produced code does, not only what type-checks. It defaults to true when target is ES2022 or later, which under TypeScript 7 is every supported target.

The two ways: [[Define]] (the standard, with the setting on) creates the property with Object.defineProperty, always. [[Set]] (the old TypeScript behaviour, with the setting off) does a plain assignment, which runs any inherited setter.

class Base {
  name = 'base';
  constructor() { this.describe(); }
  describe(): void { console.log('Base constructor sees name =', this.name); }
}

class Sub extends Base {
  name = 'sub';
}

const s = new Sub();
console.log('after construction:', s.name);

Base constructor sees name = base
after construction: sub

That output is the trap, and it happens at runtime. A base class constructor cannot see the field initialisers of a subclass, because they run after super() returns. Any base class that calls an overridable method from its constructor will read the base's own values, or undefined for a field the base does not declare, and no type says so.

The other consequence of [[Define]] is that a field in a derived class hides an inherited accessor instead of calling it. With a get/set pair on the base and a plain field with the same name on the derived class, the setter never runs. Under the old [[Set]] behaviour it did, which is why this is a migration hazard for older codebases and not an abstract distinction.

Two things follow for how to write classes. Do not call an overridable method from a constructor. The fix is an init() that the caller invokes, or a factory function. Declare instead of initialising when a subclass will provide the value, using declare name: string in the base, which tells the compiler about the field and produces no code.

6.15 A Static Member and a Static Block

A static member belongs to the constructor, not to instances. A static block in a class runs once, when the class is defined, and can see private members. A static block in a class is written static { … }, with no name and no parameters.

class Counter {
  static #count = 0;
  static created: string;
  static #epoch: string;

  static {
    Counter.#epoch = new Date(0).toISOString();
    Counter.created = Counter.#epoch;
  }

  static next(): number { return ++Counter.#count; }
  static get total(): number { return Counter.#count; }
}

console.log(Counter.next(), Counter.next(), Counter.total, Counter.created);

1 2 2 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z

The main use of a static block is initialising several statics that depend on each other, in order, and reaching private statics while doing so. One thing it cannot do is worth knowing, because it looks like the obvious use: a static readonly field may not be assigned from a static block.

class C { static readonly created: string; static { C.created = 'x'; } }
error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'created' because it is a read-only property.

readonly on a static allows assignment only in its own initialiser, so a computed value must either be written inline, static readonly created = new Date(0).toISOString();, or the field must be mutable, as in the example above.

Statics are inherited. class Sub extends Counter {} gets Sub.next() through the prototype chain of the constructors, and Sub.next() increments the same #count, because there is one storage slot on Counter. That shared state is the usual source of surprise with static registries.

this inside a static member is the constructor, so this.next() works in a static method and refers to the subclass when called as Sub.next(). Writing Counter.next() explicitly pins it to the base.

The restriction that trips people up is in §6.16: a static member may not refer to the class's type parameter.

6.16 A Type Parameter in a Static Member

A type parameter in a static member is not allowed if it is the class's parameter, and is perfectly fine if the member declares its own.

class Registry<T> {
  #items: T[] = [];
  add(item: T): void { this.#items.push(item); }
  get size(): number { return this.#items.length; }

  // NOT ALLOWED — a static field cannot use the class's T (TS2302):
  // static all: T[] = [];

  // Allowed — a static METHOD may declare its own type parameter.
  static of<U>(...items: U[]): Registry<U> {
    const r = new Registry<U>();
    for (const i of items) r.add(i);
    return r;
  }
}

const strings = Registry.of('a', 'b', 'c');
console.log(strings.size);

3

Uncommenting the static field produces the error verbatim:

error TS2302: Static members cannot reference class type parameters.

The reason is erasure (§1.2). Registry<string> and Registry<number> are the same constructor object at runtime, since there is one static side shared by every instantiation. A static field typed T[] would therefore be a single array claiming two incompatible element types. The restriction is the type system refusing to state something false.

A static method that declares its own parameter is unaffected, because that parameter is worked out for each call, not for each instantiation. Registry.of<U> above is the standard shape for a static factory on a generic class, and it is the workaround whenever you wanted the class's T in a static.

The other workaround, when you really need separate static state for each instantiation, is to stop using statics: use a module-level Map<string, unknown> keyed by whatever tells the instantiations apart, or a factory function that returns a fresh class expression (§6.21), which does create a separate constructor for each call.

6.17 this at Runtime in a Class

this at runtime in a class follows JavaScript's rules, and TypeScript describes them instead of changing them.

class Greeter {
  constructor(private readonly name: string) {}

  greetMethod(): string { return `Hello, ${this.name}`; }
  greetArrow = (): string => `Hello, ${this.name}`;
}

const g = new Greeter('Ada');
const detachedMethod = g.greetMethod;
const detachedArrow = g.greetArrow;

console.log(g.greetMethod(), '|', detachedArrow());
try { detachedMethod(); } catch (e) { console.log('detached method:', (e as Error).constructor.name); }

Hello, Ada | Hello, Ada
detached method: TypeError

The method loses this when it is detached, and the arrow field does not. The arrow is created for each instance with this captured from where it is written, which is why it survives being passed to addEventListener, setTimeout or a React prop.

Three ways to handle it, with the trade-offs.

An arrow field. Correct by construction. It costs one function object per instance per field, and a subclass cannot override it with a prototype method, because the field hides it.

.bind(this) in the constructor. Same cost, keeps the behaviour of a prototype method, and needs one line per method.

Bind at the call site, as in onClick={() => g.greetMethod()}. It costs nothing per instance and is the usual answer in modern code.

TypeScript's contribution is strictBindCallApply (§13.10), which checks bind, call and apply against the declared parameters, and the this parameter of §6.18, which lets a method say what receiver it needs, so that detaching it is a compile error instead of a runtime one.

6.18 A this Parameter

A this parameter in a method declares what this must be, and it makes the detachment above catchable at compile time.

class Handle {
  constructor(readonly id: string) {}

  // Declaring `this` means the checker verifies the receiver.
  describe(this: Handle): string { return `handle ${this.id}`; }
}

const h = new Handle('h1');
console.log(h.describe());

function neverCalled(): void {
  const detached = h.describe;
  // @ts-expect-error The 'this' context of type 'void' is not assignable to method's 'this' of type 'Handle'.
  detached();
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

handle h1
function

Without the annotation, detached() compiles and then throws. With it, the mistake is a compile error at the call.

The this parameter is erased and does not count as a parameter (§4.8), so Parameters<typeof Handle.prototype.describe> is [].

It is most useful on a method you expect to be passed around, and in a .d.ts that describes an API whose callbacks have a bound receiver: jQuery-style plugins, DOM handlers, and the thisArg of Array.prototype.map.

A narrower this type is legal and useful. describe(this: Handle & { verbose: true }): string requires a receiver with an extra property, so the method can only be called on instances that qualify. That is a capability check at compile time with no cost at runtime.

6.19 A this Type

A this type is the keyword this used as a type. In a class it means "the type of the actual receiver", which is the subclass when the method is called on one, and that is what makes fluent APIs inherit correctly.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

class QueryBuilder {
  protected parts: string[] = [];
  select(cols: string): this { this.parts.push(`SELECT ${cols}`); return this; }
  from(table: string): this { this.parts.push(`FROM ${table}`); return this; }
  build(): string { return this.parts.join(' ') + ';'; }
}

class PostgresBuilder extends QueryBuilder {
  returning(cols: string): this { this.parts.push(`RETURNING ${cols}`); return this; }
}

const q = new PostgresBuilder().select('*').from('users').returning('id');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof q, PostgresBuilder>>;

console.log(q.build());

SELECT * FROM users RETURNING id;

select() returned this, so on a PostgresBuilder it returns a PostgresBuilder, and .returning() is available after it. Annotate the return as QueryBuilder instead and the chain breaks at exactly that point, with an error saying that returning does not exist.

That is the whole feature, and it is why this is the right return type for any method that returns the receiver: setters in a fluent API, add, with and without builders, and change methods that support chaining.

A this type changes with the receiver, so it is not the same as writing the class name. It also works in parameter position: equals(other: this): boolean requires the argument to be the same subclass, which is stronger and occasionally what you want.

The limit: this as a type is not available in a static member, for the same reason as §6.16, since there is one static side. static create(): this is an error. The workaround is a type parameter on the static method, constrained by a construct signature.

6.20 A this-Based Type Guard

A this-based type guard is a method whose return type is this is T. It narrows the receiver itself, which no ordinary predicate can do.

abstract class FsNode {
  constructor(readonly name: string) {}
  isDirectory(): this is Directory { return this instanceof Directory; }
  isFile(): this is FileNode { return this instanceof FileNode; }
}

class FileNode extends FsNode {
  constructor(name: string, readonly bytes: number) { super(name); }
}

class Directory extends FsNode {
  readonly children: FsNode[] = [];
  add(child: FsNode): this { this.children.push(child); return this; }
}

function size(node: FsNode): number {
  if (node.isFile()) return node.bytes;                       // narrowed to FileNode
  if (node.isDirectory()) return node.children.reduce((n, c) => n + size(c), 0);
  return 0;
}

const root = new Directory('root').add(new FileNode('a.txt', 100)).add(
  new Directory('sub').add(new FileNode('b.txt', 20)),
);
console.log(size(root));

120

The narrowing applies to the receiver, so node.bytes and node.children are available in their own branches with no assertion.

The advantage of this pattern over a free-standing predicate function (§3.9) is that it is easy to find: the check lives on the type, so an editor offers isFile() on any FsNode. The disadvantage is coupling. The base class has to know about its subclasses, which is a design smell in some hierarchies and completely normal in a closed one such as a file tree or an AST.

A this is T guard on a field is also legal, and it is how you can express a state with no label field: readonly loaded: this is LoadedState on a class with a boolean field of that name. That is rarer, and worth knowing exists.

For a class hierarchy the honest alternative is a discriminated union (§3.12) of plain object types, which needs no classes at all and gives you exhaustiveness (§3.14) for free. Use this is T when you are committed to classes, and a discriminated union when you are choosing.

6.21 A Class Expression

A class expression is a class written where an expression is expected. It may be anonymous, and it creates a fresh constructor each time it is evaluated.

const Point = class {
  constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {}
  toString(): string { return `(${this.x}, ${this.y})`; }
};

console.log(String(new Point(1, 2)));

// A named class expression: the name is visible only inside the class body.
const Tagged = class Inner {
  readonly tag = Inner.name;
};
console.log(new Tagged().tag);

// A factory producing a fresh class per call — one static side each.
function makeCounter(start: number) {
  return class {
    static count = start;
    static next(): number { return this.count++; }
  };
}
const A = makeCounter(10);
const B = makeCounter(100);
console.log(A.next(), A.next(), B.next());

(1, 2)
Inner
10 11 100

The name of a named class expression is only visible inside its body, which is how Inner.name works above while Inner cannot be reached from outside.

Each evaluation creates a separate constructor with its own statics, which the counter demonstrates: A and B do not share count. That is the workaround for the restriction in §6.16 when you really need separate static state for each instantiation.

A class expression is what a mixin returns (§6.25), which is its most important use. It is also how you create a class conditionally, or with a base chosen while the program runs: class extends (isProd ? Fast : Debug) {} is legal, though its type is often any unless the base is a single known type.

The type of const Point = class {…} is the anonymous constructor type, and naming the instance type needs InstanceType<typeof Point> (§9.8), which is one more reason to prefer a declaration when you have the choice.

6.22 The override Keyword and noImplicitOverride

The override keyword marks a member as deliberately replacing one from the base class, and noImplicitOverride makes it mandatory.

// Compiled with --noImplicitOverride; without it, only the second error fires.
class Base {
  greet(): string { return 'base'; }
  farewell(): string { return 'bye'; }
}

class Good extends Base {
  override greet(): string { return 'good'; }
}

class Missing extends Base {
  // @ts-expect-error This member must have an 'override' modifier because it overrides a member in the base class 'Base'.
  greet(): string { return 'missing'; }
}

class Wrong extends Base {
  // @ts-expect-error This member cannot have an 'override' modifier because it is not declared in the base class 'Base'.
  override fairwell(): string { return 'typo'; }
}

console.log(new Good().greet(), new Base().greet(), typeof Missing, typeof Wrong);

good base function function

Both errors are real bugs. The missing-override case is a method that silently replaced a base implementation, usually because someone added it to the base later, and now the unrelated method in the subclass hides it. The wrong-override case is a typo: fairwell was meant to override farewell, and without the keyword it would simply be a new method that nothing ever calls.

That second one is the more valuable catch, and it is invisible without the setting. A subclass that meant to override and misspelled the name compiles, runs, and uses the base implementation forever.

noImplicitOverride is not part of strict and has to be switched on separately. tsc --init includes it commented out. It is cheap to adopt: the fix is mechanical, and the compiler tells you every place.

override on a member that also exists in an implemented interface is not required, because implements is a check and not inheritance (§6.6). The keyword is only about the prototype chain.

6.23 An Abstract Class and an Abstract Member

An abstract class cannot be instantiated. An abstract member declares a signature that a concrete subclass must implement.

abstract class Shape {
  constructor(readonly name: string) {}

  abstract area(): number;                 // no body: subclasses must supply one
  abstract readonly sides: number;

  describe(): string { return `${this.name}: ${this.area().toFixed(2)} (${this.sides} sides)`; }
}

class Square extends Shape {
  readonly sides = 4;
  constructor(private readonly side: number) { super('square'); }
  area(): number { return this.side ** 2; }
}

console.log(new Square(3).describe());

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Cannot create an instance of an abstract class.
  new Shape('x');
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

square: 9.00 (4 sides)
function

abstract is entirely erased. The class that comes out is an ordinary one, and new Shape('x') at runtime, reached through an any or from JavaScript, works and produces an object whose area is undefined. The protection exists only at compile time.

An abstract member may be a method, a property, an accessor or an index signature, and a concrete subclass must implement every one. A subclass that is itself abstract may leave some unimplemented.

describe() calling this.area() is the template-method pattern, and it is the main reason to use an abstract class instead of an interface: the base supplies shared behaviour that depends on what the subclass provides. An interface can only declare.

The choice against an interface: use an abstract class when there is shared implementation or state, and an interface when there is only a contract. And remember the warning in §6.14: an abstract base must not call an overridable method from its constructor, because the fields of the subclass are not yet set.

6.24 An Abstract Construct Signature

An abstract construct signature, abstract new (...args) => T, describes a constructor that may be abstract. It is what a factory or a registry needs when the classes it stores include abstract bases.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

abstract class Animal { abstract speak(): string; }
class Dog extends Animal { speak(): string { return 'woof'; } }

type Concrete<T> = new (...args: never[]) => T;
type AnyCtor<T> = abstract new (...args: never[]) => T;

const concrete: Concrete<Animal> = Dog;          // ✅ Dog is concrete
const anyCtor: AnyCtor<Animal> = Animal;         // ✅ abstract accepted here

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Cannot assign an abstract constructor type to a non-abstract constructor type.
  const bad: Concrete<Animal> = Animal;
}

console.log(new concrete().speak(), typeof anyCtor, typeof neverCalled);

woof function function

A concrete construct signature correctly rejects an abstract class, because you cannot new it. That is the check working, and it is the error people hit when writing a mixin or a dependency-injection container.

abstract new accepts both, which is what you want for anything that describes constructors without creating instances: a registry of subclasses, the parameter of a decorator, the base constraint of a mixin (§6.25).

You cannot call new on a value of an abstract construct type, which is the trade-off: the type says "this may be abstract", so the compiler will not let you instantiate it. If you need both, accepting abstract bases and creating instances, you need the concrete signature and must exclude abstract classes.

The never[] in the parameter list is the §8.4 idiom: it matches every constructor without bringing in any. For a factory that must also check the arguments, use a generic tuple (§7.9).

6.25 A Mixin and a Constrained Mixin

A mixin is a function that takes a class and returns a subclass of it with extra members. It is the standard way to combine behaviours in a language with single inheritance, and TypeScript types it with a construct signature plus a class expression.

type Constructor<T = {}> = new (...args: any[]) => T;

function Timestamped<TBase extends Constructor>(Base: TBase) {
  return class extends Base {
    readonly stamped = 1700000000000;
    age(now: number): number { return now - this.stamped; }
  };
}

function Serialisable<TBase extends Constructor>(Base: TBase) {
  return class extends Base {
    toJSON(): string { return JSON.stringify({ ...this }); }
  };
}

class Note { constructor(public text = 'hello') {} }

const Rich = Serialisable(Timestamped(Note));
const n = new Rich('hi');
console.log(n.text, n.age(1700000000010), n.toJSON());

hi 10 {"text":"hi","stamped":1700000000000}

Three details make this work, and each is a place where it commonly does not.

new (...args: any[]) => T is the one place where any[] is truly required. The class a mixin returns must pass any constructor arguments on to Base, and never[], correct everywhere else in this course, makes the extends Base clause reject them. This is a documented exception, not a slip.

The return type is inferred, and it has to be: writing it out would mean naming an anonymous class expression. That is why a mixin is written as a function returning a class, and why its result is used directly and not annotated.

The mixin returns a class expression (§6.21), so each call creates a fresh constructor.

A constrained mixin requires the base to have particular members, which is how a mixin can use what it extends:

type Constructor<T = {}> = new (...args: any[]) => T;
type HasName = { name: string };

function Loggable<TBase extends Constructor<HasName>>(Base: TBase) {
  return class extends Base {
    log(): string { return `[${this.name}] ok`; }     // `name` guaranteed by the constraint
  };
}

class Service { constructor(public name = 'svc') {} }
const LoggableService = Loggable(Service);
console.log(new LoggableService('auth').log());

[auth] ok

TBase extends Constructor<HasName> is the constraint, and it is checked at the call: Loggable(class {}) is an error that names the missing name. That turns "this mixin only works on classes that have a name" from a comment into a contract checked at compile time.

What This Section Established

Fields, constructors, methods, getters and statics are JavaScript. TypeScript adds annotations, visibility and abstractness on top, and all of the additions are erased. private is a design rule that JSON.stringify ignores. #private is real, is a JavaScript feature, and #field in x is the only brand check that nothing can fake.

Two constructs produce code and should be known as such: a parameter property (banned by erasableSyntaxOnly) and the field set-up rules that useDefineForClassFields chooses. That is why a base constructor sees base, not sub, and why calling an overridable method from a constructor is a bug.

this has three roles in the type layer: a parameter that constrains the receiver, a return type that makes fluent chains inherit, and a this is T guard that narrows the receiver itself. A static member may not use the class's type parameter, because there is one constructor object and one static side, and a static method's own parameter is the workaround.

override with noImplicitOverride catches the misspelled override that silently does nothing, which is invisible otherwise. Abstract classes give you the template-method pattern, and need abstract new in any signature that must accept them. And a mixin is a function that returns a class expression, with any[] in the constructor signature as the one place this course allows it.

Exercises

1. Encapsulate four ways. Take a class holding a token that must not leak. Implement it with private, with #, with a closure, and with a WeakMap, then show for each whether the token appears in JSON.stringify, in Object.keys, and under an as unknown as assertion. Say which you would ship and why.

2. Find the initialisation bug. Write a base class whose constructor calls an overridable method, a subclass with a field that the base's method reads, and show the value it actually sees. Then fix it two ways, one that keeps the base's call and one that removes it, and say which setting or construct made the bug invisible.

3. Build a constrained mixin pipeline. Write two mixins, one unconstrained and one requiring an id: string, compose them onto a class, and show: a working composition, a compile error from applying the constrained mixin to a class without id, and the resulting instance's type including the members of both mixins, checked with a type test.

Solution

1. Four encapsulations.

class WithPrivate { constructor(private token: string) {} }

class WithHash { #token: string; constructor(t: string) { this.#token = t; } }

function makeClosure(token: string) {
  return { use(): number { return token.length; } };
}

const tokens = new WeakMap<object, string>();
class WithWeakMap {
  constructor(t: string) { tokens.set(this, t); }
  use(): number { return tokens.get(this)?.length ?? 0; }
}

const p = new WithPrivate('secret');
const h = new WithHash('secret');
const c = makeClosure('secret');
const w = new WithWeakMap('secret');

console.log('private :', JSON.stringify(p), Object.keys(p), (p as unknown as { token: string }).token);
console.log('#hash   :', JSON.stringify(h), Object.keys(h));
console.log('closure :', JSON.stringify(c), Object.keys(c), c.use());
console.log('weakmap :', JSON.stringify(w), Object.keys(w), w.use());

private : {"token":"secret"} [ 'token' ] secret
#hash   : {} []
closure : {} [ 'use' ] 6
weakmap : {} [] 6

private leaks all three ways: it is in the JSON, in the keys, and one assertion reads it. The other three leak none.

Ship #. It is a language feature, it survives every transform including type stripping (§6.10), it costs nothing, and #token in x gives you an unforgeable brand check as a bonus. The closure version cannot take part in a class hierarchy and creates every method again for each instance. The WeakMap version works but adds a module-level global and a lookup on every access, which makes it the right choice only when you must add private state to objects you did not construct.

2. The initialisation bug.

class BaseBroken {
  constructor() { console.log('base sees:', this.label()); }
  label(): string { return 'base'; }
}

class SubBroken extends BaseBroken {
  prefix = '>>';
  override label(): string { return `${this.prefix} sub`; }
}

new SubBroken();

base sees: undefined sub

this.prefix is undefined, and the type says it is string. The subclass's field initialisers run after super() returns, so the base constructor calls an override that reads a field that does not exist yet.

Fix A — keep the call, move the work out of the constructor:

class BaseA {
  init(): void { console.log('base sees:', this.label()); }
  label(): string { return 'base'; }
}
class SubA extends BaseA {
  prefix = '>>';
  override label(): string { return `${this.prefix} sub`; }
}
const a = new SubA();
a.init();

base sees: >> sub

Fix B — remove the call, and let the subclass pass the value up:

class BaseB {
  constructor(label: string) { console.log('base sees:', label); }
}
class SubB extends BaseB {
  constructor(readonly prefix = '>>') { super(`${prefix} sub`); }
}
new SubB();

base sees: >> sub

What made the bug invisible is the standard field behaviour of useDefineForClassFields (§6.14) combined with the type system having no idea of the order of initialisation. prefix is declared string and is undefined at that moment, and nothing in the type layer can say "not yet". strictPropertyInitialization does not help, because the field is initialised, just later than the read.

Fix B is the better one. A constructor that calls an overridable method is a hazard even when it works today, because a future subclass brings the same bug back.

3. A constrained mixin pipeline.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Constructor<T = {}> = new (...args: any[]) => T;

// Unconstrained: adds behaviour that needs nothing from the base.
function Versioned<TBase extends Constructor>(Base: TBase) {
  return class extends Base {
    readonly version = 1;
    bump(): number { return this.version + 1; }
  };
}

// Constrained: requires `id`, and uses it.
function Auditable<TBase extends Constructor<{ id: string }>>(Base: TBase) {
  return class extends Base {
    audit(action: string): string { return `${this.id}:${action}`; }
  };
}

class Record_ { constructor(public id: string) {} }

const Full = Auditable(Versioned(Record_));
const r = new Full('r1');

type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof r.version, 1>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof r.audit>, string>>;

console.log(r.id, r.version, r.bump(), r.audit('read'));

class NoId { constructor(public name = 'x') {} }
function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Property 'id' is missing in type 'NoId'.
  const Bad = Auditable(NoId);
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

r1 1 2 r1:read
function

The order of composition matters, and the constraint checks the combined base. Auditable(Versioned(Record_)) works because the class that Versioned returns still has id: a mixin's return type includes the base's members, which is what makes chaining possible at all.

The constraint fires at the call, naming the missing member: Auditable(NoId) is an error on that line and not inside the body of the mixin. That is the value of Constructor<{ id: string }> over a bare Constructor: the requirement is part of the signature.

The type tests confirm that the members of both mixins survive. r.version and r.audit are both present and correctly typed on the final instance, without any of the three classes being named in an annotation. The whole chain is inferred, which is why a mixin's return type must not be written out.

SECTION 7

Generics

A function that works for one type is easy to write. A function that works for every type and still says something true about how its input relates to its output is what generics are for, and the second half of that sentence is the part people skip. function first(arr: any[]): any works for every type, but it throws away the one interesting fact: the result has the same type as the elements of the array you passed in.

That is the whole idea: a generic is a type with a blank in it, and the blank is filled in each time you use it. Array<T> is not one type but a family of them, and so are Promise<T>, Map<K, V>, Set<T> and Record<K, V>. When you make something generic you write a rule that connects the types on the way in with the types on the way out, and the checker applies that rule at every call.

The section builds this up in order: parameters and arguments, then inference (the compiler filling the blank for you), then constraints (limits on what may fill it), then three refinements (defaults, const, and factories). Its second half tackles the part that is genuinely hard and rarely taught: variance, the answer to "is a Box<Dog> also a Box<Animal>?", which explains a whole family of assignability errors that otherwise look arbitrary. It closes with the question worth asking before all of it: is a generic the right tool here at all?

7.1 Type Parameters and Type Arguments

A type parameter is declared in angle brackets and is a variable that stands for a type. A type argument is what you fill it in with where you use it. Keep the two words straight, because the error messages use them precisely.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// T is a type parameter; it is declared once and used twice in the signature.
function firstOr<T>(items: readonly T[], fallback: T): T {
  return items.length > 0 ? items[0]! : fallback;
}

// `string` here is a type argument, supplied explicitly.
const a = firstOr<string>(['x', 'y'], 'z');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof a, string>>;

console.log(firstOr([1, 2, 3], 0), firstOr<string>([], 'empty'));

1 empty

Read the signature as a promise about relationships, not as three separate annotations. It says: whatever T turns out to be, the array holds Ts, the fallback is a T, and the result is a T. The compiler holds you to all three, which is what stops firstOr(['a'], 0), a mistake that any[] would have accepted silently.

A note on names, because they tell the next reader something. T is the usual single parameter, K and V are a key and a value, E is an element, and R is a result. Beyond two parameters, use words: <Row, Key> reads better than <T, U>, and the compiler does not care. The one really bad habit is a single-letter name for a parameter that appears in six places, because then the error messages say T and you have to go and look it up.

A type parameter belongs only to the thing that declares it. In the function above, T exists for the length of one call, and two calls of firstOr have unrelated Ts. That is what makes a type parameter different from a type alias: the alias names one fixed type, while the parameter names a different type each time it is used.

Giving a type argument explicitly, as firstOr<string>([], 'empty') does, is the exception, not the rule. It is needed when there is nothing to infer from (an empty array here), and it is useful for pinning a type down on purpose. Most of the time you leave it out, and §7.2 is about what happens then.

7.2 Generic Inference from Arguments

Generic inference from arguments is why generics are pleasant to use instead of noisy. When you leave out the type arguments, the checker looks at the values you passed, matches them against the parameter types, and works out each type parameter.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function pair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B] { return [a, b]; }

const p = pair('id', 42);
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof p, [string, number]>>;

// Two candidates for one parameter: the checker picks their best common supertype.
type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };
declare const dog: Dog;
declare const animal: Animal;
function bothOf<T>(a: T, b: T): T[] { return [a, b]; }
const widened = bothOf('x', 'y');
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof widened, string[]>>;      // two literals -> string
const supertyped = bothOf(dog, animal);
type _3 = Expect<Equal<typeof supertyped, Animal[]>>;   // Dog and Animal -> Animal
// @ts-expect-error string and number have no common supertype among the candidates
bothOf('x', 3);

// Inference through a callback: T comes from the array, U from the return.
function mapAll<T, U>(items: readonly T[], f: (item: T, index: number) => U): U[] {
  return items.map(f);
}
const lengths = mapAll(['aa', 'bbb'], (s) => s.length);
type _4 = Expect<Equal<typeof lengths, number[]>>;
console.log(lengths);

[ 2, 3 ]

Three behaviours are visible there, and each explains a kind of confusion.

Each parameter is inferred on its own. pair('id', 42) works out A from the first argument and B from the second, with no interaction.

When one parameter has several candidates, they are reconciled to the best common supertype, not to their union. This is worth measuring instead of assuming, because the union answer is widely repeated and wrong. bothOf('x', 'y') gives string[]: two literal candidates widen to the type that covers both. bothOf(dog, animal) gives Animal[]: one candidate is a supertype of the other, so it wins. And bothOf('x', 3) is a compile error, because none of the candidates covers both, so the checker fixes T from the first argument and reports the second as a mismatch. A union appears only when a single argument's own type is already a union: allOf(['x', 3]) infers (string | number)[], because the element type of the array literal was a union before inference started. When you want the union across parameters, say so with an explicit type argument, bothOf<string | number>('x', 3), and when you want inference to consider only one argument, §4.17's NoInfer is the tool.

Inference goes left to right through the parameter list, which is why the callback in mapAll gets a typed parameter for free. By the time the checker reaches f, it has already worked out T from items, so the arrow's s is known to be string with no annotation. Reverse the parameters, mapAll(f, items), and the arrow's parameter becomes an implicit any under noImplicitAny, because nothing has told the checker what T is yet. Put the value you infer from before the callback that uses it. It is the most important ordering decision in a generic signature.

Inference works from the types of the arguments, and those come from ordinary inference, so a literal in an argument position widens. pair('id', 42) gave [string, number], not ['id', 42]. The const type parameter of §7.8 is the switch that changes this, and it exists because "I want the literal" is a common request that nothing else can meet.

7.3 Generic Types and Generic Interfaces

A generic type is a type alias with type parameters, and a generic interface is the same idea for an interface. Both are used by supplying type arguments, and neither exists at runtime.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };

interface Repository<Entity, Id> {
  find(id: Id): Entity | undefined;
  save(entity: Entity): Id;
}

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Result<number, string>, { ok: true; value: number } | { ok: false; error: string }>>;

// A generic interface can be partially applied by aliasing it.
type UserRepo = Repository<{ id: string; name: string }, string>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Parameters<UserRepo['find']>, [id: string]>>;

Result<T, E> is the type worth understanding well, because it is the shape most real error handling wants (§10.20), and it shows a generic type doing something an ordinary alias cannot: the relationship between ok and which of value or error is present is kept for every pair of type arguments.

The choice between a generic type and a generic interface follows the same rule as in the non-generic case (§2.10), with one addition. An interface can be extended and merged, and an alias can be a union, an intersection, a conditional or a mapped type. Result above must be an alias, because an interface cannot be a union. Repository could be either, and interface is the usual choice for a shape that implementations will declare themselves against.

Type arguments are supplied by name and number: Repository on its own is an error ("Generic type 'Repository' requires 2 type arguments"), unless a parameter has a default (§7.7). A generic type with the wrong number of arguments is one of the clearest errors the compiler produces, and one of the few where the message tells you exactly how to fix it.

One thing that surprises people coming from Java or C#: two uses of a generic type are compared by shape, not by name. Repository<User, string> and a hand-written object with matching find and save are the same type, and Box<string> and Container<string> are interchangeable if their members match. The type parameter is not a name tag. §7.13's phantom type parameter exists to buy that property back when you need it.

7.4 A Type Parameter in a Class

A type parameter in a class is declared on the class and is available to every instance member. It behaves like a function's type parameter, with one hard restriction worth knowing before you hit it.

class Stack<T> {
  #items: T[] = [];
  push(item: T): this { this.#items.push(item); return this; }
  pop(): T | undefined { return this.#items.pop(); }
  get size(): number { return this.#items.length; }
  map<U>(f: (item: T) => U): Stack<U> {
    const out = new Stack<U>();
    for (const item of this.#items) out.push(f(item));
    return out;
  }
}

const numbers = new Stack<number>().push(1).push(2).push(3);
const labels = numbers.map((n) => `#${n}`);
console.log(numbers.size, labels.pop(), numbers.pop());

3 #3 3

Two type parameters are at work here. T belongs to the class and is fixed for the life of an instance, while U belongs to the map method and is worked out for each call. That is the standard arrangement, and it is how Array.prototype.map is typed.

The restriction: a static member cannot use the class's type parameter. There is exactly one static side per class, shared by every instantiation, so there is no T for it to refer to:

class Registry<T> {
  static all: unknown[] = [];        // ✅
  // @ts-expect-error Static members cannot reference class type parameters.
  static typed: T[] = [];
  add(item: T): void { Registry.all.push(item); }
}
console.log(new Registry<string>().add('a'), Registry.all.length);

undefined 1

That is not an arbitrary rule. It is the erasure story (§1.2) again: Registry<string> and Registry<number> are the same constructor object at runtime, so a static field typed T[] would be one array claiming two incompatible types. §6.16 covers the workaround: a static method may declare its own type parameter, which is how a generic factory (§7.9) is usually written.

The inference note for classes is that new Stack() with no argument and no annotation gives Stack<unknown>, because there is nothing to infer from. Either annotate the variable, supply the type argument, or give the constructor a parameter that carries the type. The third is usually best: new Stack([1, 2, 3]) needs no annotation at all.

7.5 Generic Constraints

An unconstrained type parameter is genuinely opaque. T could be anything, so you may not read a property from it, call it, or compare it. A generic constraint, written T extends Something, limits what T can be and, in exchange, tells the checker what it may assume inside.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T {
  return a.length >= b.length ? a : b;      // .length is legal: the constraint promises it
}

console.log(longest('hello', 'hi'), longest([1, 2], [1, 2, 3]).length);

// The constraint is a lower bound on what callers may pass, not on what they get back.
const kept = longest([1, 2], [3]);
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof kept, number[]>>;

// @ts-expect-error a number has no length
const bad = longest(1, 2);

hello 3

The return type is T, not { length: number }, and that is the whole reason to write the generic instead of annotating the parameters as { length: number } directly. longest([1, 2], [3]) gives back a number[] with all its array methods intact, while the non-generic version would give back something that only has a length.

A generic constraint is checked at the call with ordinary assignability, so it goes by shape: anything with a numeric length qualifies, including a string, an array, a NodeList and an object you wrote this morning.

The constraints you will actually write are a short list, and each has a reason:

  • T extends object: excludes primitives, so spreading and looping over keys are safe.
  • T extends PropertyKey: a string | number | symbol, for anything used as a key.
  • T extends readonly unknown[]: a tuple or array, where readonly means "I will not change it", so callers may pass a readonly array too.
  • T extends (...args: never[]) => unknown: any function, without bringing in any (§8.4).
  • T extends Record<string, unknown>: a plain object used as a dictionary.

And the one to avoid: T extends any and T extends unknown restrict nothing, and are usually a sign that the parameter should not be generic at all, or that a distributive conditional (§8.5) was what you actually meant.

7.6 Using a Type Parameter in a Constraint

Using a type parameter in a constraint, as in K extends keyof T, is what makes a generic relational instead of just polymorphic (working for any type at all). It is the pattern behind every type-safe property accessor, and once you have seen it you will use it constantly.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function getProp<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}

const user = { id: 7, name: 'Ada', active: true };

const userName = getProp(user, 'name');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof userName, string>>;
const userId = getProp(user, 'id');
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof userId, number>>;

console.log(userName, userId);
// @ts-expect-error 'emial' is not a key of user
getProp(user, 'emial');

Ada 7

Notice what the signature achieves that no non-generic one could: the return type depends on the value of the argument. getProp(user, 'name') is string and getProp(user, 'id') is number, from one declaration. The mechanism is that K is inferred as the literal type 'name'. It stays a literal because the parameter type keyof T is a union of literal types, and inference against a union of literals does not widen. Then T[K] (§8.2) looks the type up.

The same shape with a setter is where the safety really shows:

function setProp<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K, value: T[K]): T {
  return { ...obj, [key]: value };
}

const user = { id: 7, name: 'Ada', active: true };
console.log(setProp(user, 'name', 'Grace').name, setProp(user, 'active', false).active);
// @ts-expect-error the value must match the type at that key
setProp(user, 'id', 'seven');

Grace false

value: T[K] ties the third argument to the second, so setProp(user, 'id', 'seven') is rejected while setProp(user, 'id', 8) is fine: one signature covering every property of every object, each with the right type.

The general point is worth stating: using a type parameter in a constraint lets one type parameter be defined in terms of another, and the order matters only in that a parameter may refer to ones declared before it. <T, K extends keyof T> is legal, and <K extends keyof T, T> is not.

7.7 Generic Parameter Defaults

A generic parameter default supplies a type argument when the caller leaves it out, with exactly the syntax of a default function parameter: <T = string>.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type ApiResult<Data, Meta = Record<string, never>> = {
  data: Data;
  meta: Meta;
};

type _1 = Expect<Equal<ApiResult<string>, { data: string; meta: Record<string, never> }>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<ApiResult<string, { page: number }>, { data: string; meta: { page: number } }>>;

// A default may refer to an earlier parameter.
type Dict<V, K extends PropertyKey = string> = Record<K, V>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Dict<number>, Record<string, number>>>;

Three rules govern them, and all three are inherited from defaults for values.

A parameter with a default must come after every parameter without one, for the same reason that f(a = 1, b) is illegal. A default may refer to earlier type parameters, as Dict does. And a default is not a constraint: <T = string> still accepts any type argument, while <T extends string = 'a'> both constrains and defaults, which is usually what you want when the default is meaningful.

The most valuable use of a generic parameter default is letting an API grow. Adding a type parameter to a published generic type is a breaking change, because every existing use now has the wrong number of arguments, unless the new parameter has a default, in which case every existing use keeps working unchanged. React's own types do this again and again, and it is why useState and Component have gained parameters over the years without breaking anyone.

The one that catches people: a default is used only when the argument is left out, never as a fallback when inference fails. In a generic function, if T cannot be inferred, the default applies. But if T is inferred as something unhelpful, the default does not step in and correct it. That is a job for a constraint or for NoInfer (§4.17), not for a default.

7.8 A Const Type Parameter

By default, inference widens: pass 'a' and T is string. A const type parameter, written <const T>, tells the checker to infer as if the argument had as const applied, which keeps literal types and turns arrays into readonly tuples.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function tupleOf<const T extends readonly unknown[]>(...xs: T): T { return xs; }
const t1 = tupleOf('a', 'b');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof t1, readonly ['a', 'b']>>;

function looseOf<T extends readonly unknown[]>(...xs: T): T { return xs; }
const t2 = looseOf('a', 'b');
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof t2, [string, string]>>;

console.log(t1, t2);

[ 'a', 'b' ] [ 'a', 'b' ]

The two calls produce identical values at runtime and different types. readonly ['a', 'b'] remembers exactly which strings, in which order, while [string, string] remembers only how many. A const type parameter costs nothing at runtime, since it is purely an instruction for inference, which is what makes it the right default for any API whose usefulness depends on literals.

That covers most configuration- and schema-shaped APIs:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function defineRoutes<const T extends Record<string, string>>(routes: T): T { return routes; }

const routes = defineRoutes({ home: '/', profile: '/me' });
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof routes, { readonly home: '/'; readonly profile: '/me' }>>;
type RouteName = keyof typeof routes;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<RouteName, 'home' | 'profile'>>;

console.log(routes.profile);
// @ts-expect-error the values are literal types now, not string
routes.home = '/other';

/me

Before const type parameters existed, the caller had to remember as const at every call, and forgetting it quietly degraded the types. Moving the instruction into the signature means the author of the API decides once, and no caller can get it wrong. That is the general argument for the feature.

Two limits. const affects inference, not the constraint: const T extends readonly unknown[] is needed for a rest parameter, because the inferred tuple is readonly and a mutable unknown[] constraint would reject it. And const has no effect when the argument is already a variable of a widened type: const xs = ['a', 'b']; tupleOf(...xs) infers from string[], because the widening happened at the const xs declaration, before the call.

7.9 A Generic Factory

A generic factory is a function that takes a constructor and returns instances of it, with the instance type preserved. It needs a construct signature (§4.3) as the constraint, and it is the standard shape for dependency injection, plugin registries and object pools.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Ctor<T, A extends readonly unknown[] = []> = new (...args: A) => T;

function createAll<T, A extends readonly unknown[]>(
  C: Ctor<T, A>, count: number, ...args: A
): T[] {
  return Array.from({ length: count }, () => new C(...args));
}

class Job {
  constructor(public queue: string, public id = 1) {}
  describe(): string { return `${this.queue}#${this.id}`; }
}

const jobs = createAll(Job, 2, 'email');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof jobs, Job[]>>;
console.log(jobs.map((j) => j.describe()));

// @ts-expect-error the constructor argument types are enforced too
createAll(Job, 1, 42);

[ 'email#1', 'email#1' ]

Both type parameters are inferred from one argument: T is the instance type and A is the parameter tuple of the constructor, both read off typeof Job. That is why the third argument is checked against the constructor of Job, and why the result is Job[] and not object[].

The construct signature is the constraint that makes this work, and it is where a generic factory usually goes wrong. Ctor<T> with a fixed empty argument list rejects any class whose constructor takes arguments, and new (...args: any[]) => T accepts everything and checks nothing. The tuple parameter A is the version that both accepts every class and keeps the arguments checked.

An abstract class cannot be passed to this factory, and the error message says so plainly: an abstract construct signature (§6.24) cannot be assigned to a concrete one. That is correct, because you cannot create an instance of an abstract class. When you really want "any subclass constructor", the fix is abstract new (...args: A) => T as the constraint, which accepts both.

7.10 Variance: Covariance, Contravariance and Invariance

Here is the question this subsection answers: given that a Dog is an Animal, is a Box<Dog> a Box<Animal>? The answer depends entirely on what Box does with its parameter, and the three possible answers have names.

Covariance means the container moves in the same direction as the parameter: Box<Dog> can be used as a Box<Animal>. This is correct when the parameter appears only in output positions, meaning you only read it. You can read a Dog wherever an Animal was expected.

Contravariance means it moves in the opposite direction: Box<Animal> can be used as a Box<Dog>. This is correct when the parameter appears only in input positions, meaning you only pass it in. A function that accepts any Animal can be used wherever one that accepts Dogs is needed.

Invariance means neither direction is allowed. This is correct when the parameter appears in both positions.

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

// Written as function-typed PROPERTIES, not methods — a method's parameters are
// checked bivariantly (§4.14), which would defeat the whole demonstration.
interface Producer<T> { get: () => T }                 // T is an output → covariant
interface Consumer<T> { set: (v: T) => void }          // T is an input  → contravariant
interface Cell<T> { get: () => T; set: (v: T) => void }   // both → invariant

declare let pAnimal: Producer<Animal>;
declare let pDog: Producer<Dog>;
pAnimal = pDog;              // ✅ covariance: a dog-producer is an animal-producer
// @ts-expect-error the reverse would let you read an Animal and call .bark()
pDog = pAnimal;

declare let cAnimal: Consumer<Animal>;
declare let cDog: Consumer<Dog>;
cDog = cAnimal;              // ✅ contravariance: something that eats any animal eats dogs
// @ts-expect-error the reverse would let you pass a cat to a dog-consumer
cAnimal = cDog;

declare let cellAnimal: Cell<Animal>;
declare let cellDog: Cell<Dog>;
// @ts-expect-error invariance: neither direction is safe for a read-write cell
cellAnimal = cellDog;

The reason for each is a one-line thought experiment, and it is worth doing them instead of memorising the words.

Covariance is safe for outputs because every Dog you read out really is an Animal. The reverse is unsafe: if pDog = pAnimal were allowed, pDog.get().bark() would type-check and then fail on a cat.

Contravariance is safe for inputs because a consumer prepared for any Animal is certainly prepared for a Dog. The reverse is unsafe: cAnimal = cDog would let someone hand a cat to a function that calls .bark().

Invariance follows from having both. cellAnimal = cellDog would let you set a cat into a Cell<Dog>, and cellDog = cellAnimal would let you get a cat and bark at it. Neither direction survives, so neither is allowed.

The property syntax in that example matters, and it is worth saying why before §10.4 says it at length. A member written as a method, set(v: T): void, has its parameters checked in both directions, so every rejection above would silently become an acceptance and the three cases would be impossible to tell apart. Written as a property that holds a function, strictFunctionTypes applies and the contravariant rule holds. If a variance demonstration ever fails to demonstrate anything, that is the first thing to check.

TypeScript works out variance automatically by looking at where each type parameter appears, and one deliberate exception is worth naming here because it explains a surprising amount of real code: arrays are treated as covariant even though they can be both read and written, so Dog[] can be used as Animal[], and then animals.push(cat) corrupts it. That is unsoundness by design (§1.12), because the alternative made too much ordinary code fail, and readonly T[] is the genuinely covariant and genuinely safe version.

7.11 Variance Annotations

The checker works out variance from the structure of the type, which is right but not always fast and not always what you meant. A variance annotation states it explicitly: out T for covariant, in T for contravariant, and in out T for invariant.

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

interface Producer<out T> { get(): T }
interface Consumer<in T> { set(v: T): void }
interface Cell<in out T> { get(): T; set(v: T): void }

declare let pAnimal: Producer<Animal>;
declare let pDog: Producer<Dog>;
pAnimal = pDog;              // ✅

declare let cDog: Consumer<Dog>;
declare let cAnimal: Consumer<Animal>;
cDog = cAnimal;              // ✅

declare let cellAnimal: Cell<Animal>;
declare let cellDog: Cell<Dog>;
// @ts-expect-error still invariant, now by declaration rather than by inference
cellAnimal = cellDog;

A variance annotation does two things, and both are worth having on a large, deeply generic type.

It is checked. Writing out T on an interface that uses T in an input position is an error, so the annotation is a claim that the compiler verifies, not a comment. That makes it a good place to record a design intention: "this type is read-only in T, and if you add a setter you will hear about it".

It saves the checker work. Computing variance from the structure means walking the whole type, and for a large recursive generic that walk is measurable. Stating the answer lets the checker skip it, which is why typescript's own compiler sources and libraries like RxJS carry these annotations. §17.6 covers when this matters. The short version is that it is a micro-optimisation everywhere except in library declaration files, where it can be worth several percent of check time.

The syntax is only legal on type alias and interface declarations, not on the type parameters of functions or classes, and only in the declaration, never where the type is used. If you find yourself wanting a variance annotation on a function's type parameter, what you actually want is usually a different parameter position, or readonly on an array.

7.12 Higher-Order Generic Inference

When a generic function is passed to another generic function, the checker can sometimes keep the result generic instead of fixing it too early. Higher-order generic inference is the name for that, and it is what makes pipe and compose usable.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

declare function pipe<A, B, C>(f: (a: A) => B, g: (b: B) => C): (a: A) => C;
declare function identity<T>(x: T): T;
declare function box<T>(x: T): { value: T };
declare function toLength(s: string): number;

// Both arguments concrete: an ordinary instantiation.
const composed = pipe(identity<string>, toLength);
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof composed, (a: string) => number>>;

// A free type variable survives: the result is itself generic.
const boxer = pipe(identity, box);
const boxed = boxer(42);
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof boxed, { value: number }>>;

boxer has the type <T>(a: T) => { value: T }. The T of identity was not fixed to unknown when pipe was called, but was carried through into the result of pipe, so boxer(42) still infers number. Without higher-order generic inference, boxer would be (a: unknown) => { value: unknown }, and every composition of generic functions would lose its types at the first step.

Two limits are worth knowing, because they explain why pipe chains sometimes lose their types for no visible reason.

It only applies to a single free type parameter passing through a single call. Compose three generic functions and the parameters of the middle one are usually fixed to their constraints. This is why every functional utility library ships fifteen hand-written overloads of pipe, one per number of arguments, instead of one recursive signature.

A type test that compares generic signatures needs care. Equal<typeof boxer, <T>(a: T) => { value: T }> reports false even though the displayed types match, because an exact comparison of two generic signatures tells their type parameters apart. The reliable way to check the type of a generic function is to call it, as _2 does: check what boxer(42) returns instead of what boxer is.

7.13 A Phantom Type Parameter

A phantom type parameter is one that appears in the parameter list of a type but not in any of its members. It carries information for the checker and describes nothing about the data, which sounds useless and is the basis for every state machine that runs at compile time.

declare const phantom: unique symbol;
type Tagged<T, Tag> = T & { readonly [phantom]?: Tag };

type Metres = Tagged<number, 'm'>;
type Feet = Tagged<number, 'ft'>;

declare function walk(distance: Metres): void;
declare const distanceInFeet: Feet;

// @ts-expect-error a Feet is not a Metres, even though both are numbers
walk(distanceInFeet);
walk(3);          // ✅ — and this is the difference from a brand

Read that last line carefully, because it is the difference between a phantom type parameter and the branded types of §8.11. The marker property here is optional, so a plain number satisfies it and walk(3) compiles. Make it required and you have a brand: raw values are rejected, and the only way in is an assertion. The optional version is the right choice when you want the distinctions enforced but do not want to force every literal through a constructor. The required version is right when the type records a fact that must be established.

The more interesting use is a state machine in the type layer:

declare const state: unique symbol;
type Conn<S extends 'open' | 'closed'> = { id: string; readonly [state]?: S };

declare function connect(id: string): Conn<'open'>;
declare function send(c: Conn<'open'>, msg: string): void;
declare function close(c: Conn<'open'>): Conn<'closed'>;

const c = connect('c1');
send(c, 'hello');            // ✅ open
const done = close(c);
// @ts-expect-error you cannot send on a closed connection
send(done, 'again');

The phantom type parameter S never appears in the object at runtime: Conn<'open'> and Conn<'closed'> are both { id: string }. And yet "send after close" is now a compile error. A whole class of bug has moved from a runtime check into the type layer at no cost at runtime.

The real limit of the technique is honest to state: it is a discipline you follow one step at a time, not a proof. c is still in scope after close(c), so a caller who keeps the old reference can still pass it to send. The example works because close returns the new state and the old variable is not used again. Some languages enforce this with types that can only be used once, and TypeScript does not, so the convention (const next = close(c), never touch c again) is carried by code review and not by the compiler.

7.14 When Not to Reach for a Generic

Every subsection so far has been an argument for generics. This one is the counterweight, and it matters because an unnecessary type parameter makes a signature harder to read, harder to change and, in the worst case, less safe than the concrete version.

The test is simple and mechanical. A type parameter earns its place only if it appears at least twice in the signature. Once is not enough, because a parameter used once does not relate anything to anything else.

// Pointless: T appears once, so this is `(x: unknown) => void` with extra steps.
declare function logIt<T>(value: T): void;
declare function logItBetter(value: unknown): void;

// Worse than pointless: T appears once and is asserted, so it is `any` in disguise.
function parse<T>(json: string): T { return JSON.parse(json) as T; }
const user = parse<{ id: number }>('{"id": "not a number"}');
console.log(typeof user.id);   // the type says number; the runtime disagrees

string

parse<T> is the most common bad generic in TypeScript, and the output above is the argument against it: the caller supplies a type argument, the function asserts it without checking, and the type system now states something false with full confidence. The honest signature returns unknown and makes the caller narrow it, which is the argument of §16.21 ("parse, don't validate") and the point of §10.15 about where an assertion belongs.

Three more cases where the concrete version is better.

When the constraint is doing all the work. function area<T extends { w: number; h: number }>(s: T): number returns number regardless, so T relates nothing. function area(s: { w: number; h: number }): number says the same thing and reads better. The generic version is only justified if the return type mentions T.

When a union would do. function pick<T extends 'a' | 'b'>(k: T): void is a more complicated way of writing function pick(k: 'a' | 'b'): void, unless the return depends on k.

When the abstraction is speculative. A generic added because "we might need other types later" costs every reader now and pays off only if that future arrives. Write it concrete first, and make it generic when the second use case shows up. The change is mechanical, and the compiler finds every call.

The counterweight to the counterweight: do not remove a generic that is preserving information. firstOr<T> (§7.1), getProp<T, K> (§7.6) and createAll<T, A> (§7.9) all mention their parameters at least twice, and each would lose something real if it were flattened. Two appearances is the line.

What This Section Established

A type parameter is a blank in a type, and a type argument fills it. Inference fills it for you from the arguments, left to right, which is why the value comes before the callback. A generic constraint says what T must be and gives you the right to use it, and K extends keyof T relates two parameters and is the shape behind every safe property accessor. Defaults keep a generic API open to growth, const type parameters keep literals, and a construct-signature constraint is what makes a factory keep its instance types.

The second half is the part that repays re-reading. Variance is not just vocabulary: it is the reason Producer<Dog> is a Producer<Animal> and Cell<Dog> is not, and it explains array assignability, how callback parameters are checked, and half the confusing generic errors you will meet. Higher-order inference is what keeps a composed generic function generic. And a phantom type parameter puts a fact into the type layer that the data does not carry.

The last subsection is the one that should change your code most: a type parameter that appears once is not doing anything, and parse<T>(json: string): T is any in disguise.

Exercises

1. A type-safe pluck. Write pluck(rows, key) returning an array of the values at that key, with the element type derived from both arguments. It must reject a key that is not on the row type, must give string[] for a string-valued key and number[] for a number-valued key, and must work on a readonly array. Check all three with type tests and one call at runtime.

2. Variance by construction. Define EventStream<T> with only a subscribe method and EventSink<T> with only an emit method, annotate each with the correct variance annotation, and show with four assignments, two accepted and two rejected, that one is covariant and the other contravariant. Then explain in one sentence why combining both into one interface must be invariant.

3. A phantom-typed builder. Model a query builder where .from() must be called before .where(), and .build() is only available once both have been called, enforced entirely by a phantom type parameter with no checks at runtime. Show a correct chain that produces a string, and two chains that are rejected.

Solution

1. A type-safe pluck.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(rows: readonly T[], key: K): T[K][] {
  return rows.map((row) => row[key]);
}

const rows = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Ada', active: true },
  { id: 2, name: 'Grace', active: false },
] as const;

const names = pluck(rows, 'name');
const ids = pluck(rows, 'id');

type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof names, ('Ada' | 'Grace')[]>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof ids, (1 | 2)[]>>;

console.log(names, ids);
// @ts-expect-error 'emial' is not a key of the row type
pluck(rows, 'emial');

[ 'Ada', 'Grace' ] [ 1, 2 ]

Two type parameters, each mentioned twice, which is the test of §7.14 passing: T appears in the array parameter and in the return, and K in the key parameter and in the indexed access. Flatten either one and the result type collapses.

readonly T[] instead of T[] is a deliberate choice, and it is what let the as const array be passed at all. A readonly parameter type accepts more from the caller, since every mutable array can be assigned to it, and it documents that pluck does not change its input. Any generic function that only reads an array should take readonly T[].

The element types came out as the literal unions 'Ada' | 'Grace' and 1 | 2 because the input was as const. With a plain array literal they would be string[] and number[]. That is inference behaving normally, not the generic doing anything special, and it is worth knowing so that the test you write matches the input you give.

2. Variance by construction.

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

interface EventStream<out T> { subscribe(fn: (event: T) => void): void }
interface EventSink<in T> { emit(event: T): void }

declare let animalStream: EventStream<Animal>;
declare let dogStream: EventStream<Dog>;
animalStream = dogStream;      // ✅ covariant: a stream of dogs is a stream of animals
// @ts-expect-error the reverse would promise dogs and deliver cats
dogStream = animalStream;

declare let animalSink: EventSink<Animal>;
declare let dogSink: EventSink<Dog>;
dogSink = animalSink;          // ✅ contravariant: a sink that takes any animal takes dogs
// @ts-expect-error the reverse would let a cat reach a dog-only sink
animalSink = dogSink;

A combined EventChannel<T> with both members must be invariant, because a covariant assignment would let a caller emit a cat into something whose subscribers expect dogs, and a contravariant assignment would let subscribers expecting cats receive dogs. Neither direction is safe, so the compiler rejects both.

The out and in annotations are checked, not just decoration. Adding an emit to EventStream<out T> is an error at the declaration: "Type 'T' is not usable as an output type because it is used in an input position". That is what makes them worth writing: the annotation becomes a design constraint that a later edit cannot quietly break.

Note that subscribe(fn: (event: T) => void) still leaves T in an output position overall, despite the function parameter nested inside.
