Two contravariant positions combine into a covariant one: the parameter of the callback is an input to the callback, but the callback is an input to subscribe. It is the same double-negative rule that makes ((T) => void) => void covariant in T.

3. A phantom-typed builder.

declare const has: unique symbol;
type Stages = { from?: true; where?: true };
type Query<S extends Stages> = {
  readonly sql: string;
  readonly [has]?: S;
};

function query(): Query<{}> { return { sql: 'SELECT *' }; }
function from<S extends Stages>(q: Query<S>, table: string): Query<S & { from: true }> {
  return { sql: `${q.sql} FROM ${table}` };
}
function where<S extends { from: true }>(q: Query<S>, cond: string): Query<S & { where: true }> {
  return { sql: `${q.sql} WHERE ${cond}` };
}
function build(q: Query<{ from: true; where: true }>): string { return `${q.sql};`; }

const ok = build(where(from(query(), 'users'), 'active'));
console.log(ok);

// @ts-expect-error .where() before .from(): the stage set has no 'from'
where(query(), 'active');
// @ts-expect-error .build() without .where(): the stage set is missing 'where'
build(from(query(), 'users'));

SELECT * FROM users WHERE active;

The phantom parameter accumulates instead of being replaced. Each step returns Query<S & { stage: true }>, so the type parameter grows into the record of the stages completed so far: {} at the start, { from: true } after the first call, { from: true; where: true } after the second. build demands exactly that final record, so any chain that skipped a step fails to match.

A record instead of a union is the detail that makes it work, and the union version is a trap worth naming because it looks correct. Written as Query<never> accumulating into Query<S | 'from'>, with where<S extends 'from'>, the whole thing compiles and checks nothing: query() produces Query<never>, and never can be assigned to every type, including 'from', so the constraint is satisfied and where(query(), …) is accepted. An intersection of object types has no such escape, because {} genuinely does not satisfy { from: true }, which is why the stages are modelled as required properties.

There are no checks at runtime at all, and the JavaScript that comes out has no trace of the stages: has is a declare const (§12.3) that produces nothing, and the property is optional and never assigned. The whole ordering rule costs zero bytes and zero cycles, which is the argument for doing it in the type layer instead of with a #stage field and a thrown error.

The honest limitation, as in §7.13: the discipline only works one step at a time, by convention. Keeping a reference to the intermediate from(query(), 'users') and passing it to where twice is legal, because the type system tracks the stages a value has reached and not how many times it was used.

SECTION 8

Type Operators and Type-Level Programming

Until now every type has been written out by hand. You declared User, you declared UserUpdate, and when a field changed you edited both. That works until the second file. After that, the types slowly drift away from the code they describe and start telling lies. That is worse than having no types at all, because a lie that type-checks is invisible.

This section is about the other way to get a type: compute it. The type layer of TypeScript is a small programming language of its own. It has values (which are types), a way to look things up, an if-else, pattern matching, a way to loop over a set of keys, string handling and recursion. Given User, you can derive UserUpdate, and from then on a field that changes in User changes in every derived type at the same moment, because there is only one declaration.

The order is deliberate, because each piece builds on the one before. First two operators that connect values and types, then indexing, then the conditional and its pattern-matching half, then looping, then strings, then recursion. By §8.9 you will write types that read a string at compile time. By §8.11 you will be able to make TypeScript reject a plain string where a UserId was wanted, something its shape-based type system cannot normally do.

One tool first, because the rest of the section leans on it.

8.1 Reading a Computed Type, and the Two Bridges

A computed type is only useful if you can see what it computed. In an editor you hover over it. In a course, and in a test suite, you need something the compiler will answer out loud. That is a type test: a check written in the type layer that fails to compile when the type is not what you claimed.

// The two-line test harness used throughout this section.
type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type A = { a: string };
type _ok = Expect<Equal<A, { a: string }>>;      // ✅ compiles: the claim is true
type _no = Expect<Equal<A, { a: number }>>;      // ❌ Type 'false' does not satisfy the constraint 'true'.
type _any = Expect<Equal<any, string>>;          // ❌ 'false' — and this is the point of the odd shape

Equal looks strange, and the strangeness is on purpose. A naive X extends Y ? Y extends X ? true : false : false reports true for Equal<any, string>, because any can be assigned in both directions to everything. Putting the comparison inside an unresolved generic signature makes the checker compare the types for exact identity instead of by assignability, so any, unknown and never are all told apart. §17.15 turns this into a real test suite. Here it is simply how the section shows its work: every claim in the pages that follow was compiled before it was written down.

Now the two bridges. The type layer and the value layer are separate worlds, which is what §1.2 called type erasure, and there are exactly two operators that carry information from the value side to the type side.

The keyof type operator takes an object type and gives you the union of its keys. The typeof type operator, used where a type is expected, takes a value and gives you its type.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Point = { x: number; y: number };
type _1 = Expect<Equal<keyof Point, 'x' | 'y'>>;

// keyof over index signatures is where people are surprised.
type _2 = Expect<Equal<keyof { [k: string]: number }, string | number>>;   // number too — see below
type _3 = Expect<Equal<keyof { [k: number]: number }, number>>;

const settings = { retries: 3, mode: 'fast' } as const;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<typeof settings, { readonly retries: 3; readonly mode: 'fast' }>>;

class Box { constructor(public v: number) {} static origin = new Box(0); }
type _5 = Expect<Equal<typeof Box, { new (v: number): Box; prototype: Box; origin: Box }>>;
type _6 = Expect<Equal<InstanceType<typeof Box>, Box>>;

Three results worth stopping on.

keyof on a string index signature is string | number, not string. That is not a quirk. It is JavaScript being described accurately: obj[1] and obj['1'] reach the same property, because a property key is always turned into a string, so a type that accepts every string key necessarily accepts every number key too. The reverse does not hold, which is why keyof { [k: number]: T } is just number.

typeof on a class gives the static side. Box as a value is the constructor function, so typeof Box carries the construct signature, the prototype property and every static member, and not the instance members. The instance type is written Box, and InstanceType<typeof Box> (§9.8) recovers it from the constructor when that is all you have. This is the most common confusion in the whole language, because Box names two different things in two different worlds.

typeof reads what inference found, so as const changes what it returns. Without the const assertion, typeof settings would be { retries: number; mode: string } and every type derived from it would be useless. "Declare the data as a value with as const, then derive the types from it" is the workhorse pattern of §8, and the keyof type operator and the typeof type operator are what make it possible.

The two together make the phrase you will write most often: keyof typeof value, which turns a real object into the union of its keys.

const routes = { home: '/', profile: '/me', settings: '/settings' } as const;
type RouteName = keyof typeof routes;            // 'home' | 'profile' | 'settings'

function go(name: RouteName): string { return routes[name]; }
console.log(go('profile'), go('home'));
// @ts-expect-error 'about' is not a key of routes
go('about');

/me /

Add a route to the object and RouteName grows on its own. Delete one and every call that used it fails to compile. There is one declaration of the truth, and the typeof type operator and the keyof type operator between them keep the type layer tied to it.

8.2 Indexed Access Types

Having a union of keys is only half of it. You also want the type at a key. An indexed access type is written exactly like a property access, but where a type is expected: T[K].

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type User = { id: number; name: string; tags: string[] };

type _1 = Expect<Equal<User['id'], number>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<User['id' | 'name'], number | string>>;   // a union key gives a union type
type _3 = Expect<Equal<User[keyof User], number | string | string[]>>;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<User['tags'][number], string>>;           // number indexes an array type

Four rules are visible there and they are the whole feature.

The index must be a type, not a value. User['id'] works, but const k = 'id'; User[k] does not, because k is a value and the type layer cannot see values. What you want is User[typeof k], and with const k = 'id' that is User['id']. This is the typeof bridge doing its job again.

A union used as the index gives a union of results. User['id' | 'name'] is number | string.

T[keyof T] is therefore the union of all the value types, which is how you say "any of the things this object holds".

number is a legal index into an array or tuple type, and T[number] means "the type of an element". That last one is the most used indexed access type in real code:

const LEVELS = ['debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error'] as const;
type Level = (typeof LEVELS)[number];            // 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error'

const THRESHOLD: Record<Level, number> = { debug: 10, info: 20, warn: 30, error: 40 };
function atLeast(level: Level): Level[] {
  return LEVELS.filter((l) => THRESHOLD[l] >= THRESHOLD[level]);
}
console.log(atLeast('warn'));

[ 'warn', 'error' ]

The array is the single source of truth: it is the value that gets looped over at runtime and the origin of the union at compile time. Adding 'fatal' to LEVELS immediately makes THRESHOLD incomplete, and the code stops compiling until you supply the number. A forgotten case becomes a build failure, through one indexed access type and one as const.

Note the parentheses in (typeof LEVELS)[number]. Without them, typeof LEVELS[number] is read as typeof (LEVELS[number]), which is a value expression and not what you meant. Whenever an indexed access type is applied to a typeof, the parentheses are required.

8.3 Conditional Types

A conditional type is an if for the type layer, written with the same extends keyword that constrains a generic: T extends U ? X : Y. It reads "if T can be assigned to U, the type is X, otherwise Y".

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type IsArray<T> = T extends readonly unknown[] ? true : false;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<IsArray<string[]>, true>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<IsArray<string>, false>>;

// Unwrap one level of Promise, or leave the type alone.
type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Unwrap<Promise<number>>, number>>;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<Unwrap<number>, number>>;

Because extends here means can be assigned to, a conditional type follows the rules of assignability and not your intuition about "kinds". never extends string is true, because never can be assigned to everything. string extends any is true. { a: 1; b: 2 } extends { a: number } is true, because the object type has at least the required member, which is shape-based typing (§10.1) all the way down.

A conditional type constraint is the second, quieter half of the feature: the extends clause in a conditional does more than choose a branch, it also narrows T inside the true branch. In the true branch of T extends { length: number } ? ... : ..., the checker knows T has a length, so T['length'] is legal there and illegal outside.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// The conditional type constraint lets the true branch index into T.
type LengthOf<T> = T extends { length: number } ? T['length'] : never;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<LengthOf<[1, 2, 3]>, 3>>;      // a tuple's length is a literal
type _2 = Expect<Equal<LengthOf<string[]>, number>>;  // an array's is not
type _3 = Expect<Equal<LengthOf<number>, never>>;

LengthOf<[1, 2, 3]> being 3 and not number is the first sign that tuples can carry arithmetic (§8.9 uses it to count). The conditional type constraint is what made T['length'] writable at all: without the check, T has no limits and no length to look up.

Two habits keep conditional types readable. Put the interesting case first: T extends X ? special : general reads better than the negation. And do not nest more than about three deep. Past that, a chain of named type aliases is easier to debug than one big expression, and §17.13 argues that a clever type nobody can read is a liability, not an asset.

In summary, the vocabulary here is a conditional type constraint.

8.4 The infer Keyword

Unwrap above used it already. The infer keyword declares a type variable inside the extends clause of a conditional type, and gives it whatever the checker had to fill in to make the match succeed. It is pattern matching, and it is the most powerful single tool in the type layer.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Ret<F> = F extends (...args: never[]) => infer R ? R : never;
type Arg1<F> = F extends (first: infer A, ...rest: never[]) => unknown ? A : never;
type Elem<T> = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never;

declare function save(user: { id: number }, force: boolean): Promise<string>;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Ret<typeof save>, Promise<string>>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Arg1<typeof save>, { id: number }>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Elem<readonly number[]>, number>>;

// A constraint on the inferred variable (`infer X extends C`) filters the match.
type FirstNum<T> = T extends [infer H extends number, ...unknown[]] ? H : never;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<FirstNum<[1, 'a']>, 1>>;
type _5 = Expect<Equal<FirstNum<['a', 1]>, never>>;

The infer keyword can appear anywhere inside the pattern: a return type, a parameter, an array element, a slot in a tuple, a property, or a segment of a template literal (§8.8). It can appear more than once, and where it appears changes what the repeated occurrences are combined into.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// Two covariant positions: the results are unioned.
type Both<T> = T extends { a: infer U; b: infer U } ? U : never;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Both<{ a: string; b: number }>, string | number>>;

// Two contravariant positions (function parameters): they are intersected.
type BothArgs<T> = T extends { a: (x: infer U) => void; b: (x: infer U) => void } ? U : never;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<BothArgs<{ a: (x: string) => void; b: (x: number) => void }>, string & number>>;

That is not an arbitrary rule, and it is worth understanding, because it is the same variance story as §7.10. A value that is produced in two places could be either one, so the union is the safe answer. A value that is consumed in two places must satisfy both consumers, so the intersection is the safe answer. string & number is never in practice, which is exactly right: no single argument works for both functions.

One practical note. Writing (...args: never[]) => infer R instead of (...args: any[]) => infer R in a pattern is the more careful spelling: never[] can be passed to any parameter list, so it matches every function, and it avoids bringing in an any that could leak (§10.21). The standard library's own ReturnType (§9.8) uses any for historical reasons. In your own utilities, prefer never.

8.5 Distribution

Here is the behaviour that surprises everyone once, and then explains half of their confusing type errors forever. A distributive conditional type is one whose checked type is a bare type parameter, T, not [T] or T[]. When such a conditional is given a union, it is applied to each member separately, and the results are joined back into a union.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<ToArray<string | number>, string[] | number[]>>;   // NOT (string | number)[]

// Preventing distribution: wrap both sides in a one-tuple.
type ToArrayWhole<T> = [T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<ToArrayWhole<string | number>, (string | number)[]>>;

// And the case that catches people out: never is the empty union.
type _3 = Expect<Equal<ToArray<never>, never>>;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<ToArrayWhole<never>, never[]>>;

Read _3 slowly. ToArray<never> is never, not never[]. A distributive conditional type goes over the members of the union it is given, never is the union with no members, so there is nothing to go over and the result is the empty union, which is never again. Any generic helper that must handle never honestly has to switch distribution off, and preventing distribution is the [T] extends [U] idiom shown above: wrapping the checked type in a tuple means it is no longer bare, so the conditional sees the union as one thing.

Distribution is not a nuisance to work around. Most of the time it is exactly what you want, and it is how the standard library's filtering utilities are built:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// This is essentially the real definition of Exclude (§9.6).
type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<MyExclude<'a' | 'b' | 'c', 'b'>, 'a' | 'c'>>;

// Filtering a union of objects by a discriminant — the everyday use.
type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; r: number } | { kind: 'rect'; w: number; h: number };
type ByKind<K extends Shape['kind']> = Extract<Shape, { kind: K }>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<ByKind<'circle'>, { kind: 'circle'; r: number }>>;

MyExclude works only because it distributes: each member is tested on its own and either kept or replaced by never, and never vanishes from a union. Written with [T] extends [U] it would test the whole union at once and return never for 'a' | 'b' | 'c' against 'b', which is useless.

The rule to remember, in one line: a bare T on the left of extends in a conditional type distributes over unions, and anything else does not. When a helper misbehaves on a union input, that is the first thing to check, and preventing distribution or deliberately turning it on is usually the whole fix.

8.6 Mapped Types

A mapped type goes through a union of keys and builds an object type. The syntax is a for...of for the type layer: { [K in Keys]: ValueType }.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Flags<K extends string> = { [P in K]: boolean };
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Flags<'read' | 'write'>, { read: boolean; write: boolean }>>;

// The everyday form: map over the keys of an existing type.
type Nullable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null };
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Nullable<{ a: string; b: number }>, { a: string | null; b: number | null }>>;

A mapping modifier adds or removes readonly and ? as the mapped type is built. Writing readonly or ? plainly adds the modifier, and prefixing it with - removes it. The explicit + prefix is legal and means "add", which is occasionally worth writing for symmetry.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;
type User = { id: number; name?: string; readonly tag: string };

type Add<T> = { +readonly [K in keyof T]+?: T[K] };
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Add<{ a: number }>, { readonly a?: number }>>;

type Strip<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Strip<User>, { id: number; name: string; tag: string }>>;

Look hard at _2, because the widely repeated description of -? is wrong. Removing optionality with a mapping modifier also removes undefined from the property type: name?: string becomes name: string, not name: string | undefined. That is what makes the standard Required<T> (§9.2) useful instead of merely cosmetic, and it is why Required cannot be written as a plain { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } with an annotation.

The other thing _2 shows is the property that makes mapped types worth trusting. A homomorphic mapped type is one written as { [K in keyof T]: ... }, where the keys come straight from keyof T. It automatically keeps the modifiers of the source type unless a mapping modifier says otherwise. Nullable<User> keeps name optional and tag readonly without being asked. A mapped type over some other union of keys does not:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;
type User = { id: number; name?: string; readonly tag: string };

// Homomorphic: modifiers survive.
type Copy<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Copy<User>, { id: number; name?: string; readonly tag: string }>>;

// Not homomorphic: the key source is a literal union, so modifiers are lost.
type FromKeys<T> = { [K in 'id' | 'name' | 'tag']: T[K & keyof T] };
type _2 = Expect<Equal<FromKeys<User>, { id: number; name: string | undefined; tag: string }>>;

name came out required, holding string | undefined, and tag lost its readonly. Homomorphism is not a detail: a helper written the non-homomorphic way silently changes the shape of every optional and readonly property it touches, and the resulting type will reject { id: 1, tag: 'x' } in places where the original accepted it. When you write a mapped type over an object, write [K in keyof T] unless you have a specific reason not to.

A homomorphic mapped type has one more special power: applied to an array or a tuple, it maps the elements and stays an array or a tuple, instead of turning into an object with numeric keys.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Boxed<T> = { [K in keyof T]: { value: T[K] } };
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Boxed<[string, number]>, [{ value: string }, { value: number }]>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Boxed<string[]>, { value: string }[]>>;

That is how the return type of Promise.all is written, and it is why a mapped type is the right tool for "transform every element of this tuple" as well as for "transform every property of this object".

8.7 Key Remapping via as

A mapped type as described so far keeps the key it went through. Key remapping via as lets the key itself be computed: { [K in keyof T as NewKey]: ... }, where NewKey is any type expression that produces a key.

Two things follow, and the second is the surprising one.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// 1. Rename: derive a handler shape from a state shape.
type Handlers<T> = { [K in keyof T & string as `on${Capitalize<K>}Change`]?: (v: T[K]) => void };
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Handlers<{ name: string }>, { onNameChange?: (v: string) => void }>>;

// 2. Filter: a key remapped to `never` is dropped from the result entirely.
type Methods<T> = { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends (...a: never[]) => unknown ? K : never]: T[K] };
type API = { load(): void; url: string; save(x: number): void };
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Methods<API>, { load(): void; save(x: number): void }>>;

type Without<T, Drop extends keyof T> = { [K in keyof T as Exclude<K, Drop>]: T[K] };
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Without<{ id: number; name: string }, 'id'>, { name: string }>>;

Remapping a key to never removes the property. That is the mechanism behind every "pick the properties whose values are functions" or "drop the internal fields" helper you will ever write, and it is why key remapping via as covers both Pick and Omit (§9.4): those two are just this operator with a particular key expression.

Key remapping via as does not cost you homomorphism. Without above is still written [K in keyof T as ...], so readonly and ? still survive the trip. That was measured in §8.6 with Copy<User>, and adding an as clause does not change it. What does break homomorphism is changing where the keys come from: [K in 'a' | 'b'] instead of [K in keyof T].

A caution about the union you go through. keyof T can include number and symbol, and a template literal type only accepts string | number | bigint | boolean | null | undefined in its slots. keyof T & string, as Handlers uses it, limits the loop to string keys, and it is the usual fix for the "Type 'symbol' is not assignable to type 'string'" error that a first attempt at a renaming mapped type always produces.

8.8 Template Literal Types

A template literal type is written with the same backtick syntax as a template string, but where a type is expected, and its slots hold types instead of values. What comes out is a literal string type, or, if any slot is a union, a union of literal string types.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Size = 'sm' | 'lg';
type Colour = 'red' | 'blue';
type Cls = `${Size}-${Colour}`;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Cls, 'sm-red' | 'sm-blue' | 'lg-red' | 'lg-blue'>>;

Every slot that holds a union multiplies out, giving every combination. That is the feature's headline and also its main hazard: four unions of ten members each make ten thousand string types, and §17.6 shows what that does to check time. Two or three small unions are a good tool. A combinatorial explosion is a slow build.

TypeScript ships four intrinsic string types that no code of your own could implement, because they call into the compiler's own string functions. Uppercase<S> and Lowercase<S> convert a whole literal, while the Capitalize type and the Uncapitalize type change only the first character.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Uppercase<'get' | 'post'>, 'GET' | 'POST'>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Lowercase<'GET'>, 'get'>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Capitalize<'name'>, 'Name'>>;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<Uncapitalize<'Name'>, 'name'>>;

// They distribute over unions, so they compose with template literals directly.
type Ev = `on${Capitalize<'click' | 'focus'>}`;
type _5 = Expect<Equal<Ev, 'onClick' | 'onFocus'>>;

Uppercase<S> and Lowercase<S> are the two you reach for when a wire format disagrees with your code style, such as an HTTP method arriving as 'get' and wanted as 'GET'. The Capitalize type and the Uncapitalize type are what turn a property name into a method name, which is the Handlers pattern from §8.7.

The other half of template literal types is that they can be matched, not only built. String union inference is infer inside a template literal pattern, and it turns the type layer into a parser:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// Split a dotted path.
type Split<S extends string> = S extends `${infer H}.${infer R}` ? [H, ...Split<R>] : [S];
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Split<'a.b.c'>, ['a', 'b', 'c']>>;

// Trim whitespace, one character at a time, from both ends.
type Trim<S extends string> =
  S extends ` ${infer R}` ? Trim<R> : S extends `${infer R} ` ? Trim<R> : S;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Trim<'  hi  '>, 'hi'>>;

// Pull the parameter names out of an Express-style route.
type PathParams<S extends string> =
  S extends `${string}:${infer P}/${infer R}` ? P | PathParams<`/${R}`>
  : S extends `${string}:${infer P}` ? P
  : never;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<PathParams<'/users/:id/posts/:postId'>, 'id' | 'postId'>>;

String union inference is greedy in a specific way that matters: in `${infer A}.${infer B}` the first placeholder matches as little as possible, so Split<'a.b.c'> binds A to 'a' and B to 'b.c'. If you want the last separator instead, match the tail recursively rather than trying to make one pattern do it.

And the limit that keeps this honest: a template literal type can only match a literal string type. PathParams<string> is never, because a plain string has no characters to look at. Every use of string union inference therefore begins by getting a literal in, which in practice means a generic parameter inferred from a string argument, an as const, or a const type parameter (§7.8).

8.9 Recursive Types and the Depth Limit

Split, Trim and PathParams were all recursive conditional types: a conditional type whose branches refer to the alias being defined. The type layer allows this, and it is a language that always finishes, since the checker enforces a limit instead of hanging, but the limit is real and you will meet it.

There are two limits, not one, and which one you get depends on the shape of the recursion.

// Tail-recursive: the recursive call IS the whole branch result.
type Count<N extends number, A extends unknown[] = []> =
  A['length'] extends N ? A : Count<N, [...A, unknown]>;
type Ok = Count<999>;        // ✅ fine — a tuple of 999 unknowns
type Deep = Count<1000>;     // ❌ Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite.

// Not tail-recursive: the recursive call is nested inside a tuple being built.
type Wrap<N extends number, A extends unknown[] = []> =
  A['length'] extends N ? [] : [unknown, ...Wrap<N, [...A, unknown]>];
type Ok = Wrap<47>;          // ✅
type Deep = Wrap<48>;        // ❌ Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite.

Those two numbers were measured against the installed compiler, by bisection, with each type compiled on its own: a tail-recursive type reaches 999 iterations and fails at 1,000, while the same computation written without tail recursion fails at 48.

The isolation matters, and it is worth knowing so that you do not trust the numbers too far. Put both types in one file and Wrap<48> compiles, because the failure moves out past 48: the checker's depth accounting is affected by what it has already worked out. So the reliable statement is the ratio, not either figure: tail recursion buys roughly twenty times the depth, and neither limit is a constant you can design against. The factor of twenty comes from an optimisation that the checker applies only when it can. A tail-recursive type is one where the recursive step is the entire result of a branch, with no work left to do around it. The checker runs it as a loop instead of nesting one step inside another, so it uses up the 1,000-instantiation budget one step at a time instead of stacking frames.

The practical consequence is a rewrite you should recognise, and it is the same accumulator trick as in ordinary recursion:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// Non-tail: the `[H, ...` wrapper means work remains after the recursive call.
type SplitSlow<S extends string> = S extends `${infer H}.${infer R}` ? [H, ...SplitSlow<R>] : [S];

// Tail: the accumulator carries the answer, and the recursive call is the whole branch.
type SplitFast<S extends string, Acc extends string[] = []> =
  S extends `${infer H}.${infer R}` ? SplitFast<R, [...Acc, H]> : [...Acc, S];

type _1 = Expect<Equal<SplitFast<'a.b.c'>, ['a', 'b', 'c']>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<SplitSlow<'a.b.c'>, ['a', 'b', 'c']>>;

Both are correct, and only one survives a long input. When a recursive conditional type reports type instantiation depth, meaning error TS2589, "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite", the first thing to try is moving the accumulation into a parameter so that the recursion becomes tail-recursive. If that is not enough, the honest answer is usually that the computation does not belong in the type layer at all (§17.13).

TS2589 is also raised for types that really are infinite, which is the error doing its real job:

type Infinite<T> = { value: T; next: Infinite<T[]> };   // never bottoms out
declare const x: Infinite<number>;
const y: string = x.next.next.next.value;   // ❌ number[][][] is not a string

Note that recursion in an object type is unrestricted, because it is lazy: type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json } is legal and cheap, since the checker only expands a branch when something asks for it. The depth limit applies to instantiation, meaning working out a conditional or a mapped type, and not to a shape that refers to itself. A recursive type alias that describes a tree is fine. A recursive conditional type that counts to a thousand is not.

What to carry forward from this subsection: type instantiation depth.

8.10 satisfies

A satisfies expression checks a value against a type without changing the type that the value is inferred to have. That one sentence is the whole feature, and it resolves a tension that had no good answer before it existed.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Palette = Record<'primary' | 'accent', string | [number, number, number]>;

const theme = { primary: '#1d4ed8', accent: [255, 128, 0] } satisfies Palette;
theme.primary.toUpperCase();      // ✅ the checker still knows this one is a string
theme.accent.map((c) => c + 1);   // ✅ and this one is a tuple of numbers

const wide: Palette = { primary: '#1d4ed8', accent: [255, 128, 0] };
wide.primary.toUpperCase();       // ❌ Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'string | [number, number, number]'.

type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof theme, { primary: string; accent: [number, number, number] }>>;

The annotated version is checked and then forgets: wide.primary is string | [number, number, number] because that is what Palette says, and every use needs a narrowing step that the author knows is unnecessary. The satisfies expression checks the same constraint and keeps what inference found. You get the error when a key is misspelled or a value has the wrong shape, and you also get the precise type afterwards.

Three details decide whether you reach for it correctly.

A satisfies expression still uses the target as a hint for typing. accent came out as the tuple [number, number, number] and not number[] precisely because Palette asked for a tuple there. That is what makes satisfies better than nothing at all for arrays and functions, whose inferred types are otherwise too loose.

It does not stop literals from widening on its own. typeof theme.primary is string, not '#1d4ed8', because const on the variable does not freeze the object literal all the way down (§2.13). When you want both the check and the literal types, combine the two:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;
type Palette = Record<'primary' | 'accent', string | [number, number, number]>;

const theme = { primary: '#1d4ed8', accent: [255, 128, 0] } as const satisfies Palette;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof theme, { readonly primary: '#1d4ed8'; readonly accent: [255, 128, 0] }>>;

Read that result carefully, because it is not what the short description of as const predicts. The properties came out readonly, but accent is the mutable tuple [255, 128, 0] and not readonly [255, 128, 0]: the type asked for by satisfies Palette was a mutable tuple, and it won. Written the other way round (satisfies Palette as const) it would not even parse. as const satisfies T is the order that works.

Excess property checking still applies. { primary, accent, extra: 1 } satisfies Palette is an error, which is exactly what you want from a configuration object: a satisfies expression is the tool for "this must conform, and I still want to know precisely what I wrote".

The rule of thumb: annotate a parameter, satisfies a constant. A parameter's type is a contract with the caller and should be the wide one. A constant's type is a description of one specific value and should be as narrow as the value allows.

8.11 Branded Types

§1.3 called TypeScript's type system structural: two types are the same if their members match, and names do not matter. That is right almost all of the time, and wrong in one specific, expensive way. UserId, OrderId, Metres and Celsius are all string or number structurally, so nothing stops a function from being handed the wrong one, and those are exactly the bugs that survive review.

A nominal type pattern imitates identity by name inside a shape-based system, and a branded type is the standard way to do it: combine the underlying type with a marker property that nothing can produce by accident.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

declare const brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly [brand]: B };

type UserId = Brand<string, 'UserId'>;
type OrderId = Brand<string, 'OrderId'>;

function asUserId(s: string): UserId {
  if (!/^u_[0-9]+$/.test(s)) throw new Error(`not a user id: ${s}`);
  return s as UserId;                    // the one assertion, inside the one validator
}

declare function loadUser(id: UserId): void;
declare const oid: OrderId;

loadUser(asUserId('u_1'));   // ✅
loadUser('u_1');             // ❌ Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'UserId'.
loadUser(oid);               // ❌ Type '"OrderId"' is not assignable to type '"UserId"'.
const plain: string = asUserId('u_2');   // ✅ a UserId is still usable as a string

Four properties make this pattern work, and each is a design decision worth understanding.

The brand key is a unique symbol declared with declare const. It has no existence at runtime at all, because declare produces no code (§12.3), so Brand<string, 'UserId'> is just a string at runtime with zero overhead, and the property cannot be created by accident because no code can name that symbol.

The brand goes one way. A UserId can be assigned to string, so every string API keeps working, while a string cannot be assigned to UserId. That asymmetry is exactly what you want, and it is why the branded type is built by intersecting and not by wrapping.

The brand string tells the brands apart. Without the B parameter, UserId and OrderId would be the same type, and the second error above would not appear. The message even names the mismatch: '"OrderId"' is not assignable to type '"UserId"'.

There is exactly one assertion, and it lives inside a validator. asUserId is the only place in the program that says as UserId, and it does so after checking. That is the whole discipline: a nominal type pattern is only as strong as its entry point is narrow, and a codebase that scatters as UserId around its calls has bought nothing. §16.22 makes the general form of this argument ("parse, do not validate"), and a branded type is what gives "parsed" a name the compiler can check.

The same pattern applies to units and to states, not only to identifiers. Brand<number, 'Metres'> and Brand<number, 'Feet'> cannot be added together, and Brand<string, 'SafeHtml'> cannot be produced except by a sanitiser. In each case the type is not describing the shape of the data, which is string or number. It is recording a fact that was established, and a shape-based type system cannot express that any other way.

What This Section Established

The type layer is a programming language, and you now have all of it. keyof and typeof bring values into it, T[K] looks inside, a conditional type chooses, infer matches a pattern, a mapped type goes through keys, key remapping via as renames and filters, template literal types build and parse strings, and recursion closes the loop, with a measured budget of 999 tail-recursive instantiations to spend. satisfies checks a value without flattening it, and a branded type buys identity by name inside a shape-based system.

The trap that the whole section pushes against is that all of this is fun, and fun is not the criterion. A derived type is one that cannot drift from its source, and that is the argument for using it. A type that took an hour to write and that nobody else on the team can change has a cost that no amount of cleverness repays. §17.13 gives that argument its own subsection, and it is the one to remember when the next conditional type reaches four levels deep.

Exercises

1. DeepPartial<T>. Write a homomorphic mapped type that makes every property optional, all the way down, but that does not go into functions or primitives, and that maps arrays element by element instead of making their indices optional. Check it with Expect<Equal<...>> against a configuration type containing a nested object, an array and a callback.

2. A typed path builder. Given a route template like '/users/:id/posts/:postId', write PathParams<S> to pull out the parameter names, and a buildPath whose second argument must supply exactly those keys, no more and no fewer. Then implement it at runtime and show it producing the right string.

3. A branded, validated quantity. Model Celsius and Fahrenheit as branded numbers so that a conversion function cannot be called with the wrong one and its result cannot be confused with its input. Provide a single validating constructor for each, and show three calls: one correct, one passing a raw number, and one passing the other unit.

Solution

1. DeepPartial<T>.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Primitive = string | number | boolean | bigint | symbol | null | undefined;

type DeepPartial<T> =
  T extends Primitive | ((...a: never[]) => unknown) ? T
  : T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? readonly DeepPartial<E>[]
  : { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> };

type Cfg = {
  db: { host: string; ports: number[] };
  onError: (e: Error) => void;
  debug: boolean;
};

type _1 = Expect<Equal<DeepPartial<Cfg>, {
  db?: { host?: string; ports?: readonly number[] };
  onError?: (e: Error) => void;
  debug?: boolean;
}>>;

The order of the branches is the whole exercise. The primitive and function check must come first: a function is an object structurally, so the mapped-type branch would otherwise turn (e: Error) => void into {} and silently delete the call signature. The array check must come before the object branch for the same reason, since { [K in keyof T]?: ... } over number[] produces something with optional numeric keys instead of an array.

The readonly DeepPartial<E>[] result is a deliberate choice, not an accident. A partly specified array cannot be safely written to by code that expects the full element type, and marking it readonly says so. If you would rather keep it mutable, DeepPartial<E>[] is the one-word change.

2. A typed path builder.

type PathParams<S extends string> =
  S extends `${string}:${infer P}/${infer R}` ? P | PathParams<`/${R}`>
  : S extends `${string}:${infer P}` ? P
  : never;

type ParamsObject<S extends string> = { [K in PathParams<S>]: string };

function buildPath<const S extends string>(template: S, params: ParamsObject<S>): string {
  return template.replace(/:([A-Za-z0-9_]+)/g, (_, name: string) =>
    encodeURIComponent((params as Record<string, string>)[name]!));
}

console.log(buildPath('/users/:id/posts/:postId', { id: '7', postId: 'a b' }));
console.log(buildPath('/health', {}));

// @ts-expect-error 'nope' is not a parameter of this template
buildPath('/users/:id', { id: '1', nope: 'x' });
// @ts-expect-error 'id' is required by this template
buildPath('/users/:id', {});

/users/7/posts/a%20b
/health

The recursion is the interesting part. The first branch matches a parameter that is followed by a /, captures the name, and continues on the rest with a / glued back on so that the same pattern can match again. The second branch matches a parameter at the end. The third returns never, which is why PathParams<'/health'> is never and ParamsObject<'/health'> is the empty object type, so buildPath('/health', {}) is correct and not an error.

const S extends string, a const type parameter (§7.8), is what keeps the argument a literal type. Without const, S is inferred as string for a variable argument and every parameter check silently disappears. The type is still valid, it just stops proving anything, which is the quiet way every template-literal-based API can fail.

3. Branded units.

declare const unit: unique symbol;
type Unit<T extends string> = { readonly [unit]: T };

type Celsius = number & Unit<'Celsius'>;
type Fahrenheit = number & Unit<'Fahrenheit'>;

function celsius(n: number): Celsius {
  if (!Number.isFinite(n) || n < -273.15) throw new RangeError(`not a temperature: ${n}`);
  return n as Celsius;
}
function fahrenheit(n: number): Fahrenheit {
  if (!Number.isFinite(n) || n < -459.67) throw new RangeError(`not a temperature: ${n}`);
  return n as Fahrenheit;
}

function toFahrenheit(c: Celsius): Fahrenheit {
  return ((c * 9) / 5 + 32) as Fahrenheit;
}

console.log(toFahrenheit(celsius(100)), toFahrenheit(celsius(-40)));

// @ts-expect-error a raw number is not a Celsius
toFahrenheit(100);
// @ts-expect-error a Fahrenheit is not a Celsius
toFahrenheit(fahrenheit(212));

212 -40

The arithmetic still works: c * 9 is legal because a Celsius is a number, and that is the property that makes branded numbers practical instead of a straitjacket. What does not work is passing the wrong one in, which is the bug being prevented.

The result needs its own assertion. (c * 9) / 5 + 32 is a plain number, because arithmetic on a branded number produces an unbranded one. Branding it again at the return is correct here, and it is the one place the assertion is justified, since the function is the thing that establishes the fact. Note the asymmetry that makes this safe: the assertion is inside the converter and not at any call, so there is a single audited place where a raw number becomes a temperature, and a single place where a Celsius becomes a Fahrenheit.

-40 is the fixed point of the conversion, which makes it the test case worth keeping: a sign error, a swapped multiplier or a dropped offset can all still produce 212 from 100 in some arrangement, but only the correct formula also maps -40 to -40.

SECTION 9

Utility Types

Every type in this section is written in TypeScript itself, in a file you can open. The file lib.es5.d.ts ships with the compiler, and the utility types (the ready-made helpers such as Partial and Pick) are ordinary declarations in it, built from exactly the operators §8 covered: a mapped type here, a conditional type there, one infer. Nothing in this section is magic. Four of the twenty are called intrinsic only because string manipulation cannot be written in the type layer at all.

That matters for two reasons. First, reading a definition is the fastest way to understand what a helper does: Partial stops being surprising once you see that it is just three tokens of mapped type. Second, the standard set is small on purpose and stops well short of what real code needs, so you will write your own. Yours should look like the ones that shipped, because in a codebase where RequireKeys and Partial follow the same conventions, the next person can read both.

The order groups them by what they do, not alphabetically: the ones that change modifiers, the ones that construct types, the ones that filter unions, the function helpers and the this helpers. Then come the two subsections that matter most in the long run: writing your own, and combining several without producing a type nobody can read. One of the standard helpers is also actively unsafe on a kind of type you will certainly write, and §9.5 is about that.

9.1 What a Utility Type Is

A utility type is a generic type alias that the standard library makes available everywhere. There is no import: Partial is simply in scope, the same way Array is. Every one of them is a pure function from types to types. Given the same arguments it gives the same result, it has no effect on the code that is produced, and it disappears completely at runtime.

Here are three of them written out, exactly as the standard library defines them:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// The real definitions, renamed so they do not collide with the globals.
type MyPartial<T> = { [P in keyof T]?: T[P] | undefined };
type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] };
type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;

type _1 = Expect<Equal<MyPartial<{ a: number }>, Partial<{ a: number }>>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<MyPick<{ a: number; b: string }, 'a'>, Pick<{ a: number; b: string }, 'a'>>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<MyExclude<'a' | 'b', 'b'>, Exclude<'a' | 'b', 'b'>>>;

A mapped type with a ? modifier, a mapped type over a narrowed union of keys, and a distributive conditional type. That is the entire toolkit, and it is the toolkit from §8.

Two habits follow from knowing that. When a utility type does something unexpected, expand its definition by hand. Almost every surprise in this section (Omit on a union, Required deleting undefined, Parameters producing a labelled tuple) becomes clear once the definition is on the screen. And when the standard set does not have what you need, write it instead of contorting the code. A three-line type alias in a types.ts is cheaper than a Partial<Pick<Omit<...>>> stack at every call, which is the argument §9.11 makes at length.

One note on names that saves confusion later: the community and the handbook both say "utility types", and library documentation sometimes says "type helpers" or "type-level functions". They are all the same thing, and a utility type you write yourself is not second-class in any way: it is looked up, worked out and cached by exactly the same machinery.

9.2 Partial, Required and Readonly

These three are the modifier utilities. Each is a homomorphic mapped type (§8.6) that adds or removes one modifier and leaves everything else alone.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type U = { id: number; name?: string; readonly tag: string };

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Partial<U>, { id?: number; name?: string; readonly tag?: string }>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Required<U>, { id: number; name: string; readonly tag: string }>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Readonly<U>, { readonly id: number; readonly name?: string; readonly tag: string }>>;

Read the three results against the input and the design is visible. Partial<T> adds ? and keeps readonly: tag came out as readonly tag?. Required<T> removes ? and keeps readonly. Readonly<T> adds readonly and keeps ?. Each utility touches exactly one modifier, because each is written with exactly one mapping modifier, and homomorphism carries the rest across untouched.

The detail worth pinning down is what Required<T> does to the type of a property, because it is more than cosmetic. Under strictNullChecks, name?: string means the property may be missing and that reading it gives string | undefined. Required removes both halves: the result is name: string, with undefined gone. That is -? doing what §8.6 measured, and it is why Required is genuinely useful for the "I have filled in every default" step of a configuration pipeline:

type Options = { retries?: number; timeoutMs?: number; verbose?: boolean };

const DEFAULTS: Required<Options> = { retries: 3, timeoutMs: 5_000, verbose: false };

function withDefaults(opts: Options): Required<Options> {
  return { ...DEFAULTS, ...opts };
}

const resolved = withDefaults({ retries: 1 });
console.log(resolved.retries + resolved.timeoutMs, resolved.verbose);

5001 false

resolved.retries + resolved.timeoutMs compiles because both are number and not number | undefined, with no !, no ?? 0 and no defensive check. Everything after withDefaults works with a fully filled-in object and can say so in its own signatures. That is the pattern: Options is the type at the boundary, Required<Options> is the type inside, and one function converts.

Two cautions. Readonly<T> is shallow. Readonly<{ db: { host: string } }> stops you reassigning db and does nothing about db.host, and the DeepPartial of §8 exercise 1 shows the recursive shape if you need it. And Partial<T> is not a good type for an update payload on its own, because it allows {}, which usually means "update nothing" and is usually a bug. RequireAtLeastOne is a custom utility (§9.10) worth having for that case.

9.3 Record

The Record type builds an object type from a union of keys and a value type: Record<K, V>. It is the one utility that builds a shape from nothing instead of transforming an existing one.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// The definition: a mapped type over an arbitrary key union.
type MyRecord<K extends keyof never, V> = { [P in K]: V };
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Record<'a' | 'b', number>, { a: number; b: number }>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<MyRecord<'a', number>, Record<'a', number>>>;

// With a wide key type it degenerates into an index signature.
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Record<string, number>, { [k: string]: number }>>;

The two uses are quite different, and it is worth naming them separately.

With a finite union of keys, the Record type gives you exhaustiveness. Every key must be present, so adding a member to the union breaks the object until you fill it in: a missing case becomes a compile error instead of an undefined at runtime.

type Level = 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error';

const COLOUR: Record<Level, string> = {
  debug: 'grey', info: 'blue', warn: 'amber', error: 'red',
};

function render(level: Level, msg: string): string {
  return `[${COLOUR[level]}] ${msg}`;
}
console.log(render('warn', 'disk almost full'));
// @ts-expect-error 'trace' is not a Level
render('trace', 'x');

[amber] disk almost full

COLOUR[level] is string, with no chance of undefined, because the Record type guarantees that every Level is a key. That guarantee is the entire reason to prefer it over a plain object literal here.

With string as the key it is an index signature, and the guarantee disappears: Record<string, number> claims that every string key holds a number, which is false for every real dictionary. This is the one place where noUncheckedIndexedAccess (§5.19) earns its keep: with that setting on, record[key] is number | undefined and you are made to handle the miss.

keyof never as the constraint is a small puzzle worth solving. keyof never is string | number | symbol, the set of all possible property keys, which is also spelled PropertyKey. Writing the constraint that way is a historical leftover in the standard library. In your own utilities, write PropertyKey.

9.4 Pick and Omit

The Pick type keeps the listed keys, and the Omit type drops them. They are the two halves of narrowing an object type down, and they are used constantly: a public shape derived from an internal one, a form model derived from a record, a function argument that wants three fields out of twenty.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type U = { id: number; name?: string; readonly tag: string; secret: string };

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Pick<U, 'id' | 'tag'>, { id: number; readonly tag: string }>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Omit<U, 'secret' | 'id'>, { name?: string; readonly tag: string }>>;

// The definitions.
type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] };
type MyOmit<T, K extends keyof never> = Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<MyOmit<U, 'secret'>, Omit<U, 'secret'>>>;

Both keep modifiers, as the readonly tag results show. The difference in their constraints is the thing to notice, because it explains a class of bug that the compiler will not catch for you:

The Pick type limits K to keyof T. The Omit type does not. Pick<U, 'nmae'> is a compile error, while Omit<U, 'nmae'> is perfectly legal and silently omits nothing. That is deliberate, since Omit is often used with keys that a subtype has (a more specific type, such as one with extra properties), but it means a typo in an Omit is invisible. If you want the strict version, it is one line:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;
type U = { id: number; name: string };

type StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<StrictOmit<U, 'id'>, { name: string }>>;

type Typo = Omit<U, 'nmae'>;          // legal, and does nothing
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Typo, U>>;     // ✅ — the misspelling was silently ignored
// @ts-expect-error StrictOmit rejects the typo
type Caught = StrictOmit<U, 'nmae'>;

The other everyday use of the Omit type is deriving a creation payload from a stored entity, and it is worth writing out because the & in it is the composition idiom of §9.11:

type Stored = { id: string; createdAt: string; title: string; body: string };
type NewPost = Omit<Stored, 'id' | 'createdAt'>;

let nextId = 1;
function create(post: NewPost): Stored {
  return { ...post, id: `p${nextId++}`, createdAt: '2026-09-01T00:00:00Z' };
}
console.log(create({ title: 'Hello', body: 'World' }));
// @ts-expect-error the server assigns the id, so the caller may not
create({ title: 'x', body: 'y', id: 'p99' });

{
  title: 'Hello',
  body: 'World',
  id: 'p1',
  createdAt: '2026-09-01T00:00:00Z'
}

One derived type, and the API now refuses a client-supplied id at compile time. Change Stored and NewPost follows.

9.5 Why Omit Is Unsafe on a Union

This is the one entry in the standard library that will quietly ruin a type, and the failure is total, not partial: applied to a discriminated union, Omit can produce a type that accepts anything.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Shape =
  | { kind: 'circle'; r: number }
  | { kind: 'rect'; w: number; h: number };

type _1 = Expect<Equal<keyof Shape, 'kind'>>;      // NOT 'kind' | 'r' | 'w' | 'h'
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Omit<Shape, 'kind'>, {}>>;  // the empty object type

const anything: Omit<Shape, 'kind'> = { totally: 'unrelated' };   // ✅ and that is the disaster
console.log(anything);

{ totally: 'unrelated' }

Trace it through the definitions and there is no mystery, only two correct rules combining into a useless answer. keyof of a union is the intersection of the members' keys, because the only property you can safely read from "a circle or a rectangle" is one that both have, and here that is kind alone. Omit<T, K> is defined as Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>, so this is Pick<Shape, Exclude<'kind', 'kind'>>, which is Pick<Shape, never>, which is {}. And {} in TypeScript means "anything except null and undefined", so the annotation stops checking altogether.

Nothing warns you. The code compiles, the editor offers no completions on the resulting type (which is the only visible symptom), and every later assignment is accepted.

The fix is to distribute the Omit over the union yourself, using the bare-type-parameter rule from §8.5:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Shape =
  | { kind: 'circle'; r: number }
  | { kind: 'rect'; w: number; h: number };

type DistributiveOmit<T, K extends PropertyKey> = T extends unknown ? Omit<T, K> : never;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<DistributiveOmit<Shape, 'kind'>, { r: number } | { w: number; h: number }>>;

// @ts-expect-error now rejected, as it should always have been
const bad: DistributiveOmit<Shape, 'kind'> = { totally: 'unrelated' };

T extends unknown ? ... : ... is a conditional that always says yes, and its only purpose is to make T bare, so the utility is applied to each member and the results are joined back into a union. The same wrapper fixes Pick on a union, and the same reasoning explains why Partial<Shape> is safe: it is a homomorphic mapped type, and those spread over unions on their own.

Two rules to carry away. Any time you Omit or Pick from something that might be a union, use the distributive version. And more generally, when a derived type stops offering completions in the editor, it has probably collapsed to {} or never. That is the cheapest available signal that a type-level composition went wrong, and it costs nothing to notice.

9.6 Exclude, Extract and NonNullable

These three filter a union, and all three are one-line distributive conditional types.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Exclude<'a' | 'b' | 'c', 'b'>, 'a' | 'c'>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Extract<'a' | 'b' | 1 | 2, string>, 'a' | 'b'>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<NonNullable<string | null | undefined>, string>>;

// The definitions, in full.
type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;
type MyExtract<T, U> = T extends U ? T : never;
type MyNonNullable<T> = T & {};

The Exclude type removes every member that can be assigned to the second argument, and the Extract type keeps them. They are complements, and the second argument is a pattern, not a list: Extract<Shape, { kind: 'circle' }> selects by shape, which is how you pull one variant out of a discriminated union:

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type AppEvent =
  | { type: 'click'; x: number; y: number }
  | { type: 'key'; key: string }
  | { type: 'scroll'; dy: number };

type EventOf<K extends AppEvent['type']> = Extract<AppEvent, { type: K }>;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<EventOf<'key'>, { type: 'key'; key: string }>>;

type Handlers = { [K in AppEvent['type']]: (e: EventOf<K>) => void };
const handlers: Handlers = {
  click: (e) => console.log('click at', e.x, e.y),
  key: (e) => console.log('key', e.key),
  scroll: (e) => console.log('scroll', e.dy),
};
function dispatch(e: AppEvent) { (handlers[e.type] as (ev: AppEvent) => void)(e); }
dispatch({ type: 'key', key: 'Escape' });
dispatch({ type: 'click', x: 3, y: 4 });

key Escape
click at 3 4

Every handler's parameter is the specific variant, worked out and not annotated, and adding a fourth event type makes handlers incomplete until it is written. That is the Extract type earning its place: without it, each handler would take the whole Event union and start with a narrowing step.

NonNullable<T> deserves a second look because its definition changed, and the current one is instructive. It is T & {}, not a conditional at all: intersecting with the empty object type removes null and undefined, the only two types that cannot be assigned to {}, and leaves everything else. That makes it cheaper for the checker than the conditional it replaced, and it explains why NonNullable<any> is {} and not any.

The most common use of these three is not a hand-written type at all, but the result of a filter: arr.filter((x) => x != null) does not narrow on its own, and writing the callback as a type predicate that returns x is NonNullable<T> (§3.9) is how you make it.

The terms above, gathered: the exclude type.

9.7 Awaited

Awaited<T> is the type-level version of await: it unwraps a promise, and keeps unwrapping until there is nothing promise-like left.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Awaited<Promise<number>>, number>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>, number>>;   // recursive
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Awaited<number>, number>>;                      // non-promise passes through
type _4 = Expect<Equal<Awaited<Promise<string> | number>, string | number>>;  // distributes

The recursion in _2 is not a nicety. It is the type layer telling the truth about the runtime. await on a promise of a promise gives you the inner value, because the promise resolution procedure keeps unwrapping thenables, so a type that unwrapped only one level would be wrong. Awaited<T> is a recursive conditional type built on infer and a check for then, which is why it also handles a custom thenable and not just a native Promise.

Where it actually gets used is in working out the result of an async function you did not write:

async function loadUser(id: string) {
  await Promise.resolve();
  return { id, name: 'Ada', roles: ['admin'] };
}

export type User = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof loadUser>>;

function describe(u: User): string { return `${u.name} (${u.roles.join(', ')})`; }

const u = await loadUser('u_1');
console.log(describe(u));

Ada (admin)

ReturnType<typeof loadUser> is Promise<{ id: string; name: string; roles: string[] }>, and Awaited strips the promise. The pair is the most common combination in the whole section, and the reason is that an async function's useful type is the resolved one while its declared type is the wrapped one. Deriving User this way means the function stays the source of truth: change what it returns and every consumer's type follows, with no interface to keep up to date.

Awaited<T> also appears in the standard library's own signatures. Promise.all returns Promise<{ -readonly [P in keyof T]: Awaited<T[P]> }>, a homomorphic mapped type over a tuple (§8.6) whose element types are each awaited, which is exactly why Promise.all([a, b]) gives you a correctly ordered tuple and not an array of a union.

9.8 Parameters, ReturnType, ConstructorParameters and InstanceType

These four take a callable apart, and every one of them is a conditional type with an infer in it, the same patterns that §8.4 built by hand.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

declare function save(user: { id: number }, force?: boolean): Promise<string>;
class Conn { constructor(host: string, port: number) {} query(sql: string) { return sql; } }

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Parameters<typeof save>, [user: { id: number }, force?: boolean]>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof save>, Promise<string>>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<ConstructorParameters<typeof Conn>, [host: string, port: number]>>;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<InstanceType<typeof Conn>, Conn>>;

The Parameters type produces a labelled tuple, keeping the parameter names and which ones are optional: [user: { id: number }, force?: boolean], not [{ id: number }, boolean]. The labels are not decoration. They show up in editor hints when the tuple is spread back into a call, which is what makes the wrapper pattern below readable.

ReturnType<T> is the return type as declared, so for an async function it is the Promise, and combining it with Awaited (§9.7) is how you get the resolved value.

ConstructorParameters<T> and InstanceType<T> both take the static side, typeof Conn and not Conn. That is the §8.1 distinction doing real work: Conn is the instance type and has no construct signature, so ConstructorParameters<Conn> is an error and ConstructorParameters<typeof Conn> is what you meant.

The reason these exist is wrappers. Anything that takes a function and returns a function of the same shape needs a way to name that shape, and these four are how:

const durations: number[] = [];

function timed<F extends (...args: never[]) => unknown>(
  fn: F,
): (...args: Parameters<F>) => ReturnType<F> {
  return (...args) => {
    const started = performance.now();
    const out = fn(...(args as never[]));
    durations.push(performance.now() - started);
    return out as ReturnType<F>;
  };
}

const add = (a: number, b: number) => a + b;
const wrapped = timed(add);
console.log(wrapped(2, 3));
// @ts-expect-error the wrapper kept the original signature
wrapped('2', 3);
console.log('calls timed:', durations.length, '| all non-negative:', durations.every((d) => d >= 0));

5
calls timed: 2 | all non-negative: true

wrapped has the argument types and the return type of add, derived instead of repeated, so the wrapper works for any function and never has to be updated when one changes. Note what the example does not claim: the elapsed times differ on every run, so the output reports how many were recorded and that none is negative, instead of any particular duration. That is a rule worth keeping whenever an example measures time.

The never[] in the constraint is the §8.4 point again: (...args: never[]) => unknown matches every function without bringing in any. The two assertions inside are the honest cost of writing a fully generic wrapper: within the function the checker cannot connect args to the parameters of F, and §10.15 discusses when an assertion at an internal boundary like this one is the right call.

One line each, for reference: the Parameters type gives a labelled tuple of a function's parameters, ReturnType<T> gives its declared return, ConstructorParameters<T> gives the parameters of a class's constructor, and InstanceType<T> gives the instances it produces.

9.9 ThisParameterType, OmitThisParameter and ThisType

Three utilities deal with the this type. They are the least used of the standard set, but the last one enables a pattern that nothing else can express.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

function format(this: { prefix: string }, msg: string): string {
  return `${this.prefix}${msg}`;
}

type _1 = Expect<Equal<ThisParameterType<typeof format>, { prefix: string }>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<OmitThisParameter<typeof format>, (msg: string) => string>>;

const bound = format.bind({ prefix: '> ' });
console.log(bound('hello'));

> hello

ThisParameterType<T> extracts the declared this parameter (§6.18) and is unknown for a function that has none. OmitThisParameter<T> removes it, giving the type the function has after being bound. That is exactly what bind returns, and it is how the standard library types Function.prototype.bind under strictBindCallApply (§13.10).

ThisType<T> is different in kind from every other utility in this section. It computes nothing. It is a marker that the checker looks for in the type of an object literal, and it changes what this means inside that literal's methods. It only has an effect with noImplicitThis on, which strict implies, and it is the mechanism behind every "options object whose methods can see the data" API:

type ObjectDescriptor<D, M> = {
  data?: D;
  methods?: M & ThisType<D & M>;      // `this` inside methods is D & M
};

function makeObject<D, M>(desc: ObjectDescriptor<D, M>): D & M {
  return { ...(desc.data as D), ...(desc.methods as M) };
}

const point = makeObject({
  data: { x: 0, y: 0 },
  methods: {
    moveBy(dx: number, dy: number) { this.x += dx; this.y += dy; return this.describe(); },
    describe() { return `${this.x},${this.y}`; },
  },
});

console.log(point.moveBy(3, 4));
console.log(point.describe());

3,4
3,4

Inside moveBy, this.x type-checks against the data object and this.describe() type-checks against its sibling method, and neither of them exists on the literal being written. Without ThisType<D & M> both are errors under noImplicitThis, and the only alternative is annotating a this parameter on every method by hand, which defeats the point of the helper. Vue's options API and a good deal of older configuration-object tooling is typed this way.

To restate the three in one line: ThisParameterType<T> extracts a declared this, OmitThisParameter<T> removes it, and ThisType<T> is a marker that changes what this means inside the methods of an object literal.

Use ThisType<T> when you are designing such an API. If you are only using one, you will never write it, and if you are writing new code, an object built from a real class or a closure is usually clearer than a descriptor whose methods depend on a sibling key.

Gathered here, because the rest of the course uses them: ThisParameterType<T> and OmitThisParameter<T>.

9.10 Writing a Custom Utility Type

The standard set stops at twenty entries, and real codebases need perhaps five more. Writing a custom utility type is the ordinary case, not an advanced one, and the four below are the ones worth having in every project.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// 1. Remove readonly — the missing complement of Readonly.
type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Mutable<{ readonly a: number; readonly b?: string }>, { a: number; b?: string }>>;

// 2. The union of an object's value types.
type ValueOf<T> = T[keyof T];
type _2 = Expect<Equal<ValueOf<{ a: 1; b: 2 }>, 1 | 2>>;

// 3. Make specific keys required, leave the rest as they are.
type RequireKeys<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K> & Required<Pick<T, K>>;

// 4. Make specific keys optional.
type PartialKeys<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K> & Partial<Pick<T, K>>;

RequireKeys and PartialKeys follow the same three-step recipe, and it is the recipe for most custom utilities: split, change one half, put the halves back together. Omit<T, K> is the untouched half, Required<Pick<T, K>> is the changed half, and & joins them again.

type RequireKeys<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K> & Required<Pick<T, K>>;

type Draft = { id?: number; title?: string; body?: string };
type Publishable = RequireKeys<Draft, 'title' | 'body'>;

function publish(post: Publishable): string {
  return `${post.title.toUpperCase()}: ${post.body.slice(0, 20)}`;   // no `!` needed
}

console.log(publish({ title: 'Hello', body: 'A short body.' }));
// @ts-expect-error body is required by Publishable
const incomplete: Publishable = { title: 'Hello' };

HELLO: A short body.

post.title is string and post.body is string, while post.id stays optional: the transformation touched two keys and left the third alone.

Three conventions make a custom utility type behave like a standard one, and each is a real trap if skipped.

Constrain the type parameters. RequireKeys<T, K extends keyof T> rejects a misspelled key, while without the constraint the typo silently does nothing, exactly as the missing constraint on Omit does (§9.4).

Write it homomorphically when it maps an object. { [K in keyof T]: ... } keeps modifiers and works on tuples, while { [K in SomeUnion]: ... } does neither (§8.6).

Decide explicitly whether it distributes. A utility that will meet a union needs either a bare T on the left of a conditional or the [T] extends [U] guard, and the choice should be deliberate. DistributiveOmit in §9.5 exists precisely because the standard Omit made the other choice.

Finally, give it a test. Expect<Equal<...>>, the harness from §8.1, is two lines and turns a utility type into something a future change cannot silently break. §17.15 makes this a proper suite. Even one assertion per utility is worth having, because a type that used to be right and has become {} produces no error at its definition, only at the far-away place that used it.

9.11 Composing Utility Types

Utility types combine well, which is their strength, and they combine without any of the readability aids that ordinary code has: no intermediate variables, no line breaks that mean anything, no names. A composition four levels deep is genuinely hard to read.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Row = { id: string; name: string; email: string; passwordHash: string; createdAt: Date };

// Hard to read: what does this describe?
type A = Partial<Omit<Pick<Row, 'id' | 'name' | 'email'>, 'id'>>;

// The same thing, named in steps.
type PublicRow = Pick<Row, 'id' | 'name' | 'email'>;
type EditableRow = Omit<PublicRow, 'id'>;
type RowPatch = Partial<EditableRow>;

type _1 = Expect<Equal<A, RowPatch>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<RowPatch, { name?: string; email?: string }>>;

Both spellings produce the identical type, and the second is the one to write. Composing utility types works best in named steps, for three reasons that are all practical, not aesthetic.

Error messages quote the alias you named. A failure against RowPatch says RowPatch, while a failure against the nested version prints the whole expression, expanded, in a message that scrolls. §17.4 covers this as its own technique: an alias exists partly to give the compiler something short to say.

The intermediate steps are usually needed anyway. PublicRow is a real concept in that codebase, since it is what the API returns, and giving it a name means the next derived type starts from it instead of working out the same Pick again.

Order matters, and names make it visible. Partial<Omit<T, 'id'>> and Omit<Partial<T>, 'id'> happen to agree here, but Required<Partial<T>> and Partial<Required<T>> do not: the first makes everything required and the second makes everything optional. Written as a nest, the reading order is right to left and mistakes are easy. Written as steps, each line applies one transformation to a named thing.

There is a real cost to depth as well as a readability cost. Each layer is an instantiation that the checker works out and caches, and a deep composition applied across a large union multiplies out. §17.6 measures this, and interfaces are cheaper than intersections (§17.8) is the specific finding that most often applies to a &-based composition like RequireKeys.

The practical rule: two levels inline, three or more named. And if the composition is used in more than one file, name it whatever its depth, because the name is what makes it searchable.

What This Section Established

Twenty standard utilities, all written in the operators of §8, all readable in lib.es5.d.ts. The three modifier utilities (Partial, Required, Readonly) each move one modifier and keep the others. Record builds a shape and gives exhaustiveness with a finite union of keys. Pick and Omit narrow, with Omit unconstrained and therefore blind to typos, and dangerous on a union, where keyof is the intersection of the keys and the result collapses to {}.
