Exclude, Extract and NonNullable filter unions. Awaited unwraps promises recursively and pairs with ReturnType constantly. The four callable utilities take a function or a typeof Class apart, and the three this utilities cover a corner that only ThisType makes reachable.

Then the two subsections that outlive the list: write your own, constrained and homomorphic and tested, and combine in named steps instead of nested expressions, because the compiler's error messages, the next reader and the checker's own performance all reward a name.

Exercises

1. DeepRequired and the Partial/Required asymmetry. Write DeepRequired<T> making every property required all the way down, without going into arrays or functions. Then show, with Expect<Equal<...>>, that Required<Partial<T>> and Partial<Required<T>> are not the same type, and explain in one sentence which one round-trips.

2. RequireAtLeastOne. Partial<T> accepts {}, which is usually a bug in an update payload. Write RequireAtLeastOne<T> that accepts an object with at least one of the keys of T and rejects the empty object, then show it accepting two valid payloads and rejecting the empty one.

3. A safe Omit for a union, applied. Take a three-variant discriminated union describing an API response. Show that Omit<Response, 'status'> collapses to {}, write the distributive replacement, and use it to build a withoutStatus function whose return type is the union of the stripped variants, checked by a type test and by a call at runtime.

Solution

1. DeepRequired and the asymmetry.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Primitive = string | number | boolean | bigint | symbol | null | undefined;

type DeepRequired<T> =
  T extends Primitive | ((...a: never[]) => unknown) ? T
  : T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? DeepRequired<E>[]
  : { [K in keyof T]-?: DeepRequired<T[K]> };

type Cfg = { db?: { host?: string; pool?: { max?: number } }; tags?: string[] };

type _1 = Expect<Equal<DeepRequired<Cfg>, {
  db: { host: string; pool: { max: number } };
  tags: string[];
}>>;

// The asymmetry.
type T0 = { a: number; b?: string };
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Required<Partial<T0>>, { a: number; b: string }>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Partial<Required<T0>>, { a?: number; b?: string }>>;
// @ts-expect-error the two orders are genuinely different types
type _4 = Expect<Equal<Required<Partial<T0>>, Partial<Required<T0>>>>;

Required<Partial<T>> round-trips, and Partial<Required<T>> does not. Partial then Required makes everything optional and then makes everything required again, landing on "all required", which equals the original only when the original had no optional properties, and here b came back as a required string. Required then Partial ends with everything optional and has thrown away the original modifiers for good.

The -? in the mapped type is what does the work in DeepRequired, and, as §8.6 measured, it removes undefined from the property type as well as the ?, which is why host is string and not string | undefined.

2. RequireAtLeastOne.

type RequireAtLeastOne<T, K extends keyof T = keyof T> =
  Omit<T, K> & { [P in K]-?: Required<Pick<T, P>> & Partial<Omit<T, P>> }[K];

type Patch = { name?: string; email?: string; age?: number };
type ValidPatch = RequireAtLeastOne<Patch>;

function update(id: string, patch: ValidPatch): string {
  return `${id}: ${Object.keys(patch).sort().join(',')}`;
}

console.log(update('u1', { name: 'Ada' }));
console.log(update('u2', { email: 'a@b.c', age: 36 }));
// @ts-expect-error an empty patch updates nothing
update('u3', {});

u1: name
u2: age,email

The trick is a mapped type used to generate a union, not to build an object. { [P in K]: ... }[K] builds an object whose value at each key is "that key required, everything else optional", and then immediately indexes it with K, which by the union-index rule of §8.2 produces the union of those value types. So ValidPatch is {name: string; email?: ...; age?: ...} | {email: string; ...} | {age: number; ...}, and {} matches none of the three, because each demands one specific key.

Omit<T, K> at the front is there for the general case where K is a subset of the keys: those properties keep their original modifiers and are unaffected by the "at least one" rule. With the default K = keyof T it contributes nothing, which is why the two-argument form is what makes this utility reusable.

3. A safe Omit on a union.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type ApiResponse =
  | { status: 'ok'; data: string[] }
  | { status: 'error'; message: string; code: number }
  | { status: 'pending' };

// The broken version.
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Omit<ApiResponse, 'status'>, {}>>;

// The distributive replacement.
type DistributiveOmit<T, K extends PropertyKey> = T extends unknown ? Omit<T, K> : never;
type ResponseBody = DistributiveOmit<ApiResponse, 'status'>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<ResponseBody, { data: string[] } | { message: string; code: number } | {}>>;

function withoutStatus(r: ApiResponse): ResponseBody {
  const { status, ...rest } = r;
  return rest;
}

console.log(withoutStatus({ status: 'ok', data: ['a', 'b'] }));
console.log(withoutStatus({ status: 'error', message: 'nope', code: 500 }));
console.log(withoutStatus({ status: 'pending' }));

{ data: [ 'a', 'b' ] }
{ message: 'nope', code: 500 }
{}

Omit<ApiResponse, 'status'> is {} because keyof ApiResponse is 'status' alone, the intersection of the keys of the three variants, so Exclude<'status', 'status'> is never and Pick<T, never> is the empty object type. Every property of every variant was thrown away by a type that looks like it removes one field.

The distributive version keeps the variants apart, and note that the third member of the result genuinely is {}: the pending variant has nothing but a status, so stripping it correctly leaves nothing. That is a real empty object in a union of three, not the collapse of the whole type into one, and the difference is exactly what _1 and _2 pin down.

The runtime implementation is a rest destructure, which mirrors the type operation precisely: const { status, ...rest } = r removes one key and keeps the others, and because r is a union the checker narrows rest for each variant. Writing it as delete (r as any).status would have produced the same result at runtime and thrown away both the type and the immutability of the argument.

SECTION 10

Assignability and the Escape Hatches

Every error message that starts with "Type X is not assignable to type Y" is an answer to one question, and this section is about that question. Assignability means "can a value of this type be used where that type is expected?". The checker asks it over and over: for an assignment, an argument, a return value, a property, a type argument. Once you know its rules, a wall of error messages becomes something you can predict.

The section has two halves, placed side by side on purpose. The first half is the rules: how shapes are compared, the special case of any, how functions compare, how enums and classes differ from plain objects, and where the deliberate looseness lives. The second half is the escape hatches: any, assertions, double assertions, @ts-ignore and @ts-expect-error. These are the tools for telling a checker that is usually right "I know better".

The judgement that organises it all is this: every escape hatch is a claim that nobody verifies, and its cost grows with how far it travels. An any that is narrowed right where the data enters is cheap. An any that flows three modules deep silently switches off checking in all of them, which is why §10.21 closes the section. Use them when you need them, and use the narrowest one that does the job.

10.1 Structural Typing

Structural typing is the rule that types are compared by their members. §1.3 introduced it. Here is the precise statement that the checker implements.

S can be assigned to T if, for every member of T, S has a matching member that can be assigned to it. Members of S that T does not mention do not matter.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Named = { name: string };

class Employee { constructor(public name: string, public salary: number) {} }
const literal = { name: 'Ada', extra: true };

function greet(x: Named): string { return `Hello ${x.name}`; }

console.log(greet(new Employee('Ada', 1)), greet(literal), greet({ name: 'Grace' }));

Hello Ada Hello Ada Hello Grace

Three sources, a class, a variable holding an object literal and an inline literal, none of which declares any relationship to Named. That is the whole rule, and it is what lets TypeScript describe JavaScript that was written before the types existed.

Four things sit on top of the structural rule as deliberate exceptions, and each has its own subsection: excess property checking on object literals written directly (§5.4), weak type detection (§5.22), private and protected members that make classes name-based (§10.10), and branded types (§8.11), which use the rule against itself.

The mental model to carry: assignability asks "can a value of S be used everywhere a T is expected?", and the answer is worked out member by member, recursively, with a cache. When an error message surprises you, the useful question is which member disagreed, and the deepest line of the error is where the checker tells you (§1.8).

10.2 Assignability

Assignability is the relation itself, and it appears in more places than the name suggests.

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };
declare const dog: Dog;

// All six of these are the SAME check: is Dog assignable to Animal?
const asVariable: Animal = dog;
function takesAnimal(a: Animal): void { console.log(a.name); }
takesAnimal(dog);
function returnsAnimal(): Animal { return dog; }
const inArray: Animal[] = [dog];
const inProperty: { pet: Animal } = { pet: dog };
type IsAssignable = Dog extends Animal ? true : false;

console.log(asVariable.name, returnsAnimal().name, inArray.length, inProperty.pet.name);

Rex Rex 1 Rex

The last one is worth pausing on. S extends T in a conditional type is the same assignability check (§8.3), which is why never extends string is true, and why a conditional type sometimes takes a branch that "looks wrong": it is following assignability, not your intuition about kinds.

The special cases, all of which are asymmetries you should be able to recite:

any can be assigned to everything, and everything can be assigned to any. It is both the top and the bottom of the hierarchy, which is exactly why it switches checking off (§10.12).

unknown accepts everything and can be assigned to nothing except unknown and any.

never can be assigned to everything, and nothing can be assigned to it except never.

null and undefined can only be assigned to themselves, to any, to unknown, and to a union that contains them, under strictNullChecks. Without it they can be assigned to everything, which is the behaviour from before 2016 and the biggest source of unchecked crashes.

10.3 Subtype Versus Assignment Compatibility

TypeScript has two compatibility relations, not one, and knowing that resolves several apparent contradictions. Subtype versus assignment compatibility is the distinction.

The subtype relation is the strict one, and it is used for things like finding the best common supertype during inference (§7.2). The assignment relation is slightly more permissive, and it is what an assignment, an argument or a return uses.

The difference is small and specific: assignment compatibility additionally allows any in both directions, and allows a numeric enum and number in both directions.

declare let anyValue: any;
let n: number = 0;

n = anyValue;          // ✅ assignment compatibility
anyValue = n;          // ✅ both directions

enum Priority { Low = 1, High = 2 }
let p: Priority = Priority.Low;
let asNumber: number = p;      // ✅ a numeric enum is a number
p = 1;                          // ✅ and a number literal is accepted back

console.log(n, asNumber, p, Priority[p]);

0 1 1 Low

p = 1 compiling is a real hole, and it is the reason string enums (§15.2) are safer: p = 3 is also accepted, producing a Priority with no name, and Priority[3] is undefined.

You will rarely need to think about which relation applies, because the assignment relation is what almost everything uses. Where it shows up is in inference: bothOf(dog, animal) picking Animal[] (§7.2) is the subtype relation choosing a best common supertype, which is why the answer is a supertype and not a union.

The practical takeaway is narrower than the theory: any and numeric enums are the two places where assignability goes both ways, and both are places to be careful.

10.4 Function Parameter Bivariance

Function parameter bivariance is TypeScript's most consequential deliberate looseness, and §4.14 demonstrated it. Here is why it exists.

Sound parameter checking is contravariant: a function that accepts Animal may be used where one that accepts Dog is expected, and not the reverse. TypeScript checks the parameters of a method in both directions.

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

// A METHOD: bivariant, so this compiles.
type MethodHolder = { handle(a: Animal): void };
const bivariant: MethodHolder = { handle(d: Dog) { d.bark(); } };

let outcome = 'no error';
try { bivariant.handle({ name: 'Whiskers' }); }
catch (e) { outcome = (e as Error).constructor.name; }
console.log(outcome);

TypeError

The reason is Array<T>. Its methods, push(...items: T[]), concat, indexOf, every, all take T as a parameter. Under contravariant checking, Dog[] could not be assigned to Animal[], and neither could Promise<Dog> to Promise<Animal>, or a Map<string, Dog> to a Map<string, Animal>. The amount of code that works in practice and would stop compiling was judged unacceptable, so method parameters were made bivariant and the built-in generics work.

The scope of the hole is exactly "members written with method syntax". A property that holds a function is checked strictly under strictFunctionTypes (§10.5), and so is a standalone function type. So the escape is available whenever you own the declaration:

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

type PropertyHolder = { handle: (a: Animal) => void };
function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Types of parameters 'd' and 'a' are incompatible.
  const strict: PropertyHolder = { handle: (d: Dog) => d.bark() };
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

function

Declare callbacks as properties in any interface you own. It is a one-word change that switches on the sound rule, and it is the most valuable habit from this section.

10.5 strictFunctionTypes

strictFunctionTypes turns on contravariant parameter checking for function types, and, as measured above, not for members written with method syntax. It is part of strict.

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

// Function TYPE: checked contravariantly.
type AnimalHandler = (a: Animal) => void;
type DogHandler = (d: Dog) => void;

declare let handleAnimal: AnimalHandler;
declare let handleDog: DogHandler;

handleDog = handleAnimal;      // ✅ contravariance: accepting more is fine

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Type 'DogHandler' is not assignable to type 'AnimalHandler'.
  handleAnimal = handleDog;
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

function

The rule reads backwards at first, and the reason is one sentence: a handler that copes with any animal can stand in for one that only had to cope with dogs, while the reverse would let a cat reach code that calls .bark().

The exemption for methods is documented, not accidental, and the setting's own description says so. That is why the pair of examples in §10.4 matters more than the setting itself: turning strict on does not fix a bivariant method, and rewriting the member as a property does.

Two practical notes.

Turning it on rarely breaks much. Most callbacks in application code either match exactly or are already contravariant. The errors it does produce are usually real: a handler narrowed to a subtype of what the API will actually pass.

It changes inference in one visible way: a callback parameter whose type would previously have been accepted silently now has to match, so a handler taken out into its own function sometimes needs a wider annotation. That is the check doing its job.

10.6 Comparing Two Function Types

Comparing two function types combines the parameter and return rules, and the full check is worth stating once so that the error messages make sense.

(p1: P1, p2: P2) => R can be assigned to (q1: Q1, q2: Q2) => S when:

  • the source has no more parameters than the target (fewer is fine);
  • each Qn can be assigned to the matching Pn, which is contravariant, under strictFunctionTypes;
  • R can be assigned to S, which is covariant;
  • S being void accepts any R (§4.9).
type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Target = (a: { id: number; name: string }) => { ok: boolean; code: number };

// Fewer parameters: ✅. Wider parameter: ✅. Narrower return: ✅.
const source: Target = () => ({ ok: true, code: 200, extra: 'ignored' });
console.log(source({ id: 1, name: 'x' }));

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error the return type is missing 'code'
  const badReturn: Target = (a) => ({ ok: true });
  // @ts-expect-error the parameter is narrower than the target's
  const badParam: Target = (a: { id: number; name: string; role: string }) => ({ ok: true, code: 1 });
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

{ ok: true, code: 200, extra: 'ignored' }
function

The extra: 'ignored' property survived because a return type only has to cover what the target promises, and this is not an object literal written directly in an annotated position, so excess property checking does not fire.

Generic signatures are compared by relating their parameters, which is why Equal<> reports false for two generic function types that have the same shape (§7.12). For a generic function the reliable test is to call it.

Overloaded signatures are compared loosely: a source with several overloads can be assigned if any of them can be assigned to the target, and a target with several requires the source to satisfy all of them. That asymmetry is a common source of confusion when a .d.ts overload set does not fit an interface.

10.7 Optional and Rest Parameter Compatibility

Compatibility of optional and rest parameters has one asymmetry worth memorising, because it is the opposite of what people guess.

type RequiredBoth = (a: string, b: number) => void;
type OptionalSecond = (a: string, b?: number) => void;
type RestTuple = (...args: [string, number]) => void;

declare let required: RequiredBoth;
declare let optional: OptionalSecond;
declare let rest: RestTuple;

required = optional;      // ✅ an optional parameter accepts a required call
rest = required;          // ✅ a tuple rest matches a positional list
required = rest;          // ✅ and back

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Type 'RequiredBoth' is not assignable to type 'OptionalSecond'.
  optional = required;
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

function

required = optional works and optional = required does not, which reads backwards until you check what each promises. A variable of type OptionalSecond may be called with one argument, and a RequiredBoth would then receive undefined for a parameter declared number. The error message says exactly that: Type 'undefined' is not assignable to type 'number'.

A rest parameter with a tuple type is interchangeable with the positional list it describes, in both directions. That is what makes (...args: Parameters<F>) => ReturnType<F> a drop-in replacement for F (§9.8), and it is the mechanism behind every typed wrapper.

A rest parameter with an array type accepts any number of arguments, so (...args: number[]) => void can be assigned to a target with two, three or zero number parameters. That is the loosest form, and the right one for a callback that really takes any number of arguments.

The practical advice: declare a callback's parameters as required in the type, and let implementations leave out the ones they do not want (§4.14). Declaring them optional buys nothing and blocks the assignment above.

10.8 Enum Compatibility

Enum compatibility has three rules, and the difference between numeric and string enums is large enough to drive a design decision.

enum Numeric { Low = 1, High = 2 }
enum AlsoNumeric { Low = 1, High = 2 }
enum Answer { Yes = 'yes', No = 'no' }

let n: Numeric = Numeric.Low;
const asNumber: number = n;      // ✅ a numeric enum IS a number
n = 2;                            // ✅ ...and a number that is a declared member's value

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error 99 is not the value of any Numeric member
  n = 99;
  // @ts-expect-error different enums are never compatible with each other
  n = AlsoNumeric.Low;
  // @ts-expect-error a string enum is not assignable from a string
  const t: Answer = 'yes';
}

console.log(n, Numeric[n], asNumber, typeof neverCalled);

2 High 1 function

Three results, and the first is a fact about the current version that is worth checking and not just recalling. A numeric enum can be assigned from a number only for values that some member actually declares: n = 2 compiles because High = 2, and n = 99 does not. Older TypeScript accepted any number at all, and a great deal of writing about enums still says so. Under the installed compiler that is false, and the same tightening applies to computed members (c = 3 against enum C { A = 1 << 0, B = 1 << 1 } is rejected).

The direction that is still wide open is the other one. const asNumber: number = n compiles, so a numeric enum flows freely into arithmetic and into any number parameter, and nothing stops Numeric.Low + Numeric.High. Assignment compatibility goes both ways for numeric enums (§10.3), and only one half of it was narrowed.

A string enum is name-based in both directions. Answer accepts only Answer.Yes and Answer.No, a bare 'yes' is rejected, and an Answer cannot be assigned to string without a widening step, so the set of possible values really is the declared one.

Two enums are never compatible with each other, however identical they are. That is the one place where enums are genuinely name-based, and it is occasionally useful, although a branded type (§8.11) achieves the same thing without producing any code.

The conclusion that §15.9 argues in full: prefer a union of string literals to an enum. It gives you the safety of a string enum with no generated code, no compatibility surprises and no numeric hole.

10.9 Class Compatibility

Class compatibility goes by shape like everything else, with one exception that makes it name-based, covered in §10.10.

class Point2D { constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {} }
class Vector2D { constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {} }

let p: Point2D = new Vector2D(1, 2);      // ✅ identical shapes, unrelated classes
const alsoP: Point2D = { x: 3, y: 4 } as Point2D;

console.log(p.x, alsoP.y, p instanceof Point2D);

1 4 false

p instanceof Point2D is false while p type-checks as a Point2D. That is shape-based typing being honest: the type describes a shape and the prototype describes an identity, and they are different questions. Any code that relies on instanceof must not rely on the annotation alone.

Three details.

Only instance members are compared. Statics and the constructor belong to the static side of the class, typeof C (§8.1), and are compared separately. So a class with a three-argument constructor can be assigned to one with none, as long as the instances match.

A class can be assigned to an interface without implements, which is the usual way a class satisfies a contract in shape-based code. implements adds a check at the declaration and nothing else (§6.6).

A subclass can be assigned to its base, both by shape and by inheritance, and the two agree, which is why this rarely comes up until private members enter the picture.

10.10 Private and Protected Members in Compatibility

Private and protected members in compatibility are the one place where TypeScript's type system becomes name-based: a private or protected member is compared by the place it was declared, not by name and type.

class VaultA { private key = 'k'; }
class VaultB { private key = 'k'; }

declare let a: VaultA;
declare let b: VaultB;

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Types have separate declarations of a private property 'key'.
  a = b;
}

// Without the modifier, the same two classes are interchangeable.
class OpenA { key = 'k'; }
class OpenB { key = 'k'; }
declare let oa: OpenA;
declare let ob: OpenB;
oa = ob;

// A subclass shares the declaration, so it is compatible.
class VaultC extends VaultA {}
declare let c: VaultC;
a = c;

console.log(typeof neverCalled, oa.key, a === c);

function k false

The check is "did this member come from the same declaration?" VaultA and VaultB each declare their own key, so they are different types. VaultC inherits VaultA's, so it is compatible.

Two consequences, one useful and one painful.

Useful: a private member is a free brand. A class with a private brand member cannot be satisfied by an object literal or by another class, which gives you name-based typing without the machinery of §8.11. The cost is that it requires a class.

Painful: two copies of a package produce an unreadable error. Type 'Foo' is not assignable to type 'Foo'. Types have separate declarations of a private property '_x'. The two Foos come from different node_modules paths. When you see a type compared to itself and failing, that is nearly always the cause, and npm ls <package> is the diagnosis.

#private fields behave the same way for compatibility, and are also genuinely private at runtime (§6.10), so they are the better choice when you want both effects.

10.11 Generic Compatibility

Generic compatibility compares two uses of a generic type by comparing what the type parameter is used for, which is variance (§7.10).

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

// Covariant use (output only).
type Producer<T> = { get(): T };
declare let pDog: Producer<Dog>;
let pAnimal: Producer<Animal> = pDog;          // ✅

// Contravariant use (input only).
type Consumer<T> = { set: (v: T) => void };
declare let cAnimal: Consumer<Animal>;
let cDog: Consumer<Dog> = cAnimal;             // ✅

// A generic function type compares by relating its parameters.
type Id = <T>(x: T) => T;
declare const id: Id;
const forStrings: (x: string) => string = id;  // ✅ instantiated on assignment

console.log(typeof pAnimal, typeof cDog, forStrings('a'));

object object a

A generic type that has not been given its arguments is compared by relating the parameters, which is why Id can be assigned to a concrete function type: the checker fills in T to make the assignment work.

A generic class with a private member is invariant whatever its use, because the private-member rule (§10.10) applies first.

A type parameter with no constraint behaves as unknown for compatibility inside the body of the generic, and as whatever it was filled in with outside. That is why code inside a generic function often cannot do what the caller obviously can: the body must work for every possible instantiation.

When two uses of a generic refuse to relate and you expected them to, the question to ask is which member uses T in the other position. A single method that takes T makes the whole type invariant, and the in and out annotations of §7.11 are how you both document and enforce what you intended.

10.12 The any Escape Hatch

The any escape hatch switches checking off for a value. Every operation on it is allowed, and its results are any too.

const parsed: any = JSON.parse('{"id": 1}');

console.log(parsed.id, parsed.nothing, parsed.a?.b?.c);
const asString: string = parsed;          // assignable to anything
const called = parsed.id.toFixed(2);      // and every operation is allowed
console.log(typeof asString, called);

1 undefined undefined
object 1.00

asString is annotated string and holds an object. That is any doing precisely what it is documented to do.

There are three legitimate uses, and they share one shape: the alternative is worse.

Describing genuinely dynamic behaviour in a .d.ts for a library whose API cannot be typed, although unknown is nearly always better even there.

A mixin's constructor signature (§6.25), where new (...args: any[]) => T is required for the extends Base clause to accept the arguments passed on. This is the one place this course allows it.

An in-progress migration, where a module is not yet typed and the choice is between any and not compiling.

And the rule that keeps it manageable: an any must not escape the function it enters. Narrow it, validate it, or assert it at the boundary, and let a real type travel onwards. §10.21 shows what happens when you do not.

noImplicitAny (§2.4) removes the accidental kind. @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any flags the deliberate kind, and running it as a warning with a required comment is a good middle position: it does not ban the tool, but it makes each use a decision.

10.13 unknown as the Safe any

Unknown as the safe any is the substitution to make almost everywhere. unknown accepts every value exactly as any does, and allows nothing until it has been narrowed.

function lengthOf(value: unknown): number {
  if (typeof value === 'string') return value.length;
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return value.length;
  if (value instanceof Set || value instanceof Map) return value.size;
  if (value !== null && typeof value === 'object' && 'length' in value
      && typeof value.length === 'number') return value.length;
  return 0;
}

console.log(lengthOf('abc'), lengthOf([1, 2]), lengthOf(new Set([1])), lengthOf({ length: 7 }), lengthOf(42));

function neverCalled(): number {
  const v: unknown = 'abc';
  // @ts-expect-error 'v' is of type 'unknown'.
  return v.length;
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

3 2 1 7 0
function

The fourth branch is the interesting one: narrowing unknown down to "an object with a numeric length" takes three checks, and the checker follows all of them. That is unknown making you write down what you actually know, and the result is code whose assumptions are visible.

Three substitutions worth making today.

catch (e: any) → catch (e) under useUnknownInCatchVariables (§10.19).

JSON.parse(...) becomes JSON.parse(...) as unknown straight away, or goes into a Json type (§5.17). The standard library returns any, which is a hole in the middle of every API boundary.

(x: any) => … becomes (x: unknown) => … in any function that will narrow anyway.

unknown absorbs everything in a union and changes nothing in an intersection, which makes it the top of the type hierarchy. The one thing it is not is a constraint: T extends unknown restricts nothing (§7.5).

10.14 A Double Assertion

A double assertion is x as unknown as T, and it exists to defeat the one guard that a single assertion has.

const n = 42;

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Conversion of type 'number' to type 'string' may be a mistake.
  const single = n as string;
}

// The double assertion is accepted — the relatedness check is gone.
const double = n as unknown as string;
console.log(typeof double, double, typeof neverCalled);

number 42 function

double is annotated string, holds the number 42, and typeof says number. A double assertion removes the last check the compiler was applying, so it is the most dangerous construct in the language after any.

The guard on a single assertion is that the two types must be related, meaning one can be assigned to the other (§2.11). Going through unknown breaks the chain into two steps, each of which is legal on its own, so any type can be asserted to any other.

There are two honest uses.

Crossing a boundary the type system cannot describe, where you have knowledge from outside: a value from a worker, a postMessage payload, or a deserialised structure whose shape a validator has just confirmed. Even here, a type predicate (§3.9) after a real check is better, because it is verified.

A test double, where you deliberately build a partial object and assert it into the full type. { id: 1 } as unknown as User in a test is a considered decision to skip the fields the test does not use.

Everything else is a bug being hidden. If a single assertion is rejected, the compiler has found that the two types are unrelated, which is information, not an obstacle.

10.15 Casting Through unknown

Casting through unknown is the same construct as §10.14, seen from the design side: where should an assertion live, and what should surround it?

The rule this course has applied throughout: an assertion belongs at a boundary, immediately after the check that justifies it, and it should be the only one.

type User = { id: string; name: string };

function isUser(v: unknown): v is User {
  return typeof v === 'object' && v !== null
    && 'id' in v && typeof v.id === 'string'
    && 'name' in v && typeof v.name === 'string';
}

function parseUser(json: string): User {
  const raw: unknown = JSON.parse(json);
  if (!isUser(raw)) throw new TypeError('not a user');
  return raw;                                     // no assertion needed: the guard narrowed it
}

console.log(parseUser('{"id":"u1","name":"Ada"}'));
try { parseUser('{"id":1}'); } catch (e) { console.log((e as Error).message); }

{ id: 'u1', name: 'Ada' }
not a user

There is no as in that function at all. The guard did the work, the narrowing followed, and the return type is honest. That is the shape to aim for: an assertion replaced by a check whose conclusion the checker carries forward.

Where an assertion genuinely remains, three rules keep it auditable.

One per boundary, and name the boundary. A parseUser, a fromWireFormat, a toBranded: one function whose whole job is the conversion, so there is one place to review.

Assert to the narrowest useful type, not to any. as User at least keeps checking downstream, while as any removes it.

Write down what makes it safe. A comment naming the invariant is the only record that survives, because the compiler will not remind you.

The timed wrapper of §9.8 and the asUserId of §8.11 are the two shapes this produces: an assertion inside a generic wrapper where the checker cannot relate a type parameter to itself, and an assertion inside a validator that has just checked. Both are internal, both are one line, and both have the check right above them.

10.16 Suppressing an Error

Suppressing an error is the last resort, below assertions, and TypeScript gives you two comments for it plus one configuration option.

// @ts-expect-error <reason>   — suppress, and require that an error exists
// @ts-ignore <reason>         — suppress, whether or not an error exists
// @ts-nocheck                 — at the top of a file: check nothing in it

All three are comments that apply to a line or a file, not type constructs, and all three are invisible to anyone reading the JavaScript that comes out.

The order of preference is not a matter of taste.

Fix the type. Nearly every suppression in a mature codebase is a missing generic, a missing narrowing, or a .d.ts that is wrong.

Assert, if you know something the checker cannot (§10.15). An assertion is at least a typed claim.

@ts-expect-error with a reason, if the error is genuinely a limitation of the compiler or of a library.

@ts-ignore — almost never; see §10.18.

@ts-nocheck, only for a file you are migrating, and with a ticket.

A suppression comment applies to the next line only, which is worth knowing because a multi-line expression is only suppressed at its first line. And none of them suppresses syntax errors: a TS1xxx is a parse failure, and no comment makes it go away.

10.17 A ts-expect-error Comment

A ts-expect-error comment suppresses the error on the next line and fails if there is no error there.

type Options = { retries: number };

// @ts-expect-error the config file is untyped and may omit retries
const partial: Options = {};

console.log(partial.retries);

undefined

The second half is the whole value. @ts-expect-error is a claim that the next line does not compile, so when the underlying problem is fixed (a library ships types, a compiler bug is closed, your own type is corrected), the comment itself becomes an error:

error TS2578: Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive.

That turns every suppression into a marker that cleans itself up. A codebase that uses @ts-expect-error cannot pile up stale suppressions, because each one is checked on every build.

It is also the right tool for testing types, which is how this whole course uses it: a line marked @ts-expect-error is a verified claim that something does not compile, and tooling in the style of check_marks can audit it. Expect<Equal<…>> (§8.1) covers the positive claims and @ts-expect-error the negative ones.

Always write a reason after it. The directive accepts trailing text, and a bare // @ts-expect-error tells the next reader nothing about whether the suppression is still justified.

Since TypeScript 5.5, a @ts-expect-error on a line inside a JavaScript file checked through JSDoc works the same way, so the tool is available during a migration too.

10.18 A ts-ignore Comment

A ts-ignore comment suppresses the error on the next line, and says nothing if there is no error.

// @ts-ignore
const a: number = 'not a number';

// @ts-ignore — and this one suppresses nothing at all, silently
const b: number = 1;

console.log(typeof a, b);

string 1

The second comment is dead, and nothing says so. That is the whole difference from @ts-expect-error, and it is why @ts-ignore should be treated as deprecated in its favour.

The failure is specific and common. A @ts-ignore is added for a real problem. A year later the problem is fixed, the comment stays, and it now silently suppresses whatever error appears on that line next. A change that breaks the line produces no diagnostic. That is a suppression that outlived its reason and became a blind spot.

The one case where @ts-ignore is correct is a line whose error depends on configuration: it errors under one tsconfig and not another, for instance in a monorepo (one repository holding several packages) where the same file is checked twice with different lib settings. @ts-expect-error would fail in the configuration where there is no error, while @ts-ignore is silent in both.

@typescript-eslint/ban-ts-comment is the lint rule, and its default configuration is the right one: @ts-expect-error allowed with a description, @ts-ignore and @ts-nocheck banned.

10.19 useUnknownInCatchVariables

useUnknownInCatchVariables types the variable in a catch clause as unknown instead of any. It is part of strict.

function risky(): string {
  try {
    throw new RangeError('too big');
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof RangeError) return `range: ${e.message}`;
    if (e instanceof Error) return `error: ${e.message}`;
    return `thrown: ${String(e)}`;
  }
}

console.log(risky());

function neverCalled(): void {
  try { risky(); } catch (e) {
    // @ts-expect-error 'e' is of type 'unknown'.
    console.log(e.message);
  }
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

range: too big
function

The setting is right because JavaScript can throw anything. throw 'a string', throw { code: 42 } and throw undefined are all legal, and a rejected promise carries whatever the rejecting code passed. Typing the variable as Error would be a lie that the language lets you break on the next line.

The explicit annotations are catch (e: unknown) and catch (e: any). Those are the only two allowed, and writing catch (e: Error) is an error whatever the setting. So the setting chooses the default, and you can opt out at each place.

The cost is one instanceof per catch block, which is the check you wanted anyway. The pattern above (most specific first, then Error, then a String(e) fallback) is the shape that §10.20 develops.

Note the interaction with Promise rejection: an await inside a try produces the rejection value in the same catch, with the same unknown type, and the same reasoning applies.

10.20 Type-Safe Error Handling

Type-safe error handling is a design problem, not a syntax one, because TypeScript has no throws clause: a function's type says nothing about what it can throw, so the compiler can never tell you that you failed to handle something.

Two strategies, and the choice is architectural.

Strategy one: throw, and narrow at the boundary. Use subclasses of Error so that instanceof can tell them apart.

class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly status: number, message: string) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'HttpError';
  }
}
class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly field: string) {
    super(`invalid ${field}`);
    this.name = 'ValidationError';
  }
}

function handle(e: unknown): string {
  if (e instanceof HttpError) return `HTTP ${e.status}`;
  if (e instanceof ValidationError) return `field ${e.field}`;
  if (e instanceof Error) return `${e.name}: ${e.message}`;
  return `non-error thrown: ${String(e)}`;
}

console.log(handle(new HttpError(404, 'nope')), '|', handle(new ValidationError('email')));
console.log(handle(new TypeError('bad')), '|', handle('a bare string'));

HTTP 404 | field email
TypeError: bad | non-error thrown: a bare string

Strategy two: return a result, and make the failure part of the type. This is the one the type system can actually enforce.

type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };

function parsePort(raw: string): Result<number, string> {
  const n = Number(raw);
  if (!Number.isInteger(n)) return { ok: false, error: `not an integer: ${raw}` };
  if (n < 1 || n > 65535) return { ok: false, error: `out of range: ${n}` };
  return { ok: true, value: n };
}

for (const raw of ['8080', 'abc', '99999']) {
  const r = parsePort(raw);
  console.log(r.ok ? `port ${r.value}` : `failed: ${r.error}`);
}

port 8080
failed: not an integer: abc
failed: out of range: 99999

The Result version is checked and the throw version is not. r.value cannot be reached without testing r.ok. The discriminated union (§3.12) makes the failure case impossible to ignore, and adding a third outcome produces errors at every consumer.

Use Result for expected failures and throw for bugs. A malformed port from user input is expected and belongs in the type, while an assertion violation is a bug and should throw. The mistake in both directions is common: throw for a validation failure buries it, and a Result for a programming error clutters every call.

Always attach cause. new Error('load failed', { cause: e }) keeps the original error, and it is the one piece of error hygiene that costs nothing and is skipped most often.

10.21 Why any Is Contagious

Why any is contagious is the closing argument of this section, and it is a property of how types propagate, not a warning about discipline.

Every operation on an any produces an any. A property access, a call, an index, the result of arithmetic, an await: all of them.

const config: any = JSON.parse('{"db": {"pool": {"max": "10"}}}');

const db = config.db;                    // any
const pool = db.pool;                    // any
const max = pool.max;                    // any — actually the string "10"

function describe(limit: number): string { return `limit ${limit + 1}`; }
console.log(describe(max), max * 2, max + 2, typeof max);

limit 101 20 102 string

Four variables and a function call, none of them annotated any, and every one of them unchecked. describe(max) accepted the string "10" into a parameter declared number and returned limit 101, because "10" + 1 joins strings. Note how close it comes to escaping detection: max * 2 really is 20, since multiplication converts the string to a number, so any test that exercises that path passes. It is the one operation that does not convert, +, that produces the wrong answer, and the single any at the top is what allowed a string to reach it.

That is the mechanism, and three consequences follow.

The damage follows the flow of data, not the file. An any returned from a module spreads through every consumer that does not annotate.

It defeats the tools silently. There is no error, no warning and no lint finding at the point where checking stopped, and the describe(max) line looks perfectly ordinary.

It survives review, because the any is usually in a different file from the bug.

The rule for containing it is one sentence: convert at the boundary. The moment an any enters, through JSON.parse, an untyped library or a .d.ts you did not write, narrow it, validate it, or annotate it into a real type, in the same function. const config: unknown = JSON.parse(...) followed by a validator (§16.21) is the whole fix, and the example above then fails to compile at config.db instead of producing NaN in production.

@typescript-eslint's no-unsafe-assignment, no-unsafe-member-access, no-unsafe-call, no-unsafe-return and no-unsafe-argument are the type-aware rules that make the spread visible (§17.18). They are noisy on a codebase with a lot of any, which is exactly the measurement they exist to give.

What This Section Established

Assignability is one relation, asked in many places and worked out member by member. any works both ways, and so does a numeric enum against number: those are the two two-way holes. unknown accepts everything and allows nothing, and never is the reverse.

Functions compare with fewer parameters allowed, covariant returns and contravariant parameters, except that the parameters of methods written with method syntax are bivariant on purpose, and strictFunctionTypes only fixes properties that hold functions. Declaring callbacks as properties is a one-word way to switch on the sound rule. Optional and required parameters relate in one direction only: required = optional compiles and the reverse does not.

A numeric enum flows freely into number, which is a real hole, and two enums are never compatible with each other, which is the one place where they are name-based. Classes go by shape until a private or protected member appears, at which point they are compared by where the member was declared: a free brand, and the cause of the "Type 'Foo' is not assignable to type 'Foo'" error that means two copies of a package.

Then the escape hatches, in order of preference: fix the type; assert at a boundary with the check beside it; @ts-expect-error with a reason, which cleans itself up when the underlying problem is fixed; and @ts-ignore almost never, because it silently suppresses whatever appears on that line next. A double assertion removes the last guard the compiler had. And any spreads with the flow of data and not with files, which is why the rule is to convert it in the function it enters.

Exercises

1. Predict eight assignments. For each pair, say whether the assignment compiles and why: number ← any; Dog[] ← Animal[]; Animal[] ← Dog[]; (a: Animal) => void ← (d: Dog) => void; { handle(a: Animal): void } ← { handle(d: Dog): void }; Priority ← 2; VaultA ← VaultB where both declare private key; readonly number[] ← number[]. Then run them and check.

2. Contain an any. Take a module that reads a JSON config with JSON.parse and passes values three functions deep. Show the wrong output that the any produces, then contain it at the boundary in two ways, with a type predicate and with a Result, and show the compile errors that now appear at the point of the mistake.

3. Replace three suppressions. Given a @ts-ignore over a real gap in a library, a @ts-ignore over a missing narrowing, and a @ts-ignore that no longer suppresses anything, give the correct treatment of each and explain what happens to each one when the underlying situation changes.

Solution

1. Eight assignments.

type Animal = { name: string };
type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void };

declare let anyValue: any;
declare let animals: Animal[];
declare let dogs: Dog[];
declare let handleAnimal: (a: Animal) => void;
declare let handleDog: (d: Dog) => void;
declare let methodAnimal: { handle(a: Animal): void };
declare let methodDog: { handle(d: Dog): void };
enum Priority { Low = 1, High = 2 }
let priority: Priority = Priority.Low;
class VaultA { private key = 'k'; }
class VaultB { private key = 'k'; }
declare let va: VaultA;
declare let vb: VaultB;
declare let mutable: number[];

let n: number = anyValue;              // ✅ 1. any is assignable to everything
animals = dogs;                        // ✅ 3. arrays are covariant (unsoundly)
handleDog = handleAnimal;              // ✅ 4b. contravariance: wider parameter is fine
methodAnimal = methodDog;              // ✅ 5. METHOD parameters are bivariant
priority = 2;                          // ✅ 6. a numeric enum accepts any number
const ro: readonly number[] = mutable; // ✅ 8. mutable widens to readonly

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error 2. Property 'bark' is missing — Animal[] is not a Dog[]
  dogs = animals;
  // @ts-expect-error 4a. contravariance forbids a narrower parameter
  handleAnimal = handleDog;
  // @ts-expect-error 7. Types have separate declarations of a private property 'key'
  va = vb;
}
console.log(n, animals.length, typeof handleDog, priority, ro.length, typeof neverCalled);

undefined 0 function 2 0 function

The two that trip people are 3 and 5. Animal[] ← Dog[] compiles because arrays are covariant despite being mutable (§1.12), and pushing an Animal into the widened alias then corrupts the original. The method case compiles for the same family of reasons, since the signatures of Array<T> itself require bivariance, and the property-syntax version of the identical declaration does not.

8 is the safe direction, and there is no reverse. number[] → readonly number[] is always fine, and readonly number[] → number[] is always an error, which is why a readonly parameter type accepts more from callers.

2. Containing an any.

type Config = { db: { pool: { max: number } } };

// The uncontained version.
const loose: any = JSON.parse('{"db":{"pool":{"max":"10"}}}');
function poolSize(c: any): number { return c.db.pool.max; }
function budget(size: number): string { return `budget ${size + 5}`; }
console.log('uncontained:', budget(poolSize(loose)));

// Containment A — a type predicate at the boundary.
function isConfig(v: unknown): v is Config {
  return typeof v === 'object' && v !== null && 'db' in v
    && typeof (v as { db: unknown }).db === 'object'
    && typeof ((v as Config).db?.pool?.max) === 'number';
}

function parseConfigA(json: string): Config {
  const raw: unknown = JSON.parse(json);
  if (!isConfig(raw)) throw new TypeError('bad config');
  return raw;
}

try { parseConfigA('{"db":{"pool":{"max":"10"}}}'); }
catch (e) { console.log('predicate:', (e as Error).message); }
console.log('predicate ok:', budget(parseConfigA('{"db":{"pool":{"max":10}}}').db.pool.max));

// Containment B — a Result, so the failure is in the type.
type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };
function parseConfigB(json: string): Result<Config, string> {
  const raw: unknown = JSON.parse(json);
  return isConfig(raw) ? { ok: true, value: raw } : { ok: false, error: 'bad config' };
}

const r = parseConfigB('{"db":{"pool":{"max":"10"}}}');
console.log('result:', r.ok ? budget(r.value.db.pool.max) : `failed: ${r.error}`);

uncontained: budget 105
predicate: bad config
predicate ok: budget 15
result: failed: bad config

budget 105 is the uncontained answer, produced with no error anywhere. poolSize returned the string "10" from a function whose declared return type is number, and "10" + 5 is "105". The correct answer for the same code with real data is 15, as the validated call two lines down shows. A single any at the parse turned an off-by-ninety into a silent one.

With unknown at the boundary, raw.db no longer compiles at all. The error appears in parseConfigA, at the line that reads a property off unvalidated data, which is where the mistake is. That is the whole benefit: the diagnostic moved from "nowhere" to "the boundary".

The Result version additionally makes the failure impossible to ignore. r.value cannot be reached without testing r.ok, so a caller cannot forget the bad-config case. The predicate version throws, which is correct only if something up the stack catches.

3. Three suppressions.

// (a) A genuine library gap -> @ts-expect-error with a reason.
declare const legacy: { render(): void };
// @ts-expect-error @types/legacy@1.2 omits renderAsync; remove when 1.3 lands
legacy.renderAsync?.();

// (b) A missing narrowing -> fix the type, no suppression at all.
function lengthOfWrong(v: string | undefined): number {
  // the @ts-ignore that was here is replaced by a check
  return v !== undefined ? v.length : 0;
}

// (c) A suppression over a line that no longer errors -> delete it.
const fine: number = 1;

console.log(lengthOfWrong('abc'), lengthOfWrong(undefined), fine);

3 0 1

(a) @ts-expect-error is right precisely because the situation will change. When @types/legacy@1.3 ships renderAsync, the line stops erroring and the directive itself becomes TS2578: Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive. That is a build failure that tells you to delete the comment and, more importantly, that the workaround is no longer needed. A @ts-ignore there would sit silently forever.

(b) The right treatment is no suppression. The original error was 'v' is possibly 'undefined', which is a real fact about the input, and a narrowing states how to handle it. Every suppression over a nullability error is a crash that was reported and dismissed.

(c) The third one is the argument for banning @ts-ignore. It suppresses nothing today and will suppress whatever error appears on that line next, so a change that breaks the assignment produces no diagnostic at all. @ts-expect-error in the same position would have failed the build the day the underlying error was fixed, which is the behaviour you want from every suppression.

Configure @typescript-eslint/ban-ts-comment at its defaults (@ts-expect-error allowed with a description, @ts-ignore and @ts-nocheck banned) and the three treatments above become the only ones the linter permits.

SECTION 11

Modules

Modules are where TypeScript stops being only a type checker and starts acting as a build tool, and they trip up experienced people more often than any other part of the language. The reason is that three separate systems are stacked on top of each other, each with its own rules: JavaScript's own module rules, Node's way of finding files, and TypeScript's removal of types from the import graph. An error about a default import can come from any of the three.

The plan is to keep those layers apart. First, the syntax TypeScript adds: type-only imports and exports, and the two settings that make them mandatory. Then the three questions the compiler answers about every import you write: what kind of file does this produce (module), where does this import point (moduleResolution), and what did the package say about itself (exports, imports and conditions). Then working with CommonJS, the older module format, where most of the historical mess lives. Last, the two newest pieces: a package that ships both formats, and import defer.

Everything that depends on the version was measured against the installed compiler rather than recalled from memory, because this is the area of TypeScript that changed most in versions 5 and 6. Two options you will find in every older tutorial, baseUrl and esModuleInterop: false, no longer exist at all.

11.1 An ES Module in TypeScript

An ES module in TypeScript is an ordinary ES module with type annotations. There is no TypeScript module system: import and export mean what they mean in JavaScript, the bindings are live, the order of evaluation is the standard one, and the type layer sits on top without changing any of it.

// geometry.ts
export type Point = { x: number; y: number };
export const ORIGIN: Point = { x: 0, y: 0 };
export function distance(a: Point, b: Point): number {
  return Math.hypot(a.x - b.x, a.y - b.y);
}
export default distance;

// main.ts
import distanceDefault, { type Point, ORIGIN, distance } from './geometry.js';
import * as geometry from './geometry.js';

const p: Point = { x: 3, y: 4 };
console.log(distance(ORIGIN, p), distanceDefault(ORIGIN, p), geometry.ORIGIN);

The one thing that looks wrong and is right: the specifier says ./geometry.js while the file on disk is geometry.ts. That is not a typo and not a compiler quirk. It is TypeScript refusing to rewrite your specifiers. The main.js that comes out will import ./geometry.js, which is the file that will exist at runtime, and a specifier ending in .ts would produce a broken import. §11.14 covers the two settings that change this, and the default is worth remembering: you write the specifier that the output needs.

A module specifier is the string in the from clause, and there are three kinds, told apart by their first character. A relative specifier begins with ./ or ../ and is resolved from the importing file. A bare specifier is a package name, such as react, node:fs or @scope/pkg, and is resolved by looking through node_modules and the package's own exports map (§11.12). An absolute specifier begins with / and is resolved from the root of the filesystem, which almost nothing should do.

The type layer's contribution is that types are exported and imported with exactly the same syntax as values. Point and ORIGIN travel together in one import statement. That convenience is also the problem that the next three subsections solve: because a type and a value look identical where they are imported, the compiler has to work out which of them exist at runtime before it can produce any output.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: a module specifier.

11.2 A Non-Module File, Module Detection and moduleDetection

A non-module file, called a script in the specification, is a file with no top-level import or export. Its top-level declarations go into the global scope, which is occasionally what you want (a .d.ts that declares globals, §12.4) and is usually a surprise.

Module detection is the rule the compiler uses to decide which of the two a file is, and it is not simply "does it have an import".

// coll.ts — no imports, no exports
const name = 'collides with the DOM global in a script';
console.log(name);

Whether that file compiles depends on two things that are nowhere in the file. Measured against the installed compiler with lib including dom:

package.json moduleDetection Result
"type": "module" auto (default) compiles — the file is a module, name is local
"type": "module" legacy error — a script, and name redeclares the DOM's global name
"type": "module" force compiles — everything is a module
no "type" field auto error — a script
no "type" field legacy error — a script
no "type" field force compiles

The moduleDetection option has three values, and auto is the default. Under auto a file is a module if it has an import or export, or if the nearest package.json says "type": "module", or if it is a .mts or .cts file. Under legacy only the import-or-export rule applies, which is how TypeScript behaved before 4.7. Under force every file is a module regardless, which is the setting to use for application code: it removes a whole class of "why is my const a global" confusion, and it makes every file's behaviour independent of a package.json several directories up.

The classic symptom of getting this wrong is the error above: Cannot redeclare block-scoped variable 'name'. A top-level const name, const status, const location, const origin, const closed or const length in a script file collides with a DOM global, and the message points at your file while the cause is that the file is not a module. The one-line fix is export {}; at the bottom of the file, which makes module detection classify it as a module. The better fix is "moduleDetection": "force" in the config, so the question never comes up.

Note the asymmetry that makes this worth understanding instead of memorising: module detection changes scoping, not syntax. A script and a module both compile the same statements, and they differ in whether the top level is global. That is why the error is never "this file is a script" but always some downstream consequence.

11.3 Type-Only Imports and Exports

A type does not exist at runtime, so an import that brings in only types must not appear in the JavaScript that comes out. Working out which imports those are is a question about the whole program: the compiler has to look inside geometry.ts to know whether Point is a type, and that is exactly the analysis that a tool working on one file at a time cannot do. A type-only import and a type-only export are the syntax that makes the answer local.

// Three ways to say "this is a type".
import type { Point } from './geometry.js';              // the whole import is type-only
import { type Point as P, ORIGIN } from './geometry.js'; // the type modifier on a named import
import type * as Types from './geometry.js';             // a type-only namespace import

export type { Point };                                    // a type-only export
export { type Point as PublicPoint } from './geometry.js';

const p: P = ORIGIN;
export const q: Point = p;

import type erases the entire statement. Nothing is produced, and the module is never loaded at runtime. That matters when importing it would have a side effect (running code that changes something, such as registering a plugin), and it matters a great deal for build speed in a large project.

The type modifier on a named import is the finer-grained form: import { type Point, ORIGIN } keeps the import statement (because ORIGIN is a value) and erases only that one name. It is the right spelling when a module gives you both, and it avoids the two-import-statements-from-one-module pattern that older codebases are full of.

A type-only export is the mirror image, and it has one use that the plain form cannot cover: re-exporting a type through a barrel file, meaning a file that only re-exports other files. export { Point } from './geometry.js' is ambiguous to a tool that works on one file at a time, and under isolatedModules (§11.5) it is an error, while export type { Point } is unambiguous and always correct.

One rule catches everyone once. import type may not be used for something you then use as a value, and the reverse is also enforced:

import type { distance } from './geometry.js';
// @ts-expect-error 'distance' cannot be used as a value because it was imported using 'import type'
console.log(distance);

That is a good error to meet, because it means the type-only marker really matters and is not decoration: the compiler is telling you that the file it produces will not contain this name.

A note on import type * as: it imports the namespace type of the module, so Types.Point is a type and Types.ORIGIN is the type of ORIGIN. It is the type-position equivalent of a namespace import, and it pairs naturally with the import() type of §11.6.

11.4 verbatimModuleSyntax

verbatimModuleSyntax removes the guessing entirely: with it on, every import and export is written to the output exactly as you wrote it, and any import that is not marked type is kept. The compiler stops removing anything, so an import of a type that you forgot to mark becomes an error instead of a silent removal.

// Without verbatimModuleSyntax the compiler silently elides this import.
// With it on:
import { A } from './dep.js';
// error TS1484: 'A' is a type and must be imported using a type-only import
// when 'verbatimModuleSyntax' is enabled.
export const g = (a: A) => a.id;

The fix is import { type A } or import type { A }, and the point is that after the fix the JavaScript that comes out is a mechanical change to the source: delete every construct marked type, and leave everything else. That property is worth a great deal.

Three things it buys you, and each solves a real problem.

Any transpiler produces the same output. A transpiler is a tool that converts source code from one language to another, here TypeScript to JavaScript. esbuild, swc, Babel and Node's own type stripping (§15.24) all work on one file at a time and cannot know whether A is a type. Under verbatimModuleSyntax they do not need to know, because you said.

Imports with side effects survive. Without the setting, import { something } from './register-plugin.js', where something is a type, has the whole statement removed, and the plugin is never registered. That is a bug that only appears in the built output and never during development. With the setting, the import stays because you did not mark it as a type.

ESM and CommonJS do not get mixed by accident. The setting makes it an error to write import x = require(...) in a file that will produce ESM, and the other way round, so the format of the output matches the syntax you wrote.

verbatimModuleSyntax is the setting to turn on for new code. Turning it on in an existing codebase produces a large but entirely mechanical diff, in which every unmarked type import becomes a marked one. The consistent-type-imports rule of typescript-eslint (§17.18) can make the whole edit automatically.

11.5 isolatedModules

isolatedModules is the older, weaker relative of verbatimModuleSyntax, and it is worth knowing separately because it flags a different set of constructs: those that cannot be compiled correctly one file at a time, whatever the transpiler does.

// error TS1205: Re-exporting a type when 'isolatedModules' is enabled
// requires using 'export type'.
export { A } from './dep.js';

Under isolatedModules the compiler refuses any construct whose output depends on information from another file. The full list is short, and each entry has the same shape.

A re-export of a type without export type, as above: the transpiler cannot know whether to write out the re-export.

An export = or an ambient const enum from another file (§15.7), because the values of a const enum are copied in from the file that declares it. Ambient means declared with declare: it describes something that exists without supplying its code.

A file with no imports or exports, which under isolatedModules must be a module. export {} is the fix, exactly as in §11.2.

The difference from verbatimModuleSyntax is worth stating precisely, because the two are often described as the same thing. isolatedModules says "do not write anything that needs knowledge of other files in order to be compiled". verbatimModuleSyntax says "the output is a literal deletion of what you marked". The second implies the first for imports and exports, but isolatedModules also covers const enum and a few declaration-merging cases that verbatimModuleSyntax says nothing about. Modern configurations turn on both, and tsc --init does exactly that.

If your build runs tsc and nothing else, neither setting is strictly required. Every real pipeline has a second tool in it (a bundler, the transform in a test runner, Node's own stripping), and the moment that is true, isolatedModules is the setting that turns "works in tsc, breaks in the bundler" into a compile error you see immediately.

11.6 The import() Type

An import() type brings a type in without an import statement, anywhere a type is expected: import('./config.js').Config. It is TypeScript's answer to two problems that a statement cannot solve.

// A type from a module, used inline — no import statement at the top of the file.
type Config = typeof import('./config.js');
type Port = import('./config.js').Port;

// Which matters most in a .d.ts that must not become a module (§12.4).
declare global {
  interface Window { appConfig: import('./config.js').Config }
}
export {};

The trap is the difference between import('m') and typeof import('m'). import('./config.js').Port names an exported type called Port. typeof import('./config.js') is the type of the module's namespace object, the thing you would get from import * as ns. Writing import('./config.js') on its own, expecting the namespace, produces a specific and helpful error:

error TS1340: Module './config.js' does not refer to a type, but is used as a type here.
Did you mean 'typeof import('./config.js')'?

Three places where an import() type is the only option.

Inside declare global. A .d.ts that adds to the global scope must be a script (§11.2), and adding an import statement would make it a module and switch the augmentation off. An import() type is an expression, not a statement, so the file stays a script.

In a circular reference that the statement form cannot express. Circularity between types is fine, but an import statement creates a real link between modules, while an import() type in a type position does not, because it is erased.

For a one-off reference. Naming a type from a module that you use in exactly one signature does not deserve a line at the top of the file, and writing it inline is genuinely more readable there.

An import() type is completely erased and can be generic: import('./repo.js').Repository<User> works, and so does typeof import('./mod.js')['default'] for the type of a default export.

11.7 export = and import require

Before ES modules existed, TypeScript needed a way to describe a CommonJS module whose entire export is a single value: module.exports = function () {}, which is what most of the npm registry from before 2015 looks like. Export equals and import require are that syntax, and they are the only two module constructs in TypeScript that are not JavaScript.

// legacy.d.cts — describing `module.exports = greet`
declare function greet(name: string): string;
export = greet;

// consumer.cts — the matching import form
import greet = require('./legacy.cjs');
console.log(greet('Ada'));

Both blocks are shown untagged as TypeScript deliberately: compiled as ES modules they do not even parse, and the errors say why: TS1203: Export assignment cannot be used when targeting ECMAScript modules and TS1202: Import assignment cannot be used when targeting ECMAScript modules. The .cts extension is what makes them legal, and it is the mechanism §11.10 describes.

export = replaces the entire exports of the module with one entity, a function, a class, a namespace or an object, and a module that uses it may have no other exports. import x = require('m') is the matching import, and it binds x to that entity directly instead of to a namespace object.

Two constraints decide when you may use them, and both are checked.

They are only legal in a file that produces CommonJS. Under module: node16 or nodenext that means a .cts file, or a .ts file in a package without "type": "module". In an ESM file the compiler rejects them, because there is no ESM syntax that means what they mean.

In new code you almost never write them. The place you meet export = is a hand-written declaration file for an old package (§12.20), and the place you meet import = require is a .cts file that uses one. Everything else should use import and export, and the interop machinery of §11.15 is what lets an ESM file use an export = module with a plain default import.

There is a second, unrelated use of the import x = ... syntax that is worth recognising so you do not confuse the two: an import alias, import Shortcut = Some.Nested.Namespace, which creates a local name for a member of a namespace (§15.11). It uses the same keyword, with no require and no module involved.

To have in hand before moving on: export equals.

11.8 An Ambient Module

An ambient module is a declaration for a module that TypeScript cannot see the source of: an untyped npm package, a virtual module provided by a bundler, or a file type that your build tool turns into a value.

// globals.d.ts — a SCRIPT file: no top-level import or export anywhere in it
declare module 'legacy-lib' {
  export function greet(name: string): string;
  const version: string;
  export default version;
}

declare module '*.svg' {
  const url: string;
  export default url;
}

// Now both resolve, with types.
import version, { greet } from 'legacy-lib';
import logoUrl from './logo.svg';
console.log(greet('Ada'), version, logoUrl);

The wildcard form is the one that earns its keep. declare module '*.svg' gives types to every SVG import at once, which is how a bundler's asset imports get types. '*.css', '*.graphql' and '*?raw' are the same pattern.

The rule that makes ambient modules fail is subtle and worth stating loudly: the file that declares them must be a script, not a module. Put a declare module 'legacy-lib' inside a file that has any top-level import or export and it stops being an ambient declaration and becomes a module augmentation (§12.6), which is a request to add members to an existing module. The compiler says so:

error TS2664: Invalid module name in augmentation, module 'legacy-lib' cannot be found.

That message names the real problem badly. The trouble is not that the module cannot be found. It is that your file is a module, so the declaration was read as an augmentation of something that does not exist. Move the declare module into a .d.ts with no imports or exports and it works. If you need a type from elsewhere inside it, use an import() type (§11.6) instead of an import statement, precisely because the statement would break the file's status as a script.

An ambient module is a promise, not a check: nothing verifies that legacy-lib really exports a greet. That is the cost of the escape hatch, and §12.20 covers how to write one carefully. The short version is to type only what you use, and to prefer unknown over a guess.

11.9 The module Option and the Output Format

The module compiler option answers one question: what module syntax should the JavaScript that comes out use? It does not affect what you write, because you write import and export regardless, and on its own it does not decide how specifiers are resolved. The module output format is its only job.

Compiled from the same source, with the type annotations stripped:

// m.ts
import type { A } from './types.js';
import { helper } from './helper.js';
export type { A };
export const use = (a: A) => helper(a.id);

With tsc --module esnext, and --module preserve gives the same output here:

import { helper } from './helper.js';
export const use = (a) => helper(a.id);

With tsc --module node16, in a CommonJS package:

"use strict";
Object.defineProperty(exports, "__esModule", { value: true });
exports.use = void 0;
const helper_js_1 = require("./helper.js");
const use = (a) => (0, helper_js_1.helper)(a.id);
exports.use = use;

Two details in the CommonJS output are worth reading instead of skimming, because they explain behaviour you will meet.

Object.defineProperty(exports, "__esModule", { value: true }) is the marker that tells a compatibility layer "this CommonJS module was compiled from ESM", and it is what makes import x from './m.js' give you the default export and not the whole namespace (§11.15).

(0, helper_js_1.helper)(a.id) is a comma expression whose only purpose is to call the function with this unset, since a direct helper_js_1.helper(...) would pass the namespace object as this. It is noise in the output and also a correctness fix.

module: esnext produces ES modules always, and is what a bundler wants. module: commonjs produces CommonJS always, which is the legacy setting. Note that under the installed compiler it may not be combined with moduleResolution: node16, and the message says so: TS5110: Option 'module' must be set to 'Node16' when option 'moduleResolution' is set to 'Node16'.

Four values that every older tutorial mentions no longer exist: module: amd, module: umd and module: system are removed (TS5108), and so is outFile, which was the option that made them useful. If you meet them in a config, the migration is to a bundler, and §14.16 lists the removals in full.

Gathered here, since each is referred to later: the module output format, the module compiler option, module preserve and module esnext.

11.10 module node16, nodenext and preserve

The three values you should actually choose between are node16, nodenext and preserve, and they differ in who decides the format.

Module node16 and nodenext, meaning module: node16 and module: nodenext, hand the decision to Node's own rules: the format of each file is decided by its extension and by the "type" field of the nearest package.json. A .mts file is always ESM, a .cts file is always CommonJS, and a .ts file is whichever the package says. nodenext follows the latest Node behaviour and node16 stays with that of Node 16, and in practice nodenext is the one to use for anything running on Node today.

The consequence is that under these settings one project can contain both formats, and the compiler checks each file against the rules of its own format. export = in a .cts file is fine and in a .mts file is an error. A bare require in an ESM file is an error. The extension in a relative specifier is mandatory in ESM and optional in CommonJS. All of that is Node's behaviour, faithfully reproduced.

module: preserve does something different and newer: it writes your import and export syntax out unchanged and leaves the question of format to whatever runs next. Written with import, you get import, and written with require, you get require. It exists for setups with a bundler, where the bundler, not tsc and not Node, decides the output format, and it pairs with moduleResolution: bundler.

A summary of when each is right:

Setting Use when
nodenext The output runs on Node directly. Format follows the file extension and package.json.
preserve A bundler consumes the output, or tsc runs with noEmit for checking only.
esnext You want ESM output unconditionally, and you control the runtime.
commonjs A legacy build that must stay CommonJS everywhere.

Getting this wrong is the most common cause of module errors in TypeScript, and it has one characteristic symptom: everything type-checks and the output crashes at runtime with ERR_REQUIRE_ESM or Cannot use import statement outside a module. It is always the same kind of mistake: the module setting and the actual runtime disagree about the format. Under nodenext this class of bug is largely designed out, because the compiler applies exactly the rules the runtime will.

In summary, the vocabulary here is module node16 and nodenext.

11.11 The moduleResolution Option

The moduleResolution option answers the second question: given the specifier './helper.js' or 'lodash', which file is that? In principle it is independent of module, and in practice it is constrained by it, since the compiler refuses combinations that no runtime implements.

The values that still exist are node16, nodenext and bundler. Three that were the default for years are gone: classic, node10 and node, the umbrella name for the last one, all report TS5108: has been removed.

moduleResolution: nodenext implements Node's ESM and CommonJS resolution exactly, including the parts people find strict.
