In an ESM file, a relative specifier must carry its extension, './helper.js' and not './helper', and a directory specifier does not resolve to index.js. Those are Node's rules, not TypeScript's, and the compiler enforcing them is the whole point: the alternative is a build that succeeds and a runtime that cannot find the file.

moduleResolution: bundler relaxes exactly those two rules, because bundlers relax them: extensionless specifiers and directory indexes both resolve. It still reads the exports and imports fields of package.json, so it is not the old node10 algorithm with a new name. It is "modern resolution, minus the extension requirement". It is only legal with module: esnext or module: preserve, which is the compiler recording that this resolution mode only makes sense when a bundler comes after it.

# The pairing the compiler enforces, and what happens if you break it:
--module commonjs --moduleResolution node16
  error TS5110: Option 'module' must be set to 'Node16' when option
  'moduleResolution' is set to 'Node16'.

--module amd --moduleResolution bundler
  error TS5095: Option 'bundler' can only be used when 'module' is set to
  'preserve' or to 'es2015' or later.

The resolution mode also decides which types a package gives you. The exports map of a package may point at different declaration files for the import and require conditions, so the same package can present different types to an ESM file and a CommonJS file in the same project. That is a feature, since a package published in both formats (§11.16) genuinely has two shapes, and it is why moduleResolution belongs to the file and not just to the project.

What to take from this subsection: module commonjs for an unconditional CommonJS build, and moduleResolution bundler, the relaxed algorithm, when a bundler comes after tsc.

11.12 Package Exports, Conditions and Subpath Imports

Modern packages describe their own entry points, and TypeScript reads that description. Three fields matter.

// node_modules/mylib/package.json
{
  "name": "mylib",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".":     { "types": "./index.d.ts", "default": "./index.js" },
    "./sub": { "types": "./sub.d.ts",   "default": "./sub.js" }
  }
}

// The importing package's own package.json
{ "name": "app", "type": "module", "imports": { "#config": "./src/config.js" } }

import { one } from 'mylib';         // resolves via exports["."]
import { two } from 'mylib/sub';     // resolves via exports["./sub"]
import { PORT } from '#config';      // a subpath import, from the app's own package.json

import type { Options } from 'mylib/missing';
// error TS2307: Cannot find module 'mylib/missing' or its corresponding type
// declarations. — the exports map does not list this subpath

exports is an allow-list, not a hint. A subpath that the map does not name cannot be reached, and TypeScript reports TS2307: Cannot find module 'mylib/missing', which is exactly what Node would do at runtime. Under the removed node10 resolution the same import would have found the file on disk and worked, which is why upgrading a project's moduleResolution sometimes brings out a pile of new errors: they were always real, and the old algorithm ignored the package's own rules.

resolvePackageJsonExports is the setting that controls that behaviour, and it is on by default under node16, nodenext and bundler. Its sibling resolvePackageJsonImports does the same for the imports field. You would only turn either off to work around a broken package, and the better fix is to report the package.

A subpath import is a specifier that starts with #, defined in the imports field of your own package.json. It is the standard replacement for the removed baseUrl and paths combination (§11.13) for anything you publish, because, unlike paths, it is a runtime feature that Node implements. #config works in the built output with no bundler and no path rewriting.

customConditions adds names to the list of conditions used when matching an entry in exports or imports. The built-in conditions are import, require, types, node and default. A monorepo commonly adds one such as "customConditions": ["source"], so that internal packages resolve to their TypeScript sources during development and to built output in production, with one exports map serving both.

The terms above, gathered: resolvePackageJsonExports, resolvePackageJsonImports and customConditions, all of which control how a bare specifier is matched against a package's own manifest.

11.13 paths Mapping

Paths mapping rewrites specifiers for the type checker, and only for the type checker. "paths": { "@app/*": ["./src/*"] } makes import { x } from '@app/a' resolve to ./src/a.ts at compile time and writes out '@app/a' unchanged, so something later in the chain must know what that means.

// tsconfig.json — measured working with the installed compiler
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "paths": { "@app/*": ["./src/*"] }
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

paths no longer requires baseUrl, because baseUrl has been removed. That is the most important fact about the current version in this subsection: every tutorial written before TypeScript 6 pairs the two, and baseUrl now reports TS5102: Option 'baseUrl' has been removed. Relative entries in paths are resolved from the directory that contains the tsconfig.json, which is what you almost always wanted, and ${configDir} (§13.5) makes that explicit when the config is extended from elsewhere.

The warning that goes with the feature: paths mapping is a lie unless something enforces it at runtime. tsc will type-check happily and write out an import of @app/a that Node cannot resolve. You need one of:

  • a bundler with a matching alias configuration (every bundler has one);
  • a hook for the runtime's resolver;
  • or, better, a subpath import (§11.12) instead, which Node implements natively.

For application code that a bundler consumes, paths is fine and convenient. For a published package it is a trap: your users get the unresolvable specifier in the .js and the .d.ts you ship. The rule is simple: paths for apps, imports for libraries.

11.14 File Extensions in Specifiers

The ./geometry.js specifier that points at geometry.ts (§11.1) is the default, and two settings change it, with sharply different consequences.

allowImportingTsExtensions lets you write the real extension:

import { helper } from './dep.ts';

# without the flag:
error TS5097: An import path can only end with a '.ts' extension when
'allowImportingTsExtensions' is enabled.

On its own this setting requires noEmit (or emitDeclarationOnly), because the JavaScript that comes out would import a .ts file that does not exist at runtime. That makes it the right setting for a tsc that only checks, in a project where a bundler or a runtime with type stripping does the real work.

rewriteRelativeImportExtensions is the setting that makes .ts specifiers work when emitting: it rewrites .ts to .js in the output.

// rw.ts
import { helper } from './dep.ts';
export const h = helper(1);

Compiled with tsc --allowImportingTsExtensions --rewriteRelativeImportExtensions:

// rw.ts
import { helper } from './dep.js';
export const h = helper(1);

Only the extension changed: the specifier keeps its original quotes, and the // rw.ts comment stays with the statement it belongs to.

.mts becomes .mjs and .cts becomes .cjs by the same rule. The rewrite applies only to relative specifiers, deliberately: a bare specifier ending in .ts refers to a file inside someone else's package, and rewriting it would be a guess.

The reason to want any of this is that ./dep.ts is what every other tool in the ecosystem accepts (editors, Deno, Bun, Node's type stripping), while ./dep.js pointing at a .ts file is a TypeScript-specific convention that confuses newcomers and breaks "go to file". The reason to be careful is that the two settings have different requirements, and turning on the first without the second in a project that emits produces TS5096.

For a project that emits with tsc, use the .js convention, or turn on both settings together. For a project that only type-checks, use allowImportingTsExtensions alone, with noEmit.

11.15 ESM and CJS Interoperability

ESM and CJS interoperability is the messiest area in the whole ecosystem, and TypeScript's part in it has become much simpler in version 7, because the two options that used to control it have been removed and their permissive behaviour is now permanent.

The underlying mismatch is this. A CommonJS module has one value, module.exports. An ES module has named bindings and possibly a default. When an ESM file imports a CommonJS one, something must decide whether import x from 'cjs-thing' means "the whole module.exports" or "module.exports.default".

esModuleInterop was the setting that chose. It writes out helper code that checks the __esModule marker (§11.9) at runtime and hands back the right thing, and it makes a default import of an export = module type-check. It can no longer be turned off:

--esModuleInterop false
  error TS5108: Option 'esModuleInterop=false' has been removed.

--allowSyntheticDefaultImports false
  error TS5108: Option 'allowSyntheticDefaultImports=false' has been removed.

Both were measured against the installed compiler. allowSyntheticDefaultImports is the type-only half of the same idea: it makes the default import type-check without changing the output, and it is what esModuleInterop implies. Since neither can be disabled, the practical rule is: a default import of a CommonJS module works, and gives you module.exports. Delete both options from any config you inherit.

What remains for you to get right is the direction that TypeScript cannot fix:

CommonJS importing ESM is genuinely hard. require() of an ES module fails on older Node with ERR_REQUIRE_ESM, and newer Node can require an ES module that is fully synchronous, but not one with top-level await. The reliable answer in a .cts file is a dynamic await import('esm-thing'), and TypeScript types that correctly.

Named imports from CommonJS are best-effort. import { readFile } from 'some-cjs-package' relies on the runtime's static analysis of the CommonJS file finding that name. Node's detection is good and not perfect, while a default import plus a property access always works.

Under verbatimModuleSyntax the format of a file is fixed by its extension, which removes the last piece of ambiguity: a .mts file is ESM and its import statements stay imports, and a .cts file is CommonJS and must use import = require.

11.16 A Dual-Published Package

A dual-published package ships both formats so that both kinds of user work. It is more work than it looks, and the type layer is where it goes wrong, so it is worth seeing a correct one.

// package.json
{
  "name": "mylib",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "import": { "types": "./dist/esm/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/esm/index.js" },
      "require": { "types": "./dist/cjs/index.d.cts", "default": "./dist/cjs/index.cjs" }
    }
  },
  "files": ["dist"]
}

Four rules make this work, and each corresponds to a way it commonly breaks.

Each format needs its own declaration file, with the matching extension. index.d.ts describes the ESM build and index.d.cts the CommonJS one. Shipping one .d.ts for both is the most common bug: the CommonJS user then sees ESM-shaped types, and export = versus export default differ in exactly the way that matters.

types must come first inside each condition object. Conditions are matched in the order they are written, and a default listed before types wins, so the types are never found. This is a silent failure: the package works and has no types.

The CommonJS build needs "type": "commonjs" in its own directory, meaning a dist/cjs/package.json containing exactly {"type": "commonjs"}, or the .cjs and .d.cts extensions everywhere. Otherwise the root "type": "module" claims those files are ESM.

The dual-package hazard is real. A dependency graph that loads both builds gets two copies of every class and every module-level singleton, so instanceof fails across the boundary. If your package holds state that carries identity, prefer publishing ESM only and letting require(esm) handle the rest.

Verifying a dual publish is not something to do by eye. tsc --noEmit with moduleResolution: nodenext in a consuming project of each kind is the real test, and the community tool @arethetypeswrong/cli checks the whole matrix of conditions against your published package. Both are worth putting in CI for a package you publish, because every one of the four failures above type-checks perfectly in the package's own repository.

11.17 import defer

Import defer is the newest module syntax TypeScript supports, and it addresses a cost that static imports in ESM otherwise make unavoidable: a module you might not need is still evaluated at startup.

import defer * as heavy from './heavy-analytics.js';

export function onFirstInteraction(): void {
  // ./heavy-analytics.js is evaluated HERE, on the first property access —
  // not when this module was loaded.
  heavy.track('interaction');
}

The meaning is precise and worth stating exactly. The module is fetched and parsed straight away, and evaluated only when needed, on the first access to a property of the namespace object. That is the difference from await import(), which postpones the fetch as well and is therefore asynchronous. import defer is synchronous at the point of use, because the code is already loaded.

Three constraints, all measured against the installed compiler:

Only the namespace form is allowed. import defer * as ns from 'm' is the syntax, and there is no import defer { x } from 'm', because a named import would have to evaluate the module to produce the binding.

It requires an ESM output format. Under --module node16 the compiler reports TS18060: Deferred imports are only supported when the '--module' flag is set to 'esnext' or 'preserve'.

TypeScript writes it out unchanged under esnext and preserve. The output is import defer * as heavy from "./heavy-analytics.js", so the runtime must implement it.

And that last point is the check on the current situation that matters: Node 24 does not support import defer, and the syntax is a parse error there. Chromium ships it, and the proposal is at stage 3. The practical position today is that import defer is available to you if your bundler implements it (several do, by turning it into a lazy getter) and not otherwise. Write it when your toolchain says yes, and use await import() when you need something that works everywhere. The two solve overlapping problems, and only one of them is available everywhere in 2026.

What This Section Established

A TypeScript module is an ES module. The type layer adds import type, export type and the type modifier so that erasure can be decided one file at a time, and verbatimModuleSyntax plus isolatedModules make that discipline mandatory. Module detection decides whether a file is a module or a script at all, and moduleDetection: force removes the question.

Then the three separate questions. module decides the output format: nodenext when Node runs the output, preserve when a bundler does, and amd, umd and system no longer exist. moduleResolution decides where a specifier points: nodenext for Node's real rules, bundler for the relaxed ones, and classic and node10 are gone. And the package's own exports, imports and conditions decide what a bare specifier is allowed to reach, with #subpath imports being the replacement that works at runtime for the removed baseUrl.

Interop is simpler than it was: esModuleInterop and allowSyntheticDefaultImports can no longer be switched off, so a default import of a CommonJS module works everywhere. What remains genuinely hard is CommonJS using ESM, and publishing in both formats, where four separate silent failures all type-check inside the package's own repository.

Exercises

1. Diagnose four module errors. For each of these, name the setting that causes it and the one-line fix: (a) Cannot redeclare block-scoped variable 'name' in a file with no imports; (b) 'A' is a type and must be imported using a type-only import; (c) Cannot find module 'mylib/internal' for a file that visibly exists in node_modules/mylib/; (d) a built bundle that no longer registers a plugin that an import { PluginHandle } from './register.js' was supposed to load.

2. Configure three projects. Write the module and moduleResolution pair, and one sentence of justification for each, for: a CLI that Node runs directly from dist/; a browser library that a bundler consumes and that is published to npm; and a monorepo package that is only ever type-checked, never emitted, because a bundler compiles the sources.

3. Make a specifier work at runtime. Take import { PORT } from '@app/config' backed by "paths": { "@app/*": ["./src/*"] }. Explain why the built output fails under node dist/main.js, then rewrite it in two ways, once so that a bundler resolves it and once so that Node resolves it with no bundler at all, and say which you would publish.

Solution

1. Four diagnoses.

(a) Cannot redeclare block-scoped variable 'name'. The file has no top-level import or export, so module detection classified it as a script and its const name landed in the global scope, where lib.dom already declares name. The one-line fix is export {}; at the bottom of the file, and the fix for the whole project is "moduleDetection": "force", which makes every file a module regardless of its contents. Note that the message names the symptom and not the cause: the same collision happens with status, location, origin, closed and length.

(b) 'A' is a type and must be imported using a type-only import. This is TS1484, raised only under verbatimModuleSyntax. The fix is import { type A } or import type { A }. The setting is doing its job: without it the compiler would silently delete the import, and a tool working one file at a time downstream would either keep a dead import or crash.

(c) Cannot find module 'mylib/internal' for a file that exists. The exports map of the package does not list ./internal, and under node16, nodenext and bundler resolution that map is an allow-list: resolvePackageJsonExports is on and the file on disk is irrelevant. The fix is to use a subpath that the package really exports. If you genuinely need the internal file, that is a request to the package author, not a config change. The reason this appears during an upgrade is that the removed node10 algorithm ignored exports entirely.

(d) The plugin is never registered. PluginHandle is a type, so without verbatimModuleSyntax the compiler removed the entire import statement, including its side effect. The fix is import './register.js'; as a separate import for its side effect, plus import type { PluginHandle } from './register.js' for the type. This is the bug that only appears in the built output, and it is the strongest single argument for turning verbatimModuleSyntax on.

2. Three configurations.

# (a) A CLI that Node runs directly from dist/
"module": "nodenext",  "moduleResolution": "nodenext"

Node is the runtime, so the compiler should apply Node's exact rules: the format comes from the file extension and package.json, extensions are mandatory in ESM specifiers, and exports is honoured. Anything looser lets a build succeed that Node cannot load.

# (b) A browser library, bundled and published to npm
"module": "preserve",  "moduleResolution": "bundler"

The bundler decides the output format, so preserve writes the syntax out unchanged instead of guessing, and bundler resolution matches what the bundler will actually do with extensionless specifiers. For the published artefact this must be paired with a real exports map and, because it is a library, no paths.

# (c) A monorepo package that is type-checked only
"module": "preserve",  "moduleResolution": "bundler",  "noEmit": true

Nothing is emitted, so the output format is irrelevant and preserve is the honest setting. This is also the configuration where allowImportingTsExtensions is safe, because there is no output to break, and with customConditions: ["source"] the internal packages resolve straight to their TypeScript sources.

3. Making a specifier real.

The built output fails because paths is a rewrite that exists only at compile time. tsc resolves @app/config to src/config.ts for checking, then writes out import { PORT } from '@app/config' unchanged. Node has no idea what @app is, has no node_modules/@app to look in, and fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. Nothing in the type check could have caught it, because the type check is the half that was configured.

The version a bundler resolves keeps paths and adds a matching alias so the two agree:

// tsconfig.json
{ "compilerOptions": { "module": "preserve", "moduleResolution": "bundler",
                       "paths": { "@app/*": ["./src/*"] } } }

// the bundler's config — the half that makes it true at runtime
{ "alias": { "@app": "./src" } }

The Node-resolved version uses a subpath import, which Node implements natively:

// package.json
{ "type": "module", "imports": { "#config": "./dist/config.js" } }

import { PORT } from '#config';

Publish the second. A subpath import is in the package manifest, so it works for anyone who uses the built output, with a bundler or without one, from an ESM file or a CommonJS one. A paths entry ships an unresolvable specifier inside your .js and your .d.ts, and the user's error message will name your package and point at a file they cannot fix. The general rule from §11.13, restated: paths for applications, imports for anything published.

Two details worth noting in the imports version. The mapping points at ./dist/config.js, the built path, because imports is resolved at runtime against the shipped package, not against your sources. And the # prefix is required by the specification: it is what makes the specifier unmistakably internal, so it can never collide with a real package name.

SECTION 12

Declaration Files and the Ecosystem

Most of the code your program runs was not written in TypeScript. The browser's built-in APIs, Node's built-in modules, a decade of npm packages and your own older files are all JavaScript, and all of them still need types that live somewhere else. A declaration file is TypeScript's answer.

That "somewhere else" is a .d.ts file, and this section covers writing them, using them, generating them and shipping them. The idea that ties it together is declare: a keyword that means "this exists, take my word for it, and produce no code for it". Everything here is a variation on that: an ambient module (types for a module you do not control), a global variable, an augmentation (adding to a type you do not own).

There are two halves. The first is about describing things: ambient declarations, merging, augmentation, and triple-slash directives, an older mechanism that predates modules. The second is about producing declarations: the declaration setting, source maps for types, isolatedDeclarations, and what a published package must put in its package.json so that a user's compiler can find its types. The section ends with typing JavaScript in place using JSDoc comments, a way to migrate without renaming a single file.

12.1 A Declaration File

A declaration file has the extension .d.ts and contains types and no implementations. It produces no code, and it exists to tell the compiler about code it cannot see.

// shapes.d.ts — types only, no runtime code anywhere in the file
export interface Point { x: number; y: number }
export declare function distance(a: Point, b: Point): number;
export declare const ORIGIN: Point;

Three sources produce them, and it is worth knowing which one you are looking at.

The compiler generates them from your .ts sources when declaration is on (§12.14). This is what a published TypeScript package ships.

A package author writes them by hand for a library that is implemented in JavaScript, and points the types field of package.json at them (§12.19).

The community writes them for a package whose author did not, and publishes them to @types (§12.11).

A .d.ts follows the same module rules as any other file (§11.2): with a top-level import or export it is a module, and without one it is a script whose declarations are global. That distinction decides everything about how it behaves, and getting it wrong is the most common failure in this section. §12.4 and §12.8 are both about it.

The extension variants match the source ones: .d.mts describes an ESM module and .d.cts a CommonJS one, and a package published in both formats needs both (§11.16).

12.2 An Ambient Declaration

An ambient declaration describes something that exists at runtime without providing it. Every declaration in a .d.ts is ambient. The term is used for the ones you write to describe an environment.

// env.d.ts
declare const BUILD_ID: string;
declare function analytics(event: string, payload?: Record<string, unknown>): void;

declare namespace App {
  interface Config { debug: boolean }
}

declare module 'untyped-package' {
  export function doThing(): void;
}

declare module '*.svg' {
  const url: string;
  export default url;
}

Four shapes, one meaning: this will be there, and here is its type.

Nothing verifies an ambient declaration. If BUILD_ID is not actually injected by your bundler, the code compiles and then crashes with a ReferenceError. That is the price of being able to describe anything, and it is why an ambient declaration should be as narrow as the truth allows: unknown where you are guessing, and only the members you actually use.

An ambient declaration may not have an implementation. declare function f() { return 1; } is an error ("An implementation cannot be declared in ambient contexts"), which is the compiler making sure the file produces no code.

Ambient declarations do real work in ordinary projects for constants set at build time, such as process.env.NODE_ENV replacements, a version string or a feature flag, and for imports that are not code, which is what the '*.svg' wildcard covers (§11.8).

12.3 The declare Keyword

The declare keyword marks a declaration as type-only: it describes something without creating it, and it produces no code.

// In a .ts file, `declare` says "assume this exists".
declare const injectedByBundler: string;
declare function externalHelper(n: number): string;

// In a class, it says "the type is here; the field is created elsewhere".
class Base {
  declare readonly kind: string;         // no initialiser emitted
  describe(): string { return `kind=${this.kind}`; }
}
class Derived extends Base {
  readonly kind = 'derived';
}

console.log(new Derived().describe());

kind=derived

declare on a class field is the fix for the initialisation hazard of §6.14. Writing readonly kind: string in the base would, under useDefineForClassFields, produce a field initialiser that overwrites nothing. Declaring it in the base and initialising it in the derived class is the normal pattern, and declare is what stops the base from producing a competing definition.

declare is implicit inside a .d.ts, so writing it there is redundant for most constructs. It is still required for const, let, var and function, which is why generated .d.ts files are full of export declare function.

declare global (§12.5) and declare module (§11.8, §12.6) are the two block forms, and they are the only way to reach outside the current file.

The rule to remember: declare means "no code is produced, and nothing checks that this is true". It is the most powerful and least verified construct in the language, and it belongs at boundaries where something outside the type system genuinely provides the value.

12.4 Declaring a Global

Declaring a global puts a name into the global scope, and the mechanism is a .d.ts file that is a script: no top-level import and no top-level export anywhere in the file.

// globals.d.ts — a SCRIPT. Adding one `import` here breaks everything below.
declare const APP_VERSION: string;
declare function reportError(e: unknown): void;

interface Window {
  appConfig?: { debug: boolean };
}

// Any file in the project can now use them, with no import.
declare const APP_VERSION: string;
console.log(typeof APP_VERSION);

undefined

Note what the runtime says: undefined. The declaration promises that the global exists, and nothing provides it here, which is exactly the risk described in §12.2, shown instead of described.

interface Window { … } without declare global works only in a script, because in a script the interface is already in the global declaration space and merges (§12.7) with the DOM's Window. In a module it would declare a local interface called Window that hides nothing useful.

The moment the file needs an import, it stops being a script, and every declaration in it becomes local to the module. There are two ways out: use an import() type (§11.6), which is an expression and not a statement, or switch to declare global (§12.5) in a module.

Where to put the file. Anywhere that the include of the tsconfig reaches. A conventional types/ or src/types/ directory is fine. The file does not have to be imported, only included, which is why a .d.ts outside include silently does nothing, a common and confusing failure.

12.5 Global Augmentation

Global augmentation adds to the global scope from inside a module, using a declare global block.

// This file is a module (it has an export), so `declare global` is required.
export {};

declare global {
  interface Window {
    appConfig?: { debug: boolean };
  }
  var APP_BUILD: string;             // `var`, not `const` — see below
}

globalThis.APP_BUILD = 'abc123';
console.log(APP_BUILD, typeof globalThis.APP_BUILD);

abc123 string

Three rules, each of which produces a confusing error when broken.

The file must be a module. declare global in a script is an error: "Augmentations for the global scope can only be directly nested in external modules or ambient module declarations". The export {} at the top is the usual way to force module status (§11.2).

Use var for a global variable, not const or let. Only var declarations create a property on globalThis, so declare global { const X: string } accepts the bare identifier X and rejects globalThis.X. This is the one place where the modern advice to avoid var does not apply.

An interface in declare global merges with the existing declaration (§12.7), while a type alias does not and will clash. That is why every global augmentation you will read uses interfaces.

The everyday uses are adding a property to Window, extending NodeJS.ProcessEnv with your own environment variables, and, in a test setup file, declaring the globals that a test framework injects.

12.6 Module Augmentation

Module augmentation adds members to a module you do not own, using declare module 'specifier' inside a module file.

// express-augmentation.ts — the file must be a module
import 'express';

declare module 'express' {
  interface Request {
    user?: { id: string; roles: readonly string[] };
  }
}

// Now, anywhere in the project:
import type { Request } from 'express';
function requireAdmin(req: Request): boolean {
  return req.user?.roles.includes('admin') ?? false;
}

The difference from an ambient module (§11.8) is whether the target already exists. In a script, declare module 'x' declares a new module. In a module, it augments an existing one, and if the module cannot be found you get an error that names the wrong thing:

error TS2664: Invalid module name in augmentation, module 'express' cannot be found.

That message means "your file is a module and express is not installed", or "your file is a module and you meant to declare a module, not augment one". Both are common.

Three rules.

You must import the module you are augmenting, or the augmentation has nothing to attach to. import 'express'; for its effect alone is the usual way.

You may only add, not change. A new member on an existing interface is fine. Redeclaring an existing one with a different type is an error, because merging requires compatibility (§12.7).

You cannot add a new top-level export. declare module 'express' { export const newThing: number } does not work: augmentation extends existing declarations and does not add to the list of exports of the module.

This is how every framework plugin adds its fields: the Request of express, the FastifyInstance of fastify, the ComponentCustomProperties of vue, and the DefaultTheme of styled-components.

12.7 Declaration Merging

Declaration merging is the rule underneath §12.5 and §12.6: two declarations of the same name in the same declaration space are combined.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

interface Config { host: string }
interface Config { port: number }
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Config, { host: string; port: number }>>;

// A function and a namespace merge: the namespace's members become properties.
function counter(): number { return counter.count++; }
namespace counter { export let count = 0; }

console.log(counter(), counter(), counter.count);

0 1 2

Not everything merges, and the list is short. An interface merges with an interface. A namespace merges with a namespace, a function, a class or an enum. A class merges with a namespace or an interface. A type alias merges with nothing: a second declaration is a duplicate-name error.

Three declaration spaces exist, and merging happens within one: type, value and namespace. A class occupies the type and value spaces at once, which is why typeof Box and Box name different things (§8.1). An interface occupies only the type space, which is why an interface and a function with the same name can coexist.

Members must be compatible. Two host: string declarations merge, while host: string and host: number do not. Function members become overloads, with the signatures of the later declaration placed first, which is what lets an augmentation add a more specific overload that wins.

The function + namespace merge above is the classic pattern for a callable with properties, and it is the type-level counterpart of the call signature in §4.2. It produces code, because a namespace does (§15.10).

12.8 Merging Namespaces

Merging namespaces combines two namespace blocks with the same name, and the rule that catches people is about exports.

namespace Shapes {
  export interface Circle { r: number }
  const secret = 'not exported';
  export function area(c: Circle): number { return Math.PI * c.r ** 2; }
}

namespace Shapes {
  export interface Square { side: number }
  export function areaOf(s: Square): number { return s.side ** 2; }
  // `secret` from the other block is NOT visible here.
}

console.log(Shapes.area({ r: 1 }).toFixed(2), Shapes.areaOf({ side: 3 }));

3.14 9

Only exported members are shared between merged blocks. A const that is not exported stays private to its own block, even though the two blocks form one namespace. That is a real source of confusion when a large namespace is split across files.

Nested namespaces merge the same way, all the way down, which is how the .d.ts files of large libraries are organised.

A namespace merged into a module is how a .d.ts describes a library that has both a default export and nested types. declare namespace Express { … } next to declare module 'express' is exactly that shape, and it is why augmenting Express requires the nested Express.Request path in some versions.

Namespaces are legacy for organising your own code (§15.12), because modules do the job and produce less output. The reason to understand merging is that you will read it in .d.ts files constantly, and that augmenting a library often requires writing it.

12.9 Merging a Namespace with a Class

Merging a namespace with a class attaches static members and nested types to a class after the fact. It is the mechanism behind an API like Album.AlbumLabel.

class Album {
  constructor(public title: string, public label: Album.Label) {}
  describe(): string { return `${this.title} [${this.label.name}]`; }
}

namespace Album {
  export interface Label { name: string }
  export const UNKNOWN: Label = { name: 'unknown' };
  export function of(title: string): Album { return new Album(title, UNKNOWN); }
}

console.log(Album.of('Kind of Blue').describe(), Album.UNKNOWN.name);

Kind of Blue [unknown] unknown

The namespace must come after the class, because the declaration of the class must be in scope first. Reversing them is an error.

The exported members of the namespace become statics on the class, and its exported types become nested types reachable as Album.Label, including from inside the class, as the constructor's parameter type shows.

This is the one namespace pattern still worth writing occasionally, because the alternative, a class plus a separate namespace of types plus manual assignment of statics, is more code for the same result. But it produces code (§15.10), so erasableSyntaxOnly forbids it, and a plain static member plus an exported type is the modern equivalent.

Where you will read it is in the .d.ts files of older libraries: this is how moment, older React and much of the Node ecosystem attach their nested types.

12.10 A Triple-Slash Directive

A triple-slash directive is a single-line comment containing an XML tag, and it must appear before any statement in the file. It predates modules, and three forms still matter.

/// <reference path="./globals.d.ts" />
/// <reference types="node" />
/// <reference lib="dom" />

reference path includes another file in the compilation. It is how a .d.ts pulls in a sibling file, and it is the mechanism tsc uses when it generates declarations that depend on each other.

reference types declares a dependency on an @types package. /// <reference types="node" /> at the top of a published .d.ts says "my types need Node's types", which is the correct way for a library to say so (§12.12).

reference lib pulls in one of the compiler's built-in libraries, so a .d.ts that uses Promise can require lib.es2015.promise without depending on the lib setting of the person using it.

In your own application code you should almost never need any of them. include in the tsconfig picks up your .d.ts files, and an import expresses a real dependency. The exception is a .d.ts that must stay a script (§12.4) and still refer to another file.

Their placement is strict: before any statement, with only comments before them. A directive after the first import is silently ignored, with no error and no effect, which is the failure to recognise.

12.11 An @types Package

An @types package is a package that contains only declarations, published from the DefinitelyTyped repository and named @types/<package>.

npm install --save-dev @types/node
npm install --save-dev @types/express

The compiler finds them automatically. Every package under node_modules/@types is included in the compilation by default, without an import and without a reference, which is why installing @types/node makes process and Buffer appear everywhere.

That automatic inclusion is convenient and is occasionally the problem: a @types/jest that came in as a dependency of something else can put describe and it into the global scope of your production code. types (§12.12) is the option that restricts it.

Three checks before installing one.

Does the package already ship types? Most modern ones do. The types field of package.json, or the types condition of an exports map, says so (§12.19), and installing an @types package next to it gives you two competing declarations.

Is the version aligned? The convention is that @types/foo@4.17.x targets foo@4.17.x: the major and minor numbers follow the library, and the patch number is the types' own revision.

Is it a devDependency? Almost always yes, because types are erased. The exception: if your own published .d.ts files refer to a type from an @types package, it becomes a real dependency, because the compilers of your users must find it too.

12.12 The types Compiler Option

The types compiler option restricts which @types packages are included automatically.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "types": ["node"]
  }
}

With that setting, only @types/node is included automatically, and everything else under node_modules/@types is ignored unless it is imported explicitly.

The default is "every package under every typeRoots directory", which is convenient until it is not. It causes two problems:

Global pollution. A @types/mocha that arrives as a dependency of something else puts describe, it and before into the global scope of your application code, where they compile and do not exist.

Slower checks. Every package that is included automatically is parsed and checked on every build, whether you use it or not.

Setting types to [] turns off automatic inclusion entirely, which is the right setting for a library that should not depend on any ambient types. Anything still needed is then brought in with an explicit import type or a /// <reference types="…" />.

The two-configuration pattern is worth knowing: the application tsconfig lists ["node"], and a tsconfig.test.json extends it with ["node", "vitest/globals"]. The test globals then exist in tests and nowhere else, which is exactly the property you want and which a single config cannot give you.

12.13 typeRoots

typeRoots lists the directories that the compiler scans for packages of types to include automatically. It defaults to every node_modules/@types from the current directory upwards.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "typeRoots": ["./node_modules/@types", "./src/types"]
  }
}

Setting it replaces the default instead of adding to it, which is the trap: writing "typeRoots": ["./src/types"] silently stops @types/node from being found, and the errors are about process and Buffer and not about the setting.

A directory in typeRoots is scanned for packages, not for .d.ts files. Each subdirectory is treated as a package of types and must contain an index.d.ts or a package.json that points at one. Dropping my-globals.d.ts straight into src/types and adding it to typeRoots does nothing.

For your own global declarations, include is the mechanism, not typeRoots. A .d.ts anywhere inside include is part of the compilation, and if it is a script its declarations are global (§12.4). That is simpler, and it is what almost every project should do.

typeRoots earns its keep in a monorepo where shared ambient types are published as a real package, or where a copied directory shaped like @types must be found. Outside those cases, leaving it at the default and using types (§12.12) to restrict is the better arrangement.

12.14 Declaration Emit

Declaration emit is tsc generating .d.ts files from your sources, controlled by the declaration setting.

// src/index.ts
export interface User { id: string; name: string }
export const VERSION = '1.0.0';
export function greet(u: User): string { return `hi ${u.name}`; }
export default greet;

Compiled with tsc --declaration --emitDeclarationOnly, the generated index.d.ts:

export interface User {
    id: string;
    name: string;
}
export declare const VERSION = "1.0.0";
export declare function greet(u: User): string;
export default greet;

Two details in that output are worth reading.

export declare const VERSION = "1.0.0" keeps the literal type, not string. Declaration emit keeps what inference produced, so a user of the package gets the literal, which is usually what you want and occasionally a surprise when a value changes.

The implementation is gone and the signature remains. That is the whole transformation.

emitDeclarationOnly produces the .d.ts files and no JavaScript, which is the right setting when a bundler produces the JavaScript and tsc is only there for the types, an extremely common modern arrangement.

The failure to expect is a type that cannot be named. If a public signature refers to a type that is not exported, declaration emit fails with "has or is using name 'X' from external module but cannot be named". The fix is to export the type. A related message, "The inferred type of 'x' cannot be named without a reference to '…'", means the inferred type of a public API reaches into the internals of a dependency, and the fix is an explicit annotation.

12.15 declarationMap

declarationMap produces a .d.ts.map next to each declaration file, so that "go to definition" on a symbol you use lands in the original .ts source and not in the generated .d.ts.

// dist/index.d.ts.map — measured, abbreviated
{"version":3,"file":"index.d.ts","sourceRoot":"","sources":["../src/index.ts"],
 "names":[],"mappings":"AAAA,MAAM,WAAW,IAAI;…"}

// and the declaration file gains a trailing comment
//# sourceMappingURL=index.d.ts.map

The benefit is entirely for developers, and it is large in a monorepo. Without it, jumping to the definition of a function in a sibling package lands on greet(u: User): string; with no body. With it, you land in the real source, can read the implementation, and, in most editors, can rename across the package boundary.

It requires the sources to be shipped, because the sources field of the map points at ../src/index.ts. For an internal monorepo package that costs nothing. For a published npm package it means including src/ in files, which is a trade-off in size that many libraries make deliberately and many do not.

sourceRoot and mapRoot adjust the paths when the published layout differs from the build layout, and getting them wrong produces a map that points at nothing, which fails silently, exactly like the map not being there.

Turn it on for anything inside a workspace. For a published package, turn it on if you are willing to ship src.

12.16 isolatedDeclarations

isolatedDeclarations requires every exported declaration to have an explicit type annotation, so that a .d.ts can be generated from a single file without type-checking it.

// With --isolatedDeclarations:
export function annotated(a: number): number { return a * 2; }   // ✅ explicit return type
export const obj = { a: 1 };                                      // ✅ an object literal is inferable

export const version: string = '1.0.0';
console.log(annotated(21), obj.a, version);

42 1 1.0.0

Remove the return type and the flag fires:

error TS9013: Expression type can't be inferred with --isolatedDeclarations.

The purpose is parallelism. Generating declarations normally needs the full type checker and the whole program, because an inferred return type may depend on another file. With every export annotated, a .d.ts is a purely local transformation, which means a build tool can generate declarations for a thousand files in parallel, and other tools (esbuild, swc, oxc) can do it at all.

The cost is an annotation on every export. In a library that is a reasonable discipline and arguably an improvement, since an explicit return type on a public function is good practice anyway (§2.3). In application code with many small exported helpers it is noise.

Note what it does not require. export const obj = { a: 1 } compiles, because an object literal of members with literal types can be worked out locally. What cannot is anything whose type depends on a call, on a generic instantiation or on another module.

Turn it on for a published library, especially in a monorepo where generating declarations is on the critical path. Leave it off for an application.

12.17 skipLibCheck

skipLibCheck stops the compiler from type-checking .d.ts files, both your dependencies' declarations and your own.

{ "compilerOptions": { "skipLibCheck": true } }

What it does not do is skip using them. Every declaration is still read, still resolved, and still used to check your code. What is skipped is checking the declaration files against themselves: whether two @types packages contradict each other, and whether the .d.ts of a library is consistent within itself.

The reason it is on by default in tsc --init is that a large tree of dependencies routinely contains declaration files that do not type-check together: two versions of @types/react, a package whose types assume lib.dom while you target Node, an @types package written for an older compiler. None of those is your bug, and all of them would fail your build without this setting.

The cost is real and worth stating. With skipLibCheck on, an error inside your own .d.ts files is not reported, including the ones you write by hand for a JavaScript library (§12.20). A codebase that writes its own declarations should check them, which means either turning the setting off or running a second tsc --noEmit over just those files with it off.

It is also a large saving in build time: lib.dom.d.ts alone is 2.3 MB. §17.6 measures it, and on a project with a heavy tree of dependencies it is frequently the single biggest lever on check time.

The recommendation: on for an application, off for a library that ships hand-written declarations, with a clear idea of what each choice hides.

12.18 Publishing Types

Publishing types means making sure that a user's compiler can find and use your declarations. Four things must line up, and each has a characteristic failure.

The declarations must exist and be in the published package. files in package.json must include the output directory, and npm pack --dry-run is the check.

package.json must point at them (§12.19), through types or, better, through a types condition in exports.

They must be resolvable under the user's moduleResolution. A package with an exports map and a top-level types field will be found differently by bundler and by nodenext, and only the exports route works for a subpath.

They must be self-contained. A .d.ts that refers to a type from a package listed only in devDependencies breaks for every user, because their compiler cannot resolve it. That is the most common real failure, and it never shows up in the package's own repository.

The tooling that catches these before your users do:

npm pack --dry-run                     # is the .d.ts actually in the tarball?
npx @arethetypeswrong/cli --pack .     # does every condition resolve, for every consumer shape?
tsc --noEmit                           # in a scratch consumer project of each module kind

The last one is the real test. Create a consumer with "type": "module" and one without, install the packed package into each, import it, and run tsc --noEmit with moduleResolution: nodenext. Every failure in this subsection shows up there and nowhere else.

12.19 The types Field in package.json

The types field in package.json tells the compiler of a user where the declarations are. There are two places to put it, and they are not equivalent.

{
  "name": "mylib",
  "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",          // the legacy field — still read
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",      // the modern one, per condition
      "default": "./dist/index.js"
    }
  }
}

Under moduleResolution: node16, nodenext or bundler, the exports map wins, and the top-level types field is only a fallback for very old users. Keeping both is harmless, and it is what most packages do.

types must be listed first inside a condition object. Conditions are matched in the order they are written, so a default placed before types wins and the types are never found. The symptom is a package that works and has no types, with no error anywhere, and it is the most common packaging bug in the ecosystem.

typings is a deprecated alias for the top-level field. It still works, and there is no reason to write it.

For a package published in both formats, each condition needs its own declaration file with the matching extension: .d.ts for import and .d.cts for require (§11.16). Shipping one .d.ts for both means the CommonJS user sees ESM-shaped types, and export = versus export default differ in exactly the way that matters.

If the entry point is index.d.ts next to index.js, TypeScript finds it even with no field at all, which is a useful fallback and not one to rely on.

12.20 Writing a Declaration File for a JavaScript Library

Writing a declaration file for a JavaScript library is the skill that unblocks an untyped dependency. The method is the same every time.

// types/legacy-chart.d.ts
declare module 'legacy-chart' {
  export interface ChartOptions {
    width: number;
    height: number;
    /** Defaults to 'line' if omitted. */
    type?: 'line' | 'bar' | 'pie';
  }

  export interface Chart {
    render(el: HTMLElement): void;
    destroy(): void;
  }

  export function createChart(data: readonly number[], options: ChartOptions): Chart;
  export const version: string;
}

Five rules, in order of how much trouble each saves.

Type only what you use. A library with two hundred exports needs declarations for the four you call. Anything else is unverified guessing that will be wrong.

Prefer unknown to a guess. A parameter whose shape you are unsure of should be unknown, which forces a narrowing at your call, and that is where you actually know.

Match the runtime shape exactly. If the library does module.exports = createChart, the declaration needs export = (§11.7) and not a named export. Getting this wrong produces "is not a function" at runtime with a clean build.

Check it against reality. Write a small file that calls the library through your declarations, run it, and confirm that it does what the types say. Nothing else verifies a .d.ts.

Turn skipLibCheck off for your own declarations (§12.17), or they are the one part of the project that nothing checks.

Where to put it: a .d.ts inside include (§12.4). And if the library is popular, the better end state is a pull request to DefinitelyTyped, so nobody else has to write it twice.

12.21 allowJs

allowJs lets .js files be part of the compilation: resolved, written out and, with checkJs (§12.22), checked.

{ "compilerOptions": { "allowJs": true, "outDir": "dist" } }

Without it, an import of a .js file that has no .d.ts next to it fails to resolve. That is the immediate reason to turn it on during a migration: a mixed codebase where some modules are still JavaScript needs the compiler to see them.

With it, the types of a .js module are inferred. The compiler reads the JavaScript, follows assignments and JSDoc comments, and produces a best-effort type, which is far better than any and far worse than a real annotation. That inference is what makes a gradual migration practical: a .ts file that imports an untyped .js module still gets useful completion.

The effect on output matters. With allowJs and an outDir, .js files are copied into the output (and converted to an older syntax if target requires it), which means the output directory contains everything. Without an outDir, tsc refuses to overwrite its own inputs.

allowJs plus declaration generates .d.ts files from JavaScript, using the same inference plus JSDoc. That is how a JavaScript library can ship types without being rewritten, and it is a genuinely good option for a small package.

The setting is off by default, and there is no reason to turn it on in a pure TypeScript project, because it only widens what the compiler will read.

12.22 checkJs

checkJs type-checks .js files as well as reading them. It requires allowJs.

{ "compilerOptions": { "allowJs": true, "checkJs": true } }

Or per file, which is the better way to start:

// @ts-check
// at the top of a single .js file — checks this one, whatever the config says

// @ts-nocheck
// the opposite: exempt this file when checkJs is on globally

The per-file // @ts-check comment is the cheapest possible way into TypeScript. No config change, no build step and no rename: add one comment to one JavaScript file and the editor starts reporting real errors in it. For a team that is not ready to adopt TypeScript, this is the demonstration that costs nothing.

The checking is genuine but weaker than in a .ts file, because there is nowhere to put annotations except JSDoc (§12.23). Inference does most of the work: assignments, default parameters, JSDoc, and the shapes of object literals.

strict applies. strictNullChecks in a checked .js file reports the same nullability errors it would in TypeScript, which is where most of the value is.

The migration path this makes possible, in order: // @ts-check on a few files, then checkJs for the whole project with // @ts-nocheck on the stragglers, then JSDoc types on the public functions, then rename to .ts when the file is already clean. §16.24 covers the full ratchet.

12.23 A JSDoc Type Annotation

A JSDoc type annotation puts a type in a comment, where TypeScript reads it. The type syntax inside the braces is TypeScript's, not Closure's.

// lib.js
// @ts-check

/** @typedef {{ id: string, name: string }} User */

/**
 * @param {User} user
 * @param {number} [times]   — the brackets make it optional
 * @returns {string}
 */
export function greet(user, times = 1) {
  return `hi ${user.name}`.repeat(times);
}

/** @type {User} */
export const admin = { id: 'a', name: 'Admin' };

/** @type {string} */
export const wrong = 42;

lib.js(22,14): error TS2322: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'.

The tags that cover almost everything:

@type {T} annotates a variable or an expression. @param {T} name and @returns {T} annotate a function. @typedef and @callback declare named types. @template T declares a type parameter. @implements and @extends {Base<T>} relate classes. @readonly, @private, @protected and @public correspond to the modifiers.

@import, added in TypeScript 5.5, is the modern way to bring in a type: /** @import { User } from './types.js' */. Before it, the usual way was @typedef {import('./types.js').User} User, which still works and which you will read constantly.

Optional parameters use brackets: @param {number} [times], and [times=1] documents the default. A | undefined union works too, and is more explicit.

The limitation to know: there is no JSDoc syntax for a type assertion in an expression, so /** @type {Foo} */ (expr), with the parentheses, is the substitute, and the parentheses are mandatory.

12.24 JSDoc Types in JavaScript

JSDoc types in JavaScript are a complete alternative to .ts files for a whole project, and it is worth knowing what the trade really is instead of dismissing it.

What you get. Full type-checking, editor completion, strict mode, generics, conditional types, and generated .d.ts files (§12.21). The type system is the same one, with no cut-down dialect.

What you give up. Mainly weight of syntax: a three-line comment where an annotation would be twelve characters. And a handful of constructs have no JSDoc spelling: satisfies did not until recently (§12.25), and some advanced generic positions are awkward.

What you gain that TypeScript does not offer. The files run with no build step. node lib.js works, the source in the repository is the source that runs, source maps are unnecessary, and there is no compilation that could be out of date. For a small library or a Node tool that is a real advantage, and it is why several well-known projects (notably Svelte, which moved to JSDoc from TypeScript) made this choice deliberately.

// A generic function in JSDoc — the same type system, more characters.
/**
 * @template T
 * @param {readonly T[]} items
 * @param {(item: T) => boolean} predicate
 * @returns {T | undefined}
 */
export function findFirst(items, predicate) {
  for (const item of items) if (predicate(item)) return item;
  return undefined;
}

The honest comparison: with Node's own type stripping (§15.24) now able to run .ts files directly, the "no build step" argument for JSDoc is much weaker than it was in 2023. For a new project, TypeScript syntax is the default. For an existing JavaScript project, JSDoc is a migration that never has to be finished, which is often worth more.

12.25 The JSDoc satisfies Tag

The JSDoc satisfies tag is the JSDoc spelling of the satisfies operator of §8.10: check the value against a type without changing the type that was inferred for it.

// config.js
// @ts-check

/** @satisfies {Record<string, number>} */
export const limits = { max: 10, min: 1 };

// The check fires:
/** @satisfies {Record<string, number>} */
export const broken = { max: 'ten' };

config.js(9,26): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

It is checked and it does not annotate. @type {Record<string, number>} would have made limits.max a number and lost the fact that the object has exactly those two keys, while @satisfies keeps the inferred shape and verifies that it conforms.

The same caveat as for the operator applies, and it is worth measuring instead of assuming: satisfies supplies a type as a hint, so limits.max comes out as number and not the literal 10, because the target says number and that is what the property is typed from. Getting literal types as well needs the JSDoc equivalent of as const, which is /** @type {const} */, supported since TypeScript 5.5, applied to the expression.

It arrived in TypeScript 5.0 together with the operator, so it is available anywhere the operator is.

The use is identical: a configuration object, a route table, a lookup map, anything where you want the keys checked against a contract and the precise shape kept for deriving other types afterwards.

What This Section Established

declare means "this exists, produce no code, and nothing checks that I am right". Every construct in this section is a form of it, and each is only as good as the care taken in writing it.

Whether a .d.ts is a script or a module decides everything. A script's declarations are global, and interface Window merges with the DOM's. A module needs declare global to reach out, and a declare module 'x' inside one becomes an augmentation whose failure message misleadingly says the module cannot be found. Adding one import to a file of globals switches all of this off, and an import() type is the way to avoid that.

Declaration merging is the engine: interfaces merge, namespaces merge with functions and classes, and type aliases merge with nothing. That is why every augmentation you will read uses interfaces, why var, not const, is required for a global variable, and why types must be listed first inside an exports condition or the declarations are silently never found.

On the producing side, declaration writes .d.ts files, declarationMap makes "go to definition" land in the real source, isolatedDeclarations trades an annotation on every export for generating them in parallel, and skipLibCheck, on by default, hides errors in your own hand-written declarations along with everyone else's. And JSDoc gives the entire type system to a .js file for the price of some comment syntax, which is the migration that never has to finish.

Exercises

1. Fix four declaration files. Each of these fails in a way whose error message points somewhere else. Diagnose and fix: (a) a globals.d.ts declaring APP_VERSION that stopped working after someone added import type { Config } from './config' to it; (b) a declare global { const API_URL: string } where globalThis.API_URL is an error; (c) a declare module 'chart-lib' that reports "module cannot be found" even though the package is installed; (d) a published package whose users report "could not find a declaration file", though dist/index.d.ts exists and exports names it.

2. Type an untyped library. Given a JavaScript library whose shape at runtime is module.exports = { createClient, VERSION }, where createClient(url, opts) returns an object with get(path) and close(), write the declaration file, say where it must live for the compiler to find it, and show two calls: one valid, and one that your declarations correctly reject.

3. Migrate a file three ways. Take a small .js module with one exported function that takes an options object. Show it (a) unchecked, (b) with // @ts-check and JSDoc types, including one deliberate error that the check catches, and (c) converted to .ts. Say what each step cost and what it bought, and which of the three you would stop at for a library that must run without a build.

Solution

1. Four declaration files.

(a) The globals file became a module. A top-level import makes the file a module (§11.2), so every declare const in it is now local to the module and the globals vanish, with errors at every place they are used, saying Cannot find name 'APP_VERSION', and none in the file that caused it.

Two fixes. Replace the import with an import() type, which is an expression and leaves the file a script:

declare const APP_VERSION: string;
declare const config: import('./config').Config;

Or keep the import and wrap everything in declare global, which is the right choice if the file needs several imports:

import type { Config } from './config';
export {};
declare global {
  const APP_VERSION: string;
  const config: Config;
}

(b) const in declare global does not create a globalThis property. Only var declarations do. That is a JavaScript rule about the global object, faithfully modelled. declare global { var API_URL: string } fixes it, and the bare identifier API_URL keeps working either way. This is the one context where var is correct.

(c) The file is a module, so declare module is an augmentation. With a top-level import or export present, declare module 'chart-lib' means "add members to the existing chart-lib", and if chart-lib ships no types there is nothing to augment, which produces TS2664: Invalid module name in augmentation. The message names the wrong problem. Move the declaration into a .d.ts with no top-level import or export, where it declares a new ambient module (§11.8).

(d) types is not first in the exports condition. Conditions match in the order they are written, so this:

"exports": { ".": { "default": "./dist/index.js", "types": "./dist/index.d.ts" } }

matches default first and never reaches types. Swapping them fixes it. The failure is silent in the package's own repository, because its internal imports resolve by path, and only appears for users, which is why @arethetypeswrong/cli in CI is worth the two minutes (§12.18).

2. Typing an untyped library.

// types/chart-client.d.ts — a .d.ts with no top-level import or export, inside `include`
declare module 'chart-client' {
  export interface ClientOptions {
    timeoutMs?: number;
    headers?: Record<string, string>;
  }

  export interface Client {
    get(path: string): Promise<unknown>;
    close(): void;
  }

  export function createClient(url: string, opts?: ClientOptions): Client;
  export const VERSION: string;
}

import { createClient, VERSION } from 'chart-client';

const client = createClient('https://api.example.com', { timeoutMs: 5000 });
const body = await client.get('/health');          // Promise<unknown> — narrow at the call site
console.log(VERSION, typeof body);

// @ts-expect-error 'timeout' is not a ClientOptions property
createClient('https://api.example.com', { timeout: 5000 });

Where it lives: anywhere the include of the tsconfig reaches, conventionally types/ or src/types/. It does not need to be imported. Being included is what matters, and a .d.ts outside include silently does nothing (§12.4).

Two decisions in the declaration are deliberate. get returns Promise<unknown> and not Promise<any>, so every caller narrows at the point where it actually knows the shape, which is the rule of §10.13 applied to a boundary you are defining. And the shape at runtime is module.exports = { createClient, VERSION }, a CommonJS object with named properties, so named exports are correct here. Had it been module.exports = createClient, the declaration would need export = (§11.7), and a plain named export would produce "is not a function" at runtime with a clean build.

The rejected call is the excess property check (§5.4) doing its job on an object literal written directly: timeout instead of timeoutMs is exactly the typo the check exists for, and it is caught only because the declaration named the property precisely.

3. Three migration steps.

// (a) Unchecked JavaScript. Nothing is verified.
export function connect(options) {
  return `${options.host}:${options.port ?? 5432}`;
}

// (b) // @ts-check plus JSDoc.
// @ts-check

/**
 * @typedef {object} ConnectOptions
 * @property {string} host
 * @property {number} [port]
 */

/**
 * @param {ConnectOptions} options
 * @returns {string}
 */
export function connect(options) {
  return `${options.host}:${options.port ?? 5432}`;
}

connect({ host: 'db' });
// error TS2561: Object literal may only specify known properties, but 'hostname'
// does not exist in type 'ConnectOptions'. Did you mean to write 'host'?
connect({ hostname: 'db' });

// (c) Converted to TypeScript.
type ConnectOptions = { host: string; port?: number };

export function connect(options: ConnectOptions): string {
  return `${options.host}:${options.port ?? 5432}`;
}

console.log(connect({ host: 'db' }), connect({ host: 'db', port: 5433 }));

db:5432 db:5433

(a) to (b) cost one comment and no configuration, and bought the whole type system for that file: the hostname typo is caught, options.port is known to be possibly undefined, and the editor completes the shape. Nothing about the build changed, and node still runs the file unmodified.

(b) to (c) cost a rename and a build step, and bought roughly twelve characters of syntax per annotation plus access to the handful of constructs that JSDoc spells awkwardly. The checking is identical, and that is the point that surprises people: step (b) already has strict TypeScript.

Stop at (b) for a library that must run without a build. The file in the repository is the file that runs, there are no source maps, no dist, and no chance of the published output being out of date. That calculation has shifted since Node gained type stripping (§15.24), which lets .ts run directly, but stripping still requires a flag and still produces no .d.ts, so for a small published package (b) remains a defensible and occasionally better choice.

SECTION 13

Configuring the Type Checker

A tsconfig.json is your project's agreement with the compiler: which files it covers, how strict to be, and what the running environment is assumed to provide. It is also the most copied file in the ecosystem, which means most projects run settings that nobody actually chose.

This section is about choosing them. The options fall into three groups that answer three different questions:

  • Which files? include, exclude, extends, and the ${configDir} variable that makes a shared base configuration work.
  • How strict? The strict family of settings, plus five settings that are not part of it and are worth adding.
  • What exists at runtime? target, lib and jsx, which decide which APIs the checker believes are there.

The options about building output (outDir, incremental, project references, and the removed options) are in §14. The split is on purpose: everything here changes which errors you see, and everything there changes which files you get.

One recommendation up front: turn on more than strict. strict is a fixed bundle that was defined before several of the most valuable checks existed, so the five settings in §13.11–§13.15, and the four in §5.18–§5.21, stay off unless you switch them on.

13.1 tsconfig.json

tsconfig.json is the file that marks the root of a TypeScript project and holds its settings. Because it is there, you can run tsc with no arguments, and an editor's language server reads it to decide how to check the file you have open.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "esnext",
    "module": "preserve",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

The compiler finds it by walking up from the current directory, so tsc in a subdirectory uses the nearest one above. tsc -p path/to/tsconfig.json names it explicitly. tsc --showConfig prints the fully-resolved result, which is the most useful diagnostic in this section because it shows what extends and the defaults actually produced.

Files named on the command line bypass the config entirely. TypeScript 7 now says so instead of doing it silently:

error TS5112: tsconfig.json is present but will not be loaded if files are specified
on commandline. Use '--ignoreConfig' to skip this error.

That diagnostic is new, and it prevents a real confusion: a tsc src/index.ts that seems to ignore every setting in the project.

tsc --init generates a documented starter config. Run it once and read the comments, even if you then delete most of them. The generated file turns on strict, esModuleInterop, skipLibCheck and forceConsistentCasingInFileNames, and comments out the rest.

A project may have several configs. For example, tsconfig.json for the application, tsconfig.test.json extending it with test globals (§12.12), and tsconfig.build.json with noEmit off. Each is a separate program, and each needs its own tsc run.

13.2 The compilerOptions Object

The compilerOptions object holds every setting that changes how the compiler behaves. The reference lists 136 of them. The ones that matter fall into six groups.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    // Language and environment
    "target": "esnext",
    "lib": ["esnext"],
    "jsx": "react-jsx",

    // Modules
    "module": "preserve",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "moduleDetection": "force",
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,

    // Type checking
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,
    "noUnusedLocals": true,
    "noUnusedParameters": true,
    "noImplicitReturns": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,

    // Emit
    "noEmit": true,

    // Interop and performance
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

That is a complete configuration for an application whose bundler produces the output, and every line in it is explained somewhere in this course.

Options are not inherited by subdirectories. There is one compilerOptions per project, and a nested tsconfig.json is a separate project, not an override.

An unknown option is an error, not a warning: TS5023: Unknown compiler option. That protects you when a setting is renamed or removed, and it is how you find out that baseUrl no longer exists (§14.16).

Relative paths inside compilerOptions resolve against the config file's own directory, not the working directory. The one exception is in §13.5, where extends makes "the config file" ambiguous.

13.3 The include and exclude Fields

The include and exclude fields decide which files are in the program. They sit outside compilerOptions, and there is one rule about them that people get wrong.

{
  "include": ["src/**/*", "types/**/*.d.ts"],
  "exclude": ["**/*.test.ts", "dist"]
}

exclude filters include. It does not remove a file that something imports. A file excluded here is still pulled in if an included file imports it. exclude decides which files are roots (where the compiler starts), not which files are reachable from them. This is why excluding a directory does not stop its errors from appearing.

The defaults are broad. With neither field, include defaults to **/*, meaning every .ts, .tsx and .d.ts under the config's directory. exclude defaults to node_modules, bower_components, jspm_packages and the outDir. Setting include replaces its default entirely, and setting exclude replaces its default too, which is why an explicit exclude should usually list node_modules.

files is the third field. It takes an exact list with no globs, and it does not accept directories. It suits a tiny project or a generated config.

A .d.ts must be inside include to have any effect (§12.4). A globals file in a directory the config does not reach does nothing, with errors at every place it is used and none at the file.

A pattern worth adopting: include: ["src"] and nothing else, with tests in a separate tsconfig.test.json that extends it. That keeps test globals out of application code and makes each program smaller.

13.4 The extends Field

The extends field makes one config inherit from another. It is how a monorepo shares settings and how the @tsconfig/* base packages work.

// tsconfig.base.json at the repository root
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "target": "esnext",
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "types": []
  }
}

// packages/api/tsconfig.json
{
  "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": { "types": ["node"] },
  "include": ["src"]
}

Four rules govern it.

Merging is shallow and per-option. The child's compilerOptions overrides the parent's key by key, and arrays are not merged. types: ["node"] above replaces the parent's [] instead of adding to it.

files, include and exclude from the child overwrite the parent's entirely. They are not merged.

extends accepts an array. The entries apply left to right and later ones win, which is how you combine a base config with a framework preset.

A bare specifier resolves as a package. "extends": "@tsconfig/node22/tsconfig.json" works after npm i -D @tsconfig/node22, and the community maintains a base for every runtime.

Relative paths in the parent resolve against the parent's directory. That is right for extends targets and wrong for almost everything else: a parent's outDir: "./dist" would put every package's output in the repository root. §13.5 is the fix.

13.5 The configDir Template Variable

The configDir template variable stands for the directory of the config that is doing the extending. That is what makes path options usable in a shared base.

// tsconfig.base.json — shared by every package
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "outDir": "${configDir}/dist",
    "rootDir": "${configDir}/src"
  }
}

// packages/api/tsconfig.json
{ "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json", "include": ["src"] }

$ cd packages/api && tsc --showConfig
{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "outDir": "./dist",          <- resolved relative to packages/api, not the root
        "strict": true,
        ...
    }
}

That output is measured, and it is the whole feature. Without ${configDir}, outDir: "./dist" in the base would resolve against the base's directory, and every package would write into one shared folder.

It was added in TypeScript 5.5. It works in the path-valued options: outDir, rootDir, include, exclude, files, paths, typeRoots, declarationDir and tsBuildInfoFile.

Before it existed, the workaround was to repeat every path option in every package's config. That is why older monorepos have large, nearly identical tsconfig.json files. Replacing that duplication with ${configDir} in one base is usually a same-day cleanup.

It is not a general variable system. There is no ${workspaceRoot} and no environment interpolation. configDir is the only one, and it means exactly "the directory of the innermost config in the extends chain".

13.6 The strict Flag

The strict flag turns on a family of checks at once. With the installed compiler it implies:

alwaysStrict                    noImplicitAny
noImplicitThis                  strictBindCallApply
strictFunctionTypes             strictNullChecks
strictPropertyInitialization    useUnknownInCatchVariables
strictBuiltinIteratorReturn

Each check has its own subsection somewhere in this course, and each can be overridden individually. "strict": true, "strictPropertyInitialization": false is legal, and it is the mechanism behind a strictness ratchet (§16.24).
