strict: true is the correct setting for every new project, without qualification. The cost grows with how much untyped code you already have, and on day one that is zero.

What strict does not include matters, because the list is long and each entry closes a real hole:

noUncheckedIndexedAccess              (§5.19)  arr[i] is T | undefined
exactOptionalPropertyTypes            (§5.18)  optional means absent, not undefined
noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature    (§5.20)  brackets for index-signature keys
noImplicitOverride                    (§6.22)  a misspelled override is an error
noUnusedLocals / noUnusedParameters   (§13.11) dead code is an error
noImplicitReturns                     (§13.13) every path returns
noFallthroughCasesInSwitch            (§13.14) an accidental fallthrough is an error

They are excluded for compatibility. strict is meant to be a stable set, and adding to it would break existing builds whenever the compiler is upgraded. So it is a floor, not a ceiling.

Turning strict on in an existing codebase produces most of its errors from strictNullChecks, and the count is an honest measure of how much of the code was already wrong. §16.24's ratchet, one flag at a time with its own commit, is the way through.

13.7 alwaysStrict

alwaysStrict makes the compiler parse every file in ECMAScript strict mode (a stricter, safer set of JavaScript rules) and emit "use strict" at the top of the output. It is part of strict.

{ "compilerOptions": { "alwaysStrict": true } }

For a module, it does nothing new, because ES modules are always in strict mode by specification. Every .ts file with an import or an export is already strict, and the emitted "use strict" is redundant. That is why you rarely see any effect.

It matters for a script (§11.2): a file with no imports or exports, compiled to a .js that a <script> tag loads. There the directive is what turns assignment to an undeclared variable into a ReferenceError instead of a silent global.

What strict mode itself changes is worth listing once, because the checks depend on it: - assigning to an undeclared variable throws - this in a plain function call is undefined and not the global object - duplicate parameter names are an error - delete on a variable is an error - octal literals are rejected

The this behaviour is the one that connects to the type layer. noImplicitThis (§13.8) reports a this of type any in a function. alwaysStrict makes that this actually be undefined at runtime, and not the global object. Together they turn a silent bug into two errors.

Leave it on. In modern code there is no case where the non-strict behaviour is what you want.

13.8 noImplicitThis

noImplicitThis reports a this whose type would otherwise be an implicit any, meaning a type the compiler could not work out and so silently made any. It is part of strict.

type Point = { x: number; y: number; scale(f: number): Point };

// An object literal's method gets `this` from the literal — no annotation needed.
const p: Point = {
  x: 1,
  y: 2,
  scale(f) { return { ...this, x: this.x * f, y: this.y * f }; },
};

console.log(p.scale(3).x, p.scale(3).y);

3 6

Extract the same function and there is nothing left to infer this from:

// @ts-expect-error 'this' implicitly has type 'any' because it does not have a type annotation.
const scale = function (f: number) { return this.x * f; };

// The fix: declare the receiver (§4.8).
const scaleTyped = function (this: { x: number }, f: number) { return this.x * f; };
console.log(scaleTyped.call({ x: 2 }, 5), typeof scale);

10 function

The flag forces you to write the this parameter wherever the checker cannot work it out. That turns a silent any into a documented contract.

It also makes this in class methods get checked properly. It is a prerequisite for ThisType<T> (§9.9) to have any effect: that utility is documented as doing nothing without noImplicitThis.

A case that feels like a false positive is a callback that a library binds: a jQuery each, a Mocha it with this.timeout, a DOM handler. In every case the correct fix is a this parameter. The library's own types usually declare one already, so if you are annotating by hand, check whether the library's callback type has it.

13.9 strictBuiltinIteratorReturn

strictBuiltinIteratorReturn was added in TypeScript 5.6 and is part of strict. It gives the result of next() on the built-in iterators an honest type.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const it = [1, 2][Symbol.iterator]();
const first = it.next();

// With the flag on, `value` is `number | undefined` — because a finished
// iterator's result has `value: undefined`.
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof first.value, number | undefined>>;

console.log(first.value, it.next().value, it.next().value);

1 2 undefined

The output is the justification. The third next() really does produce undefined, and before this flag the type said number.

The change applies only to the built-in iterators: arrays, Map, Set, strings, NodeList, and generators from the standard library. A user-defined iterator declares its own types and is unaffected.

for...of is unaffected, because the loop only visits results where done is false. That is why the flag costs so little in practice. The pattern that has to change is a manual .next() call, and those are rare outside library code.

The correct handling is a done check, which narrows:

const it = [1, 2][Symbol.iterator]();
const r = it.next();
if (!r.done) console.log(r.value.toFixed(1));    // narrowed to number
console.log('done?', it.next().done, it.next().done);

1.0
done? false true

It is in strict, so it arrives with a compiler upgrade and not as a decision you make. Knowing what it changed is what makes the resulting errors easy to read.

13.10 strictBindCallApply

strictBindCallApply checks Function.prototype.bind, call and apply against the function's actual signature. It is part of strict.

function area(this: { unit: string }, width: number, height: number): string {
  return `${width * height}${this.unit}`;
}

console.log(area.call({ unit: 'm2' }, 3, 4));
console.log(area.apply({ unit: 'm2' }, [3, 4]));
const bound = area.bind({ unit: 'cm2' }, 5);
console.log(bound(6));

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error the second argument must be a number
  area.call({ unit: 'm2' }, 3, '4');
  // @ts-expect-error the receiver must have a `unit`
  area.call({}, 3, 4);
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

12m2
12m2
30cm2
function

Without the flag, all three methods take any[] and return any. So every one of those errors goes unreported, and the result is unchecked downstream (§10.21).

bind with partial application is typed correctly. area.bind({unit}, 5) returns (height: number) => string, with the first parameter used up. The standard library's own declarations do this with the tuple manipulation of §5.14.

The this parameter is checked too, which is why declaring one (§4.8, §6.18) pays off here. Without it the receiver is unchecked, and area.call({}, 3, 4) compiles.

The limitation: an overloaded function binds against its last signature only, which is the same limitation Parameters has (§9.8). For a heavily overloaded function the check is weaker than it looks.

13.11 noUnusedLocals and noUnusedParameters

noUnusedLocals reports a declared variable that is never read. noUnusedParameters does the same for parameters. Neither is in strict.

{ "compilerOptions": { "noUnusedLocals": true, "noUnusedParameters": true } }

error TS6133: 'unusedVar' is declared but its value is never read.
error TS6133: 'b' is declared but its value is never read.

A leading underscore exempts a parameter. This is measured, not assumed: function f(a: number, _b: number) reports nothing under noUnusedParameters. It is the convention for a parameter you must declare in order to reach a later one, such as a callback's (value, _index, array).

Only trailing parameters could ever be removed, which is why the underscore convention exists at all. An unused parameter followed by a used one cannot simply be deleted, so the underscore is how you mark it as intentional.

An unused import is reported by noUnusedLocals. Most of its findings come from this in practice, and it is a real correctness check as well as tidiness: an import that nothing uses may still have a side effect, and being told about it is how you notice.

The argument against these two flags is that they fail the build during ordinary editing: comment out three lines and the imports they used become errors. The counter-argument is that a lint rule doing the same check produces a warning nobody reads. The middle position most teams settle on: flags off locally, on in CI, using a tsconfig.ci.json that extends the main one.

13.12 noImplicitReturns

noImplicitReturns requires every code path in a function to return a value, whenever any path does.

// With --noImplicitReturns
function classify(n: number): string {
  if (n < 0) return 'negative';
  if (n > 0) return 'positive';
  return 'zero';                     // without this line: TS2366
}

console.log(classify(-1), classify(0), classify(1));

negative zero positive

Remove the last line and the compiler reports:

error TS2366: Function lacks ending return statement and return type does not
include 'undefined'.

Note which error it is. Under strictNullChecks, the annotated return type string already makes the missing path an error, so noImplicitReturns adds nothing there. Its value is for functions with an inferred return type. There the missing path would silently add undefined to the type, and the mistake would show up at some distant call site.

It does not fire when no path returns a value. That is correct: a void function with no returns is fine. The rule is "if some path returns, all must".

The common false-positive shape is a function whose final branch always throws, or calls something that does. Annotating the throwing helper as never (§4.12) resolves it. That is worth doing anyway, because it also makes control flow analysis treat the following code as unreachable.

Turn it on. It is the cheapest of the five non-strict checks, and it catches a real class of bug: a switch that grew a case, or an if chain that grew a condition, where nobody added the return.

13.13 noFallthroughCasesInSwitch

noFallthroughCasesInSwitch reports a non-empty switch case that falls through into the next one.

// With --noFallthroughCasesInSwitch
function label(n: number): string {
  switch (n) {
    case 1:
    case 2:
      return 'small';          // an EMPTY case above is fine — that is grouping
    case 3: {
      const doubled = n * 2;
      return `medium ${doubled}`;
    }
    default:
      return 'large';
  }
}

console.log(label(1), label(2), label(3), label(9));

small small medium 6 large

// A case with a body and no terminator:
error TS7029: Fallthrough case in switch.

Empty cases are exempt, and that is the whole design: case 1: case 2: return 'small' is the standard grouping idiom and is never a mistake. What gets reported is a case that has statements in it and then falls into the next. That is occasionally deliberate and almost always an omitted break.

When fallthrough is intended, you can restructure (extract a function called from both cases), or end the case with an explicit // falls through comment and turn the flag off for that file. TypeScript has no per-line suppression for this, so restructuring is usually right.

It pairs with exhaustiveness checking (§3.14). The never assignment in the default catches a missing case, and this flag catches a leaking one. Together they make a switch over a discriminated union genuinely safe.

Turn it on. The false-positive rate is near zero, and the bug it catches, an omitted break in a case that also has a body, reads correctly and behaves wrongly.

13.14 allowUnreachableCode

allowUnreachableCode has three states instead of two, which is unusual and is the thing to know.

"allowUnreachableCode": undefined   // the DEFAULT: an editor suggestion, greyed out, no error
"allowUnreachableCode": false       // an error
"allowUnreachableCode": true        // silence

function afterReturn(): number {
  return 1;
  console.log('never runs');       // with the flag false: TS7027
}
console.log(afterReturn(), typeof afterReturn);

1 function

Compiled with --allowUnreachableCode false:

error TS7027: Unreachable code detected.

Leaving the option out is not the same as true. It is a third state in which the editor greys the code out as a suggestion and the compiler reports nothing. That is why unreachable code looks faded in your editor and does not fail the build.

Setting it to false is worth doing, because unreachable code after a return or a throw is almost always a real mistake: a misplaced return, an inverted condition, or a block that was meant to move.

Its sibling allowUnusedLabels works the same way, with the same three states. It reports an unused label, which catches label: written where an object literal was meant.

Note what is not unreachable. Code after a call to a function that always throws counts as reachable for the checker, unless that function is annotated never (§4.12). That is one more reason to annotate a fail() helper properly: it makes both this flag and noImplicitReturns behave correctly.

13.15 The target Option

The target option selects the ECMAScript version that the emitted JavaScript must run on. It has two effects: it decides which syntax is rewritten for older engines (called downlevelling), and it decides which lib files are included by default.

{ "compilerOptions": { "target": "esnext" } }

es5 has been removed. This is the most important currency fact in this subsection, measured against the installed compiler:

$ tsc --target es5 file.ts
error TS5108: Option 'target=ES5' has been removed. Please remove it from your
configuration.

es2015 and later are all still accepted: es2015, es2016, es2020, es2022, es2023 and esnext were each verified. A config copied from a 2022 tutorial will name es5 and will not compile.

target implies a default lib. target: es2022 includes lib.es2022, so Object.hasOwn and Array.prototype.at are available without asking. Setting lib explicitly (§13.16) overrides that default. That is how you say "compile for older syntax but assume newer APIs are polyfilled" (supplied at runtime by a library that adds the missing functions).

The right value depends on where the output runs. For Node, match the oldest Node you support: es2022 for Node 18 and later, or esnext if you control the deployment. For the browser through a bundler, use esnext and let the bundler downlevel, because it knows your browserslist (the list of browsers you support) and the compiler does not.

Downlevelling has a cost that the flag hides. Emitting async/await for an older target generates a state machine, and class fields become constructor assignments. For anything modern this does not arise, which is one more argument for a high target plus a bundler.

13.16 The lib Option

The lib option lists which built-in type declarations are included. That decides which APIs the checker believes exist.

// With --lib esnext (no dom):
const title = document.title;

error TS2584: Cannot find name 'document'. Do you need to change your target
library? Try changing the 'lib' compiler option to include 'dom'.

// With --lib esnext,dom the same line compiles.

The default comes from target, and setting lib replaces it entirely instead of adding to it. So "lib": ["dom"] alone removes every ECMAScript declaration and produces hundreds of errors. The correct spelling is always a full list: ["esnext", "dom", "dom.iterable"].

The error message names the fix, which is unusually helpful:

error TS2550: Property 'groupBy' does not exist on type 'ObjectConstructor'.
Do you need to change your target library? Try changing the 'lib' compiler option
to 'es2024' or later.

That was produced by calling Object.groupBy under --lib es2015, and it tells you exactly which library version introduced the API.

The lib is a claim, not a polyfill. Adding es2024 does not make Object.groupBy exist in an older runtime. It only makes the compiler stop complaining. The whole discipline is matching lib to what your deployment target actually implements, or to what your polyfills provide.

For Node, lib should not include dom. Including it makes document, window, fetch and localStorage type-check in code that will crash. That is one of the most common misconfigurations, and @tsconfig/node22 avoids it by setting lib correctly.

13.17 libReplacement

libReplacement controls whether the compiler looks for @typescript/lib-* packages that stand in for the built-in library files.

{ "compilerOptions": { "libReplacement": false } }

How it works: when libReplacement is on, resolving lib.dom.d.ts first checks for a node_modules/@typescript/lib-dom package and uses that instead if it is there. That is how a project pins a specific version of the DOM types, independently of the compiler version. @types/web publishes exactly such a package.

Turning it off is a performance setting. With it on, the compiler does a module resolution for every lib file on every startup. With it off, it uses its built-ins directly. On a project with a large lib list the difference is measurable, and that is why the flag exists as a switch and is not simply implied.

Set it to false unless you are substituting a lib. That covers the overwhelming majority of projects. With nothing in node_modules/@typescript/, the resolution finds nothing and the work is pure overhead.

When you do want a replacement, the case is a project that must target a specific DOM API surface. An example is a library verifying against an older browser baseline. Pinning @types/web there gives a stable set of declarations that a compiler upgrade will not move.

It is the newest option in this section and the least likely to matter to you. Knowing it exists explains what a @typescript/lib-* package in a dependency tree is doing.

13.18 The jsx Option

The jsx option decides what .tsx syntax compiles to, and it is required for any file that contains JSX.

"jsx": "react-jsx"        // the modern transform: imports jsx() from react/jsx-runtime
"jsx": "react-jsxdev"     // the same, with debug information — for development builds
"jsx": "preserve"         // emit .jsx unchanged, for a downstream tool to handle
"jsx": "react"            // the legacy transform: React.createElement
"jsx": "react-native"     // preserve, but emit .js

All five were verified as still accepted by the installed compiler.

react-jsx is the right choice for React 17 and later. It emits an import of react/jsx-runtime, so a .tsx file no longer needs import React from 'react' just to use JSX. That requirement belonged to the react transform, and it is one of the most persistent stale habits in React codebases.

preserve is the right choice when a bundler handles JSX. Then tsc type-checks and emits .jsx (or nothing at all with noEmit), and Vite or esbuild does the transform. This is the common modern setup.

jsxImportSource changes which package the runtime is imported from, for example "jsxImportSource": "preact" or "solid-js". It can also be set per file with a /** @jsxImportSource … */ pragma, which is how a codebase mixes two JSX libraries.

The cost of .tsx is that the angle-bracket type assertion is unavailable (§1.9), because <T>expr parses as JSX. expr as T works in both kinds of file, which is why this course uses it throughout.

§16.11 covers what the option means for typing JSX: the JSX namespace, intrinsic elements and attribute checking.

What This Section Established

A tsconfig.json marks a project. tsc --showConfig prints what extends and the defaults actually produced. Naming files on the command line now bypasses the config with an explicit TS5112, not silently. include decides the roots and exclude filters them, and neither removes a file that something imports.

extends merges shallowly and per-option, and arrays replace instead of appending. ${configDir} is what makes a shared base config's path options resolve per package, so they do not all land in the repository root.

strict is nine checks and a floor, not a ceiling. noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature, noImplicitOverride, noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters, noImplicitReturns and noFallthroughCasesInSwitch are all outside it and all worth adding. allowUnreachableCode has three states, and its default is a silent editor hint and not an error.

The environment options are claims, not guarantees. target: es5 no longer exists. lib replaces its default instead of adding to it, so ["dom"] alone removes ECMAScript entirely. Including dom in a Node project makes document type-check in code that will crash. And jsx: react-jsx is why a modern .tsx file needs no import React.

Exercises

1. Write two configs. Produce a complete tsconfig.json for (a) a Node 22 CLI that tsc compiles to dist/, and (b) a React application a bundler compiles, where tsc only type-checks. Justify every line that differs between them, and say which flags outside strict you included and why.

2. Diagnose four config errors. For each, name the setting and the fix: a project where document type-checks but crashes at runtime under Node; a monorepo where every package's output lands in the repository root; a .d.ts full of globals that has no effect; a build that fails with TS5023: Unknown compiler option 'baseUrl'.

3. Find what strict misses. Write a module that compiles cleanly under strict and contains four distinct bugs, each of which is caught by one of the flags outside strict. Show the error each flag produces and the minimal fix.

Solution

1. Two configs.

// (a) A Node 22 CLI that tsc compiles.
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2023",
    "lib": ["es2023"],
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "moduleDetection": "force",
    "types": ["node"],

    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": "src",
    "sourceMap": true,
    "declaration": false,

    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,
    "noImplicitReturns": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
    "allowUnreachableCode": false,

    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "libReplacement": false
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

// (b) A React application; a bundler emits, tsc only checks.
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "esnext",
    "lib": ["esnext", "dom", "dom.iterable"],
    "module": "preserve",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "moduleDetection": "force",
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "types": [],

    "noEmit": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,

    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,
    "noImplicitReturns": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
    "allowUnreachableCode": false,

    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "libReplacement": false
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

The differences all follow from who emits the output and where it runs. (a) uses nodenext for both module and moduleResolution because Node is the runtime and its exact rules must apply (§11.10). (b) uses preserve/bundler because the bundler decides the format (§11.11). (a) sets outDir/rootDir/sourceMap. (b) sets noEmit, and can therefore safely add allowImportingTsExtensions (§11.14), which requires it.

lib differs, and it is the important difference. (a) omits dom deliberately: including it would make document and fetch-shaped browser globals type-check in code running on a server. (b) includes it, and dom.iterable too.

types differs. (a) needs ["node"] for process and fs. (b) sets [], so that a stray transitive @types/mocha cannot put describe into the application's global scope (§12.12).

The non-strict flags are identical in both, because they are about code quality and not about the environment. noUnusedLocals and noUnusedParameters are deliberately absent from both. They belong in a tsconfig.ci.json (§13.11), so that commenting out a line during development does not fail the build.

2. Four config errors.

(a) document type-checks under Node. lib includes dom, either explicitly or because target was set high and lib was never set at all. The fix is an explicit "lib": ["es2023"] with no dom entry. The symptom is the worst kind: a clean build, and then ReferenceError: document is not defined in production.

(b) Every package's output lands in the repository root. The shared base config has "outDir": "./dist", and relative paths in a config resolve against that config's directory (§13.4). The fix is "outDir": "${configDir}/dist" (§13.5), which resolves against the extending config instead. tsc --showConfig in one package is the diagnosis, because it prints the absolute path the option actually got.

(c) A globals .d.ts has no effect. There are two candidates, and both are common. Either the file is outside include (§13.3), so it is not in the program at all. Or someone added a top-level import to it, which made it a module, so its declarations are module-scoped (§12.4). The tell is that the errors are all at use sites and none are in the file itself.

(d) TS5023: Unknown compiler option 'baseUrl'. baseUrl was removed in TypeScript 7 (§14.16). The fix is to delete it: paths no longer requires it and resolves relative entries against the config's own directory (§11.13). If the project really needed the "resolve bare specifiers from a root directory" behaviour that baseUrl provided on its own, the replacement is an explicit paths entry, or better a subpath import (§11.12).

3. What strict misses.

// Compiles cleanly under `strict`. Four bugs.
type Level = 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn';

class BaseLogger {
  format(msg: string): string { return msg; }
}

export class Logger extends BaseLogger {
  // BUG 3: meant to override `format`, misspelled it.
  fromat(msg: string): string { return `[log] ${msg}`; }

  // BUG 1: rows[0] is typed `string` and may be undefined.
  first(rows: string[]): string { return rows[0]; }

  // BUG 2: the 'warn' case falls through into `describe`'s next case.
  describe(level: Level): string {
    switch (level) {
      case 'debug': return 'verbose';
      case 'warn': const prefix = '!';
      case 'info': return 'normal';
      default: return 'unknown';
    }
  }

  // BUG 4: a path with no return, and no return annotation to catch it.
  classify(n: number) {
    if (n < 0) return 'negative';
    if (n > 0) return 'positive';
  }
}

Each flag names its own bug:

noUncheckedIndexedAccess
  error TS2322: Type 'string | undefined' is not assignable to type 'string'.

noFallthroughCasesInSwitch
  error TS7029: Fallthrough case in switch.

noImplicitOverride
  error TS4114: This member must have an 'override' modifier because it overrides
  a member in the base class 'BaseLogger'.        <- on `format`, once renamed

noImplicitReturns
  error TS7030: Not all code paths return a value.

The minimal fixes: rows[0] ?? '' or a length check; a break or a return in the 'warn' case; renaming fromat to format and adding override; and a final return 'zero'.

Bug 4 is deliberately written without a return annotation, because that is the only shape noImplicitReturns catches that strict does not. Annotate it : string and plain strictNullChecks reports TS2366 at the function. Leave it inferred and the return type quietly becomes string | undefined, and the error, if any, appears at whichever call site first assigns it to a string. That is exactly the "reported far from the mistake" problem that §2.3 recommends return annotations for. noImplicitReturns covers the functions where you did not write one.

Bug 3 is the one worth dwelling on, because it is invisible without the flag and invisible in review. fromat compiles, runs, and is never called, so every caller gets the base implementation forever, and the class looks entirely reasonable. noImplicitOverride reports it from the other direction: once the method is spelled correctly it demands the override keyword, and the keyword on a method the base does not have is also an error (§6.22). The typo cannot survive in either spelling.

SECTION 14

Project Structure, Build and Migration

§13 was about what the compiler checks. This section is about what it produces, how fast it does that, and how to get a project from wherever it is now to a configuration worth keeping.

It has three themes:

  • Layout and output. Where the files go and what shape they take, plus two settings (noEmit and emitDeclarationOnly) that separate checking from building, which is how most modern projects are set up.
  • Speed. incremental, composite, project references and noCheck, all measured on this machine instead of just described.
  • Change. What TypeScript 7 removed, how to move away from it, and how to raise the strictness of a codebase that cannot absorb a thousand errors in one commit.

One number to set expectations, measured in §1.6 and refined here: with the native compiler, a 200-file project checks in 0.91s from a cold start (nothing saved from an earlier run) and 0.58s when warm (with saved results). That is fast enough that most of the machinery in this section is unnecessary for a project that size, and essential at ten times that size. Knowing which situation you are in is most of the skill.

14.1 outDir

outDir is the directory the emitted JavaScript goes into. Without it, the output lands beside each input file, which is almost never what you want.

{
  "compilerOptions": { "outDir": "dist" },
  "include": ["src"]
}

src/index.ts        ->  dist/index.js
src/util/parse.ts   ->  dist/util/parse.js

The folder structure under outDir mirrors the common root of the input files, not the project root. The common root is the deepest folder that contains all of them. This causes the most common surprise in this section. Add one file outside src, such as a scripts/build.ts or a root-level config.ts, and the common root moves up. Every output path then gains a src/ segment, and dist/index.js becomes dist/src/index.js.

rootDir (§14.2) is what pins the root in place, and setting both together is the reliable arrangement.

outDir is added to the default exclude, so the compiler does not try to compile its own output. If you set exclude explicitly you replace that default and must list it yourself (§13.3). Otherwise the second build reads dist/*.js as input, which under allowJs produces a confusing cascade of errors.

declarationDir puts .d.ts files somewhere else. That is occasionally wanted for a package that publishes types separately from JavaScript. By default they land beside their .js in outDir, which is where a consumer's module resolution expects them.

14.2 rootDir

rootDir declares the input root explicitly, so the output layout does not depend on which files happen to be in the program.

{
  "compilerOptions": { "outDir": "dist", "rootDir": "src" },
  "include": ["src"]
}

Its real job is to give you an error instead of a surprise. With rootDir: "src", a file outside src that gets pulled in reports:

error TS6059: File '/project/scripts/build.ts' is not under 'rootDir' '/project/src'.
'rootDir' is expected to contain all source files.

Without it, that file silently changes every output path. The error is much better than the silence, which is why rootDir belongs in any config that has an outDir.

It does not change which files are compiled. That is include and exclude (§13.3). rootDir only limits where they may be, and controls the output layout.

In a monorepo, rootDir must be set per package. ${configDir} (§13.5) makes that possible from a shared base: "rootDir": "${configDir}/src" resolves against each package and not against the repository root.

rootDirs (plural) is a different option. It declares several directories that should be treated as one virtual root, so generated files in a separate folder can import source files by relative path. It is niche: worth recognising, not worth reaching for.

14.3 The incremental Flag

The incremental flag makes the compiler save a .tsbuildinfo file that records what it checked, so a later run can skip work on files that have not changed.

{ "compilerOptions": { "incremental": true, "outDir": "dist" } }

Measured on this machine, a 200-file project with declaration: true:

cold (no .tsbuildinfo)      0.91s
warm, nothing changed       0.58s
one LEAF file changed       0.62s
one ROOT file changed       0.81s

Three things to read from those numbers.

The floor is about 0.58s. That is process startup plus reading the build info, and no amount of incremental building removes it. On a project this size the flag saves roughly a third of a second.

Changing a leaf costs almost nothing, and changing a root costs almost everything. A leaf is a file nothing else imports, and a root is one that many files depend on. m0.ts is imported, directly or through other files, by 199 files, so changing it invalidates them all and the run approaches the cold time. Every incremental build works this way. It is the argument for good dependency structure over compiler flags: a widely-imported module makes every rebuild expensive.

The saving grows with project size. That is why this flag is essential at ten thousand files and optional at two hundred.

The .tsbuildinfo is written into outDir and named after the config: dist/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo, as verified above. tsBuildInfoFile (§14.6) moves it, which matters when noEmit is on and there is no outDir to put it in.

Delete the file to force a full rebuild. A stale or corrupt build info produces errors that make no sense against the source, and removing it is the first diagnostic step.

14.4 The composite Flag

The composite flag marks a project as something other projects may reference. It turns on several other settings and adds one requirement.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "composite": true,        // implies: incremental, declaration, and a required rootDir
    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": "src"
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

What it turns on: incremental is on, declaration is on, and rootDir defaults to the config's directory and not to the computed common root.

What it requires: every input file must be listed by files or matched by include. A composite project cannot rely on a file being included only because something imported it. A project that references this one needs to know the full input list without following imports.

Why declarations are mandatory is the key idea. A project that references this one reads its .d.ts output, not its source. That is what makes project references fast, because the referencing project never type-checks the referenced one's implementation. It is also what makes them strict, because anything not in the public declarations cannot be reached.

The consequence for a monorepo is that a referenced package must be built before the package that uses it can be checked. That is the trade-off. tsc --build (§14.15) handles the ordering, and a plain tsc -p packages/app fails with "output file has not been built from source file" until the referenced package has been built.

composite on its own does nothing useful. It exists so that the references in §14.5 can work.

14.5 A Project Reference

A project reference declares that this project depends on another composite project. It is TypeScript's answer to the monorepo (one repository holding several packages).

// packages/app/tsconfig.json
{
  "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "include": ["src"],
  "references": [{ "path": "../core" }]
}

// tsconfig.json at the root — a solution file that builds nothing itself
{
  "files": [],
  "references": [{ "path": "./packages/core" }, { "path": "./packages/app" }]
}

$ tsc --build --verbose
Projects in this build:
    * packages/core/tsconfig.json
    * packages/app/tsconfig.json
    * tsconfig.json

Project 'packages/core/tsconfig.json' is out of date because output file
'packages/core/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo' does not exist
Building project 'packages/core/tsconfig.json'...
Building project 'packages/app/tsconfig.json'...

$ tsc --build --verbose        # a second time
Project 'packages/core/tsconfig.json' is up to date because newest input
'packages/core/src/index.ts' is older than output 'packages/core/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo'

That transcript is measured, and it shows the three things references give you.

Ordering is worked out for you. tsc --build sorts the dependency graph and builds in dependency order.

Up-to-date checks are per project. A change in app does not rebuild core, and the second run above rebuilds nothing at all.

The boundary is enforced. app sees core's .d.ts, so it cannot reach into core's internals, and a type that core did not export is genuinely unavailable.

The root "files": [] is the solution file idiom: a config that compiles nothing and exists only to name the projects, so that one tsc --build at the root builds everything.

The cost is that references commit you to a build order. Editors handle them well now, but a fresh clone must build before it can check, and a circular reference is an error and not just a slow build. For a two-package repository this is more machinery than it is worth. At fifteen packages it is what keeps the check time survivable.

14.6 tsBuildInfoFile

tsBuildInfoFile relocates the incremental build's state file.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "incremental": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "tsBuildInfoFile": "./node_modules/.cache/tsbuildinfo.json"
  }
}

Its main use is with noEmit. With no outDir, the default location is beside the config, as ./tsconfig.tsbuildinfo in the project root. Nobody wants that file in their repository. Pointing it at a cache directory keeps the root clean.

It must be gitignored, always. The file records absolute paths and file versions from the machine that wrote it. A committed copy is at best useless and at worst causes wrong up-to-date decisions on another machine.

Caching it in CI is worthwhile, and controlling its location is the main reason to do so. A restored .tsbuildinfo plus unchanged sources turns a cold check into a warm one. On the project measured in §14.3 that is 0.91s to 0.58s, and proportionally more on a large one. The cache key must include the compiler version and the config, because a change in either invalidates it.

With composite and --build, each project gets its own, named after its config, and tsBuildInfoFile overrides it per project. In a monorepo the usual arrangement is to leave them in each package's outDir and gitignore that whole directory.

14.7 noEmit

noEmit runs the checker and writes nothing. It is the most-used way of running tsc in modern projects.

{ "compilerOptions": { "noEmit": true } }

$ tsc --noEmit              # check once
$ tsc --noEmit --watch      # and keep checking

The arrangement it enables is the standard one. A fast tool (Vite, esbuild, swc, or Node's own type stripping) removes the types and produces the output without checking. Then tsc --noEmit checks without producing output. Each tool does the half it is good at.

noEmitOnError is a different flag. It applies when tsc is the tool producing output, and it makes the compiler refuse to write anything when errors were found. The default is to write output anyway, which surprises people the first time a build succeeds with forty type errors.

noEmit works together with incremental, but you need tsBuildInfoFile (§14.6) to say where the saved state goes.

It is a prerequisite for allowImportingTsExtensions (§11.14), because a .ts import specifier cannot be written to the output honestly. That pairing, noEmit plus real file extensions, is the most pleasant setup available for a project whose bundler handles the transform.

noEmit is wrong for a package that publishes types. Something must generate the .d.ts files, and only tsc can. emitDeclarationOnly (§14.8) is the configuration for that.

14.8 emitDeclarationOnly

emitDeclarationOnly writes .d.ts files and no JavaScript.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "declaration": true,
    "emitDeclarationOnly": true,
    "outDir": "dist"
  }
}

This is the correct configuration for a published library in a modern toolchain. A bundler produces the JavaScript, with the tree-shaking (dropping unused code), minification and format conversion it is good at. tsc produces the declarations, which only it can.

It requires declaration, and it is an error without it. It also pairs with declarationMap (§12.15) when you ship sources, and with isolatedDeclarations (§12.16) when generation time matters.

The output layout follows outDir and rootDir exactly as JavaScript output does, so the .d.ts tree mirrors the source tree. That is what a consumer's resolution expects when package.json points at dist/index.d.ts (§12.19).

A package published in two formats needs two runs (§11.16), one per format, each with its own outDir and its own extension: a .d.ts for the ESM build and a .d.cts for CommonJS. Shipping one for both is a packaging bug that type-checks perfectly inside your own repository and fails for half your consumers.

14.9 sourceMap

sourceMap writes a .js.map file beside each output file, so a debugger or a stack trace can point at the TypeScript source and not at the generated JavaScript.

{ "compilerOptions": { "sourceMap": true, "outDir": "dist" } }

Three related options and what each is for.

inlineSourceMap puts the map inside the .js file as a base64 data URI, not in a separate file. That is one fewer file to deploy and a larger bundle, and it cannot be combined with sourceMap.

inlineSources embeds the original TypeScript content in the map, so the debugger does not need the source files on disk. It is essential when the maps are read somewhere the sources are not, such as an error-reporting service.

sourceRoot and mapRoot rewrite the paths inside the map, for when the deployed layout differs from the build layout.

For Node, sourceMap plus --enable-source-maps is the pair that makes a production stack trace name your .ts line. Node needs the flag. Without it the map is written and ignored.

The security consideration is real. A public source map with inlineSources publishes your original code, comments included. For a browser application that is usually acceptable, and sometimes it is not. The common compromise is to generate the maps, upload them to the error tracker, and not deploy them.

Note what happens when two tools are in the chain. If a bundler consumes tsc's output, the bundler must be told to read the incoming maps. Otherwise the final map points at the intermediate JavaScript and not at your source.

14.10 importHelpers

importHelpers makes downlevelled syntax import its helper functions from tslib, and not paste a copy of them into every file. (Downlevelling means rewriting new syntax for an older target, and the helpers are small functions that the rewritten code needs.)

Measured, compiling one async function:

// f.ts
export async function f() {
  await Promise.resolve();
  return 1;
}

With tsc --target es2015, the __awaiter helper (nine lines) is pasted into this file, and into every other file that uses async:

var __awaiter = (this && this.__awaiter) || function (thisArg, _arguments, P, generator) {
    function adopt(value) { return value instanceof P ? value : new P(function (resolve) { resolve(value); }); }
    return new (P || (P = Promise))(function (resolve, reject) {
        function fulfilled(value) { try { step(generator.next(value)); } catch (e) { reject(e); } }
        function rejected(value) { try { step(generator["throw"](value)); } catch (e) { reject(e); } }
        function step(result) { result.done ? resolve(result.value) : adopt(result.value).then(fulfilled, rejected); }
        step((generator = generator.apply(thisArg, _arguments || [])).next());
    });
};
// f.ts
export function f() {
    return __awaiter(this, void 0, void 0, function* () {
        yield Promise.resolve();
        return 1;
    });
}

With tsc --target es2015 --importHelpers, the file imports it from tslib instead:

import { __awaiter } from "tslib";
// f.ts
export function f() {
    return __awaiter(this, void 0, void 0, function* () {
        yield Promise.resolve();
        return 1;
    });
}

And with tsc --target es2017 or later, neither appears, because there is nothing to downlevel:

// f.ts
export async function f() {
    await Promise.resolve();
    return 1;
}

That is the whole decision. importHelpers matters only when you are downlevelling, and how much it saves depends on how many files use the affected syntax. For a modern target it changes nothing.

It requires tslib as a real dependency. Without it the compiler reports:

error TS2354: This syntax requires an imported helper but module 'tslib' cannot be found.

And for a published package, tslib must be in dependencies and not in devDependencies, because the emitted import is in the shipped code.

The modern advice is to raise target instead. Every helper exists because a language feature was compiled away. If you target a runtime that has the feature, both the helper and the import disappear.

14.11 erasableSyntaxOnly

erasableSyntaxOnly forbids the TypeScript constructs that produce runtime code, so that any tool which only deletes the types still produces correct output.

// With --erasableSyntaxOnly, each of the four commented-out forms below is
// TS1294: "This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled."
//
//   enum Colour { Red, Green }
//   namespace Util { export const x = 1; }
//   class P { constructor(public v: number) {} }     (a parameter property)
//   const enum CE { A = 1 }

// The erasable equivalents:
const Colour = { Red: 0, Green: 1 } as const;
type Colour = (typeof Colour)[keyof typeof Colour];

class P {
  readonly v: number;
  constructor(v: number) { this.v = v; }
}

console.log(Colour.Green, new P(3).v);

1 3

All four rejections were measured against the installed compiler.

Note what remains legal. A declare enum in an ambient declaration is fine, because it produces no code. So is every type-level construct, and so are abstract, implements, visibility modifiers and override, all of which are erased.

Why you would want this: Node's own type stripping (§15.24), esbuild, swc and every "just delete the types" transform cannot produce a runtime enum or a parameter-property assignment. Without the flag, those constructs compile under tsc and then silently do nothing under the other tool: a field that is undefined, or an enum object that does not exist.

The migration cost is concentrated in parameter properties, which Angular and NestJS codebases use heavily. Each one becomes three lines. Enums are replaced by the as const object above, which is better anyway (§15.9), and namespaces are replaced by modules.

Turn it on in any new project. It costs nothing on day one, and it keeps every fast transform in the ecosystem available to you.

14.12 noCheck

noCheck produces output without type-checking. It is a build-speed option with a narrow correct use.

$ tsc --noCheck              # emit, skipping the checker entirely

The intended use is a two-phase build. Produce the output immediately with --noCheck, so that downstream work can start, and run tsc --noEmit in parallel to do the checking. Neither blocks the other, and the build fails if the check does.

On the project measured in §14.3 the saving was small: 0.60s against 0.58s warm. The native compiler's cost there is dominated by startup and reading files, not by checking. On a project where checking really dominates, the saving is the checking time.

It is dangerous when used alone. Producing output without checking is exactly the "works in the bundler, forty errors in tsc" failure that §1.7 is about. A build script that uses --noCheck without a paired check is worse than having no tsc at all.

It combines with emitDeclarationOnly, which is where it is most interesting. Generating .d.ts files needs inference but not full checking, so --noCheck --emitDeclarationOnly produces declarations quickly. With isolatedDeclarations (§12.16) on, they are guaranteed correct because every export is annotated.

Reach for it only when you have measured that checking is the bottleneck, and only when a check is running somewhere.

14.13 stableTypeOrdering

stableTypeOrdering was added in TypeScript 6.0. It makes the compiler order union and intersection members the same way every time, so the same source always produces the same type text.

{ "compilerOptions": { "stableTypeOrdering": true } }

The problem it solves is noise in the diffs of generated declarations. Without it, the order of a union's members in a .d.ts can depend on the order the files were processed. An unrelated change then reorders 'a' | 'b' into 'b' | 'a', and the diff of the declaration file fills with churn. A package that reviews its generated declarations, which is the right practice for a public API, would have real changes hidden by that noise.

It also makes error messages stable. That matters for any test suite that asserts on diagnostic text, and for a .d.ts snapshot test.

The cost is a small amount of sorting work on every union and intersection the compiler forms, which is why it is opt-in and not the default.

Turn it on for a library that publishes generated declarations, and for any project that snapshot-tests types. For an application whose .d.ts files nobody reads, it changes nothing you would notice.

It was verified as accepted by the installed compiler. Because it is new, it is the option most likely to be missing from a config inherited from before TypeScript 6.

14.14 tsc --init

tsc --init generates a starter tsconfig.json with the current recommended defaults, heavily commented.

$ npx tsc --init

The generated file turns on strict, esModuleInterop, skipLibCheck, forceConsistentCasingInFileNames and, depending on the version, isolatedModules and verbatimModuleSyntax. It comments out the rest, with a one-line description each.

Its real value is as documentation. Reading the generated comments once is a faster survey of the options than the reference is, and it tells you what the compiler team currently considers a good default.

Its limitation is that it does not know your runtime. The generated target, module, moduleResolution and lib are cautious defaults, and every project needs to set them deliberately (§13.15, §11.10, §13.16). A tsc --init config used unchanged is a working config, and not a good one.

The better starting point for most projects is an @tsconfig/* base, such as @tsconfig/node22, @tsconfig/strictest or @tsconfig/recommended, extended with your own overrides (§13.4). Those are maintained, versioned and reviewed. @tsconfig/strictest in particular turns on most of what §13.6 lists as missing from strict.

Run tsc --init once to read it, and extend a maintained base to ship.

14.15 tsc --build

tsc --build, written tsc -b, is a different mode from ordinary tsc. It reads project references, works out which projects are out of date, and builds them in dependency order.

$ tsc --build                       # build every referenced project, in order
$ tsc --build --verbose             # and explain each decision
$ tsc --build --force               # rebuild everything regardless of timestamps
$ tsc --build --clean               # delete the outputs
$ tsc --build --watch               # and keep going

The up-to-date check is based on timestamps. It compares each project's newest input against its .tsbuildinfo. --verbose prints the reasoning, and it is the only practical way to diagnose "why does it rebuild this every time". The answer is usually a generated file whose timestamp always changes.

It only makes sense with composite (§14.4). A non-composite project that another project references cannot be built this way, and the error says so.

--build ignores most command-line compiler options, because each project's settings come from its own config. That surprises people who try tsc --build --noEmit. The flags it accepts are the build-mode ones listed above.

In a monorepo, --build at the solution file is the single command that checks everything, in the right order, skipping what has not changed. That is the payoff for the setup in §14.5, and it is why the machinery is worth it above a certain size.

14.16 A Removed Compiler Option

TypeScript 6.0 deprecated a set of options, and 7.0 removed them. This is the most important currency fact for anyone reading older material, and every entry below was verified against the installed compiler.

$ tsc --target es5 file.ts
error TS5108: Option 'target=ES5' has been removed.

$ tsc --outFile out.js file.ts
error TS5102: Option 'outFile' has been removed.

$ tsc --baseUrl . file.ts
error TS5102: Option 'baseUrl' has been removed.

$ tsc --moduleResolution classic file.ts
error TS5108: Option 'moduleResolution=Classic' has been removed.

$ tsc --moduleResolution node10 file.ts
error TS5108: Option 'moduleResolution=node10' has been removed.

$ tsc --module amd file.ts
error TS5108: Option 'module=AMD' has been removed.        (also UMD, System)

$ tsc --esModuleInterop false file.ts
error TS5108: Option 'esModuleInterop=false' has been removed.

$ tsc --allowSyntheticDefaultImports false file.ts
error TS5108: Option 'allowSyntheticDefaultImports=false' has been removed.

$ tsc --downlevelIteration file.ts
error TS5102: Option 'downlevelIteration' has been removed.

And one syntax removal, which produces a different code:

module Legacy { export const x = 1; }
error TS1540: A 'namespace' declaration should not be declared using the 'module'
keyword. Please use the 'namespace' keyword instead.

What to do in each case.

target: es5 → raise it, and let a bundler downlevel if you must support older browsers. outFile and the AMD/UMD/System module formats → use a bundler; that is what they were for. baseUrl → delete it; paths no longer needs it and resolves relative to the config (§11.13), and a subpath import is better still (§11.12). moduleResolution: node/node10/classic → nodenext or bundler (§11.11). esModuleInterop: false and allowSyntheticDefaultImports: false → delete them; the permissive behaviour is now permanent (§11.15). downlevelIteration → raise target past ES2015.

Recognising them is the point. A tutorial, a Stack Overflow answer or an inherited config written before 2026 will contain several of these, and the error codes above tell you that what you are reading no longer applies.

14.17 ignoreDeprecations

ignoreDeprecations silences the warning for an option that is deprecated but not yet removed.

{ "compilerOptions": { "ignoreDeprecations": "6.0" } }

The value is a version string naming the release whose deprecations you are acknowledging. It was verified as accepted by the installed compiler.

It buys time, not permanence. An option deprecated in 6.0 gives a warning in 6.x and is removed in 7.0 (§14.16). At that point ignoreDeprecations does nothing, because the option no longer exists, and the error is has been removed and not a deprecation warning.

So the correct use is narrow: a codebase in the middle of an upgrade that must keep building on the old compiler while the migration lands, with the flag and a ticket removed together. Using it to stay on deprecated options indefinitely just moves the whole cost to the day the next major version arrives.

The deprecation warnings themselves are worth reading and not silencing, because each names its replacement. That is the cheapest possible migration guide, written by the tool that knows exactly which options you are using.

If you find ignoreDeprecations in a config you inherit, treat it as a marker. Something in that file was scheduled for removal, and on TypeScript 7 it probably already has been.

14.18 Choosing a Strictness Baseline

Choosing a strictness baseline is the decision this whole section builds to. The honest answer depends on one thing: whether the codebase already exists.

A new project: everything on, on day one.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,
    "noImplicitReturns": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
    "allowUnreachableCode": false,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true
  }
}

The cost of each flag grows with how much non-conforming code exists, and on day one that is none. Adding any of them later means fixing a backlog.

An existing project: a ratchet, one flag per commit. (A ratchet only turns one way: each flag you turn on stays on.) The order matters, because each step's errors are cheaper to fix once the previous step has landed:

1. noImplicitAny             — the biggest and the most valuable
2. strictNullChecks          — the biggest again; expect the most errors here
3. strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, noImplicitThis    — usually small
4. strictPropertyInitialization, useUnknownInCatchVariables    — small
5. "strict": true            — now a no-op, replacing the individual flags
6. noImplicitOverride, noImplicitReturns, noFallthroughCasesInSwitch  — small
7. noUncheckedIndexedAccess  — moderate, and worth every error
8. exactOptionalPropertyTypes, noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature     — moderate

Three rules make a ratchet work.

Never go backwards. A flag that is on stays on, and the config is what holds it in place. If a flag cannot be fixed today, do not turn it on today.

Measure before you commit to a step. Run tsc --noEmit with the flag on and count the errors, which tells you whether the step is an afternoon or a quarter. tsc --noEmit --strict 2>&1 | grep -c 'error TS' is the whole measurement.

Allow a scoped exception, not a global one. A file that cannot be fixed yet gets a // @ts-expect-error with a ticket (§10.17), which fails the build once the underlying problem is fixed. That is better than turning the flag off for the whole project.

The end state is the same config in both cases. The difference is only how long it takes to get there, and a project that ratchets one flag a month arrives within a year with no heroics.

What This Section Established

outDir mirrors the common root of the inputs, which is why one stray file outside src reorganises the whole output tree. rootDir turns that surprise into TS6059. noEmit plus a fast external transform is the standard modern arrangement, and emitDeclarationOnly is its counterpart for a published package, because only tsc can produce .d.ts files.

Speed, measured and not asserted: 200 files check cold in 0.91s and warm in 0.58s, a leaf change costs 0.62s and a root change 0.81s. At this size, dependency structure matters more than flags. composite plus project references make each package's boundary its .d.ts, which is what lets tsc --build skip whole projects. The cost is that a fresh clone must build before it can check.

erasableSyntaxOnly forbids the four constructs that emit code, which is what keeps every fast transform in the ecosystem usable. importHelpers matters only when downlevelling, and raising target removes the need for both it and the helpers.

And TypeScript 7 removed target: es5, outFile, baseUrl, moduleResolution: classic/node10, module: amd/umd/system, esModuleInterop: false, allowSyntheticDefaultImports: false and downlevelIteration. That is nine options that appear in nearly every configuration written before 2026, each with its own error code to tell you that what you are reading is out of date.

Exercises

1. Fix an output layout. A project has outDir: "dist", include: ["src"], and dist/index.js appears where expected — until someone adds scripts/generate.ts and imports a helper from src. Now everything is under dist/src/. Explain exactly why, give the one-line fix that produces an error instead, and give the two-line fix that keeps both directories compiling.

2. Decide on project references. For each of these, say whether project references are worth the setup and why: a single-package application of 300 files; a monorepo of 4 packages where 3 depend on 1 shared library; a monorepo of 40 packages; a library with src and test directories. Where you say no, say what you would do instead.

3. Plan a migration. A codebase compiles on TypeScript 5.2 with strict: false, baseUrl, paths, target: es5, moduleResolution: node and 60 files using enum. Write the ordered plan to get it onto TypeScript 7 with the §14.18 baseline, saying which steps are mechanical, which need judgement, and which single step you would do first if you could only do one.

Solution

1. The output layout.

Why it happened. outDir mirrors the common root of the files in the program, which is computed and not declared. With only src in the program, the common root is src/, and src/index.ts maps to dist/index.js. Adding scripts/generate.ts moves the common root up to the project directory. It is pulled in because something imports it, even though include names only src (§13.3). Every path then gains a segment: dist/src/index.js and dist/scripts/generate.js.

The one-line fix that produces an error instead:

{ "compilerOptions": { "outDir": "dist", "rootDir": "src" } }

error TS6059: File '/project/scripts/generate.ts' is not under 'rootDir' '/project/src'.
'rootDir' is expected to contain all source files.

That is strictly better than the silent reorganisation: the build now fails and names the file that caused it.

The two-line fix that keeps both compiling is a second project, not a wider root:

// tsconfig.json          -> src only
{ "compilerOptions": { "outDir": "dist", "rootDir": "src" }, "include": ["src"] }

// tsconfig.scripts.json  -> scripts only, its own output tree
{ "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": { "outDir": "dist-scripts", "rootDir": "scripts" },
  "include": ["scripts"] }

Widening rootDir to "." is the tempting third option, and it is worse, because it accepts the dist/src/ layout permanently, and every consumer path in package.json has to account for it.

2. Project references, four cases.

A single-package application of 300 files: no. There is one project, and references are between projects. The measurement in §14.3 puts a 200-file check at under a second, so incremental: true alone covers it. Instead, set incremental and cache .tsbuildinfo in CI (§14.6). If it ever becomes slow, look at the dependency structure, because a widely-imported module makes every rebuild expensive and no flag fixes that.

Four packages, three depending on one shared library: probably not. The setup cost is real: composite everywhere, a solution file, ${configDir} in the base, and a build step before any check. The saving on four packages is small. Instead, use one tsconfig.json per package with plain path resolution, or a single program covering all four. Revisit when the build is actually slow.

Forty packages: yes. This is what references are for. Each package's boundary becomes its .d.ts, so a change in one leaf does not re-check the other thirty-nine. tsc --build handles the ordering. The enforced public surface (§14.4) stops packages from reaching into each other's internals, which at forty packages is a design benefit at least as large as the speed one.

A library with src and test: no, but split the config. Tests and sources are one build unit. What you want is two configs, not two projects: tsconfig.json covering src with types: [], and tsconfig.test.json extending it with the test framework's globals (§12.12). That keeps describe and it out of the library's own scope, which is the actual problem, and needs none of the reference machinery.

3. The migration plan.

Step 0, the one to do first if you could only do one: strictNullChecks. Not the version upgrade. It finds more real bugs than every other step combined, it does not depend on the compiler upgrade, and it can start today on 5.2. Everything else is either mechanical or a prerequisite.

Phase 1 — mechanical, no judgement, one commit each.

  1. moduleResolution: node → bundler or nodenext (§11.11). Mechanical, but expect a batch of new errors from packages whose exports maps were previously ignored. Those errors are real and always were.
  2. baseUrl → delete it, and keep paths, which no longer needs it (§11.13). Mechanical.
  3. target: es5 → es2020 or later (§13.15). Mechanical, unless a genuinely old runtime is a requirement, in which case a bundler downlevels instead.
  4. Delete esModuleInterop: false / allowSyntheticDefaultImports: false if present, and downlevelIteration (§14.16).

Phase 2, the compiler upgrade. With phase 1 done, TypeScript 7 accepts the config. Expect the JS API break (§1.6) to affect any build script that imports typescript. Those move to typescript/unstable/sync.

Phase 3, the strictness ratchet, which needs judgement and time (§14.18). Go in this order: noImplicitAny, then strictNullChecks, then the small members of the family, then strict: true, then the flags outside it. Do one flag per commit, and measure before starting with tsc --noEmit --<flag> 2>&1 | grep -c 'error TS'.

Phase 4, the enums, which needs the most judgement. Sixty enum declarations block erasableSyntaxOnly (§14.11), and converting them is not purely mechanical. A string enum becomes an as const object plus a derived union with identical behaviour. A numeric enum's reverse mapping (Colour[0]) has no direct equivalent, and every use of it needs a decision. Do this last, module by module, and only if erasableSyntaxOnly is a goal. It is the one item on the list you could reasonably choose to skip.

What makes the plan work is that phases 1 and 3 are independent. The strictness ratchet can run on 5.2 while the version upgrade is being prepared, so the two streams do not block each other. And the ratchet is where the bugs are.

SECTION 15

The Features That Emit Code

Everything else in this course is erased. §1.2 made that claim, and every section since has relied on it: a type annotation, an interface, a generic parameter, implements, abstract, private, satisfies. All of it is deleted, and the JavaScript that comes out is your source with the type layer removed.

Four constructs are the exceptions, and this section covers all four: - enum produces an object. - namespace produces a function that runs immediately (an IIFE, an "immediately invoked function expression"). - A decorator produces a function call. - A parameter property produces an assignment.

Each is a real language feature and not a type annotation. Each was added before TypeScript adopted its current policy of waiting for the JavaScript standards process.

That history is why the section matters more than its size suggests. erasableSyntaxOnly (§14.11) forbids all four. The reason is practical, not ideological. esbuild, swc, Babel's TypeScript plugin and Node's own type stripping all process one file at a time, and three of the four cannot be produced by just deleting characters. A project that uses them is tied to a TypeScript-aware compiler for good.

The last two subsections follow that thread to its end: what "type-only syntax" really means, and what running TypeScript with no build step looks like today. The answer is very different from the one that was true two years ago.

15.1 A Numeric Enum

A numeric enum is the original form. Members with no initialiser (no = value) are numbered from zero, and the emitted object holds each name and each number.

enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }

console.log(Direction.Up, Direction.Right);
console.log(Object.keys(Direction).length, JSON.stringify(Direction));

0 3
8 {"0":"Up","1":"Down","2":"Left","3":"Right","Up":0,"Down":1,"Left":2,"Right":3}

Eight keys for four members. That is the reverse mapping (§15.6), and it is the first thing to know about a numeric enum. The object is twice the size you wrote, Object.keys returns eight entries, and anything that iterates it sees both directions.

Numbering continues from the last explicit value. enum E { A = 5, B, C } gives B = 6 and C = 7. That is convenient, and it is also a way to introduce a silent bug. When a member is inserted in the middle, every later value shifts, and any number you saved somewhere now means something else.

The type accepts any declared member's value. This was tightened in recent versions, and it is worth restating because it is the half people get wrong. Measured in §10.8: d = 2 compiles because Left = 2, and d = 99 does not. Older TypeScript accepted every number.

Reverse lookup on an undeclared number is undefined, not an error. A value that arrived from a database or a wire format and is out of range therefore gives undefined and not a failure.

The recommendation this section builds to is in §15.9, and it is simple: for a set of named constants, an as const object plus a derived union does the same job with none of this. A numeric enum's only real advantage is bitflag arithmetic, and even there a plain object works.

15.2 A String Enum

A string enum gives every member an explicit string value. It has no reverse mapping, and it behaves much better than the numeric form.

enum Status { Active = 'ACTIVE', Closed = 'CLOSED' }

console.log(Status.Active, Object.keys(Status));
console.log((Status as Record<string, unknown>)['ACTIVE']);

ACTIVE [ 'Active', 'Closed' ]
undefined

Two keys for two members, and Status['ACTIVE'] is undefined, because there is no reverse mapping. That is the biggest improvement over the numeric form: the emitted object is exactly what you wrote.

Every member must be initialised. There is no auto-increment for strings, so a string enum cannot silently renumber.

The type is nominal in both directions (§10.8). "Nominal" means the name matters and not just the shape. A bare 'ACTIVE' is not assignable to Status, and a Status is not assignable to string without widening. That is genuinely stronger than a union of string literals, and it is the one argument for preferring an enum: a Status cannot be forged from a string that happens to match.

The value is what crosses the wire, so choosing it deliberately matters. Active = 'ACTIVE' means the API sees "ACTIVE", and Active = 'active' means it sees "active". Changing that value later is a breaking change for every stored record. That is why the enum's name and its value should be decided separately and not by convention.

If you use enums at all, use string enums. Every hazard in §15.1 and §15.6 belongs to the numeric form.

15.3 A Heterogeneous Enum

A heterogeneous enum mixes numeric and string members. It is legal, it behaves as the sum of its parts, and it is a mistake.

enum Mixed { No = 0, Yes = 'YES' }

console.log(Mixed.No, Mixed.Yes);
console.log(Mixed[0], (Mixed as Record<string, unknown>)['YES']);
console.log(Object.keys(Mixed));

0 YES
No undefined
[ '0', 'No', 'Yes' ]

Three keys for two members, because the numeric member gets a reverse mapping and the string member does not. That asymmetry is the whole problem. Iterating the object, filtering it or serialising it gives a result that depends on which members happen to be numbers.

The rule the compiler enforces is narrow. A string member may not be followed by an implicitly numbered one. enum E { A = 'a', B } is an error, because there is nothing to increment. Everything else is allowed.

There is no situation in which this is the right model. If some members are strings, make them all strings. If you genuinely have two different kinds of value, you have two types, and a discriminated union (§3.12) is the tool.

The reason to know heterogeneous enums exist is to recognise one in code you inherit, and to understand why Object.keys on it returns something surprising.

One line each, for reference: a reverse mapping.

15.4 Constant and Computed Enum Members

A constant enum member has a value the compiler can work out at compile time. A computed enum member has one that must be evaluated at runtime. The distinction decides what the enum can do.

enum Flags {
  None = 0,                    // constant: a literal
  Read = 1 << 0,               // constant: an expression over literals and earlier members
  Write = 1 << 1,
  All = Read | Write,          // constant: an expression over earlier members
  FromRuntime = 'abc'.length,  // computed: a function call
}

console.log(Flags.Read, Flags.Write, Flags.All, Flags.FromRuntime);
console.log(Flags[3], Flags[2]);

1 2 3 3
FromRuntime Write

A constant member is one whose value the checker can evaluate. That means a numeric or string literal, a reference to an earlier constant member of the same enum, or an expression combining those with + - * / % << >> >>> & | ^ ~ and unary + -. Everything else is computed.

Only constant members take part in the union enum type (§15.5), and only they may be used in a const enum (§15.7) or an ambient enum (§15.8). A single computed member changes what the whole enum can be used for, which is why the distinction is worth recognising.

A computed member must be a number. FromRuntime = 'abc'.length is fine. A computed string member is an error, because a string enum's members must all be constant.

Bitflags are the one genuinely good use of a numeric enum, and the 1 << 0 style is why. A bitflag is one bit of a number used as an on/off switch, so several can be combined into one value. The values are meaningful, the combinations are meaningful, and All = Read | Write documents itself.

Now read Flags[3] in the output: it is 'FromRuntime', not 'All'. Both members happen to hold 3, because Read | Write is 3 and 'abc'.length is 3. The reverse mapping is a plain object built by assignment, so the last member with a given value wins, and every earlier one can no longer be reached by number. Nothing warns you about the collision. That is the reverse mapping's real hazard. It is why Flags[n] is unusable as a lookup in any enum where two members can share a value, which includes every bitflag enum that has a combination member.

Collected in one place, because the rest of the course leans on them: a computed enum member and a constant enum member.

15.5 A Union Enum

A union enum is an enum whose members are all constant. That lets the checker treat the enum type as a union of its members' literal types, and that is what makes narrowing and exhaustiveness work.

enum Status { Active = 'ACTIVE', Closed = 'CLOSED', Pending = 'PENDING' }

function describe(s: Status): string {
  switch (s) {
    case Status.Active: return 'running';
    case Status.Closed: return 'finished';
    case Status.Pending: return 'waiting';
    default: {
      const exhaustive: never = s;      // every member handled
      return exhaustive;
    }
  }
}

console.log(describe(Status.Pending), describe(Status.Active));

waiting running

The never assignment compiles only because the enum is a union enum. Add a fourth member without adding a case and it fails, naming the missing one. It is the same mechanism as §3.14 for a discriminated union.

A single computed member breaks it. If one member's value is a function call, the enum type is no longer a union of literals and narrowing by === stops refining. The exhaustiveness check then silently stops working. Nothing warns you: the default branch simply becomes reachable with s still typed as the whole enum.

A member's type is reachable individually. Status.Active is a type as well as a value, and function onlyActive(s: Status.Active) compiles. This is occasionally useful for a state machine, and it is the enum's counterpart to Extract on a union (§9.6).

Narrowing works both ways. if (s === Status.Active) narrows to Status.Active in the true branch and to Status.Closed | Status.Pending in the false one. That is why an if/else if chain over an enum behaves as you would hope.

15.6 An Enum at Runtime, and Reverse Mapping

An enum at runtime is an ordinary object built by an IIFE, and seeing the emitted code answers most questions about enums at once.

enum Direction { Up, Down }
enum Status { Active = 'ACTIVE' }

Compiled with tsc:

"use strict";
var Direction;
(function (Direction) {
    Direction[Direction["Up"] = 0] = "Up";
    Direction[Direction["Down"] = 1] = "Down";
})(Direction || (Direction = {}));
var Status;
(function (Status) {
    Status["Active"] = "ACTIVE";
})(Status || (Status = {}));

(The "use strict" is there because a file with no import or export is a script, and tsc marks scripts as strict. A module is already strict and gets no such line.)

Direction[Direction["Up"] = 0] = "Up" is one statement doing two jobs. The inner assignment sets Direction["Up"] = 0 and evaluates to 0. The outer one then sets Direction[0] = "Up". That is reverse mapping: a numeric enum stores both directions, so that Direction[0] gives back the name.

The string enum emits one assignment per member and no reverse mapping, and you can measure that: Status['ACTIVE'] is undefined (§15.2).

(Direction || (Direction = {})) is what makes an enum mergeable. A second enum Direction block, or a namespace of the same name, adds to the existing object and does not replace it (§12.7).

Three consequences for real code.

Iterating a numeric enum needs a filter. Object.keys(Direction) returns ['0','1','Up','Down']. The idiom for "just the names" is Object.keys(D).filter((k) => Number.isNaN(Number(k))), and for a string enum it is simply Object.keys(S).

The enum object is a real dependency. Importing one imports a runtime value. An enum in a types.ts that a consumer imports only for its types still pulls the object into the bundle, unless the import is import type (§11.3).

Reverse mapping is mildly a security hazard. An attacker-supplied number indexes the enum object and produces a name, and code that treats D[input] as validation gets a truthy result for any in-range integer.

15.7 A Const Enum

A const enum is not emitted at all. Every place it is used is replaced with the literal value.

const enum Direction { Up = 0, Down = 1 }

const move = Direction.Up;

Compiled with tsc:

"use strict";
const move = 0 /* Direction.Up */;

The use site became the literal, with the member's name kept only as a comment, and there is no Direction object anywhere in the output.

The saving is real and the cost is larger. There are three problems, in increasing order of seriousness.

There is no object, so there is no runtime access. Direction[0], Object.keys(Direction) and passing Direction as a value are all errors. Anything that needs to list the members cannot use a const enum.

It breaks single-file transpilation. That is why isolatedModules (§11.5) rejects a const enum imported from another file: inlining requires knowing the values in the declaring file, and a tool that handles one file at a time does not. esbuild, swc and Node's type stripping all either fail on it or silently produce a broken import.

It is forbidden by erasableSyntaxOnly (§14.11), as measured: const enum CE { A = 1 } reports TS1294.

preserveConstEnums writes the object out as well as inlining, which brings back runtime access and gives up the size saving. It exists mainly so that a .d.ts can describe a const enum honestly.

The recommendation is not to use them. Compared with a string-union as const object (§15.9), the size saving is nil, because that alternative also emits nothing when used only as a type, and it works with every tool.

15.8 An Ambient Enum
