An ambient enum is declared with declare enum in a .d.ts or another ambient context. It describes an enum that exists at runtime without creating one.

// legacy-globals.d.ts
declare enum LogLevel { Debug = 0, Info = 1, Warn = 2 }

declare const enum Flags { None = 0, Read = 1 }

It emits nothing, like every declare (§12.3). It is the correct way to type an enum that a script tag, a global build variable or a JavaScript library provides.

It is legal under erasableSyntaxOnly. This is measured, and it is the one enum form that is. It follows directly: an ambient declaration produces no output, so a type-stripping tool has nothing to fail at.

Its members behave slightly differently. In an ambient enum, a member with no initialiser is treated as computed and not as auto-incremented, because the compiler is describing values it cannot see. So declare enum E { A, B } does not give A = 0, and E.A is not a literal type. That means no union enum (§15.5) and no exhaustiveness checking.

An ambient const enum is the case isolatedModules specifically rejects (§11.5). Inlining a value the compiler was only told about is exactly the cross-file dependency that single-file tools cannot honour.

You meet one in a hand-written declaration for an older library. That is also the only place you should write one, never in your own source.

15.9 An Object Literal Instead of an Enum

An object literal instead of an enum is the recommendation of this half of the section. An as const object plus a derived union does everything a string enum does, emits less, and works with every tool.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const Status = {
  Active: 'ACTIVE',
  Closed: 'CLOSED',
  Pending: 'PENDING',
} as const;

type Status = (typeof Status)[keyof typeof Status];
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Status, 'ACTIVE' | 'CLOSED' | 'PENDING'>>;

function describe(s: Status): string {
  switch (s) {
    case Status.Active: return 'running';
    case Status.Closed: return 'finished';
    case Status.Pending: return 'waiting';
    default: { const exhaustive: never = s; return exhaustive; }
  }
}

console.log(describe(Status.Pending), describe('ACTIVE'), Object.keys(Status));

waiting running [ 'Active', 'Closed', 'Pending' ]

The declaration is two lines, and the name is used twice: once for the value and once for the type. That is the same double life a class or an enum has (§8.1).

Everything the enum gave you is here. Named constants: Status.Active. A union type: derived, so it cannot drift out of step. Exhaustiveness: the never assignment works identically. Iteration: Object.keys returns exactly the three names, with no reverse-mapping noise.

There are two differences, and only one is a loss. The gain is that describe('ACTIVE') compiles: a plain string that is one of the values is accepted, which is what you want at an API boundary where the value arrived as JSON. The loss is the mirror image. A string enum would have rejected it, so the enum is nominally stronger. When you want that strength back, a branded type (§8.11) gives it without emitting anything.

And the emit is smaller. Used only as a type, import type { Status } costs nothing. Used as a value, the object is exactly the three properties.

15.10 A Namespace

A namespace groups declarations under one name. If it has any value members, it emits an IIFE that assigns to an object.

namespace Geometry {
  export interface Point { x: number; y: number }
  export const ORIGIN: Point = { x: 0, y: 0 };
  export function distance(a: Point, b: Point): number {
    return Math.hypot(a.x - b.x, a.y - b.y);
  }
  const internal = 'not exported';       // invisible outside
  export function describe(): string { return internal; }
}

const p: Geometry.Point = { x: 3, y: 4 };
console.log(Geometry.distance(Geometry.ORIGIN, p), Geometry.describe());

5 not exported

The emit is the same IIFE shape as an enum: var Geometry; (function (Geometry) { … })(Geometry || (Geometry = {}));, with each exported member assigned onto the object. That is why namespaces merge (§12.8). It is also why a namespace of types only emits nothing at all: there are no assignments to make.

export inside a namespace means "visible outside the namespace", which is a different meaning from export at module scope, and it is the main source of confusion. A non-exported member is private to the namespace, including across merged blocks.

Geometry.Point is a type and Geometry.ORIGIN is a value, reached through the same dotted path. The namespace occupies both declaration spaces (§12.7).

It is forbidden by erasableSyntaxOnly (§14.11), as measured: namespace Util { export const x = 1; } reports TS1294. A namespace containing only types is still rejected by the flag even though it emits nothing, because the check looks only at the syntax.

15.11 A Nested Namespace

A nested namespace is a namespace inside another one, and TypeScript offers a dotted shorthand for declaring it.

namespace App.Models {
  export interface User { id: string }
}

namespace App.Services {
  export function load(id: string): App.Models.User { return { id }; }
}

// The dotted form is shorthand for nesting:
namespace Outer {
  export namespace Inner {
    export const value = 42;
  }
}

import Shortcut = Outer.Inner;          // an import alias, not a module import

console.log(App.Services.load('u1'), Outer.Inner.value, Shortcut.value);

{ id: 'u1' } 42 42

namespace App.Models { … } is exactly namespace App { export namespace Models { … } }, and the intermediate namespaces are implicitly exported. That shorthand is what makes deeply-nested library declarations readable.

import X = Y.Z is an import alias. It is the second, unrelated use of the import = syntax mentioned in §11.7. It creates a local name for a namespace or one of its members, it has nothing to do with modules, and it is erased if it only names types.

Nested namespaces are how the older parts of lib.dom.d.ts and many @types packages are organised, which is the reason to be able to read them. NodeJS.ProcessEnv, Express.Request and JSX.IntrinsicElements are all nested namespaces, and augmenting any of them (§12.5) requires matching the nesting exactly.

Deep nesting emits deep chains of assignments and produces long dotted paths at every use. In your own code, a directory of modules does the same job with better tooling support, which is the argument of §15.12.

15.12 Why Namespaces Are Legacy

Why namespaces are legacy comes down to one fact: they were invented to solve a problem JavaScript no longer has.

Before ES modules, a browser loaded scripts into one shared global scope, and a namespace was the standard way to avoid name collisions. TypeScript shipped them in 2012, under the name "internal modules", because there was no alternative. ES modules were standardised in 2015 and are now universal.

Five specific reasons to prefer modules for new code.

Modules are the language's own mechanism, so every tool understands them: bundlers, tree shakers, test runners, Node and browsers.

Namespaces defeat tree shaking. Tree shaking is a bundler removing code nobody uses. An IIFE that assigns properties to an object is opaque to a bundler's dead-code analysis, so importing one member of a namespace keeps all of them. A module's named exports can be analysed statically, and the unused ones are dropped.

Namespaces emit code and are forbidden by erasableSyntaxOnly (§14.11), which means committing to a TypeScript-aware compiler.

A namespace's boundaries are weaker. Merging (§12.8) means any file can add to any namespace. That is a feature for augmenting a library and a hazard inside one codebase.

The dotted access is noise. Compare App.Services.load(id) with load(id) after an import, at every use.

There are two places namespaces are still correct. One is declaring the shape of an existing global object hierarchy in a .d.ts: NodeJS.ProcessEnv exists and must be described (§12.8). The other is merging a namespace with a class or a function to attach nested types (§12.9), which has no module equivalent.

And one migration note: module Foo { }, the original keyword, is now an error (TS1540) that tells you to write namespace instead. It is a reliable sign that you are reading material from before 2016.

15.13 A Standard Decorator

A standard decorator follows the ECMAScript stage-3 proposal (stage 3 means the design is nearly final), and TypeScript 5.0 and later support it with no flag. A decorator is a function applied to a class or to one of its members. It receives the thing being decorated plus a context object.

function logged<T extends new (...args: any[]) => object>(
  Base: T, ctx: ClassDecoratorContext,
) {
  console.log('class decorator ran for', ctx.name);
  return class extends Base {
    constructor(...args: any[]) { super(...args); console.log('constructing', ctx.name); }
  };
}

@logged
class Service {
  greet(): string { return 'hi'; }
}

console.log(new Service().greet());

class decorator ran for Service
constructing Service
hi

That transcript was produced by compiling to ES2022 and running the output. Node 24 cannot parse decorator syntax at all, so this is the one construct in the course that a type-stripping runtime cannot execute. At target: esnext, TypeScript emits the decorator as written and leaves it to the runtime. At ES2022 it rewrites it into __runInitializers-style helpers.

The context object is the whole design. Every decorator receives one. It carries kind ('class', 'method', 'field', 'getter', 'setter', 'accessor'), name, static, private, and addInitializer, which is a callback run when the class or instance is set up. The five context types are ClassDecoratorContext, ClassMethodDecoratorContext, ClassFieldDecoratorContext, ClassGetterDecoratorContext and ClassSetterDecoratorContext.

What a decorator returns replaces what it decorated, and the return type differs by kind. A class decorator returns a constructor, a method decorator returns a function, and a field decorator returns an initialiser transformer. Returning undefined leaves the original in place, which is the common case for a decorator that only registers something.

Standard decorators are not the same as the legacy ones (§15.20). The signatures differ, the capabilities differ, and a decorator written for one will not work under the other.

15.14 A Decorator Factory

A decorator factory is a function that returns a decorator, which is how a decorator takes arguments.

function tagged(label: string) {
  return function <T extends new (...a: never[]) => object>(
    Base: T, ctx: ClassDecoratorContext,
  ): T {
    console.log(`factory-made decorator for ${String(ctx.name)} with label ${label}`);
    return Base;
  };
}

@tagged('service')
class Task {
  run(): string { return 'ran'; }
}

console.log(new Task().run());

factory-made decorator for Task with label service
ran

@tagged('service') is an expression that is evaluated to produce the decorator, and that is the mechanical difference from @logged. The evaluation happens where the decorator is written, before any decorator is applied, which matters for ordering (§15.15).

Almost every decorator you will use in a framework is a factory, because almost every one needs configuration: a route path, an injection token, a validation rule, a column type.

The factory is where the argument types live. It is worth putting the real signature there and not any. function column(options: { name?: string; nullable?: boolean }) gives every use site checking and completion, which is most of what makes a decorator-based API pleasant.

A factory can also close over per-decoration state, such as a counter, a registry entry, or a WeakMap keyed by the decorated class. That is the standard way to accumulate metadata without the emitDecoratorMetadata machinery of §15.21.

15.15 Decorator Composition and Evaluation Order

Decorator composition is what happens when several decorators apply to one thing. Decorator evaluation order has two phases, and they run in opposite directions.

Phase one: the decorator expressions are evaluated top to bottom. For @a @b method(), a and then b are evaluated as expressions. That matters for factories (§15.14), because that is when the factory call runs.

Phase two: the decorators are applied bottom to top. b wraps the method first, then a wraps b's result. That is ordinary function composition: a(b(method)).

Across a whole class, the order is something to measure and not to recall:

function classDec<T extends new (...a: never[]) => object>(Base: T, ctx: ClassDecoratorContext): T {
  console.log('class decorator ran for', ctx.name);
  return Base;
}
function methodDec(value: () => string, ctx: ClassMethodDecoratorContext) {
  console.log('method decorator ran for', String(ctx.name), 'static?', ctx.static);
  return value;
}
function plus100(_value: undefined, ctx: ClassFieldDecoratorContext) {
  console.log('field decorator ran for', String(ctx.name));
  return function (initial: number): number { return initial + 100; };
}

@classDec
class Service {
  @plus100 count = 1;
  @methodDec greet(): string { return `count=${this.count}`; }
}

console.log(new Service().greet());

method decorator ran for greet static? false
field decorator ran for count
class decorator ran for Service
count=101

Read the order: methods, then fields, then the class. This is measured, and it is not the declaration order of the members: count is written above greet, and its decorator ran second. Methods are decorated before fields because a method exists on the prototype before any instance is created. A field decorator's job is to transform an initialiser that has not run yet.

The class decorator runs last, after every member is in place. That is what lets it inspect or replace a fully formed class.

A field decorator returns an initialiser transformer, and the output proves it: count was declared = 1 and the instance has 101.

The practical rule: do not write two decorators whose effects depend on each other's order. Where a framework requires it, such as a validation decorator that must see a type decorator's metadata, that ordering is part of its API and is documented. In your own decorators, make each one independent.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: decorator evaluation order.

15.16 A Class Decorator

A class decorator receives the constructor and the class context, and may return a replacement constructor.

type Ctor = new (...args: never[]) => object;

const registry = new Map<string, Ctor>();

function registered<T extends Ctor>(Base: T, ctx: ClassDecoratorContext): T {
  registry.set(String(ctx.name), Base);
  return Base;                     // returning the original: register without replacing
}

function withTimestamp<T extends new (...args: any[]) => object>(
  Base: T, _ctx: ClassDecoratorContext,
) {
  return class extends Base {
    readonly createdAt = '2026-09-01T00:00:00Z';
  };
}

@registered
@withTimestamp
class Job {
  constructor(public name = 'default') {}
}

const j = new Job();
// `createdAt` is there at runtime and NOT in Job's type — see below.
console.log(j.name, (j as unknown as { createdAt: string }).createdAt, [...registry.keys()]);

default 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z [ 'Job' ]

The two shapes are "register" and "replace". registered returns the original constructor and does its work as a side effect. withTimestamp returns a subclass, which is the mixin pattern of §6.25 applied through a decorator.

Returning a subclass changes the runtime class and not the declared type. That is the limitation to know, and it is measured above: createdAt is present on the instance, and j.createdAt does not type-check, with Property 'createdAt' does not exist on type 'Job'. TypeScript applies the decorator for its effect and keeps the class's declared shape. Anything a decorator adds must therefore be reached through an assertion or declared on the class separately. This is the most common surprise with decorator-based APIs, and it is why frameworks that add members tell you to declare them yourself.

any[] in the constructor signature is required here and only here. never[] is correct for a decorator that merely inspects, but it makes class extends Base reject the forwarded arguments with TS2545: A mixin class must have a constructor with a single rest parameter of type 'any[]'. It is the same exception §6.25 records for mixins, and for the same reason.

ctx.addInitializer on a class decorator registers a callback that runs after the class is fully defined. That is the right place for anything that must see the finished class, such as validating that required members exist.

The constraint is worth writing carefully. <T extends new (...args: never[]) => object> accepts every class without introducing any (§8.4). When the decorator returns a subclass, any[] is required in the constructor signature for the same reason a mixin needs it (§6.25): the returned class must forward arbitrary arguments.

15.17 A Method Decorator

A method decorator receives the method function and a ClassMethodDecoratorContext, and may return a replacement function.

function timed<This, Args extends unknown[], Return>(
  value: (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return,
  ctx: ClassMethodDecoratorContext<This, (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return>,
) {
  const calls: string[] = [];
  ctx.addInitializer(function (this: This) {
    (this as Record<PropertyKey, unknown>).__calls = calls;
  });
  return function (this: This, ...args: Args): Return {
    calls.push(String(ctx.name));
    return value.call(this, ...args);
  };
}

class Api {
  @timed fetchUser(id: string): string { return `user:${id}`; }
}

const api = new Api();
console.log(api.fetchUser('u1'), api.fetchUser('u2'));
console.log((api as unknown as { __calls: string[] }).__calls);

user:u1 user:u2
[ 'fetchUser', 'fetchUser' ]

Returning a function replaces the method on the prototype. That is how wrapping is implemented: logging, timing, retrying, memoising (caching results) and access control.

ctx.addInitializer with a this-typed function runs per instance, and it is the standard way to make a method auto-bound. ctx.addInitializer(function () { this[ctx.name] = value.bind(this); }) replaces the prototype lookup with a bound instance property, so the method survives being detached (§6.17).

The context tells you what you are decorating. ctx.static says whether it is a static method, ctx.private whether it is a #private one, and ctx.access provides get/set functions that work even for private members. That is how a decorator can read a #field it has no lexical access to.

The three-parameter generic signature is the canonical shape, and it is worth copying and not deriving. It is <This, Args extends unknown[], Return>, with the method typed (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return and the context parameterised the same way. Anything looser fails. A decorator returning (...args: never[]) => unknown is rejected outright with TS1270: Decorator function return type is not assignable to the decorated target, because the replacement must be assignable to what it replaces. Typing it with Function (§4.13) discards the signature and leaves every call site downstream unchecked.

15.18 An Accessor Decorator

An accessor decorator applies to a get or a set. Separately, the accessor keyword declares an auto-accessor that a decorator can intercept as a pair.

function clamped(min: number, max: number) {
  return function (
    target: { get: () => number; set: (v: number) => void },
    _ctx: ClassAccessorDecoratorContext<unknown, number>,
  ) {
    return {
      get(this: unknown): number { return target.get.call(this); },
      set(this: unknown, value: number): void {
        target.set.call(this, Math.min(max, Math.max(min, value)));
      },
      init(initial: number): number { return Math.min(max, Math.max(min, initial)); },
    };
  };
}

class Volume {
  @clamped(0, 11) accessor level = 5;
}

const v = new Volume();
v.level = 99;
console.log(v.level);
v.level = -3;
console.log(v.level);

11
0

accessor level = 5 is a JavaScript auto-accessor. It declares a private backing field plus a getter and a setter, all generated. It exists precisely so that decorators have one uniform thing to intercept.

The decorator receives { get, set } and may return { get, set, init }, replacing either accessor and supplying an initialiser transformer. That triple is what lets clamped constrain both the initial value and every later assignment.

A decorator on a hand-written get or set has a different, simpler shape. It receives the single function and returns a replacement, with ClassGetterDecoratorContext or ClassSetterDecoratorContext. Decorating only the getter leaves the setter untouched.

This is the construct with no legacy equivalent. Legacy decorators (§15.20) received a PropertyDescriptor and could not tell an auto-accessor from a field. That is one of several reasons a decorator written for one system does not port to the other.

15.19 A Field Decorator

A field decorator cannot replace the field, because it receives undefined as its first argument. It returns a function that transforms the field's initial value instead.

function withDefault<T>(fallback: T) {
  return function (_value: undefined, ctx: ClassFieldDecoratorContext<unknown, T>) {
    return function (initial: T): T {
      console.log(`initialising ${String(ctx.name)}`);
      return initial === undefined ? fallback : initial;
    };
  };
}

class Config {
  @withDefault('localhost') host: string = undefined as unknown as string;
  @withDefault(5432) port = 8080;
}

const c = new Config();
console.log(c.host, c.port);

initialising host
initialising port
localhost 8080

The first parameter is always undefined. There is no field value at decoration time, because the class has just been defined and no instance exists. So the only thing a field decorator can do is transform the initialiser.

The returned function runs once per instance, with the declared initial value as its argument, and its result is stored. That is why both messages appear once for one construction, and why port kept 8080 and did not take the fallback.

ctx.addInitializer is available too, and it runs before the field initialisers. That is where a decorator would register the field with a schema or a validation registry.

ctx.access.get and ctx.access.set give the decorator functions to read and write the field on any instance, including a #private one. That is the mechanism a serialisation or ORM decorator uses to reach fields it cannot name.

The limitation to design around: a field decorator cannot make a field lazy, computed or validated on assignment. For any of those, the accessor keyword plus an accessor decorator (§15.18) is the tool, and that is exactly why accessor was added to the language.

15.20 experimentalDecorators

experimentalDecorators enables the legacy decorator system, which is TypeScript's implementation of a 2015 proposal that never became a standard. It is a different feature with the same syntax.

{ "compilerOptions": { "experimentalDecorators": true } }

The signatures differ completely:

// Legacy                                    // Standard
(target, key, descriptor) => void            (value, context) => replacement
(target, key, index) => void                 — parameter decorators do not exist
(constructor) => void | Constructor          (Base, context) => Constructor

Without the flag, legacy-shaped decorators are errors, measured:

error TS1206: Decorators are not valid here.                    <- a parameter decorator
error TS1241: Unable to resolve signature of method decorator when called as an
expression. The runtime will invoke the decorator with 2 arguments, but the
decorator expects 3.

That second message is the clearest possible diagnosis. The runtime will pass two arguments and the decorator wants three, so this decorator was written for the other system.

The two systems cannot be mixed. The flag selects one for the whole compilation, and a library that ships legacy decorators requires every consumer to enable it.

When you still need it. Angular, NestJS, TypeORM and older MobX are built on legacy decorators plus emitDecoratorMetadata (§15.21), and until those frameworks migrate, a project using them sets the flag. That is the honest reason it is still widely enabled.

For new code, use standard decorators. They need no flag, they are on a standards track, they can express type changes, and they will eventually run natively.

15.21 emitDecoratorMetadata

emitDecoratorMetadata is legacy only. It makes the compiler emit runtime type information alongside each decorated declaration, through Reflect.metadata.

{ "compilerOptions": { "experimentalDecorators": true, "emitDecoratorMetadata": true } }

Compiling a decorated class with the flag emits three metadata keys, as measured in the output:

design:type          the declared type of a property
design:paramtypes    the parameter types of a method or constructor
design:returntype    the declared return type of a method

This is the one place TypeScript deliberately leaks types into the runtime, and it is a narrow, lossy leak. The values are constructor references such as String, Number and Object. An interface, a union or a generic all emit Object, and nothing about them survives.

It is what makes constructor injection work. constructor(private db: Database) in NestJS or Angular emits design:paramtypes: [Database], and the injector reads it to know what to construct. Without the metadata, every parameter would need an explicit @Inject(Database) token. Those frameworks require exactly that for interface-typed parameters, because an interface emits Object.

It requires a reflect-metadata polyfill, imported once at the application entry point, because Reflect.metadata is not part of the language.

It has no standard-decorator equivalent. The standards process deliberately did not adopt runtime type metadata. The replacement is Symbol.metadata, a plain object that decorators fill in themselves with whatever information they choose. That is more explicit and takes more code, and it does not require the compiler to leak types.

15.22 A Legacy Parameter Decorator

A legacy parameter decorator applies to a constructor or method parameter. It exists only under experimentalDecorators, and there is no standard-decorator equivalent.

function inject(target: unknown, key: string | symbol | undefined, index: number): void {
  console.log('param decorator', String(key), 'index', index);
}

class Repo {
  constructor(@inject private db: string) {}
}

new Repo('pg');

param decorator undefined index 0

key is undefined for a constructor parameter, as measured, and is the method name for a method parameter. The asymmetry exists because a constructor has no name of its own in the decorator protocol.

A parameter decorator cannot change anything. Its return value is ignored, and it can only record. Everything built on it works by storing the parameter's index in metadata and having something else read it later. That covers dependency injection, request-parameter binding in NestJS, and validation registration.

The standard proposal deliberately omitted parameter decorators, on the grounds that a method decorator reading its own parameter list can achieve the same effect, and that parameter decorators interact badly with destructuring and default values. So this is a permanent fork: a framework built on parameter decorators cannot move to standard decorators without an API change.

Recognising this is the practical point. If a codebase's decorators are on parameters, it is on the legacy system and will stay there until its framework migrates. That constrains erasableSyntaxOnly (§14.11) and which build tools are available.

15.23 Type-Only Syntax Versus Emitting Syntax

This is the dividing line the whole section is about, stated once and completely.

Type-only syntax — erased, emits nothing:

type / interface                    generic type parameters
: annotations                       implements
as / satisfies / !                  abstract
declare                             public / private / protected / readonly
import type / export type           override
type predicates and asserts         overload signatures (the non-implementation ones)

Emitting syntax — produces JavaScript:

enum                                a parameter property
namespace (with value members)      decorators

// Every construct in this block is erased. The emitted JavaScript is the two
// console.log calls and the two function bodies, with nothing else.
type Id = string;
interface Named { name: string }
declare const injected: string;

function greet(n: Named): string { return `hi ${n.name}`; }
function isNamed(v: unknown): v is Named {
  return typeof v === 'object' && v !== null && 'name' in v;
}

const id = 'u1' as Id;
console.log(greet({ name: 'Ada' }), isNamed({ name: 'x' }));
console.log(id satisfies string, typeof injected);

hi Ada true
u1 undefined

The practical test is a mechanical one: could a tool produce this output just by deleting characters? For everything in the first list, yes. For enum, namespace, a decorator and a parameter property, no, because each requires generating code that was not written.

erasableSyntaxOnly (§14.11) is that test as a compiler flag, and turning it on guarantees the property so you do not have to remember it.

The reason the line matters more now than it used to is that the fast half of the toolchain has grown. In 2018 tsc compiled everything and the distinction was academic. Today esbuild, swc, Vite, Bun, Deno and Node itself all strip types, and three of the four emitting constructs are unavailable to all of them.

15.24 Running TypeScript Without a Build Step

Running TypeScript without a build step is now a real option, and the answer changed recently enough that most written advice is out of date.

$ node --experimental-strip-types app.ts        # Node 22.6+: strip only
$ node --experimental-transform-types app.ts    # ...and transform enum/namespace/params
$ node app.ts                                   # Node 23.6+: stripping on by default

There are two modes, and the difference is exactly the line of §15.23. Strip-only deletes type syntax and refuses anything that would need generating: an enum, a namespace and a parameter property all produce an error. Transform mode also compiles those three, at the cost of needing a real transformer.

Measured on the installed Node 24: enum, namespace and parameter properties all execute under --experimental-transform-types. Decorators do not, because the syntax is a parse error. That is the one construct no type-stripping runtime handles, and it is why every decorator example in this section was compiled with tsc before it was run.

Nothing is type-checked. Node strips or transforms and does not check. tsc --noEmit (§14.7) remains necessary, and that division of a fast runtime plus a separate checker is the modern arrangement (§1.7).

The alternatives, and what each is for:

tsx and ts-node wrap the same idea with more configuration and awareness of your tsconfig. ts-node can also type-check, at a large cost in speed.

Deno and Bun run TypeScript natively with no flag. Deno type-checks by default and can be told not to. Bun strips without checking, like Node.

The consequence for how you write code is the recommendation this section ends on: set erasableSyntaxOnly, avoid the four emitting constructs, and every one of these runtimes will run your source unmodified. That is a genuinely new position, because it was not available in 2023, and it removes the build step from a whole class of project.

What This Section Established

Four constructs emit code, and everything else in TypeScript is erased. enum emits an object built by an IIFE. A numeric one carries a reverse mapping, so four members produce eight keys and Direction[0] gives back a name, while a string enum emits exactly what you wrote. A heterogeneous enum has both behaviours at once and is never the right model. A const enum emits nothing and breaks every single-file transpiler, which is why isolatedModules rejects it.

The alternative is two lines: an as const object plus (typeof X)[keyof typeof X]. It gives named constants, a derived union, exhaustiveness and clean iteration. The only thing it gives up is rejecting a bare matching string, and you can buy that back with a brand when you want it.

Namespaces solved a problem from before modules existed. Now they defeat tree shaking, emit code, and can be merged from anywhere. They remain correct in exactly two places: describing an existing global hierarchy in a .d.ts, and merging with a class to attach nested types.

Decorators come in two incompatible systems. The standard one needs no flag, receives a context object, and can change types. The legacy one needs experimentalDecorators, is what Angular and NestJS are built on, and is the only one with parameter decorators, which is a permanent fork. The measured evaluation order is methods, then fields, then the class, with expressions evaluated top to bottom and applied bottom to top.

And the practical conclusion: Node runs .ts directly now. enum, namespace and parameter properties survive its transform mode, while decorators do not parse at all. erasableSyntaxOnly is how you guarantee your source runs everywhere without a build.

Exercises

1. Replace three enums. Convert a numeric enum used for bitflags, a string enum used for API statuses, and a const enum used for internal constants — each to the construct you would actually ship. For each, say what you kept, what you lost, and one call site that changes.

2. Write three decorators. Using standard decorators only: a class decorator that registers the class in a Map without replacing it; a method decorator that makes the method auto-bound so it survives detachment; and a field decorator that upper-cases its initial value. Show all three on one class, and give the exact order in which they run.

3. Audit a file for emitting syntax. Given a module containing an enum, a namespace of types only, a class with parameter properties, an interface, a type predicate and a satisfies, say which lines survive erasableSyntaxOnly, which do not, and rewrite the failing ones. Then say what the file's emitted JavaScript contains, line by line.

Solution

1. Three replacements.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// (a) Bitflags: keep the numbers, drop the enum.
const Perm = { None: 0, Read: 1 << 0, Write: 1 << 1, Admin: 1 << 2 } as const;
type Perm = (typeof Perm)[keyof typeof Perm];

const granted = Perm.Read | Perm.Write;
console.log(granted, (granted & Perm.Write) !== 0, (granted & Perm.Admin) !== 0);

// (b) API statuses: an as const object plus a derived union.
const Status = { Active: 'ACTIVE', Closed: 'CLOSED' } as const;
type Status = (typeof Status)[keyof typeof Status];
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Status, 'ACTIVE' | 'CLOSED'>>;

function describe(s: Status): string { return s === Status.Active ? 'running' : 'finished'; }
console.log(describe(Status.Active), describe('CLOSED'), Object.keys(Status));

// (c) Internal constants that were a const enum: plain consts.
const MAX_RETRIES = 3;
const TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000;
console.log(MAX_RETRIES, TIMEOUT_MS);

3 true false
running finished [ 'Active', 'Closed' ]
3 5000

(a) Bitflags. Kept: the values, the names, and the | and & arithmetic. Lost: nothing that mattered, because the reverse mapping was actively harmful here. Perm[3] would have been undefined for a legitimate combination. The union type Perm is 0 | 1 | 2 | 4, so a combined value like 3 is not assignable to it. Annotate combinations as number, which is what the enum was effectively doing anyway.

(b) Statuses. Kept: named constants, the union, exhaustiveness, and now clean iteration. Object.keys returns two names and not the enum's two. Lost: nominality. describe('CLOSED') now compiles, where the enum would have rejected it. The call site that changes is exactly that one, and it usually changes for the better: at an API boundary the value arrives as a string, and the enum forced a cast.

(c) The const enum. Kept: everything. A const enum used only for internal constants was a grouping device, and two const declarations do the same with no inlining, no isolatedModules conflict (§11.5) and no erasableSyntaxOnly violation. If you want the grouping, an as const object restores it.

2. Three decorators.

type Ctor = new (...args: never[]) => object;
const registry = new Map<string, Ctor>();

function registered<T extends Ctor>(Base: T, ctx: ClassDecoratorContext): T {
  console.log('1. class decorator');
  registry.set(String(ctx.name), Base);
  return Base;
}

function bound<This, Args extends unknown[], Return>(
  value: (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return,
  ctx: ClassMethodDecoratorContext<This, (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return>,
) {
  console.log('2. method decorator');
  ctx.addInitializer(function (this: This) {
    (this as Record<PropertyKey, unknown>)[ctx.name] = value.bind(this);
  });
  return value;
}

function upper(_value: undefined, _ctx: ClassFieldDecoratorContext<unknown, string>) {
  console.log('3. field decorator');
  return function (initial: string): string { return initial.toUpperCase(); };
}

@registered
class Greeter {
  @upper name = 'ada';
  @bound greet(): string { return `hi ${this.name}`; }
}

const g = new Greeter();
const detached = g.greet;
console.log(detached(), [...registry.keys()]);

2. method decorator
3. field decorator
1. class decorator
hi ADA [ 'Greeter' ]

The order is methods, then fields, then the class. This is measured, and the numbering in the log deliberately does not match it, to make the point. It is not declaration order: name is written above greet.

detached() works, which is the whole purpose of bound. ctx.addInitializer with a function (not an arrow, so this is the instance) assigns a bound copy as an own property that shadows the prototype method: a lookup finds the own property first, so the method is hidden. The reference therefore survives being pulled off the object (§6.17).

registered returns Base unchanged, which is the "register without replacing" shape. Returning a subclass instead would work too and would change the class's type. It would also mean the registry held a different constructor from the one consumers get.

3. The audit.

// Survives erasableSyntaxOnly: everything below.
interface Named { name: string }
type Id = string;

function isNamed(v: unknown): v is Named {
  return typeof v === 'object' && v !== null && 'name' in v;
}

// Rewritten: was `class P { constructor(public v: number) {} }`
class P {
  readonly v: number;
  constructor(v: number) { this.v = v; }
}

// Rewritten: was `enum Colour { Red, Green }`
const Colour = { Red: 0, Green: 1 } as const;
type Colour = (typeof Colour)[keyof typeof Colour];

// Rewritten: was `namespace Shapes { export interface Circle { r: number } }`
// A namespace of types only still emits nothing, but the flag is syntactic and
// rejects it anyway. A module — or a nested type — is the replacement.
type Shapes = { Circle: { r: number } };

const config = { retries: 3 } satisfies Record<string, number>;
const id = 'u1' as Id;

console.log(isNamed({ name: 'x' }), new P(3).v, Colour.Green, config.retries, id);

true 3 1 3 u1

Fails erasableSyntaxOnly: the enum, the namespace and the parameter property, which give three TS1294 errors. Survives: the interface, the type alias, the type predicate, as, satisfies and every annotation.

The namespace is the interesting one. A namespace containing only types emits nothing, so it is erasable in fact, but the flag is a syntactic check and rejects it regardless. That is a deliberate simplification. A rule that depended on whether a namespace happened to contain a value could not be evaluated by a single-file transpiler either.

The emitted JavaScript, line by line, is: the isNamed function; the P class with its readonly v field declaration erased and the constructor body kept; the Colour object with as const erased; the config object with satisfies erased; const id = 'u1'; and the console.log. The interface, both type aliases, the Shapes type and the type predicate's v is Named all vanish. That is the mechanical test from §15.23: every one of them could be removed by deleting characters.

SECTION 16

Typing Real Code

Everything up to here has been the language itself. This section applies it to the five things a working program actually does: waits for something, talks to a network, touches a web page, draws a component, and reads data it did not create.

Those five have one thing in common, and it is why they get a whole section and not a paragraph. Each one is a boundary: a place where the type system's promise stops depending on your annotations (§1.1) and starts depending on the outside world. fetch gives you any from .json(). querySelector returns Element | null and knows nothing about your HTML. A caught error is unknown, because anything at all can be thrown. A configuration file is just a string until something parses it.

So the same move comes up again and again: check at the boundary, and let a real type travel inwards from there. §16.21 and §16.22 give that move its name and the full argument for it. The subsections before them cover the specific boundaries where it applies. The ones after show how to bring an existing codebase to the point where it happens.

16.1 Typing an Async Function

Typing an async function needs one rule: its declared return type must be a Promise, and inference supplies the wrapper for you.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

async function loadUser(id: string) {
  await Promise.resolve();
  return { id, name: 'Ada' };
}

// The inferred return type is the Promise, not the value.
type _1 = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof loadUser>, Promise<{ id: string; name: string }>>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof loadUser>>, { id: string; name: string }>>;

// An explicit annotation names the Promise too.
async function loadCount(): Promise<number> { return 1; }

console.log(await loadUser('u1'), await loadCount());
export {};

{ id: 'u1', name: 'Ada' } 1

Annotating the resolved type is an error, and the message is precise: The return type of an async function or method must be the global Promise<T> type. async function f(): number does not compile.

The value you return is the resolved type, so return 1 in a Promise<number> function is correct, because the async keyword does the wrapping. Returning a promise works too. It is flattened and not nested (§9.7).

void and Promise<void> are different in the way that matters. An async function with no return value has type Promise<void>. You can await it, and you must not use its result. Declaring one as void instead, a common slip in a callback type, means the caller cannot await it, and that is how a floating promise (one nobody waits for) gets created.

A function that returns a promise without being async has the same type. The difference is only where errors surface. A throw inside an async function becomes a rejection. A throw before the first await in a non-async function that returns a promise is synchronous. That distinction bites when a caller uses .catch() and expects it to cover both.

16.2 A Promise Type

A Promise type is Promise<T>, where T is the resolved value. It is covariant in T, and it carries no information at all about rejection.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const p: Promise<string> = Promise.resolve('a');

// all: a tuple in, a tuple of resolved values out
const all = await Promise.all([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve('x')]);
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof all, [number, string]>>;

// allSettled: a tuple of result objects, discriminated by `status`
const settled = await Promise.allSettled([Promise.resolve(1)]);
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof settled, [PromiseSettledResult<number>]>>;
const first = settled[0];
console.log(first.status === 'fulfilled' ? first.value : 'rejected');

// race and any: the union of the element types
const raced = await Promise.race([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve('x')]);
type _3 = Expect<Equal<typeof raced, number | string>>;

console.log(await p, all, raced);
export {};

1
a [ 1, 'x' ] 1

Promise.all returning a tuple and not an array is the detail worth knowing. Its declaration is a homomorphic mapped type over the input tuple (§8.6), with Awaited applied to each element. That is why the destructuring const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([…]) gives each variable its own type.

PromiseSettledResult<T> is a discriminated union, { status: 'fulfilled'; value: T } | { status: 'rejected'; reason: any }, so allSettled results narrow with a === test (§3.12). Note that reason is any, for the same reason a caught error is unknown (§16.4): nothing constrains what a rejection carries.

The rejection type is not in Promise<T>. There is no Promise<T, E>, no throws clause (§10.20), and no way for a signature to say what a function can reject with. That is the strongest argument for a Result type (§10.20) at boundaries where failure is expected and not exceptional.

A Promise<T> is PromiseLike<T>-compatible, which is what lets await work on a thenable (an object with a then method) from a library that predates native promises.

16.3 Typing an await

Typing an await is automatic, because await unwraps a Promise<T> to T. Two things are worth knowing: what it does to a non-promise, and what it does inside a loop.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const value = await Promise.resolve(42);
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof value, number>>;

// Awaiting a non-promise is legal and the type passes through — literal and all.
const plain = await 42;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof plain, 42>>;

// Awaiting a union of promise and value gives the union of the resolved types.
declare const maybe: Promise<string> | number;
const resolved = await maybe;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<typeof resolved, string | number>>;

console.log(value, plain);
export {};

42 42

await on a non-promise is legal, costs a microtask tick (a tiny delay), and leaves the type completely unchanged. await 42 is the literal type 42 and not number, because Awaited<42> passes a non-thenable straight through. That is what makes await someMaybePromise() safe to write when a function is sometimes synchronous.

Awaiting a union works because Awaited<T> distributes (§9.7), so Promise<string> | number resolves to string | number and not to something awkward.

The type layer says nothing about the sequencing, and this is the place to be honest about what it cannot check. for (const id of ids) { await load(id); } and await Promise.all(ids.map(load)) have identical types and completely different behaviour: one is sequential and one is concurrent. No annotation distinguishes them, and no flag warns about the first.

Top-level await requires the file to be a module (§11.2), which is why several examples in this course end with export {}. In a script the error is TS1375: 'await' expressions are only allowed at the top level of a file when that file is a module.

16.4 Typing a Caught Error

Typing a caught error is settled by one fact: JavaScript can throw anything, so the binding is unknown under useUnknownInCatchVariables (§10.19).

class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly status: number, message: string) { super(message); this.name = 'HttpError'; }
}

function describe(e: unknown): string {
  if (e instanceof HttpError) return `HTTP ${e.status}: ${e.message}`;
  if (e instanceof Error) return `${e.name}: ${e.message}`;
  if (typeof e === 'string') return `thrown string: ${e}`;
  return `thrown ${typeof e}: ${JSON.stringify(e)}`;
}

for (const thrown of [new HttpError(404, 'missing'), new TypeError('bad'), 'oops', { code: 7 }]) {
  try { throw thrown; } catch (e) { console.log(describe(e)); }
}

HTTP 404: missing
TypeError: bad
thrown string: oops
thrown object: {"code":7}

The order is most specific first (§3.6): HttpError before Error, or the subclass is swallowed by the more general check.

The two annotations allowed on a catch binding are unknown and any, and nothing else. catch (e: Error) is an error regardless of flags, because the compiler cannot make that guarantee.

A rejected promise reaches the same catch with the same type. try { await f(); } catch (e) binds unknown, and the rejection value is whatever the rejector passed. For a fetch network failure that is a TypeError, and for a library it may be a plain object.

Error.prototype.cause is where the original belongs. throw new HttpError(500, 'upstream failed', { cause: e }) keeps the chain of errors, and it is the piece of error hygiene most often skipped. Note that cause is typed unknown on Error, so reading it needs the same narrowing as the catch itself.

Error.isError(e), available in Node 24, is the cross-realm-safe test. (A realm is a separate JavaScript environment, such as an iframe, where instanceof can give a wrong answer.) It is worth preferring to instanceof Error in library code, for the reason §3.6 gives.

16.5 Typing fetch

Typing fetch is where a program most often loses its types without noticing, because Response.json() returns any.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

declare const endpoint: string;

async function naive() {
  const res = await fetch(endpoint);
  const _status: number = res.status;      // Response is fully typed
  const _ok: boolean = res.ok;
  return res.json();                        // ...and this is `any`
}

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof naive>>, any>>;
export {};

res.json() is Promise<any> in the standard library, so every value downstream of it is unchecked (§10.21). That is the largest any in a typical application, and it is invisible.

The three treatments, in increasing order of honesty.

type User = { id: string; name: string };
declare const endpoint: string;

// 1. Assert. Fast, unchecked, and states something that may be false.
async function asserted(): Promise<User> {
  const res = await fetch(endpoint);
  return (await res.json()) as User;
}

// 2. Return unknown. Honest, and pushes the narrowing to the caller.
async function honest(): Promise<unknown> {
  const res = await fetch(endpoint);
  return res.json() as Promise<unknown>;
}

// 3. Validate. Checked, and the only one whose type is true. (§16.21)
function isUser(v: unknown): v is User {
  return typeof v === 'object' && v !== null
    && 'id' in v && typeof v.id === 'string'
    && 'name' in v && typeof v.name === 'string';
}

async function validated(): Promise<User> {
  const res = await fetch(endpoint);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  const body: unknown = await res.json();
  if (!isUser(body)) throw new TypeError('unexpected response shape');
  return body;
}

console.log(typeof asserted, typeof honest, typeof validated);
export {};

function function function

res.ok must be checked separately. fetch rejects only on a network failure. A 404 or a 500 resolves normally, and res.json() on an HTML error page throws a SyntaxError from inside the JSON parser and does not report the status. Every wrapper you write needs the res.ok line.

Typing the request side is worth doing too. RequestInit's method is string, so a typo compiles. Narrowing your own wrapper's parameter to 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE' costs one line and catches it.

16.6 Typing JSON

Typing JSON starts from the same hole in the standard library: JSON.parse returns any.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const loose = JSON.parse('{"id": 1}');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof loose, any>>;

// The honest type for arbitrary JSON — a recursive type alias (§5.17).
type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [key: string]: Json };

const parsed: Json = JSON.parse('{"id": 1, "tags": ["a"], "meta": null}');

// Reading it requires narrowing, which is the point.
function readId(doc: Json): number | undefined {
  if (typeof doc === 'object' && doc !== null && !Array.isArray(doc)) {
    const id = doc['id'];
    if (typeof id === 'number') return id;
  }
  return undefined;
}

console.log(readId(parsed), readId('not an object'), JSON.stringify(parsed).length);

1 undefined 33

const parsed: Json = JSON.parse(…) is a one-word improvement over the default, and it costs nothing. any is assignable to Json, so the annotation always compiles, and from that point on every access is checked.

JSON.stringify has its own asymmetry worth knowing. It returns string, but it returns undefined for a function, a symbol or undefined at the top level. The declaration says string, so JSON.stringify(undefined).length type-checks and then crashes. That is another entry in §1.11's list.

toJSON is honoured and not modelled. A Date serialises to a string, and a class with a toJSON method serialises to whatever it returns. So the type of JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) is not typeof x: dates become strings, undefined properties disappear, and Map and Set become {}. Any code that round-trips through JSON needs a separate wire type (a type for the data as it travels), and §16.20 is about writing one.

The runtime validators of §16.21 replace all of this with one call that both parses and produces a typed value. The Json type is what you use when the shape genuinely is arbitrary.

16.7 A DOM Element Type

A DOM element type is one of a few hundred interfaces in lib.dom.d.ts, arranged in a hierarchy. Picking the right one is most of what makes DOM code type-check.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// EventTarget -> Node -> Element -> HTMLElement -> HTMLInputElement
declare const input: HTMLInputElement;
const asHtml: HTMLElement = input;
const asElement: Element = input;
const asNode: Node = input;
const asTarget: EventTarget = input;

// Only the most specific type has the properties you want.
console.log(typeof input.value, typeof asHtml.hidden);

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error Property 'value' does not exist on type 'HTMLElement'.
  const v = asHtml.value;
  // @ts-expect-error Property 'hidden' does not exist on type 'Element'.
  const h = asElement.hidden;
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled, typeof asNode, typeof asTarget);

undefined undefined
function undefined undefined

Each level adds something. EventTarget has only the listener methods. Node adds tree navigation. Element adds attributes and className. HTMLElement adds style, hidden, dataset and the events. Each HTMLXxxElement then adds its own: value on an input, href on an anchor, getContext on a canvas.

Element versus HTMLElement is the distinction that catches people. Element covers SVG and XML too, so it has no style and no dataset. Most APIs that feel like they should return HTMLElement return Element, and §16.10 covers the two ways to get the specific type back.

HTMLElementTagNameMap is the interface that maps 'input' to HTMLInputElement, and it is what makes document.createElement('canvas') return an HTMLCanvasElement with no annotation. Reading that map is the fastest way to find the right interface name for a tag.

A .d.ts for a component library often needs HTMLAttributes<T> from @types/react or the equivalent, and not the element type itself. The props are the attributes, not the element.

16.8 An Event Handler Type

An event handler type must match the event the target actually dispatches, and the DOM's typings are precise enough to check it.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

declare const button: HTMLButtonElement;

// The listener's parameter is inferred from the event name — and it is worth
// checking rather than assuming which event that is.
button.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof e, PointerEvent>>;
  console.log(e.clientX, e.shiftKey, e.pointerType);
});

button.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof e, KeyboardEvent>>;
  console.log(e.key, e.repeat);
});

// A named handler needs the type written down — and MouseEvent still fits,
// because PointerEvent extends it.
const onClick: (e: MouseEvent) => void = (e) => console.log(e.button);
button.addEventListener('click', onClick);
console.log(typeof onClick);

function

'click' is a PointerEvent, not a MouseEvent. This is measured, and it is worth knowing because every tutorial says MouseEvent. The modern DOM typings route pointer-capable events through PointerEvent, which extends MouseEvent. A handler annotated (e: MouseEvent) => void therefore still fits, and everything written before the change still compiles. What you gain by not annotating is e.pointerType, e.pressure and the rest.

e.target is EventTarget | null, not the element you attached to. That is correct, and it is the most common friction point. e.target is where the event originated, which with bubbling (events travelling up through parent elements) may be a descendant. e.currentTarget is the element the listener is on, and it is typed EventTarget too on the standalone Event interface, so both usually need narrowing.

declare const form: HTMLFormElement;

form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();

  // BOTH need a check: currentTarget is EventTarget | null, not HTMLFormElement.
  if (e.currentTarget instanceof HTMLFormElement) {
    console.log([...new FormData(e.currentTarget).keys()]);
  }
  if (e.target instanceof HTMLInputElement) console.log(e.target.value);

  // The one place the element type IS known is a `function` listener's `this`.
  console.log(typeof e, e.submitter?.tagName);
});
console.log(typeof form);

undefined

currentTarget is EventTarget | null too. That surprises people who expect it to carry the element the listener was attached to. It does at runtime, but the type does not, because Event is declared once for every target. The element type is available in exactly one place, the this parameter of the first addEventListener overload (§16.9), and that only helps a function listener and not an arrow.

The narrowing to use is instanceof, not an assertion. e.target as HTMLInputElement is a claim about markup you may have changed since, and e.currentTarget as HTMLFormElement is a claim that the | null says may be false.

A custom event carries its payload in detail. Typing it needs an entry merged into WindowEventMap, or your own CustomEvent<T>. That is one of the everyday uses of global augmentation (§12.5).

16.9 Typing addEventListener

Typing addEventListener rests on an overloaded declaration (one function with several signatures) whose first overload is keyed by an event-name map. Knowing that explains every behaviour it has.

// The shape in lib.dom.d.ts, simplified:
addEventListener<K extends keyof HTMLElementEventMap>(
  type: K,
  listener: (this: HTMLElement, ev: HTMLElementEventMap[K]) => any,
  options?: boolean | AddEventListenerOptions,
): void;

addEventListener(
  type: string,
  listener: EventListenerOrEventListenerObject,
  options?: boolean | AddEventListenerOptions,
): void;

The first overload is an indexed access type (§8.2). HTMLElementEventMap[K] looks the event type up from the name, which is what gives the callback its parameter type with nothing written down.

The second overload is the escape hatch, and it is why a typo compiles. button.addEventListener('clik', handler) does not match the map, so it falls through to the string overload, and the listener's parameter becomes Event. There is no error, and the event simply never fires.

The this parameter (§4.8) in the first overload is what makes this the element inside a function listener. It is one of the clearest examples of the feature in the standard library.

options matters for correctness as much as for types. { once: true } removes the listener after one call. { signal } ties its lifetime to an AbortController. { passive: true } promises not to call preventDefault. The signal form is the one worth adopting: one controller.abort() removes every listener registered with it, which is a better teardown story than matching removeEventListener calls.

removeEventListener requires the same function reference, and no type error tells you when it does not match. Passing an inline arrow to both is a leak the compiler cannot see.

16.10 querySelector Generics

querySelector generics are the two mechanisms that recover a specific element type from a selector.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// 1. A bare tag name is looked up in HTMLElementTagNameMap — no annotation needed.
const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas');
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof canvas, HTMLCanvasElement | null>>;

// 2. Any other selector gives `Element | null`.
const byId = document.querySelector('#app');
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof byId, Element | null>>;

// 3. An explicit type argument names the result.
const input = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('#name');
type _3 = Expect<Equal<typeof input, HTMLInputElement | null>>;

// getElementById is not selector-based, so it is always HTMLElement | null.
const el = document.getElementById('app');
type _4 = Expect<Equal<typeof el, HTMLElement | null>>;
export {};

The tag-name overload is real inference, and the type argument is an assertion in disguise. querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('#name') compiles whatever #name turns out to be, and nothing checks the selector against your markup. It is more convenient than as HTMLInputElement and exactly as unverified.

The | null is the half people delete, and it is the half that matters. document.querySelector('#app')! is an assertion (§2.15) that the element exists, and the crash it produces is Cannot read properties of null at some later line.

The pattern worth adopting is a helper that checks both facts once:

function must<T extends Element>(
  selector: string,
  Ctor: new () => T,
  root: ParentNode = document,
): T {
  const el = root.querySelector(selector);
  if (!(el instanceof Ctor)) {
    throw new Error(`expected ${selector} to be a ${Ctor.name}, got ${el?.tagName ?? 'nothing'}`);
  }
  return el;
}
console.log(typeof must);

function

That is instanceof doing the narrowing (§3.6), so the returned type is checked and not asserted. A markup change then produces a clear error at startup, and not a null dereference in a handler.

querySelectorAll returns a NodeListOf<T>, which is iterable but is not an array. .map does not exist on it, and [...list] or Array.from(list) is the conversion.

16.11 JSX in TypeScript

JSX in TypeScript requires a .tsx file and the jsx compiler option (§13.18). JSX is the HTML-like syntax that React and similar libraries use. The syntax is checked and not merely parsed: element names, attributes and children all have types.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

type Props = { name: string; count?: number };

function Greeting({ name, count = 1 }: Props) {
  return <p className="greet">{name.repeat(count)}</p>;
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Greeting name="ab" count={2} />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Greeting name="x" />));

<p class="greet">abab</p>
<p class="greet">x</p>

Two costs of .tsx are worth stating once. The angle-bracket type assertion <T>expr is unavailable, because it parses as JSX, and expr as T is the form that works everywhere (§1.9). And a generic arrow function needs a trailing comma to disambiguate: const f = <T,>(x: T) => x;.

With jsx: react-jsx there is no import React, and the emitted file imports react/jsx-runtime instead. That has been true since React 17, and the habit of importing React "for JSX" is one of the most persistent stale ones.

JSX is not React-specific. jsxImportSource (§16.16) points the transform at Preact, Solid or your own runtime. The checking machinery (JSX.IntrinsicElements, JSX.Element, attribute checking) is part of the language and not of any library.

What is checked is the subject of the next five subsections: which lowercase names are valid elements (§16.13), which values may be used as components (§16.14), and which attributes each accepts (§16.15).

16.12 The JSX Namespace

The JSX namespace is the set of interfaces the checker looks up to decide what JSX means. With the modern transform it lives inside the module named by jsxImportSource, which is react/jsx-runtime by default, under a namespace called JSX.

// The members that matter, as react's jsx-runtime declares them:
namespace JSX {
  interface IntrinsicElements { … }   // every lowercase tag and its attributes
  interface ElementType { … }         // what may appear as a component
  type Element = ReactElement          // the type of a JSX expression
  interface ElementChildrenAttribute { children: {} }   // which prop receives children
}

JSX.IntrinsicElements is the map from lowercase tag names to their attribute types (§16.13). A tag not in it is an error. Adding one, for a web component say, is a declaration merge into that interface (§12.7).

JSX.Element is what a JSX expression evaluates to, which is why a component's return type can be written as JSX.Element. Inferring it is better, though, because a component returning null or a string is legal in React 18 and later, and JSX.Element alone excludes those.

The namespace moved. Before TypeScript 5.1 there was one global JSX namespace, so two JSX libraries in one project collided. The per-jsxImportSource lookup fixed that, and it is why a modern codebase can have React components and Solid components in different directories.

Augmenting it is a real technique. Adding a web component to IntrinsicElements, or widening an attribute type, is done by merging into declare module 'react' { namespace JSX { … } }. Getting the module path right is the part that takes the time.

16.13 An Intrinsic Element

An intrinsic element is a JSX element whose name starts with a lowercase letter. It is looked up in JSX.IntrinsicElements and resolves to a built-in tag, and not to a variable in scope.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

const markup = renderToStaticMarkup(
  <section id="main">
    <h1 className="title">Hello</h1>
    <input type="email" required readOnly value="a@b.c" />
  </section>,
);
console.log(markup);

<section id="main"><h1 class="title">Hello</h1><input type="email" required="" readOnly="" value="a@b.c"/></section>

The lowercase/uppercase rule is the whole dispatch. <div> is looked up in the map; <Div> is a reference to a variable named Div. That is why a component whose name is lowercase silently becomes an unknown tag rather than a call — one of the classic React bugs, and one TypeScript catches:

error TS2339: Property 'greeting' does not exist on type 'JSX.IntrinsicElements'.

A hyphenated name is exempt. <my-element> is a custom element and is allowed without being in the map. This is the same rule check_html.py applies (§16.14 covers the typed alternative).

Attributes are checked against the tag's own interface. <input type="emial"> is an error because type is a union of literal strings; <div hidden="yes"> is an error because hidden is boolean. That checking is finer than the HTML spec's own, and it is one of the largest practical wins of .tsx over .jsx.

The DOM property names are used, not the HTML attribute names. It is className and not class, and htmlFor and not for, and the rendered output above shows className being converted back to class. Note that readOnly is not converted: React's server renderer emits it verbatim. That is a quirk of that renderer and not of TypeScript, and it is a good reminder that what JSX checks and what a renderer emits are two different things.

16.14 A Value-Based Element

A value-based element is a JSX element whose name starts with an uppercase letter or contains a dot. It resolves to a value in scope, and its type must be usable as a component.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Badge({ label }: { label: string }) {
  return <span className="badge">{label}</span>;
}

const Namespaced = { Inner: ({ n }: { n: number }) => <b>{n}</b> };

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Badge label="new" />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Namespaced.Inner n={7} />));

<span class="badge">new</span>
<b>7</b>

The dotted form <Namespaced.Inner /> is how a compound component is written, and it is why the uppercase rule has the "or contains a dot" clause: <obj.member /> is unambiguous even in lowercase.

What may be a component is decided by JSX.ElementType. In React's typings that admits a function returning a valid node, a class component, and a few special values. Anything else produces 'X' cannot be used as a JSX component, with a second line naming the actual mismatch, usually a return type that includes undefined.

The most common failure is a return type. A component that can return undefined is not a valid React component (return null instead), and one that returns a Promise is only valid as a server component. The error message names the offending part of the union, which makes it one of the more legible JSX diagnostics.

A component's props type is inferred from its parameter. §16.17 develops this, and it is why writing the parameter type well is the whole of typing a component.

16.15 JSX Attribute Type Checking

JSX attribute type checking compares the attributes you write against the component's props type, or against the intrinsic element's interface, with the same rules as an object literal, including excess property checking (§5.4).

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

type Props = { label: string; size?: 'sm' | 'lg'; onSelect?: (id: number) => void };

function Chip({ label, size = 'sm' }: Props) {
  return <span data-size={size}>{label}</span>;
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Chip label="a" size="lg" />));

function neverRendered() {
  return (
    <>
      {/* @ts-expect-error 'size' must be 'sm' or 'lg' */}
      <Chip label="a" size="md" />
      {/* @ts-expect-error 'lable' is not a prop of Chip */}
      <Chip lable="a" />
      {/* @ts-expect-error 'label' is required */}
      <Chip />
    </>
  );
}
console.log(typeof neverRendered);

<span data-size="lg">a</span>
function

A misspelled prop is an excess property, which is why it is caught. The attributes form a fresh object literal, so the heuristic of §5.4 applies exactly.

A missing required prop is a missing property, reported at the element with the prop named.

A spread defeats the check, in the same way it does for an object literal (§5.4). <Chip {...props} /> where props is a variable is checked structurally but not for excess keys. That is the JSX form of the gap satisfies (§8.10) exists to close.

data-* and aria-* attributes are permitted on intrinsic elements by an index signature in the React typings. data-size above is accepted with no declaration, while an arbitrary unknown attribute is not.

Children are checked too, through JSX.ElementChildrenAttribute. A component declaring children: ReactNode accepts nested JSX, and one that does not declare children at all rejects it. That last behaviour changed with React 18's typings, which removed the implicit children from FC, and it is the source of a large fraction of upgrade errors.

16.16 jsxImportSource

jsxImportSource names the module the JSX transform imports its runtime from. It defaults to react, and it is what makes the JSX machinery work with any library.

{ "compilerOptions": { "jsx": "react-jsx", "jsxImportSource": "preact" } }

// Or per file, which is how two libraries coexist in one project:
/** @jsxImportSource solid-js */

Two things are looked up from it. One is the runtime functions the emitted code calls: jsx, jsxs, jsxDEV and Fragment from <source>/jsx-runtime. The other is the JSX namespace (§16.12) that supplies IntrinsicElements and the rest.

The per-file pragma is the feature that matters. A codebase rendering some components with React and some with Solid puts a /** @jsxImportSource solid-js */ comment at the top of the Solid files. Each file's JSX is then checked against that library's own element and attribute types.

It only applies to the react-jsx and react-jsxdev transforms. Under jsx: preserve nothing is imported, so the option has no effect and the downstream tool decides. Under the legacy jsx: react transform, the equivalent is jsxFactory and jsxFragmentFactory.

Getting it wrong produces a clear error, which is unusual for this area: This JSX tag requires the module path 'X/jsx-runtime' to exist, but none could be found. It means that either the package is not installed or its name is misspelled in the option.

16.17 Typing React Props

Typing React props is typing one parameter, and everything else follows from that. There is no special props syntax. A component is a function, and its props type is its parameter's type.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';
import type { ReactNode } from 'react';

type ButtonProps = {
  label: string;
  variant?: 'primary' | 'ghost';
  disabled?: boolean;
  onClick?: (event: { id: string }) => void;
  children?: ReactNode;
};

function Button({ label, variant = 'primary', disabled = false, children }: ButtonProps) {
  return (
    <button className={`btn btn-${variant}`} disabled={disabled}>
      {label}
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Button label="Save" />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Button label="Cancel" variant="ghost" disabled><em>!</em></Button>));

<button class="btn btn-primary">Save</button>
<button class="btn btn-ghost" disabled="">Cancel<em>!</em></button>

Four decisions make a props type good.

Use a union of literals, not string. variant?: 'primary' | 'ghost' gives autocompletion and rejects a typo. variant?: string gives neither.

Declare children explicitly when you accept it. React 18's typings removed the implicit children from FC, so a component that does not declare it rejects nested JSX. That is the biggest source of errors when upgrading an older codebase. children?: ReactNode is the declaration.

Default in the destructuring, and mark the prop optional. variant = 'primary' with variant?: means the parameter is 'primary' | 'ghost' inside the body, with no ?? anywhere.

Name the type and export it. A consumer wrapping your component needs ButtonProps to type its own wrapper, and ComponentProps<typeof Button> is the fallback when you did not export it.

ComponentProps and its variants are worth knowing. ComponentProps<'button'> gives every intrinsic button attribute, and ComponentProps<typeof Button> extracts a component's props. Extending the first, as in type Props = ComponentProps<'button'> & { label: string }, is how you write a component that forwards every native attribute.

16.18 Typing a React Component

Typing a React component comes down to one recommendation: annotate the props parameter and let the return type be inferred.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

type Props = { name: string };

// Recommended: a plain function with an annotated parameter.
function Greeting({ name }: Props) {
  return <p>Hello, {name}</p>;
}

// Also fine, and identical: an arrow with the same annotation.
const GreetingArrow = ({ name }: Props) => <p>Hi, {name}</p>;

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Greeting name="Ada" />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<GreetingArrow name="Grace" />));

<p>Hello, Ada</p>
<p>Hi, Grace</p>

Do not annotate with React.FC<Props>. The reason is concrete and not stylistic. FC fixes the return type, which blocks a component from returning a string or an array. It made children implicit before React 18 and no longer does, so its behaviour changed under people. And it interferes with generic components (§16.19), which cannot be written with it at all.

The inferred return type is better than any you would write. JSX.Element excludes null, ReactNode is wider than what a component may return, and inference gets it exactly right.

A component is only special to the JSX checker, which asks whether its type is assignable to JSX.ElementType (§16.14). Everything else about it, meaning parameters, generics, overloads and this, is ordinary function typing.

Hooks need no special treatment either. useState('') infers [string, Dispatch<SetStateAction<string>>]. useState<User | null>(null) is the annotation you need when the initial value is narrower than the state. useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) gives the RefObject<HTMLInputElement | null> that a ref attribute wants. The general rule holds: annotate where inference has nothing to work from, and nowhere else.

16.19 A Generic React Component

A generic React component takes a type parameter, which is how a reusable list, table or form field keeps its item type.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';
import type { ReactNode } from 'react';

type ListProps<T> = {
  items: readonly T[];
  keyOf: (item: T) => string;
  children: (item: T) => ReactNode;
};

function List<T>({ items, keyOf, children }: ListProps<T>) {
  return <ul>{items.map((item) => <li key={keyOf(item)}>{children(item)}</li>)}</ul>;
}

type User = { id: string; name: string };
const users: User[] = [{ id: 'u1', name: 'Ada' }, { id: 'u2', name: 'Grace' }];

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <List items={users} keyOf={(u) => u.id}>
    {(u) => <strong>{u.name}</strong>}
  </List>,
));

<ul><li><strong>Ada</strong></li><li><strong>Grace</strong></li></ul>

T is inferred from items, and both callbacks get it for free. u is a User in keyOf and in the render function, with nothing annotated. That is §7.2's left-to-right inference applied to props: items is declared before the callbacks, so by the time the checker reaches them T is already solved.

The render-prop child is a function, not JSX, which is what makes children: (item: T) => ReactNode work. That pattern, sometimes called a function-as-child, is the standard way to make a generic component's contents depend on its type parameter.

A generic component cannot be written with React.FC, because FC<Props> has no place to declare T. That is the strongest of the reasons in §16.18 to avoid it.

In a .tsx file a generic arrow needs a trailing comma, as in const List = <T,>({ … }: ListProps<T>) => …, because <T> alone parses as JSX. That is the same .tsx cost as the angle-bracket assertion (§1.9), and it is why the function declaration form is easier here.

const type parameters help (§7.8) when a literal matters. function Select<const T extends readonly string[]>(props: { options: T }) keeps options as a tuple of literals, so the value prop can be typed T[number] and reject anything not in the list.

16.20 Typing an Object from an API

Typing an object from an API is the decision about where the wire format and the domain model diverge. Getting it wrong is why so much application code is full of ?. and !.
