type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// The WIRE type: exactly what the API sends, warts included.
type UserWire = {
  id: string;
  display_name: string;
  created_at: string;          // an ISO string, not a Date
  deleted_at: string | null;
  roles: string[];
};

// The DOMAIN type: what the rest of the program wants.
type User = {
  id: string;
  displayName: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  deletedAt?: Date;
  roles: readonly string[];
};

function toDomain(wire: UserWire): User {
  return {
    id: wire.id,
    displayName: wire.display_name,
    createdAt: new Date(wire.created_at),
    ...(wire.deleted_at !== null && { deletedAt: new Date(wire.deleted_at) }),
    roles: wire.roles,
  };
}

const u = toDomain({
  id: 'u1', display_name: 'Ada', created_at: '2026-09-01T00:00:00Z',
  deleted_at: null, roles: ['admin'],
});
type _1 = Expect<Equal<typeof u.createdAt, Date>>;
console.log(u.displayName, u.createdAt.getUTCFullYear(), 'deletedAt' in u, u.roles);

Ada 2026 false [ 'admin' ]

Two types and one function is the whole pattern, and each half earns its place.

The wire type is honest about the format. created_at is a string because JSON has no dates (§16.6). deleted_at is string | null because that is what the server sends. Typing it as Date would be a lie that no assertion makes true.

The domain type is honest about the model. createdAt is a real Date. deletedAt is absent and not null: the conditional spread produces a key that is genuinely not there, which 'deletedAt' in u reports as false (§5.18). And roles is readonly because nothing downstream should mutate it.

The conversion is the only place that knows both, so a change in the API's naming is one edit, and the rest of the program never sees display_name.

The temptation to skip this is strongest when the shapes nearly match, and that is exactly when it costs least to do. Once the wire type is a type alias next to the domain one, adding the validator of §16.21 is a two-line change and not a refactor.

16.21 A Runtime Validator

A runtime validator is a function that checks a value's shape while the program runs and produces a typed result. It is the only construct in this course that makes a type true and not merely asserted.

type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; errors: string[] };
type Validator<T> = (input: unknown, path: string) => Result<T>;

const str: Validator<string> = (v, p) =>
  typeof v === 'string' ? { ok: true, value: v } : { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected string`] };

const num: Validator<number> = (v, p) =>
  typeof v === 'number' && Number.isFinite(v)
    ? { ok: true, value: v }
    : { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected number`] };

function object<S extends Record<string, Validator<unknown>>>(
  shape: S,
): Validator<{ [K in keyof S]: S[K] extends Validator<infer U> ? U : never }> {
  return (v, p) => {
    if (typeof v !== 'object' || v === null) return { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected object`] };
    const out: Record<string, unknown> = {};
    const errors: string[] = [];
    for (const [key, check] of Object.entries(shape)) {
      const r = check((v as Record<string, unknown>)[key], `${p}.${key}`);
      if (r.ok) out[key] = r.value; else errors.push(...r.errors);
    }
    return errors.length
      ? { ok: false, errors }
      : { ok: true, value: out as { [K in keyof S]: S[K] extends Validator<infer U> ? U : never } };
  };
}

const userValidator = object({ id: str, name: str, age: num });

const good = userValidator(JSON.parse('{"id":"u1","name":"Ada","age":36}'), 'user');
if (good.ok) console.log(good.value.name.toUpperCase(), good.value.age + 1);

const bad = userValidator(JSON.parse('{"id":1,"name":"Ada"}'), 'user');
if (!bad.ok) console.log(bad.errors);

ADA 37
[ 'user.id: expected string', 'user.age: expected number' ]

The type is derived from the validator, not declared beside it. { [K in keyof S]: S[K] extends Validator<infer U> ? U : never } is a mapped type (§8.6) with a conditional and an infer (§8.4) that pulls each field's type out of its checker. So the shape you validate and the type you get back cannot drift apart. That is the whole design, and it is what every schema library in the ecosystem does.

good.value.age + 1 is checked and true. The type says number and something confirmed it, which is the property no assertion has (§10.14).

Errors accumulate with paths. user.id and user.age are both reported from one call, because a validator that stops at the first failure makes a bad API response take three round trips to diagnose.

There is exactly one assertion in the whole implementation, at the point where the accumulated Record<string, unknown> becomes the derived type. It sits inside the function that just verified every field (§10.15). That is the shape to aim for: the assertion is next to the check that justifies it.

In production, use a library. Zod, Valibot, ArkType and TypeBox all do this and much more. Writing one once is how you understand what they are doing and why their inferred types are trustworthy.

16.22 Parse, Do Not Validate

Parse, do not validate is the principle behind §16.21 (the phrase is usually written bare, as parse do not validate). The difference it names is between a function that answers a question and one that produces a value.

type User = { id: string; name: string };

// VALIDATE: returns a boolean. The knowledge is thrown away at the return.
function isValidUser(v: Record<string, unknown>): boolean {
  return typeof v['id'] === 'string' && typeof v['name'] === 'string';
}

// PARSE: returns the narrowed value. The knowledge is in the type.
function parseUser(v: unknown): User {
  if (typeof v !== 'object' || v === null) throw new TypeError('not an object');
  const o = v as Record<string, unknown>;
  if (typeof o['id'] !== 'string') throw new TypeError('id must be a string');
  if (typeof o['name'] !== 'string') throw new TypeError('name must be a string');
  return { id: o['id'], name: o['name'] };
}

const raw: Record<string, unknown> = JSON.parse('{"id":"u1","name":"Ada","extra":1}');

// The validating version leaves the caller exactly where it started.
if (isValidUser(raw)) {
  console.log(typeof raw['id']);            // still `unknown` to the checker
}

// The parsing version hands back something the rest of the program can use.
const user = parseUser(raw);
console.log(user.id.toUpperCase(), user.name);

string
U1 Ada

isValidUser returns true and the caller learns nothing. Inside the if, raw['id'] is still unknown. The check happened, its conclusion was discarded, and every use downstream needs the same check again or an assertion.

parseUser returns a User. The check happened once, at a named boundary, and every use downstream is checked against a type that something verified.

Three consequences worth stating.

A type predicate (§3.9) is the halfway house. function isUser(v: unknown): v is User does pass the knowledge on, and it is a real improvement over a boolean. But it is an unchecked promise, whereas a parser's return type is checked against what it actually constructs.

Parsing normalises as well as checks. parseUser returns exactly { id, name } and drops extra. A predicate leaves the original object with whatever else was on it, which matters when the value is re-serialised.

"Make illegal states unrepresentable" is the same idea one level up (§3.12). Parse the input into a type that cannot express the invalid cases, and every downstream function is relieved of checking.

The name comes from Alexis King's 2019 essay, and the one-line version is the best summary there is: use a data structure that makes illegal states unrepresentable, and push the burden of proof to the edge.

To have in hand before moving on: parse do not validate.

16.23 Typing a Configuration Object

Typing a configuration object is the case where satisfies (§8.10) earns its keep most clearly, because you want two things that pull in opposite directions: the shape checked, and the exact values remembered.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type RouteConfig = Record<string, { path: string; auth: boolean; roles?: readonly string[] }>;

const routes = {
  home: { path: '/', auth: false },
  profile: { path: '/me', auth: true },
  admin: { path: '/admin', auth: true, roles: ['admin'] },
} as const satisfies RouteConfig;

// Checked: a typo or a wrong value fails at the declaration.
// Precise: the keys and the paths survive as literal types.
type RouteName = keyof typeof routes;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<RouteName, 'home' | 'profile' | 'admin'>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<(typeof routes)['admin']['path'], '/admin'>>;

function urlFor(name: RouteName): string { return routes[name].path; }
console.log(urlFor('profile'), routes.admin.roles);

/me [ 'admin' ]

as const satisfies T is the combination, in that order, because the reverse does not parse (§8.10). as const keeps the literals and makes everything readonly. satisfies checks the whole object against the contract without widening it.

An annotation would have thrown the precision away. const routes: RouteConfig = { … } type-checks identically, and then keyof typeof routes is string, routes.admin.path is string, and urlFor accepts any string at all.

The environment case is the other half of this subsection, and it needs a different tool because the values arrive as strings at runtime:

type Env = { NODE_ENV: 'development' | 'production'; PORT: number; DEBUG: boolean };

function readEnv(source: Record<string, string | undefined>): Env {
  const mode = source['NODE_ENV'] ?? 'development';
  if (mode !== 'development' && mode !== 'production') throw new Error(`bad NODE_ENV: ${mode}`);
  const port = Number(source['PORT'] ?? '3000');
  if (!Number.isInteger(port)) throw new Error(`bad PORT: ${source['PORT']}`);
  return { NODE_ENV: mode, PORT: port, DEBUG: source['DEBUG'] === 'true' };
}

const env = readEnv({ NODE_ENV: 'production', PORT: '8080', DEBUG: 'true' });
console.log(env.NODE_ENV, env.PORT + 1, env.DEBUG);

production 8081 true

That is §16.22 applied to configuration. One function converts strings into a typed object at startup and throws with a readable message when something is wrong. The rest of the program then reads a PORT that is genuinely a number. The alternative, process.env.PORT! at each use, is three assertions and a NaN.

16.24 Migrating a JavaScript File

Migrating a JavaScript file is a sequence of small steps that can each be shipped alone, and the point of doing it in steps is that each one has value on its own.

Step 1: // @ts-check. Add one comment at the top of one .js file (§12.22). No config change, no build change, no rename. The editor immediately reports real errors, and every one of them is a bug that was already there.

Step 2: JSDoc types on the exports (§12.23). Use @param, @returns and @typedef. The file is still JavaScript, still runs unmodified, and now its callers get checked too.

Step 3: rename to .ts. Do this when the file is already clean under @ts-check, so the rename produces no new errors. Convert the JSDoc to annotations mechanically.

Step 4: remove the remaining any. These are the ones that came in through untyped dependencies, JSON.parse, and the boundaries of §16.5 and §16.6.

// Step 3's output for a file that went through steps 1 and 2.
export type ConnectOptions = { host: string; port?: number; secure?: boolean };

export function connect({ host, port = 5432, secure = false }: ConnectOptions): string {
  return `${secure ? 'postgresqls' : 'postgresql'}://${host}:${port}`;
}

console.log(connect({ host: 'db' }), connect({ host: 'db', port: 5433, secure: true }));

postgresql://db:5432 postgresqls://db:5433

Four rules that keep a migration from stalling.

Convert leaves first. A leaf module has no imports of its own, so it has no untyped dependencies and its types are real immediately. If you convert an entry point first, everything it touches is any and the exercise proves nothing.

Do not mix a rename with a refactor. A commit that converts .js to .ts should change no behaviour, so that a bug afterwards can be traced to its cause.

Type the shape you have, not the shape you want. If a function genuinely returns string | undefined, say so. Improving the design is a separate commit.

Let allowJs carry the rest (§12.21). A half-migrated project compiles the whole time, which is what makes the work interruptible.

16.25 A Strictness Ratchet

A strictness ratchet is the mechanism that makes an existing codebase get stricter without ever getting looser. §14.18 gave the order of the flags, and this is how you run it.

The ratchet has three parts.

A flag that is on stays on. The tsconfig.json in the repository is what holds each flag in place. Turning one off to unblock a merge undoes the whole exercise, and the discipline is easier to keep if the rule is absolute.

Measure before each step. tsc --noEmit --<flag> 2>&1 | grep -c 'error TS' tells you whether the next flag is an afternoon or a quarter, and it costs one command:

$ tsc --noEmit --strictNullChecks 2>&1 | grep -c 'error TS'
412
$ tsc --noEmit --noUncheckedIndexedAccess 2>&1 | grep -c 'error TS'
87

Those numbers change the plan. 87 is a day and 412 is a project, and knowing which is which before you start is the difference between a ratchet and a stalled branch.

Allow a scoped exception, never a global one. A file that cannot be fixed today gets // @ts-expect-error with a ticket number (§10.17), which fails the build when the underlying problem is fixed, so the exceptions clean themselves up. Turning the flag off for the project, or adding // @ts-nocheck to the file, leaves nothing that will ever tell you it can be removed.

Two refinements worth adding when the codebase is large.

Ratchet by directory. A tsconfig.strict.json covering src/core with the stricter flags, checked in CI alongside the main one, lets a well-maintained subtree move ahead of the rest. Directories move into it one at a time.

Count, do not eliminate. A CI step asserting that the number of @ts-expect-error comments never increases is a ratchet in itself. It is easier to adopt than a flag because it never blocks a merge that improves the count.

The end state is §14.18's config, and the timeline is measured in months and not weeks. That is fine. Every step ships value, and a codebase that ratchets one flag a month arrives within a year.

16.26 Typing a Third-Party Module with No Types

Typing a third-party module with no types is the last boundary, and there are four options in decreasing order of quality.

Option 1: check whether types exist. Try npm i -D @types/<package> (§12.11), or a newer major version of the package that ships its own. This is worth thirty seconds before anything else, and it succeeds more often than people expect.

Option 2 — write a narrow ambient declaration (§11.8, §12.20).

// types/legacy-chart.d.ts — a script file, inside `include`
declare module 'legacy-chart' {
  export interface ChartOptions { width: number; height: number }
  export interface Chart { render(el: HTMLElement): void; destroy(): void }
  export function createChart(data: readonly number[], options: ChartOptions): Chart;
}

Type only what you call, prefer unknown to a guess, and match the runtime shape exactly: use export = if the module does module.exports = fn (§11.7).

Option 3 — a one-line escape, deliberately.

declare module 'legacy-chart';        // everything from it is `any`

That is honest about being untyped, and it is far better than sprinkling @ts-ignore at each import. It is the right first move when the package is used in one place and you are not sure of its shape yet.

Option 4: wrap it. Import the untyped module in exactly one file, give that file's exports real types, and let the rest of the program use the wrapper.

// The wrapper is the only place that touches the untyped module, so it is the
// only place an `any` can enter (§10.21).
type Chart = { render(el: unknown): void; destroy(): void };

declare const untypedCreateChart: unknown;

export function createChart(data: readonly number[]): Chart {
  const fn = untypedCreateChart as (d: readonly number[]) => Chart;
  return fn(data);
}
console.log(typeof createChart);

function

The wrapper is the best option for anything used in more than a couple of places. It turns "this dependency is untyped" from a property of the whole codebase into a property of one file, which is exactly the containment rule of §10.21.

And if the package is popular, write the declarations properly and send them to DefinitelyTyped. It is usually an hour, and it is the only one of the four options that stops the next person doing the same work.

What This Section Established

Five boundaries, one move. An async function's type is Promise<T>, and annotating the resolved type is an error. Promise carries no rejection type at all, which is why a Result belongs at any boundary where failure is expected. A caught error is unknown because anything can be thrown, and the narrowing goes most-specific-first.

fetch is fully typed until .json(), which is any and is the largest invisible hole in a typical application. JSON.parse is the same. Both are fixed by the same one-word change: annotate the result unknown or Json, and narrow.

The DOM's typings are more precise than people expect, and less convenient. querySelector gives Element | null unless the selector is a bare tag name. A type argument is an assertion and not inference. 'click' is a PointerEvent and not a MouseEvent. And e.currentTarget is EventTarget | null even on the element you attached to. instanceof is the narrowing that makes all of it honest.

JSX is checked and not just parsed. Lowercase names come from JSX.IntrinsicElements, and uppercase ones must satisfy JSX.ElementType. Attributes are checked with excess-property rules, and jsxImportSource makes the whole mechanism work with any library. Type the props parameter and infer everything else: React.FC fixes the return type, changed its children behaviour under everyone, and cannot express a generic component.

And the principle the section ends on: parse, do not validate. A boolean check throws its conclusion away, while a parser returns a value whose type something verified. That is the only construct in this course that makes a type true and not merely asserted, and it is what every boundary in this section should end with.

Exercises

1. Close four holes. Take a module that fetches JSON, reads two DOM elements, attaches a handler and catches an error — written the way most code is, with as, ! and no validation. Rewrite it so that no assertion remains, and say for each of the four which construct replaced the assertion.

2. Type a component three ways. Write a Select component that takes a list of options and a selected value, and make the value prop reject anything not in the list. Do it with a plain union, with a generic, and with a const type parameter, then say which you would ship and what each version costs the caller.

3. Build a parser from a schema. Extend §16.21's validator with array, optional and a literal-union checker, derive the type from the schema rather than declaring it, and validate a nested payload — showing both a success with the correct narrowed type and a failure listing every bad path.

Solution

1. Four holes closed.

type User = { id: string; name: string };

function isUser(v: unknown): v is User {
  return typeof v === 'object' && v !== null
    && 'id' in v && typeof v.id === 'string'
    && 'name' in v && typeof v.name === 'string';
}

async function loadUser(url: string): Promise<User> {
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);        // (1) res.ok, not an assertion
  const body: unknown = await res.json();                     // (2) unknown, not `as User`
  if (!isUser(body)) throw new TypeError('unexpected shape');
  return body;
}

function must<T extends Element>(selector: string, Ctor: new () => T): T {
  const el = document.querySelector(selector);                // (3) instanceof, not `!`
  if (!(el instanceof Ctor)) throw new Error(`${selector} is not a ${Ctor.name}`);
  return el;
}

function describeError(e: unknown): string {                  // (4) narrowing, not `as Error`
  if (e instanceof TypeError) return `bad data: ${e.message}`;
  if (e instanceof Error) return `${e.name}: ${e.message}`;
  return `thrown ${typeof e}`;
}

console.log(typeof loadUser, typeof must, describeError(new TypeError('x')), describeError('s'));

function function bad data: x thrown string

(1) res.ok replaced as User on a failed request. fetch resolves on a 404, so without the check the JSON parse runs on an error page and throws a SyntaxError that names nothing useful.

(2) const body: unknown replaced the assertion on res.json(). That one word is what makes the following line necessary and not optional, and it is the highest-value change in the whole exercise (§16.5).

(3) instanceof replaced querySelector(…)! as HTMLInputElement. Two assertions became one check that establishes both facts: that the element exists, and that it is the right kind (§16.10).

(4) Narrowing replaced (e as Error).message. The catch binding is unknown (§16.4), and the thrown string branch is the case the assertion would have crashed on.

2. Three Select components.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

// (a) A plain union — simple, and the options are fixed at the declaration.
type Colour = 'red' | 'green' | 'blue';
function SelectUnion({ value }: { value: Colour }) {
  return <select defaultValue={value}>{(['red', 'green', 'blue'] as const).map((c) => (
    <option key={c} value={c}>{c}</option>
  ))}</select>;
}

// (b) A generic — the options travel with the component, but a plain array widens.
function SelectGeneric<T extends string>({ options, value }: { options: readonly T[]; value: T }) {
  return <select defaultValue={value}>{options.map((o) => (
    <option key={o} value={o}>{o}</option>
  ))}</select>;
}

// (c) A const type parameter — the literals survive even from an inline array.
function SelectConst<const T extends readonly string[]>(
  { options, value }: { options: T; value: T[number] },
) {
  return <select defaultValue={value}>{options.map((o) => (
    <option key={o} value={o}>{o}</option>
  ))}</select>;
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<SelectGeneric options={['a', 'b'] as const} value="b" />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<SelectConst options={['a', 'b']} value="b" />));

function neverRendered() {
  return (
    <>
      {/* @ts-expect-error 'purple' is not a Colour */}
      <SelectUnion value="purple" />
      {/* @ts-expect-error 'c' is not one of the options */}
      <SelectConst options={['a', 'b']} value="c" />
    </>
  );
}
console.log(typeof neverRendered);

<select><option value="a">a</option><option value="b" selected="">b</option></select>
<select><option value="a">a</option><option value="b" selected="">b</option></select>
function

Ship (c). It is the only version where an inline array literal keeps its literal types, so value is checked against exactly the options the caller passed, with nothing required of them.

What each costs the caller. (a) costs a shared type they must import and cannot extend per use. (b) costs an as const at every call site, and forgetting it silently degrades T to string, so the check evaporates with no error (§7.8). (c) costs nothing, because the const moves the requirement into the signature, where the author decides once.

Note that (b) and (c) render identically. The difference is entirely in what the caller has to remember, which is the whole argument for const type parameters.

3. A parser from a schema.

type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; errors: string[] };
type Validator<T> = (input: unknown, path: string) => Result<T>;
type Infer<V> = V extends Validator<infer T> ? T : never;

const str: Validator<string> = (v, p) =>
  typeof v === 'string' ? { ok: true, value: v } : { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected string`] };
const num: Validator<number> = (v, p) =>
  typeof v === 'number' && Number.isFinite(v)
    ? { ok: true, value: v } : { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected number`] };

function literal<const T extends readonly string[]>(...allowed: T): Validator<T[number]> {
  return (v, p) => (typeof v === 'string' && (allowed as readonly string[]).includes(v))
    ? { ok: true, value: v as T[number] }
    : { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected one of ${allowed.join('|')}`] };
}

function array<V extends Validator<unknown>>(item: V): Validator<Infer<V>[]> {
  return (v, p) => {
    if (!Array.isArray(v)) return { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected array`] };
    const out: unknown[] = [];
    const errors: string[] = [];
    v.forEach((el, i) => {
      const r = item(el, `${p}[${i}]`);
      if (r.ok) out.push(r.value); else errors.push(...r.errors);
    });
    return errors.length ? { ok: false, errors } : { ok: true, value: out as Infer<V>[] };
  };
}

function optional<V extends Validator<unknown>>(inner: V): Validator<Infer<V> | undefined> {
  return (v, p) => (v === undefined ? { ok: true, value: undefined } : inner(v, p) as Result<Infer<V>>);
}

function object<S extends Record<string, Validator<unknown>>>(
  shape: S,
): Validator<{ [K in keyof S]: Infer<S[K]> }> {
  return (v, p) => {
    if (typeof v !== 'object' || v === null || Array.isArray(v)) {
      return { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected object`] };
    }
    const out: Record<string, unknown> = {};
    const errors: string[] = [];
    for (const [key, check] of Object.entries(shape)) {
      const r = check((v as Record<string, unknown>)[key], `${p}.${key}`);
      if (r.ok) out[key] = r.value; else errors.push(...r.errors);
    }
    return errors.length
      ? { ok: false, errors }
      : { ok: true, value: out as { [K in keyof S]: Infer<S[K]> } };
  };
}

const teamSchema = object({
  name: str,
  size: num,
  tier: literal('free', 'pro'),
  members: array(object({ id: str, nickname: optional(str) })),
});

type Team = Infer<typeof teamSchema>;

const good = teamSchema(JSON.parse(
  '{"name":"core","size":2,"tier":"pro","members":[{"id":"u1"},{"id":"u2","nickname":"g"}]}',
), 'team');
if (good.ok) {
  const team: Team = good.value;
  console.log(team.tier.toUpperCase(), team.members.length, team.members[1]?.nickname ?? '-');
}

const bad = teamSchema(JSON.parse(
  '{"name":1,"size":"two","tier":"enterprise","members":[{"id":5}]}',
), 'team');
if (!bad.ok) console.log(bad.errors);

PRO 2 g
[
  'team.name: expected string',
  'team.size: expected number',
  'team.tier: expected one of free|pro',
  'team.members[0].id: expected string'
]

Infer<V> is the piece that makes the whole thing compose. One conditional type with an infer (§8.4) extracts a validator's output type, and every combinator is then written in terms of it. So array(object({ … })) produces the right nested type with no declaration anywhere.

literal needs a const type parameter (§7.8) to keep 'free' | 'pro' and not widen to string[]. Without it the schema still validates correctly at runtime, and the type becomes string. That is the silent degradation §7.8 exists to prevent.

Team is derived, never declared. Change tier to add 'enterprise' and the type changes with it. There is no second place to update, and therefore no way for the two to disagree.

Every path is reported, and each names its location, including the array index in team.members[0].id. That is what makes a validator usable in production: one failing request produces one complete diagnosis and not four round trips.

SECTION 17

Type-Level Craft and Performance

The last section is about the parts of TypeScript that are not features. They are habits: how to read an error message that the compiler wrote for a machine, how to write a type that a colleague can maintain, how to find out why a build takes ninety seconds, and how to stop a type from quietly becoming wrong six months from now.

The main idea is that a type system is a tool used by people, and most of its costs are human ones. A conditional type nested four levels deep is not slow, it is unreadable. An error message that fills two screens is not wrong, it is unusable. The performance material here is real and measured, but it comes third, because with the native compiler most projects are not slow. The numbers below show a whole synthetic project checking in under a second, and a single lib entry costing more than everything else combined.

The section ends with the two things that keep a codebase's types honest over time. Type tests turn a type into something a refactor cannot silently break. Type-aware lint rules catch the kinds of mistake the compiler is not designed to catch: a promise nobody awaited, an any that keeps spreading, or a ! (non-null assertion) that nobody justified.

17.1 A Readable Type Error

A readable type error is mostly a property of the types, not of the compiler. The message is generated mechanically, and what it has to say is decided by how you wrote the declarations.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// Anonymous: the message will print this whole shape, expanded.
declare function saveAnon(u: { id: string; profile: { name: string; age: number } }): void;

// Named: the message can say `User`.
type Profile = { name: string; age: number };
type User = { id: string; profile: Profile };
declare function saveNamed(u: User): void;

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error the shapes differ at profile.age
  saveAnon({ id: '1', profile: { name: 'Ada', age: '36' } });
  // @ts-expect-error the same mistake, against a named type
  saveNamed({ id: '1', profile: { name: 'Ada', age: '36' } });
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

function

The two messages differ in exactly the way that matters:

# against the anonymous parameter
error TS2345: Argument of type '{ id: string; profile: { name: string; age: string; }; }'
is not assignable to parameter of type '{ id: string; profile: { name: string; age: number; }; }'.
  The types of 'profile.age' are incompatible between these types.
    Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

# against the named one
error TS2345: Argument of type '{ id: string; profile: { name: string; age: string; }; }'
is not assignable to parameter of type 'User'.
  The types of 'profile.age' are incompatible between these types.
    Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

One word, User instead of the expansion, and the message shortens. On a twenty-field entity that is the difference between a message you read and one you scroll past.

Four habits produce readable errors, in order of effect.

Name every type used in a public signature. The compiler prints the alias when it has one.

Annotate exported functions' return types (§2.3). An inferred return type travels onward, so the error surfaces at a call site and not at the mistake.

Prefer interface to a deep intersection for a declared shape (§5.8). An intersection is expanded in messages, while an interface prints its name.

Split a long conditional chain into named steps (§9.11). RowPatch in a message beats Partial<Omit<Pick<Row, …>, …>>.

17.2 Reading a Compiler Message

Reading a compiler message is a skill with three rules. They are worth practising deliberately, because the messages are structured and not free prose.

Rule one: read from the bottom up. The last, most-indented line is the actual disagreement, and every line above it is the path the checker took. On a nested type the top line can be a page long and the bottom line is one clause.

Rule two: the error code is more searchable than the message. TS2345 is always "argument not assignable to parameter". TS2322 is an assignment. TS2339 is a missing property. TS2551 is the same with a spelling suggestion. TS7006 is an implicit any parameter. TS2589 is instantiation depth (§17.5). TS2590 is a union that is too complex. Searching the code finds the class of problem and not one person's instance of it.

Rule three: the position is where the checker noticed, not where the mistake is. An inferred return type carries an error to its consumer. A generic's constraint failure is reported at the call. A .d.ts mismatch is reported in your code.

Four messages worth recognising on sight, with what each actually means:

"Types have separate declarations of a private property 'x'."
  -> two copies of the same package (§10.10). `npm ls <pkg>` is the diagnosis.

"Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite."   (TS2589)
  -> a recursive type hit its budget (§8.9). Make it tail-recursive, or stop.

"Expression produces a union type that is too complex to represent."   (TS2590)
  -> a combinatorial union (§17.7). Reduce the cross product.

"The inferred type of 'x' cannot be named without a reference to '...'"
  -> declaration emit needs a type you did not export (§12.14). Export it,
     or annotate the export explicitly.

And one habit that shortens most investigations: when a message is unreadable, annotate the thing it is about. Adding an explicit type to the variable, parameter or return in question moves the error to the declaration and usually reduces it to one line.

17.3 Simplifying an Inferred Type

Simplifying an inferred type is the technique for a type that is correct and unreadable, such as a chain of Omit<Pick<…>> that an editor hover prints across four lines.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type Row = { id: string; name: string; email: string; passwordHash: string };
type Patch = Partial<Omit<Row, 'id' | 'passwordHash'>>;

// The classic one-liner: a homomorphic mapped type that forces expansion.
type Prettify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {};

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Prettify<Patch>, { name?: string; email?: string }>>;

declare const p: Prettify<Patch>;
console.log(typeof p);

undefined

{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {} is the idiom, and each half does something. The mapped type re-forms the object, so the checker has a concrete list of members and not a composition to display. The & {} defeats the display that keeps the alias name, so the result is printed expanded and not as Prettify<Patch>.

It changes the display, not the type. Prettify<T> is the identity, as the Expect<Equal<…>> above confirms, so it is safe to apply anywhere. It is common to see it applied at the boundary of a library's public types purely so that consumers' hovers are legible.

It is homomorphic (§8.6), so readonly and ? survive. A non-homomorphic version would silently strip them, which is why the keyof T form matters here as much as anywhere.

The cost is one more instantiation per use. On a public type used in a hundred signatures that is measurable in principle and, per §17.6's measurements, almost never in practice. Apply it where a hover is genuinely hard to read, not everywhere.

The alternative is to not need it. Name the intermediate steps (§9.11), and the hover shows a name you chose and not a composition to decode.

17.4 An Alias for Display

An alias for display is the same idea from the other direction: a type alias exists partly so the compiler has something short to say.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

// Three ways to name the same thing; they differ only in what a message prints.
type Handler = (event: { type: string; detail: unknown }) => void;
interface HandlerInterface { (event: { type: string; detail: unknown }): void }
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Handler, HandlerInterface>>;

declare function on(name: string, handler: Handler): void;
console.log(typeof on);          // `declare` emits nothing, so at runtime: undefined

undefined

The compiler prefers to print an alias when the type has one, and it loses the alias in three situations worth knowing: after a conditional or mapped type is resolved, after an intersection is elaborated, and when the alias is generic and the instantiation is not itself named.

That is why type RowPatch = Partial<EditableRow> beats the inline nest (§9.11). The alias survives into the message, and the nest does not.

An interface's name survives more reliably than an alias's, which is the display half of §5.8's argument. For a large object type appearing in many signatures, interface is the choice that keeps diagnostics short.

Naming for display is not the same as naming for reuse. A type used once may still deserve a name purely so that its errors are legible, and that is a legitimate reason on its own. The alias costs nothing at runtime and nothing at check time.

17.5 An Excessively Deep Type

An excessively deep type is one whose instantiation exceeds the compiler's budget, and the error is TS2589: Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite.

// Tail-recursive: the recursive call IS the branch result.
type Count<N extends number, A extends unknown[] = []> =
  A['length'] extends N ? A : Count<N, [...A, unknown]>;
type Ok = Count<999>;         // ✅
type Deep = Count<1000>;      // ❌ TS2589

// Not tail-recursive: work remains after the recursive call.
type Wrap<N extends number, A extends unknown[] = []> =
  A['length'] extends N ? [] : [unknown, ...Wrap<N, [...A, unknown]>];
type Fine = Wrap<47>;         // ✅
type TooDeep = Wrap<48>;      // ❌ TS2589

Those two numbers were measured by bisection (repeatedly halving the range) in §8.9, and they are the practical limits: 999 tail-recursive instantiations, 47 otherwise.

They are deliberately in two separate blocks, and that is not presentation. Put both types in one file and Wrap<48> compiles. The failure moves out to somewhere between 48 and 100, because the checker's depth accounting is affected by what it has already instantiated. So the numbers above are the limits for a type measured on its own. The honest general statement is weaker and more useful: a tail-recursive type buys you roughly twenty times the depth, and neither limit is a constant you can design against. If a type is anywhere near either number, it is too close.

Three responses, in order.

Make it tail-recursive. Move the accumulation into a parameter, so that the recursive call is the entire result of its branch. That gains a factor of twenty, and it is usually a mechanical rewrite (§8.9's SplitSlow/SplitFast).

Reduce the input. A type-level parser over a 200-character string does 200 instantiations per pass, while one over a route template does five.

Move the computation to runtime. This is the answer more often than people expect, and §17.13 makes the argument.

A false positive is possible and rare. The checker sometimes reports TS2589 for a type that would terminate, because the budget counts instantiations and not depth. Splitting the type into two named aliases occasionally resolves it, because each gets its own budget. If that feels like a workaround, it is one, and it is a signal to reconsider the design.

17.6 Type-Checking Performance

Type-checking performance is measurable with one flag. The measurements below are the ones that matter, taken on this machine with the native compiler (§1.6).

$ tsc --noEmit --extendedDiagnostics
Files:            89
Types:         35715
Instantiations: 34231
Memory used:   65892K
Check time:    1.080s
Total time:    1.480s

The single largest lever in most projects is lib. The same two-line file, checked twice:

--lib esnext         Files: 88   Types:  9554   Memory:  15377K   Check: 0.195s
--lib esnext,dom     Files: 89   Types: 35715   Memory:  65892K   Check: 1.080s

One declaration file, lib.dom.d.ts at 2.3 MB, is 5.5× the check time and 4.3× the memory of everything else combined. For a Node project that includes dom by accident (§13.16), removing it is the cheapest performance change available. It also stops document type-checking in code that will crash.

Three more levers, in order of typical effect.

skipLibCheck: true (§12.17) skips checking every .d.ts against itself. On a heavy dependency tree this is frequently the biggest remaining win, and its cost is that errors in your own hand-written declarations go unreported.

incremental: true (§14.3), measured on a 200-file project: 0.91s cold, 0.58s warm, 0.62s after a leaf change, 0.81s after a root change. The floor is process startup.

types: [] (§12.12) stops every @types package under node_modules from being parsed on every run.

And the honest headline: on the native compiler, most projects are not slow. A 200-file project checks in under a second. Before optimising, measure. Check time in the output above is the number to watch, and if it is under a couple of seconds the work is better spent elsewhere.

17.7 A Slow Union

A slow union is one with a large number of members. The commonest way to make one by accident is a template literal type (§8.8) whose slots multiply out.

Measured, adding one 10-member union at a time to a cross product (every combination of the members):

baseline (no cross product)   Types: 35328
`${A}-${B}`         (100)     Types: 35482      +154
`${A}-${B}-${C}`  (1,000)     Types: 36503    +1,175
`${A}-…-${D}`    (10,000)     Types: 46524   +11,196
`${A}-…-${E}`   (100,000)     error TS2590

Each additional slot multiplies the member count by ten, and the type count follows. At five slots the compiler refuses outright:

error TS2590: Expression produces a union type that is too complex to represent.

That refusal is a feature. The alternative is a compiler that appears to hang.

The fix is nearly always to stop pre-computing the product. Three shapes avoid it:

Keep the parts separate. { size: Size; colour: Colour } is two 10-member unions and not one 100-member one, and it is usually a better model anyway.

Validate rather than enumerate. A `${string}-${string}` pattern accepts the right shape without listing every instance, and a runtime check (§16.21) covers what the type cannot.

Defer with a generic. A function taking <S extends Size, C extends Colour>(size: S, colour: C): \${S}-${C}`` computes one member per call and not all of them up front.

Unions of object types are cheaper than they look, because the checker compares them member by member and caches the results. It is the literal unions that multiply, and template literals are the multiplier.

17.8 Interfaces Are Cheaper Than Intersections

Interfaces are cheaper than intersections is standard advice. It is worth reporting what the measurement on the installed compiler actually showed, because the answer is not what the advice implies.

Eight four-field traits, combined two ways, with 300 fresh object literals assigned to the result:

type Entity = T0 & T1 & … & T7            Check time: 0.987s / 1.308s
interface Entity extends T0, …, T7 {}     Check time: 1.309s / 1.415s

Two runs of each, and the run-to-run variance is larger than the difference between them. The same intersection file measured 0.987s and 1.308s on consecutive runs. At this scale, on the native compiler, the performance claim is not reproducible, and reporting it as though it were would be repeating something and not measuring it.

The guidance still stands, for the other three reasons, all of which are deterministic and not statistical.

Errors are reported at the declaration. interface … extends with a conflicting member fails where it is written. An intersection produces a silent never member and fails at the first value (§5.7).

The name survives into messages. An interface prints as Entity, and an intersection is elaborated (§17.4).

A conflict is an error and not an impossibility. That is the same point as the first, and it is the one that catches real bugs.

Where the performance claim is likely to be real is a codebase two orders of magnitude larger than this measurement, where the checker's cache is under pressure. That is exactly the situation you should measure and not assume. --extendedDiagnostics before and after is one command, and it is the only thing that settles it for your project.

17.9 Project References for Build Time

Project references for build time are the structural answer to a slow monorepo, and their effect is different in kind from a flag.

The mechanism, from §14.5: each package is composite, its consumers read its .d.ts output and not its source, and tsc --build skips any project whose inputs are older than its .tsbuildinfo.

What that buys, measured as a shape and not as a number: a change in a leaf package re-checks that package and nothing else. Without references, a single program contains every file, and every change re-checks the union of what is reachable.

What it costs.

A build step before any check. A fresh clone must run tsc --build before tsc --noEmit in any consuming package succeeds. The error until then, "output file has not been built from source file", is one every new team member hits once.

Declarations on the critical path. The boundary is the .d.ts, so generating it is now part of the dependency chain. isolatedDeclarations (§12.16) is what makes that generation parallelisable, and the two features are designed to go together.

Real setup. You need composite everywhere, ${configDir} in the shared base (§13.5), a solution file at the root, and a references array per package that must stay correct.

The threshold, stated plainly: below about ten packages the setup costs more than it saves, and incremental alone covers it. Above that, it is what makes the check time survivable. §14.5's four-package example is deliberately on the "not worth it" side of that line.

17.10 Incremental Type Checking

Incremental type checking reuses the previous run's work through a .tsbuildinfo file. The numbers from §14.3 are worth repeating here with their interpretation.

200 files, strict, declaration: true
  cold (no .tsbuildinfo)     0.91s
  warm, nothing changed      0.58s
  one LEAF file changed      0.62s
  one ROOT file changed      0.81s

The floor is 0.58s, and it is process startup plus reading the saved state, not checking. That is the number to keep in mind. Incremental checking cannot take a project below its startup cost, so on a small project the flag saves a third of a second, and on a large one it saves most of the run.

A leaf change is nearly free, and a root change is nearly a full rebuild. m0.ts is imported transitively by 199 files, so changing it invalidates all of them. That is a fact about your dependency graph, not about the compiler, and it is the most actionable performance finding in this section. A module that everything imports makes every rebuild expensive. Splitting it reduces the blast radius of every future edit, whether that means types in one file and values in another, or one module per concern.

Cache .tsbuildinfo in CI (§14.6), keyed on the compiler version and the config. A restored cache turns every CI check into a warm one.

Delete it when the results stop making sense. A stale or corrupt build info produces errors that do not match the source, and removing the file is the first diagnostic step, before you doubt the compiler.

17.11 extendedDiagnostics

extendedDiagnostics prints the compiler's own breakdown of timing and counts. It is the measurement tool for everything in §17.6.

$ tsc --noEmit --extendedDiagnostics
Files:                        89
Lines:                    120458
Identifiers:              131234
Symbols:                   93117
Types:                     35715
Instantiations:            34231
Memory used:              65892K
Parse time:                0.213s
Bind time:                 0.098s
Check time:                1.080s
Emit time:                 0.000s
Total time:                1.480s

Read Check time against Parse time. If parsing dominates, the problem is how many files: a lib entry, an over-broad include, or an @types package you do not use. If checking dominates, the problem is what the types do: a combinatorial union (§17.7), a deep recursive type (§17.5), or a widely-instantiated generic.

Types and Instantiations are the two counters that respond to a fix. They are deterministic, unlike the timings, which is what makes them the right metric for a before-and-after comparison. §17.7's cross-product measurements are counts precisely because the timings were noise.

--diagnostics is the shorter version with just the totals. --listFiles prints every file in the program, which is how you find out that a stray include pattern pulled in node_modules, or that @types/jest is in your production build.

The workflow is: measure, change one thing, measure again. Two runs of the same command differ by a few hundred milliseconds (§17.8), so a single timing proves nothing, but the counts do.

17.12 generateTrace

generateTrace records a profile of the check in Chrome's tracing format, for the cases --extendedDiagnostics cannot explain.

$ tsc --noEmit --generateTrace ./trace
$ ls trace/
legend.json   trace.json   types_0.json   types_1.json   types_2.json   types_3.json

trace.json opens in chrome://tracing or ui.perfetto.dev and shows a flame chart of the check: which file, which symbol, and which type instantiation took the time. types_*.json is a dump of every type the compiler created, and legend.json maps the files.

What you are looking for is one wide bar. A single checkSourceFile or structuredTypeRelatedTo span dominating the chart names the file, and usually the expression, responsible. No counter gives you that level of detail.

Use it when the counts do not explain the time. If Types is modest and Check time is large, some specific comparison is expensive: a deeply-nested conditional, a generic instantiated with a large union, or a .d.ts with a pathological signature. The trace is the only way to find which.

The --generateTrace output is large: a 2.4 MB types_0.json for a two-line file that includes lib.dom. Do not commit it, and do not leave the flag on in CI.

@typescript/analyze-trace is the companion tool that reads the output and prints a ranked summary. It is the practical entry point, because reading a raw flame chart of a compiler is a specialist activity, and the summary usually names the culprit directly.

17.13 When Not to Reach for a Clever Type

When not to reach for a clever type is the judgement this course has been building toward, and it is worth stating as a set of tests and not as a feeling.

The maintenance test. Could a colleague who has not read §8 modify this type? If not, the cleverness has a cost that recurs every time the code changes, and it is paid by someone who did not choose it.

The error test. When a caller gets it wrong, is the message actionable? A deep conditional type produces a failure at the outermost level with the whole chain expanded, and "not assignable to never" is the least useful message the compiler produces.

The runtime test. Would a runtime check be better here? A type-level parser validates a literal, which means it validates the code you wrote and nothing that arrives from outside. A validator (§16.21) checks both, and the type comes with it.

The value test. What does this prevent? A type that prevents a real, recurring bug earns its complexity. One that prevents a mistake nobody makes is a puzzle you left for someone.

// Clever: a type-level parse of a route template.
type Params<S extends string> =
  S extends `${string}:${infer P}/${infer R}` ? P | Params<`/${R}`>
  : S extends `${string}:${infer P}` ? P : never;

// Plain: the caller states the parameters.
type Route<P extends string = never> = { template: string; params: readonly P[] };

const clever: Params<'/users/:id'> = 'id';
const plain: Route<'id'> = { template: '/users/:id', params: ['id'] };
console.log(clever, plain.params);

id [ 'id' ]

Both are defensible, and the first is right only when the template is genuinely a literal in the source. The moment routes come from a config file, a database or a generated manifest, Params<string> is never (§8.8) and the whole apparatus quietly stops checking anything.

The rule of thumb that survives review: a type-level computation is worth it when it removes a class of mistake at many call sites, and not worth it when it removes one mistake at one. The Params type in a routing library with a thousand consumers is excellent. The same type in an application with nine routes is a liability.

17.14 A Type Test

A type test is an assertion about a type that fails at compile time. Without them, a type that used to be right and is now {} (§5.21) or never produces no error at its definition. The error appears, eventually, somewhere far away.

// The two-line harness used throughout this course.
type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type RequireKeys<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K> & Required<Pick<T, K>>;
type Draft = { id?: number; title?: string };

type _1 = Expect<Equal<RequireKeys<Draft, 'title'>['title'], string>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<RequireKeys<Draft, 'title'>['id'], number | undefined>>;

// The negative half matters as much: assert what must NOT compile.
// @ts-expect-error 'nope' is not a key of Draft
type _3 = RequireKeys<Draft, 'nope'>;

declare const d: RequireKeys<Draft, 'title'>;
console.log(typeof d);

undefined

Equal is deliberately strange, and the strangeness is load-bearing. Deferring the comparison inside an unresolved generic signature makes the checker compare identically and not by assignability, which is what tells any, unknown and never apart. A naive X extends Y ? Y extends X ? true : false : false reports true for Equal<any, string>.

Both halves are needed. Expect<Equal<…>> asserts what a type is. @ts-expect-error (§10.17) asserts what does not compile, and it self-destructs when the underlying situation changes, which no positive assertion does.

Type tests cost nothing at runtime, because they are declarations, and they run as part of tsc --noEmit, so no test runner is involved. A file of them next to each utility type is the whole practice.

They are the only defence against a silent collapse. §9.5's Omit on a union produces {}, which accepts everything, and the only symptom is that the editor stops offering completions. One Expect<Equal<…>> turns that into a build failure.

17.15 An Expect-Type Assertion

An expect-type assertion is the library form of §17.14. The three in common use are worth knowing, because they differ in what they can express.

expect-type      expectTypeOf<T>().toEqualTypeOf<U>()      runtime-free, chainable
tsd              expectType<U>(value)                      a CLI over .test-d.ts files
vitest           expectTypeOf / assertType, `test-types`   integrated with the test run

// The hand-rolled equivalents, which is all any of them are underneath.
type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;
type Extends<A, B> = A extends B ? true : false;
type IsAny<T> = 0 extends 1 & T ? true : false;

type _1 = Expect<Equal<{ a: 1 }, { a: 1 }>>;
type _2 = Expect<Extends<'a', string>>;
type _3 = Expect<IsAny<any>>;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<IsAny<unknown>, false>>;
console.log('type tests are compile-time only');

type tests are compile-time only

IsAny<T> is the one worth copying. 0 extends 1 & T is true only when T is any, because 1 & any is any and 0 extends any holds. Every other T makes the intersection never or a literal, and 0 does not extend it. Detecting a stray any is the single most valuable assertion in a library's type tests, because an any that leaks into a public signature disables checking for every consumer (§10.21).

Distinguish "is exactly" from "is assignable to". toEqualTypeOf and Equal are identity, while toMatchTypeOf and Extends are assignability. Using the loose one where you meant the strict one is how a test passes while the type drifts wider.

Where to put them. A types.test-d.ts beside the implementation, included in the tsconfig so that tsc --noEmit checks it, is enough. It also means the tests run on every build and not only when someone invokes a test runner.

What to assert, in a library: every exported utility's output on a representative input, every public function's inferred return type, and, with IsAny, that no public signature contains any.

17.16 A Lint Rule for Types

A lint rule for types covers what the compiler is not designed to. The distinction is not "linters are optional extra checks". It is that the two tools answer different questions.

The compiler asks: is this consistent? It does not ask whether the code is a good idea, whether a promise was awaited, whether an any is spreading, or whether a ! was justified.

The rules worth turning on, and what each catches:

@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises        an async call nobody awaited
@typescript-eslint/no-misused-promises         an async callback where void was wanted
@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-condition    a check that can never be false
@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment        an `any` flowing into typed code
@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-member-access     ...and being read from
@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-call              ...and being called
@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-argument          ...and being passed
@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports     `import type` where it belongs
@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion       every `!`, so each is a decision
@typescript-eslint/ban-ts-comment              `@ts-expect-error` yes, `@ts-ignore` no
@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any             every deliberate `any`
@typescript-eslint/switch-exhaustiveness-check a switch missing a union member

no-floating-promises is the one to turn on first. An unawaited promise is the most common real bug the compiler cannot see. The code runs, the error is swallowed, and the failure appears as missing data and not as an exception. It is a type-aware rule (§17.18) and it needs the type information to work.

no-unsafe-* as a group is a measurement, and a noisy one on an existing codebase, which is the point. The count of findings is the size of the any surface (§10.21), and it is the only way to see it.

switch-exhaustiveness-check overlaps with §3.14's never assignment and is worth having as well. It fires on a switch with no default, where the never trick has nowhere to live.

17.17 typescript-eslint

typescript-eslint is the toolchain that lets ESLint understand TypeScript. It has a parser that produces an ESTree-compatible AST (the tree of syntax that lint rules read) from TypeScript source, and a plugin of rules written against it.

// eslint.config.js — the flat config, which is the current form
import tseslint from 'typescript-eslint';

export default tseslint.config(
  ...tseslint.configs.strictTypeChecked,
  ...tseslint.configs.stylisticTypeChecked,
  {
    languageOptions: {
      parserOptions: { projectService: true, tsconfigRootDir: import.meta.dirname },
    },
  },
);

Four preset tiers, in increasing strictness: recommended, strict, and the -TypeChecked variants of each. The type-checked ones are the only ones that include §17.18's rules, and they are the reason to use this toolchain at all.

projectService: true is the modern way to give the rules type information. It uses the same project-discovery mechanism the editor's language server uses, so it finds the right tsconfig for each file without you listing them. It replaces the older project: ['./tsconfig.json'], which had to be kept in step by hand.

Turn off the rules that duplicate the compiler. With noUnusedLocals on (§13.11), @typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars is redundant, and with strict on, several stylistic rules are too. Two tools reporting the same thing trains people to skim both.

And turn off formatting rules entirely. Formatting belongs to a formatter, and a linter that also formats produces conflicts and slow runs. That has been typescript-eslint's own recommendation since it deprecated its formatting rules.

17.18 A Type-Aware Lint Rule

A type-aware lint rule asks the compiler for the type of an expression while linting. It is what makes the most valuable rules possible, and it is the reason linting a TypeScript project is slower than linting a JavaScript one.

// Every one of these is invisible to a syntax-only linter and to the compiler.
async function save(): Promise<void> { await Promise.resolve(); }

async function caller(): Promise<void> {
  save();                       // no-floating-promises: the promise is dropped
  await save();                 // fine
}

declare const maybe: string | undefined;
function check(): string {
  if (maybe !== undefined && maybe !== null) return maybe;   // no-unnecessary-condition
  return '';
}

console.log(typeof caller, check());

function

save() on its own line is a floating promise, and nothing in the type system objects. The expression's value is simply discarded, exactly as 1 + 1; would be. Only a rule that asks what type the expression has can tell that it is a Promise, and that dropping it loses both the sequencing and the rejection.

maybe !== null after maybe !== undefined can never be false, because the declared type has no null in it. That is a rule reading the narrowed type at that point, which is again information only the compiler has.

The cost is real: type-aware linting requires a full program. In practice it roughly doubles or triples lint time compared with the syntax-only configuration, because the rules are running on top of a type-check.

Three ways to make that acceptable.

projectService: true (§17.17) and not an explicit project list, so only the files being linted are in the program.

Run type-aware rules in CI and the fast set locally, using two configs. The fast set catches the syntax-level problems at edit time, and the expensive ones run once per push.

Do not run tsc and type-aware ESLint as separate serial steps in CI when time matters, because they duplicate the type-check. Running them in parallel is the easy win. On a large project, dropping the redundant tsc --noEmit and letting the lint step's own type-check fail the build is the aggressive one.

What This Section Established

Readable errors are made by naming types, annotating exported returns, and preferring an interface to a deep intersection. The compiler prints an alias when it has one and expands when it does not. Read a message bottom-up, search the code and not the text, and remember that the position is where the checker noticed and not where the mistake is.

The performance material, measured and not repeated: lib.dom.d.ts alone takes a two-line file from 9,554 types and 0.195s to 35,715 types and 1.080s, which is the largest single lever in most projects. A template-literal cross product multiplies by ten per slot and is refused outright at 100,000 members with TS2590. A tail-recursive type gets 999 instantiations and a non-tail-recursive one 47. Incremental checking has a floor at process startup, and a root-module change costs nearly a full rebuild, which is a fact about your dependency graph and not about the compiler.

And one measurement that contradicted the advice it was meant to confirm: interfaces were not measurably cheaper than intersections at 300 assignments over eight traits, because run-to-run variance exceeded the difference. The guidance survives on its deterministic merits, which are better arguments anyway.

The two habits that outlast any of it are type tests and type-aware lint rules. Type tests matter because a type that collapses to {} produces no error at its definition. Type-aware lint rules matter because a floating promise, a spreading any and a condition that can never be false are all invisible to a compiler doing exactly its job.

Exercises

1. Make three errors readable. Take a function whose parameter is a deep anonymous object type, whose return type is inferred, and whose argument is built from a four-way intersection. Produce the error message it gives on a wrong call, then make three changes and produce the message again — quoting both and saying which change did the most.

2. Find and fix a slow check. Given a project whose Check time is 6s, list the measurements you would take in order and what each would tell you. Then, for the three most likely causes, give the change and the counter in --extendedDiagnostics that would confirm it worked.

3. Write type tests for a utility. Take §9.10's RequireKeys<T, K> and write a complete test file: three positive assertions, one that a wrong key does not compile, one that the result contains no any, and one distinguishing "is exactly" from "is assignable to". Say what each would catch if the utility were later changed carelessly.

Solution

1. Three errors made readable.

// Before: anonymous parameter, inferred return, intersection argument type.
type A = { id: string }; type B = { createdAt: string };
type C = { name: string }; type D = { tags: string[] };

declare function saveBefore(u: { id: string; meta: { name: string; age: number } }): unknown;

// After: named parameter type, annotated return, interface instead of intersection.
interface Meta { name: string; age: number }
interface User { id: string; meta: Meta }
interface Entity extends A, B, C, D {}

declare function saveAfter(u: User): string;

function neverCalled(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error age is a string
  saveBefore({ id: '1', meta: { name: 'Ada', age: '36' } });
  // @ts-expect-error the same mistake
  saveAfter({ id: '1', meta: { name: 'Ada', age: '36' } });
}
declare const e: Entity;
console.log(typeof neverCalled, typeof e);

function undefined

# before
error TS2345: Argument of type '{ id: string; meta: { name: string; age: string; }; }'
is not assignable to parameter of type '{ id: string; meta: { name: string; age: number; }; }'.
  The types of 'meta.age' are incompatible between these types.
    Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

# after
error TS2345: Argument of type '{ id: string; meta: { name: string; age: string; }; }'
is not assignable to parameter of type 'User'.
  The types of 'meta.age' are incompatible between these types.
    Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

Naming the parameter type did the most, and it is the cheapest of the three: one alias replaces the whole expansion on the right of "not assignable to". On a twenty-field entity that is a one-line message instead of a five-line one.

The return annotation did nothing here, and would have on a different call. Its value is positional. With an inferred return, a mistake inside saveBefore is reported wherever the result is used, and with an annotation it is reported at the function. That does not show up in this example precisely because the error is in the argument.

The interface-instead-of-intersection change is invisible in this message and visible in others. A conflicting member across A–D is an error at the interface Entity declaration and a silent never in the intersection (§5.7), which is a much larger difference than any message length.

2. Finding a slow check.

The measurements, in order.

1. tsc --noEmit --extendedDiagnostics     Files / Types / Parse / Check
2. tsc --noEmit --listFiles | wc -l       is the program bigger than you think?
3. tsc --noEmit --listFiles | grep node_modules | head
4. tsc --noEmit --generateTrace ./trace   only if the counts do not explain it

What each tells you. Step 1 splits the time into parse and check: parse-dominated means too many files, and check-dominated means expensive types. Step 2 gives the file count against what you expected. Step 3 shows which dependencies are in the program at all, so an unexpected @types package or a lib entry appears here. Step 4 names the specific expression when the counts are unremarkable and the time is not.

The three most likely causes, the change, and the confirming counter.

lib includes dom unnecessarily. Change: "lib": ["es2023"] (§13.16). Confirming counter: Types drops sharply. Measured, a two-line file goes from 35,715 to 9,554 types and Check time from 1.080s to 0.195s. This is the first thing to check for any Node project.

skipLibCheck is off with a heavy dependency tree. Change: "skipLibCheck": true (§12.17). Confirming counter: Check time falls while Files stays the same, because the same declarations are read and are just no longer checked against each other. The cost is that your own hand-written .d.ts files stop being checked, so check them separately.

A combinatorial union. Change: keep the parts separate, or defer with a generic (§17.7). Confirming counter: Types, which is deterministic. The cross-product measurements in §17.7 are counts precisely because the timings were noise. A drop from 46,524 to 35,482 is the 10,000-member union going away.

And measure twice. Two runs of the same command differed by more than 30% in §17.8's measurements, so a single timing proves nothing. Types and Instantiations are the metrics that respond reliably to a fix.

3. Type tests for RequireKeys.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;
type Extends<A, B> = A extends B ? true : false;
type IsAny<T> = 0 extends 1 & T ? true : false;

type RequireKeys<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K> & Required<Pick<T, K>>;

type Draft = { id?: number; title?: string; body?: string };
type Publishable = RequireKeys<Draft, 'title' | 'body'>;

// 1. The named keys became required, with `undefined` removed.
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Publishable['title'], string>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Publishable['body'], string>>;
// 2. The others are untouched.
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Publishable['id'], number | undefined>>;

// 3. A wrong key must not compile.
// @ts-expect-error 'nope' is not a key of Draft
type _4 = RequireKeys<Draft, 'nope'>;

// 4. No `any` leaked in.
type _5 = Expect<Equal<IsAny<Publishable['title']>, false>>;

// 5. "Is exactly" versus "is assignable to" — both true here, and they differ.
type _6 = Expect<Equal<Publishable['title'], string>>;      // identity
type _7 = Expect<Extends<Publishable['title'], string>>;    // assignability
// @ts-expect-error 'string' is not IDENTICAL to 'string | undefined'
type _8 = Expect<Equal<Publishable['title'], string | undefined>>;
type _9 = Expect<Extends<Publishable['title'], string | undefined>>;   // ...but it IS assignable

console.log('all assertions are compile-time only');

all assertions are compile-time only

What each would catch.

_1 and _2 catch a Required that stopped removing undefined. If someone rewrote the utility as Omit<T, K> & { [P in K]: T[P] }, the mapped type is not homomorphic in the way Required is, and title would come back as string | undefined. The code would still compile everywhere, and every consumer would just quietly need a ! again.

_3 catches over-application. A careless rewrite using Required<T> instead of Required<Pick<T, K>> would make id required too. That is the opposite of what the utility promises, and it is a change no call site reports.

_4 catches a lost constraint. Dropping K extends keyof T makes RequireKeys<Draft, 'nope'> legal and silently do nothing, which is exactly the hole the standard Omit has (§9.4). The @ts-expect-error fails the build the day the constraint is removed.

_5 catches an any leak, which is the assertion most worth having in a library. An any in a public signature disables checking for every consumer (§10.21) and produces no error anywhere.

_6–_9 are the pair that shows why the distinction matters. Extends is satisfied by anything narrower, so a utility that accidentally returned never for title would pass every Extends assertion and fail every Equal one. Assert with Equal by default, and use Extends only when you deliberately mean "at least this wide".

SECTION 18

Capstone: A Fully Typed Service

Seventeen sections of mechanisms are worth little until they meet code that has to work. This section is one single build: a small task service, taken from an empty file to something with a boundary you can trust, a domain model that cannot represent an illegal state, and a test suite that the compiler itself runs.

Build it as you read. Every stage names the sections it draws on, so if a stage misbehaves you know where to go back to, instead of searching. Every block here runs, under node --experimental-transform-types, with no build step and no dependencies. That is itself a demonstration of §15.24: nothing in this capstone uses a construct that produces extra code.

The last three stages are the ones people usually skip, and they decide whether the types are worth anything. They are the type tests, an audit against what the earlier sections measured, and an honest list of what is still wrong.

18.1 The Brief

Identity
A user id and a task id are both strings and must never be interchangeable. There is exactly one place a raw string becomes either.
State
A task is draft, active or done. An assignee exists only when active or done; a completion time only when done. No combination outside those three is representable.
Boundary
Data arrives as unvalidated JSON. Nothing downstream sees a type that something did not check. Every bad field is reported with its path, in one pass.
Failure
Expected failures are values with types. Bugs throw. The two are never confused.
Extension
An event bus and a repository, both generic, both inferring their handlers' argument types with nothing annotated at the call site.
Proof
Type tests that a careless refactor cannot pass, checked by tsc --noEmit rather than by a test runner.

18.2 Branded Identifiers

Start with identity, because everything else is built on it. There are two branded types (§8.11) and two validating constructors, and those constructors are the only doors in.

declare const brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly [brand]: B };

export type UserId = Brand<string, 'UserId'>;
export type TaskId = Brand<string, 'TaskId'>;

export function userId(raw: string): UserId {
  if (!/^u_[0-9a-z]+$/.test(raw)) throw new TypeError(`not a user id: ${raw}`);
  return raw as UserId;
}

export function taskId(raw: string): TaskId {
  if (!/^t_[0-9a-z]+$/.test(raw)) throw new TypeError(`not a task id: ${raw}`);
  return raw as TaskId;
}

declare function assign(task: TaskId, to: UserId): void;

function typeErrorsOnly(): void {
  // @ts-expect-error a raw string is not a TaskId
  assign('t_1', userId('u_ada'));
  // @ts-expect-error a UserId is not a TaskId
  assign(userId('u_ada'), userId('u_ada'));
}
void typeErrorsOnly;

console.log(taskId('t_1'), userId('u_ada'));
try { userId('t_1'); } catch (e) { console.log((e as Error).message); }

t_1 u_ada
not a user id: t_1

Three properties, and each is deliberate. The brand key is a declare const unique symbol, so it emits nothing and no code can name it (§12.3). The two ids are distinguished from each other by the brand string, which is what makes the second rejection possible. And the as lives inside the validator, after the check. That is the discipline of §10.15, and it is the reason the type means something.

taskId('t_1') printed t_1. A branded string is a string at runtime, with zero overhead. The whole apparatus exists only while the compiler is looking.

18.3 A Domain Model with No Illegal States

Now the model. There are three states, and the fields that only make sense in some of them live only in those (§3.12).

type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' };
type TaskId = string & { readonly __brand: 'TaskId' };

export type Task =
  | { readonly kind: 'draft'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string }
  | { readonly kind: 'active'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string; readonly assignee: UserId }
  | { readonly kind: 'done'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string;
      readonly assignee: UserId; readonly completedAt: string };

export function describe(task: Task): string {
  switch (task.kind) {
    case 'draft': return `${task.title} — unassigned`;
    case 'active': return `${task.title} — ${task.assignee}`;
    case 'done': return `${task.title} — done ${task.completedAt.slice(0, 10)}`;
    default: return assertNever(task);
  }
}

function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error(`unhandled variant: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`);
}

const id = 't_1' as TaskId;
const ada = 'u_ada' as UserId;

console.log(describe({ kind: 'draft', id, title: 'Write' }));
console.log(describe({ kind: 'active', id, title: 'Ship', assignee: ada }));
console.log(describe({ kind: 'done', id, title: 'Test', assignee: ada, completedAt: '2026-09-01T12:00:00Z' }));

// @ts-expect-error a draft has no assignee
const impossible: Task = { kind: 'draft', id, title: 'x', assignee: ada };

Write — unassigned
Ship — u_ada
Test — done 2026-09-01

Count the inhabitants (the number of distinct shapes a type allows). The obvious modelling, { state: string; assignee?: UserId; completedAt?: string }, permits a done task with no assignee, an active one with a completion time, and a state string nobody defined. This model permits exactly three shapes, and task.assignee is a compile error in the draft branch.

assertNever is the ratchet (§3.14). Adding a fourth variant produces an error at every switch that does not handle it, in every file, naming the missing one. That is the property that makes a discriminated union worth the extra punctuation.

18.4 Wire Types and the Boundary

The API does not speak your domain model. Give it its own type, and write one function that converts between them (§16.20).

type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' };
type TaskId = string & { readonly __brand: 'TaskId' };
type Task =
  | { readonly kind: 'draft'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string }
  | { readonly kind: 'active'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string; readonly assignee: UserId };

// Exactly what the server sends — snake_case, nullable, no branding.
export type TaskWire = {
  task_id: string;
  title: string;
  assigned_to: string | null;
};

export function toDomain(wire: TaskWire): Task {
  const id = wire.task_id as TaskId;
  return wire.assigned_to === null
    ? { kind: 'draft', id, title: wire.title }
    : { kind: 'active', id, title: wire.title, assignee: wire.assigned_to as UserId };
}

const rows: TaskWire[] = [
  { task_id: 't_1', title: 'Write', assigned_to: null },
  { task_id: 't_2', title: 'Ship', assigned_to: 'u_ada' },
];

console.log(rows.map(toDomain).map((t) => `${t.kind}:${t.title}`));

[ 'draft:Write', 'active:Ship' ]

The wire type is honest about the format, because assigned_to really is string | null. The domain type is honest about the model, where "unassigned" is a state and not a null field. One function knows both, and a rename on the server is one edit.

Note what is missing and is coming next. wire.task_id as TaskId is an unchecked assertion, and TaskWire is a claim about JSON that nothing verified. §18.5 replaces both.

18.5 A Schema-Derived Validator

The boundary needs a parser and not a cast (§16.21, §16.22). The type comes out of the schema, so the two cannot drift apart.

export type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; errors: string[] };
export type Validator<T> = (input: unknown, path: string) => Result<T>;
export type Infer<V> = V extends Validator<infer T> ? T : never;

export const str: Validator<string> = (v, p) =>
  typeof v === 'string' ? { ok: true, value: v } : { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected string`] };
