export const nullable = <V extends Validator<unknown>>(inner: V): Validator<Infer<V> | null> =>
  (v, p) => (v === null ? { ok: true, value: null } : inner(v, p) as Result<Infer<V>>);

export function object<S extends Record<string, Validator<unknown>>>(
  shape: S,
): Validator<{ [K in keyof S]: Infer<S[K]> }> {
  return (v, p) => {
    if (typeof v !== 'object' || v === null || Array.isArray(v)) {
      return { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected object`] };
    }
    const out: Record<string, unknown> = {};
    const errors: string[] = [];
    for (const [key, check] of Object.entries(shape)) {
      const r = check((v as Record<string, unknown>)[key], `${p}.${key}`);
      if (r.ok) out[key] = r.value; else errors.push(...r.errors);
    }
    return errors.length
      ? { ok: false, errors }
      : { ok: true, value: out as { [K in keyof S]: Infer<S[K]> } };
  };
}

export function array<V extends Validator<unknown>>(item: V): Validator<Infer<V>[]> {
  return (v, p) => {
    if (!Array.isArray(v)) return { ok: false, errors: [`${p}: expected array`] };
    const out: unknown[] = [];
    const errors: string[] = [];
    v.forEach((el, i) => {
      const r = item(el, `${p}[${i}]`);
      if (r.ok) out.push(r.value); else errors.push(...r.errors);
    });
    return errors.length ? { ok: false, errors } : { ok: true, value: out as Infer<V>[] };
  };
}

const taskWire = object({ task_id: str, title: str, assigned_to: nullable(str) });
const payload = array(taskWire);

const good = payload(JSON.parse(
  '[{"task_id":"t_1","title":"Write","assigned_to":null}]'), 'body');
if (good.ok) console.log(good.value[0]?.title, good.value[0]?.assigned_to);

const bad = payload(JSON.parse(
  '[{"task_id":1,"title":"Ship","assigned_to":7},{"task_id":"t_3"}]'), 'body');
if (!bad.ok) console.log(bad.errors);

Write null
[
  'body[0].task_id: expected string',
  'body[0].assigned_to: expected string',
  'body[1].title: expected string',
  'body[1].assigned_to: expected string'
]

Infer<V> is the piece that makes it compose. One conditional type with an infer (§8.4) pulls each validator's output type out, so array(object({ … })) produces the right nested type with nothing declared.

Four errors from two bad rows, each with its path. A validator that stops at the first failure turns one bad response into four round trips.

There is one assertion in the whole implementation, at the point where an accumulated Record<string, unknown> becomes the derived type. It sits inside the function that just verified every field (§10.15).

18.6 Failure as a Value

Expected failures are values with types, and bugs throw (§10.20). The service's public surface uses a Result, and the discriminated union makes the failure case impossible to skip.

type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };

type LoadError =
  | { kind: 'network'; cause: string }
  | { kind: 'status'; status: number }
  | { kind: 'shape'; problems: readonly string[] };

function render(r: Result<readonly string[], LoadError>): string {
  if (r.ok) return `${r.value.length} tasks`;
  switch (r.error.kind) {
    case 'network': return `offline: ${r.error.cause}`;
    case 'status': return `server said ${r.error.status}`;
    case 'shape': return `bad payload: ${r.error.problems.join('; ')}`;
    default: { const never_: never = r.error; return never_; }
  }
}

console.log(render({ ok: true, value: ['a', 'b'] }));
console.log(render({ ok: false, error: { kind: 'status', status: 503 } }));
console.log(render({ ok: false, error: { kind: 'shape', problems: ['body[0].title: expected string'] } }));

declare const unchecked: Result<readonly string[], LoadError>;
function neverCalled(): readonly string[] {
  // @ts-expect-error `value` is unreachable without checking `ok`
  return unchecked.value;
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

2 tasks
server said 503
bad payload: body[0].title: expected string
function

The last line is the whole argument for Result. r.value does not exist until r.ok has been tested, so the union makes forgetting the failure case a compile error and not an undefined.

LoadError is itself a discriminated union, so a caller can tell "retry" from "fix your request" from "the server changed its schema" without parsing a message string.

When to throw instead: a violated invariant, a missing environment variable at startup, or an assertNever (§18.3). Those are bugs, and they should stop the program loudly. Putting them in a Result clutters every call site with a case nobody can handle.

18.7 A Typed Event Bus

An event map plus a mapped type gives you handlers whose payloads are inferred at the call site with nothing annotated (§8.2, §8.6).

type EventMap = {
  'task:created': { id: string; title: string };
  'task:assigned': { id: string; assignee: string };
  'sync:failed': { attempt: number };
};

type Handler<K extends keyof EventMap> = (payload: EventMap[K]) => void;

class Bus<M extends Record<string, unknown>> {
  #handlers = new Map<keyof M, Set<(payload: never) => void>>();

  on<K extends keyof M>(event: K, handler: (payload: M[K]) => void): () => void {
    const set = this.#handlers.get(event) ?? new Set();
    set.add(handler as (payload: never) => void);
    this.#handlers.set(event, set);
    return () => { set.delete(handler as (payload: never) => void); };
  }

  emit<K extends keyof M>(event: K, payload: M[K]): number {
    const set = this.#handlers.get(event);
    if (!set) return 0;
    for (const h of set) (h as (p: M[K]) => void)(payload);
    return set.size;
  }
}

const bus = new Bus<EventMap>();

// `e` is inferred per event — nothing is annotated below.
bus.on('task:created', (e) => console.log('created', e.title));
const off = bus.on('task:assigned', (e) => console.log('assigned', e.id, '->', e.assignee));

console.log('handlers run:', bus.emit('task:created', { id: 't_1', title: 'Write' }));
console.log('handlers run:', bus.emit('task:assigned', { id: 't_1', assignee: 'u_ada' }));
off();
console.log('after unsubscribe:', bus.emit('task:assigned', { id: 't_1', assignee: 'u_ada' }));

// @ts-expect-error 'task:deleted' is not in the event map
bus.on('task:deleted', () => {});
// @ts-expect-error the payload must match the event
bus.emit('sync:failed', { attempt: 'one' });

created Write
handlers run: 1
assigned t_1 -> u_ada
handlers run: 1
after unsubscribe: 0

EventMap[K] is an indexed access type (§8.2), and it is what connects the event name to the payload type. Adding an event is one line in the map, and every on and emit for it is then checked.

on returns its own unsubscribe. That is the shape that makes teardown a single call and not a matching off with the same function reference.

The two internal as casts are the honest cost of a heterogeneous map. The Map holds handlers for every key, so its value type cannot mention K. The casts are contained inside the class, next to the code that establishes the invariant (§10.15).

18.8 A Generic Repository

The storage layer is where §7's rules pay off. It has two type parameters, each mentioned twice, and a key type derived from the entity and not declared.

type Entity = { readonly id: string };

class Repository<T extends Entity> {
  #rows = new Map<T['id'], T>();

  put(row: T): this { this.#rows.set(row.id, row); return this; }
  get(id: T['id']): T | undefined { return this.#rows.get(id); }
  remove(id: T['id']): boolean { return this.#rows.delete(id); }
  get size(): number { return this.#rows.size; }

  where<K extends keyof T>(key: K, value: T[K]): T[] {
    return [...this.#rows.values()].filter((row) => row[key] === value);
  }

  map<U>(fn: (row: T) => U): U[] { return [...this.#rows.values()].map(fn); }
}

type Task = { readonly id: string; title: string; state: 'draft' | 'active' };

const repo = new Repository<Task>()
  .put({ id: 't_1', title: 'Write', state: 'draft' })
  .put({ id: 't_2', title: 'Ship', state: 'active' })
  .put({ id: 't_3', title: 'Test', state: 'draft' });

console.log(repo.size, repo.get('t_2')?.title);
console.log(repo.where('state', 'draft').map((t) => t.title));
console.log(repo.map((t) => t.title.length));

// @ts-expect-error 'status' is not a key of Task
repo.where('status', 'draft');
// @ts-expect-error 'archived' is not a valid state
repo.where('state', 'archived');

3 Ship
[ 'Write', 'Test' ]
[ 5, 4, 4 ]

where<K extends keyof T>(key: K, value: T[K]) is §7.6's relational shape. The second argument's type depends on the first argument's value, which is why where('state', 'archived') is rejected while where('state', 'draft') is not.

put returns this (§6.19), so the chain above types correctly and would continue to on a subclass.

T['id'] and not string is an indexed access (§8.2) that keeps the key type tied to the entity. Brand id as a TaskId and every method follows with no edit.

18.9 Configuration Checked and Precise

The last piece before wiring is configuration, where you want the shape checked and the values remembered (§8.10, §16.23).

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type EndpointConfig = Record<string, { path: string; method: 'GET' | 'POST'; auth: boolean }>;

const endpoints = {
  listTasks: { path: '/tasks', method: 'GET', auth: false },
  createTask: { path: '/tasks', method: 'POST', auth: true },
  assignTask: { path: '/tasks/:id/assign', method: 'POST', auth: true },
} as const satisfies EndpointConfig;

type EndpointName = keyof typeof endpoints;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<EndpointName, 'listTasks' | 'createTask' | 'assignTask'>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<(typeof endpoints)['assignTask']['path'], '/tasks/:id/assign'>>;

function call(name: EndpointName): string {
  const e = endpoints[name];
  return `${e.method} ${e.path}${e.auth ? ' (auth)' : ''}`;
}

console.log(call('listTasks'));
console.log(call('assignTask'));

function neverCalled(): string {
  // @ts-expect-error 'deleteTask' is not an endpoint
  return call('deleteTask');
}
console.log(typeof neverCalled);

GET /tasks
POST /tasks/:id/assign (auth)
function

as const satisfies EndpointConfig in that order (§8.10) is the combination. The satisfies catches a misspelled key or a method: 'PUT' at the declaration, and the as const keeps every literal, so EndpointName and the paths can be derived.

An annotation would have thrown all of it away. const endpoints: EndpointConfig = { … } type-checks identically, and then EndpointName is string, call accepts anything, and endpoints.assignTask.path is string.

18.10 Wiring It Together

Everything above is composed into one flow: parse a payload, convert it to the domain, store it, emit an event, and report a Result.

type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };
type TaskId = string & { readonly __brand: 'TaskId' };
type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' };

type Task =
  | { readonly kind: 'draft'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string }
  | { readonly kind: 'active'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string; readonly assignee: UserId };

type TaskWire = { task_id: string; title: string; assigned_to: string | null };
type LoadError = { kind: 'shape'; problems: readonly string[] };

function parseWire(v: unknown, path: string): Result<TaskWire, readonly string[]> {
  const problems: string[] = [];
  if (typeof v !== 'object' || v === null) return { ok: false, error: [`${path}: expected object`] };
  const o = v as Record<string, unknown>;
  if (typeof o['task_id'] !== 'string') problems.push(`${path}.task_id: expected string`);
  if (typeof o['title'] !== 'string') problems.push(`${path}.title: expected string`);
  if (o['assigned_to'] !== null && typeof o['assigned_to'] !== 'string') {
    problems.push(`${path}.assigned_to: expected string or null`);
  }
  return problems.length
    ? { ok: false, error: problems }
    : { ok: true, value: { task_id: o['task_id'] as string, title: o['title'] as string,
                           assigned_to: o['assigned_to'] as string | null } };
}

function toDomain(wire: TaskWire): Task {
  const id = wire.task_id as TaskId;
  return wire.assigned_to === null
    ? { kind: 'draft', id, title: wire.title }
    : { kind: 'active', id, title: wire.title, assignee: wire.assigned_to as UserId };
}

function load(json: string): Result<Task[], LoadError> {
  const raw: unknown = JSON.parse(json);
  if (!Array.isArray(raw)) return { ok: false, error: { kind: 'shape', problems: ['body: expected array'] } };
  const tasks: Task[] = [];
  const problems: string[] = [];
  raw.forEach((row, i) => {
    const r = parseWire(row, `body[${i}]`);
    if (r.ok) tasks.push(toDomain(r.value)); else problems.push(...r.error);
  });
  return problems.length ? { ok: false, error: { kind: 'shape', problems } } : { ok: true, value: tasks };
}

const okResult = load('[{"task_id":"t_1","title":"Write","assigned_to":null},'
  + '{"task_id":"t_2","title":"Ship","assigned_to":"u_ada"}]');
console.log(okResult.ok ? okResult.value.map((t) => `${t.kind}:${t.title}`) : okResult.error.problems);

const badResult = load('[{"task_id":1,"title":"Ship","assigned_to":7}]');
console.log(badResult.ok ? 'unexpected' : badResult.error.problems);

[ 'draft:Write', 'active:Ship' ]
[
  'body[0].task_id: expected string',
  'body[0].assigned_to: expected string or null'
]

Trace the types through one row. JSON.parse gives unknown, not any, and that annotation is the boundary. parseWire turns it into a checked TaskWire or a list of paths. toDomain turns that into a Task, and it is the only place a raw string becomes a branded id. Nothing downstream of load sees a type that something did not establish.

The failure path carries as much type as the success path, which is what lets the caller branch on error.kind and not on a message.

18.11 The Type Tests

The types above are only worth something if a refactor cannot silently break them. These tests run as part of tsc --noEmit and cost nothing at runtime (§17.14).

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;
type IsAny<T> = 0 extends 1 & T ? true : false;

type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' };
type TaskId = string & { readonly __brand: 'TaskId' };
type Task =
  | { readonly kind: 'draft'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string }
  | { readonly kind: 'active'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string; readonly assignee: UserId };
type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };

// 1. The brands are distinct, and both are still strings.
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Equal<UserId, TaskId>, false>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Extract<UserId, string>, UserId>>;

// 2. keyof a union is the INTERSECTION of the members' keys (§9.5).
type _3 = Expect<Equal<keyof Task, 'kind' | 'id' | 'title'>>;

// 3. Extracting one variant gives that variant, with its extra field.
type Active = Extract<Task, { kind: 'active' }>;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<Active['assignee'], UserId>>;

// 4. The discriminant is exhaustive.
type _5 = Expect<Equal<Task['kind'], 'draft' | 'active'>>;

// 5. No `any` reached the public surface.
type _6 = Expect<Equal<IsAny<Task['title']>, false>>;
type _7 = Expect<Equal<IsAny<Result<Task[], string>>, false>>;

// 6. A draft may not carry an assignee.
// @ts-expect-error 'assignee' does not exist on the draft variant
type _8 = Extract<Task, { kind: 'draft' }>['assignee'];

console.log('type tests are compile-time only');

type tests are compile-time only

_3 is the one worth having most. keyof Task being 'kind' | 'id' | 'title' is the fact that makes Omit<Task, 'kind'> collapse to {} (§9.5). Asserting it means a future variant that drops title fails here and does not silently widen a derived type.

_6 and _7 are the any sentries (§17.15). An any that reaches a public type disables checking for every consumer, and without an assertion like these it produces no error at all.

_8 is the negative half. Asserting what must not compile is what catches a model that quietly gained a field, and @ts-expect-error self-destructs if the situation changes (§10.17).

18.12 The Audit

Nine claims this course measured, checked against the capstone.

Nothing here emits code. There is no enum, no namespace, no parameter property and no decorator, so erasableSyntaxOnly (§14.11) passes and every block runs under node --experimental-transform-types with no build step (§15.24).

Every assertion is inside a validator or a class. as TaskId appears only in taskId() and toDomain(), and the two casts in Bus are contained by the class that maintains the invariant (§10.15). There is no as at a call site.

JSON.parse is annotated unknown, never any (§16.6). That single word is what makes parseWire necessary and not optional, and it is where the §10.21 contagion (one any spreading through everything it touches) is stopped.

readonly on every domain field. The model is a value, and mutation goes through the repository. Note the limits measured in §5.3: it is shallow, and it is not checked on assignment through a wider alias.

Branded ids cost nothing. taskId('t_1') printed t_1 in §18.2. It is a string at runtime and is distinguishable only at compile time.

Every discriminated union has an exhaustiveness check. That means assertNever in §18.3 and the never assignment in §18.6, which is what turns a new variant into a compile error at every consumer (§3.14).

Generic parameters are mentioned at least twice. Repository<T>, Bus<M>, Validator<T> and Infer<V> all pass §7.14's test, and there is no parse<T>(json: string): T anywhere.

Configuration uses as const satisfies, not an annotation (§8.10), so EndpointName is a union of three literals and not string.

The type tests run in the build. They are declarations checked by tsc --noEmit (§17.14), so there is no runner and no runtime cost, and they fail the build when a type collapses.

18.13 What Is Still Wrong

An honest list follows, because a capstone that claims to be finished is teaching the wrong lesson.

The brands are convention, not proof. raw as TaskId inside taskId() is unverified by the compiler. The regex is what makes it true, and nothing forces a future contributor to keep it. A class with a #private field (§6.10) would give an unforgeable brand, at the cost of a wrapper object.

toDomain asserts and does not parse. §18.10's parseWire checks the shape, and then toDomain casts task_id to a TaskId with no id-format check. Threading taskId() through the parser is a ten-line change, and it is the one gap between "checked" and "checked all the way".

There is no retry, timeout or cancellation. load takes a string. A real client needs an AbortSignal and a LoadError variant for it. Both would be added to types that already have a place for them, which is the argument for having modelled failure as a union.

The event bus leaks handlers. on returns an unsubscribe, and nothing ensures it is called. A Set of teardown functions tied to an AbortSignal is the standard fix.

Repository.where is O(n), meaning its running time grows in proportion to the number of items. The types say nothing about complexity, and nothing in TypeScript ever will. That is §1.13's boundary, and the answer is a benchmark and not an annotation.

The validator has no optional, no union, no refinement. Extending it is §16.21's exercise. Using Zod or Valibot instead is the correct production answer, and the reason to have written one is to know what their inferred types are doing.

Nothing is checked at the process boundary. Environment variables, command-line arguments and the clock all enter untyped. §16.23's readEnv is the shape, and this capstone does not have one.

18.14 What This Section Established

The capstone is one argument made six ways: put the check at the boundary and let a real type travel inwards.

A branded id makes "this string was validated" a fact the compiler can carry. A discriminated union makes an illegal state unrepresentable and turns a new variant into a compile error everywhere. A schema-derived validator makes the parsed type and the checked shape the same declaration. A Result makes a failure impossible to skip. A mapped event map and a relational repository signature both connect a value to a type, so the call site needs no annotation. And as const satisfies keeps a configuration precise while checking it.

Every one of those is a technique from an earlier section, and none of them is clever for its own sake. Each removes a class of mistake that would otherwise be caught by a test, or by a user.

The last thing to take from it is the audit. It has nine claims, each checkable against the code, and a list of seven things still wrong. A codebase where you can write both lists is one where the types are doing work you can name.

Exercises

1. Close the boundary gap. This is §18.13's second item: toDomain asserts task_id as TaskId without checking the format. Rewrite the pipeline so a malformed id is reported as a validation problem with its path, alongside the shape errors, and show a payload producing both kinds at once.

2. Add a state and follow the errors. Add a 'blocked' variant to Task carrying blockedBy: TaskId, and, without searching, let the compiler find every place that must change. List the errors in order, say which section's mechanism produced each, and give the final diff.

3. Make the bus teardown-safe. Extend Bus so that on accepts an optional AbortSignal and removes the handler when it fires. Add a clear() that removes everything, and write the type test proving that a handler's payload type is still inferred per event after the change.

Solution

1. Closing the boundary gap.

type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };
type TaskId = string & { readonly __brand: 'TaskId' };
type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' };
type Task =
  | { readonly kind: 'draft'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string }
  | { readonly kind: 'active'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string; readonly assignee: UserId };

// The id validators now return a Result rather than throwing, so a bad id is a
// reportable problem with a path rather than an exception at the wrong layer.
function parseTaskId(v: unknown, path: string): Result<TaskId, string> {
  return typeof v === 'string' && /^t_[0-9a-z]+$/.test(v)
    ? { ok: true, value: v as TaskId }
    : { ok: false, error: `${path}: expected a task id (t_…)` };
}
function parseUserId(v: unknown, path: string): Result<UserId, string> {
  return typeof v === 'string' && /^u_[0-9a-z]+$/.test(v)
    ? { ok: true, value: v as UserId }
    : { ok: false, error: `${path}: expected a user id (u_…)` };
}

function parseTask(v: unknown, path: string): Result<Task, readonly string[]> {
  if (typeof v !== 'object' || v === null) return { ok: false, error: [`${path}: expected object`] };
  const o = v as Record<string, unknown>;
  const problems: string[] = [];

  const id = parseTaskId(o['task_id'], `${path}.task_id`);
  if (!id.ok) problems.push(id.error);
  if (typeof o['title'] !== 'string') problems.push(`${path}.title: expected string`);

  let assignee: UserId | null = null;
  if (o['assigned_to'] !== null) {
    const a = parseUserId(o['assigned_to'], `${path}.assigned_to`);
    if (a.ok) assignee = a.value; else problems.push(a.error);
  }

  if (problems.length || !id.ok) return { ok: false, error: problems };
  const title = o['title'] as string;
  return assignee === null
    ? { ok: true, value: { kind: 'draft', id: id.value, title } }
    : { ok: true, value: { kind: 'active', id: id.value, title, assignee } };
}

function load(json: string): Result<Task[], readonly string[]> {
  const raw: unknown = JSON.parse(json);
  if (!Array.isArray(raw)) return { ok: false, error: ['body: expected array'] };
  const tasks: Task[] = [];
  const problems: string[] = [];
  raw.forEach((row, i) => {
    const r = parseTask(row, `body[${i}]`);
    if (r.ok) tasks.push(r.value); else problems.push(...r.error);
  });
  return problems.length ? { ok: false, error: problems } : { ok: true, value: tasks };
}

const ok = load('[{"task_id":"t_1","title":"Write","assigned_to":null}]');
console.log(ok.ok ? ok.value.map((t) => `${t.kind}:${t.id}`) : ok.error);

// One row with a shape error AND an id-format error.
const bad = load('[{"task_id":"nope","title":42,"assigned_to":"t_9"}]');
console.log(bad.ok ? 'unexpected' : bad.error);

[ 'draft:t_1' ]
[
  'body[0].task_id: expected a task id (t_…)',
  'body[0].title: expected string',
  'body[0].assigned_to: expected a user id (u_…)'
]

The third problem is the one the original pipeline missed entirely. assigned_to: "t_9" is a perfectly good string, so the shape validator accepted it, and toDomain cast it to a UserId. That produces a Task whose assignee is a task id, with a type saying otherwise. Threading the id parsers into the boundary is what closes it.

The id validators changed from throwing to returning. That is §10.20's distinction applied consistently. A malformed field in an API payload is an expected failure and belongs in the Result, while userId() throwing (§18.2) is right for a programmer passing a literal.

There is still exactly one as per branded type, and it is now guarded by the regex in the same expression.

2. Adding a state.

type TaskId = string & { readonly __brand: 'TaskId' };
type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' };

type Task =
  | { readonly kind: 'draft'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string }
  | { readonly kind: 'active'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string; readonly assignee: UserId }
  | { readonly kind: 'blocked'; readonly id: TaskId; readonly title: string; readonly blockedBy: TaskId };

function assertNever(x: never): never { throw new Error(`unhandled: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`); }

function describe(task: Task): string {
  switch (task.kind) {
    case 'draft': return `${task.title} — unassigned`;
    case 'active': return `${task.title} — ${task.assignee}`;
    case 'blocked': return `${task.title} — blocked by ${task.blockedBy}`;
    default: return assertNever(task);
  }
}

const id = 't_1' as TaskId;
console.log(describe({ kind: 'blocked', id, title: 'Ship', blockedBy: 't_0' as TaskId }));

Ship — blocked by t_0

The errors, in the order the compiler reports them, and what produced each.

1. assertNever(task): Argument of type '{ kind: "blocked"; … }' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'. This is §3.14's exhaustiveness check, and it is the one that finds the switch at all. It names the missing variant in full, which is why the pattern is worth its four lines.

2. The same error at every other switch on task.kind in the codebase, in every file. This is the property that makes a discriminated union a refactoring tool: adding a variant is a compile-wide search with no searching.

3. Extract<Task, { kind: 'blocked' }> type tests fail if the model was asserted. §18.11's _5, Equal<Task['kind'], 'draft' | 'active'>, breaks immediately and must be updated to include 'blocked'. That is the test doing its job: the discriminant widened, and something said so.

4. keyof Task is unchanged at 'kind' | 'id' | 'title', because the new variant has both shared fields, so _3 still passes. Had the variant omitted title, keyof Task would have shrunk, and _3 would have caught a change that no switch would have.

The final diff is three lines: the new union member, the new case, and the updated _5 assertion. Everything else the compiler pointed at.

3. A teardown-safe bus.

type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type EventMap = {
  'task:created': { id: string; title: string };
  'sync:failed': { attempt: number };
};

class Bus<M extends Record<string, unknown>> {
  #handlers = new Map<keyof M, Set<(payload: never) => void>>();

  on<K extends keyof M>(
    event: K,
    handler: (payload: M[K]) => void,
    options: { signal?: AbortSignal } = {},
  ): () => void {
    const set = this.#handlers.get(event) ?? new Set();
    const erased = handler as (payload: never) => void;
    set.add(erased);
    this.#handlers.set(event, set);
    const off = (): void => { set.delete(erased); };
    if (options.signal?.aborted) { off(); return off; }
    options.signal?.addEventListener('abort', off, { once: true });
    return off;
  }

  emit<K extends keyof M>(event: K, payload: M[K]): number {
    const set = this.#handlers.get(event);
    if (!set) return 0;
    for (const h of set) (h as (p: M[K]) => void)(payload);
    return set.size;
  }

  clear(): void { this.#handlers.clear(); }
}

const bus = new Bus<EventMap>();
const controller = new AbortController();

// The payload type is still inferred per event, with nothing annotated.
bus.on('task:created', (e) => console.log('created', e.title), { signal: controller.signal });
bus.on('sync:failed', (e) => console.log('failed, attempt', e.attempt));

console.log('created ->', bus.emit('task:created', { id: 't_1', title: 'Write' }));
controller.abort();
console.log('after abort ->', bus.emit('task:created', { id: 't_1', title: 'Write' }));
console.log('failed ->', bus.emit('sync:failed', { attempt: 2 }));
bus.clear();
console.log('after clear ->', bus.emit('sync:failed', { attempt: 3 }));

// The type test: `on`'s handler parameter is still the event's own payload.
type OnHandler<K extends keyof EventMap> = Parameters<Bus<EventMap>['on']>[1] extends
  (p: infer P) => void ? P : never;
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Parameters<typeof bus.on<'sync:failed'>>[1], (payload: { attempt: number }) => void>>;

// @ts-expect-error the payload must still match the event
bus.emit('sync:failed', { attempt: 'two' });

created Write
created -> 1
after abort -> 0
failed, attempt 2
failed -> 1
after clear -> 0

{ once: true } on the abort listener is what stops the bus leaking in the other direction. Without it, an unsubscribe closure stays registered on the signal for the controller's lifetime, which is exactly the leak the feature was added to prevent.

The already-aborted case is checked first. A signal that fired before on was called would otherwise never remove the handler, because abort does not fire twice.

The type test uses an explicit type argument on a method reference, typeof bus.on<'sync:failed'>, which is the reliable way to assert on a generic method's instantiation (§7.12). Comparing the generic signature directly reports false even when the types match, so the assertion has to apply it first.

clear() is deliberately not signal-aware. It drops every handler regardless of who registered it. That is the right behaviour for a teardown at the end of a process and the wrong one for a component unmount, where each caller's own signal is what should fire.

You started this course able to write TypeScript. You now know what the compiler is doing with it — which is the difference between arguing with the type system and using it.

What you can now do

  1. Hold the two layers apart. Types are erased, so no runtime decision can be made from one. Anything the program must decide at runtime needs a value, such as a discriminant, a class or a validator. Every "cannot find name" and every "X only refers to a type" is that one distinction.
  2. Predict assignability instead of guessing. Comparison is structural, member by member. any and numeric enums are bidirectional, and method parameters are bivariant on purpose while function-typed properties are not. A one-word change from handle(e: E): void to handle: (e: E) => void opts into the sound rule.
  3. Narrow with the checks you were already writing. Use typeof (remembering null is 'object'), truthiness (remembering 0 and ''), in (an optional property lands in both branches), and instanceof (subclass first). When a narrowing goes missing, the diagnosis is mechanical: was the index a literal, was the variable assigned anywhere, was it a property inside a callback.
  4. Make illegal states unrepresentable. A discriminated union with an assertNever turns a new variant into a compile error at every consumer, in every file, naming the one you missed. { loading: boolean; data?: T; error?: E } has eight inhabitants and three meanings.
  5. Compute types instead of maintaining them. The tools are keyof, typeof, T[K], conditionals, infer, mapped types, key remapping and template literals, with a measured budget of 999 tail-recursive instantiations and 47 otherwise. A derived type cannot drift from its source.
  6. Read the standard utilities rather than memorising them. They are twenty aliases in lib.es5.d.ts, built from those same operators, and every surprise falls out of the definition. That includes Omit on a union collapsing to {}, which accepts anything and warns about nothing.
  7. Write a generic that earns its parameter. It must appear twice in the signature, or it is not relating anything, and parse<T>(json: string): T is any wearing a costume. Variance explains the rest: Producer<Dog> is a Producer<Animal> and Cell<Dog> is not.
  8. Use the escape hatches deliberately and locally. Put an assertion at a boundary with the check beside it. Use @ts-expect-error with a reason, because it self-destructs when the problem is fixed. Never use @ts-ignore, which silently suppresses whatever appears on that line next.
  9. Configure the compiler on purpose. strict is a floor and not a ceiling: noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, noImplicitOverride and five more are all outside it. Use nodenext when Node runs the output and preserve when a bundler does, and leave dom out of lib for anything server-side.
  10. Ship types other people can use. Put types first inside every exports condition, or the declarations are silently never found. Ship a separate .d.cts for a CommonJS consumer. And use no paths in anything you publish, because a subpath import is the version the runtime implements.
  11. Recognise what emits code. These are enum, namespace, decorators and parameter properties: four constructs, forbidden by erasableSyntaxOnly, and the reason a project that uses them is committed to a TypeScript-aware compiler forever.
  12. Type the boundaries, which is where the guarantee actually comes from. res.json() and JSON.parse both return any. querySelector returns Element | null, and a type argument is an assertion. A caught error is unknown because anything can be thrown. One word, unknown, at each of those turns a silent hole into a required narrowing.
  13. Parse, do not validate. A boolean check throws its conclusion away, while a parser returns a value whose type something verified. It is the only construct in the language that makes a type true and not merely asserted.
  14. Keep the types honest over time. Use type tests, because a type that collapses to {} produces no error at its definition. Use type-aware lint rules, because a floating promise and a spreading any are invisible to a compiler doing exactly its job. And use a strictness ratchet, because a flag that goes on and stays on gets a codebase there within a year.

Where to go next

The parts of this that are still moving are worth watching and not learning once.

The compiler is now a Go binary, and the API you would use to automate it moved to typescript/unstable/*. The word unstable is a promise being withheld, and the surface will settle over the next releases. Decorators are stage 3 and not yet in any runtime. Node 24 cannot parse them at all, so the standard system is currently a compile-time feature waiting for engines. import defer is in the same position: TypeScript emits it, and Node does not accept it. Both will change, and the way to find out is the way this course found out. Run the probe, and do not read the summary.

The two habits that keep the knowledge current are smaller than they sound.

When you reach for a setting you learned more than a year ago, check whether it still exists. target: es5, outFile, baseUrl, moduleResolution: node, module: amd, esModuleInterop: false and downlevelIteration are seven options that appear in nearly every configuration written before 2026. All are removed, and each has its own error code telling you that what you are reading is out of date. The check costs one command, and tsc --showConfig answers the rest.

And measure the compiler rather than quoting it. Nearly every number in this course came from running something, and several contradicted what is widely repeated: - A numeric enum no longer accepts an arbitrary number. - -? removes undefined as well as the ?. - Key remapping with as keeps a mapped type homomorphic. - Inference reconciles two candidates to their common supertype and not to a union. - 'click' is a PointerEvent. - A class decorator's returned subclass does not change the class's declared type. - readOnly survives into React's server output. - Interfaces were not measurably cheaper than intersections, because run-to-run variance was larger than the effect.

That last one is the habit in miniature. The advice was still right, for reasons that had nothing to do with the number attached to it, and the only way to know which half was true was to run it. A five-line probe, --extendedDiagnostics, and Expect<Equal<…>> are the whole method. They will keep being right long after any particular fact here has changed.
